decision.text: I went into the Cistern for the first time in my life, down the hatch's tray lift behind Tamsin, on Bram Coyle's service phrase in her mouth.

a3w_bram_truth.speaker: npc_c9_04
a3w_bram_truth.text: You push Hesper's sheet through the slot under the tray and hear it drop onto steel on the other side. Then you put your mouth to the slot and say his name until boots come. / "Coyle," says the voice you know from the Grille, which has never said more than three words to you at once. / He reads it. You can hear him read it, twice, the paper turning over. "Hesper," he says. "She kept it." A long breath through the slot. "Six years under the salt, and I've been waiting on the tray for her answer." / Then, differently, in the voice of a man who has decided something and will not be talked out of it by anybody, himself included: "Go to the grate. The dark end. Wait there and don't touch it."
a3w_bram_truth.again: "Go to the grate," Bram says through the slot.

a3w_bram_kind.speaker: npc_c9_04
a3w_bram_kind.text: You push the letter you wrote through the slot under the tray, hear it drop onto steel, and say his name into the slot until boots come. "Coyle." / He reads it. Halfway down he laughs, once, at something you wrote, and then he blows his nose like a man who does not care who hears. "She's all right, then," Bram says through the slot. "Edda. She's all right." You say nothing, which is the price, and you will be paying it a while. / "Go to the grate," he says. "The dark end. Wait there and don't touch it."
a3w_bram_kind.again: "Go to the grate," Bram says through the slot.

a3w_bram_told.speaker: npc_c9_04
a3w_bram_told.text: You put your mouth to the slot under the tray and say his name until boots come. "Coyle." / "Edda Lockett died six years ago," you say. "Her daughter is called Hesper. She kept the other letter." / There is no sound at all from the other side, not breathing, not anything, for long enough that you think he has gone. "Six years," Bram says. You hear him do the sum. "Hesper." Then: "Kept it." Then nothing again. Then, in the voice of a man who has decided something: "Go to the grate. The dark end. Wait there."
a3w_bram_told.again: "Go to the grate," Bram says through the slot.

a3w_bram_ask.speaker: npc_c9_04
a3w_bram_ask.text: You put your mouth to the slot under the tray and say his name until boots come. "Coyle." A pause. "You." He does not say anything about the letter; he does not need to. "You'll be wanting in." Another pause, while a man who keeps a door argues with himself, and loses. "Go to the grate. The dark end. Wait there and don't touch it."
a3w_bram_ask.again: "Go to the grate," Bram says through the slot.

a3w_bram_grate.speaker: npc_c9_04

text.text: You wait at the grate. It stands open already, its bar on the concrete where the Unwritten left it, and nothing comes up it now. Then a lamp, far down, swinging, and the top of a ladder knocking the rock, and a face coming up into the light upside down: forty-one, broad, unshaven, black under the eyes with soot. Bram Coyle looks at you for the first time in his life. "Mind the third rung," he says. "It's been loose since before I was born."

You wait at the grate. Behind the bars the fan's slow beat goes on, and then, while you are listening to it, stops: the first silence on the apron in your life. Up the lane a dog starts barking at it. A lamp comes up the throat of the intake, swinging, and the top of a ladder knocks the rock, and a key on a chain turns in the grate's bolts from below. The grate lifts. A face comes up into the light upside down: forty-one, broad, unshaven, a wrench through his belt. Bram Coyle looks at you for the first time in his life. "Mind the third rung," he says. "It's been loose since before I was born."

a3w_bram_grate.again: Bram's lamp in the intake. The ladder.

news.text: the designate went inside the Cistern, the first from Knock in living memory

decision.text: I went into the Cistern for the first time in my life, down the intake behind Bram Coyle, who lifted the grate for me once his letter came back.

text.text: The grate at the dark west end of the apron stands open, its bar on the concrete where the Unwritten left it. Nothing comes out of it now, no air, no hum: only a cold breath that smells of a fire gone out. The rungs go down into the black.
The grate at the dark west end of the apron, lifted off its bolts and laid back against the rock. Down in the throat the fan beats slow and steady; the rungs go down beside it into the warm.

At the dark west end of the apron, at knee height in the rock, the square iron grate you have walked past every day of your life, no wider than a man's shoulders. Air moves through it, cool, smelling of oil and of people. A long way down a fan beats, slow, and you feel every beat of it in your teeth. The grate is held by four bolts rusted into the rock, and there is a bar for exactly that in the post-house woodpile. The bolts are not the problem. The fan is.

again.text: The open grate. The cold breath out of it.
The grate. The fan's beat, a long way down.

passives.label: Pump Hand
passives.text: You know this grate. Every pump hand on the slope does: the Cistern's intake, the one Maud told you not to put your face to because it would steal your breath. And at the top of the hour, every spring, the fan stops for nine minutes while somebody on this side cleans the screen.

options.text: (Wait for the top of the hour, when the fan stops, and go down.)
(Find the fan's service stop on the housing, throw it, and take the grate off.)
(Take the grate off and go down between the fan's beats on a rope, counting.)

a3w_grate_mech_no.speaker: narrator
a3w_grate_mech_no.text: You go over the housing beside the grate an inch at a time, and if there is a way to stop that fan from this side, ninety years of rust and goat hair are keeping it. The bolts come out easily enough. The fan does not stop. You put your hand into the throat and the air pulls at your sleeve, hard and steady, all the way down.
a3w_grate_mech_no.again: The fan, pulling at the air, all the way down.

a3w_grate_rope_no.speaker: narrator
a3w_grate_rope_no.text: You get the grate off and your legs into the throat, and on the third rung the fan's push catches your coat and nearly takes you down by it. You come back up with the rope burning in your palms and your heart going like a hammer. Not like that. Not until you know the beat better than you do.
a3w_grate_rope_no.again: Your palms, still burning from the rope.

a3w_down_pump.speaker: narrator
a3w_down_pump.text: You wait on your heels by the grate with the bar across your knees, the way you did every spring with Corin, until the top of the hour. The fan's beat slows, and slows, and stops, and in the silence you have nine minutes. The bolts come out in your hands like rotten teeth. The rungs are where they always were, cold, slick, going down into a throat of concrete that smells of oil and wet stone and, under that, faintly, of soup.
a3w_down_pump.again: Nine minutes. The rungs going down.

options.text: (Go down, and crawl the pump run.)

a3w_down_mech.speaker: narrator
a3w_down_mech.text: It takes you an hour of looking to find what nobody has looked for in ninety years: on the housing beside the grate, under rust and goat hair and a nest of something, a steel cover held by two screws, and under it a red handle stencilled SERVICE STOP — INTAKE — NOT DURING OCCUPANCY. You throw it. The fan below winds down with a long falling note, like a breath let out, and stops. Then the bar, and the four bolts, which come out like rotten teeth, and the rungs going down into a concrete throat that smells of oil and wet stone and, under that, faintly, of soup.
a3w_down_mech.again: The red handle, thrown. The rungs going down.

options.text: (Throw the stop back behind you, so the fan turns again, and crawl the pump run.)

a3w_down_rope.speaker: narrator
a3w_down_rope.text: You lever the grate off its bolts with the bar from the woodpile, tie your rope to its frame and lie on your belly with your head in the throat, listening. The fan's beat comes up the concrete: a slow push of air, and a pull, and a push. You count it until you could count it asleep. Then you go down between one push and the next, hand under hand, with the blades going round somewhere below your boots in the dark, and you do not think about them, and you are past.
a3w_down_rope.again: The rope, the beat, the dark below your boots.

a3w_down_dark.speaker: narrator
a3w_down_dark.text: You go down the rungs into the black with a lamp in your teeth. The throat is still warm, the concrete sooted to the touch, and at the bottom the fan sits dead in its housing with paper ash caught in its blades. Somebody came this way with oil. Nobody stopped them.
a3w_down_dark.again: The dead fan, ash in its blades.

a3w_pumprun.speaker: narrator

text.text: The pump run is a concrete pipe a person can crawl, and you crawl it on your elbows, through ash. At the end of it, a hatch with a wheel, standing open: whoever came through with the oil did not close it behind them. Beyond it, a red lamp, and the sound of somebody working a hand pump, and coughing.

At the bottom the throat turns, and turns again, and becomes the pump run: a concrete pipe a person can crawl, warm and loud and wet, the pipes overhead sweating onto your back. You crawl it on your elbows for longer than you like. At the end of it, a hatch with a wheel, dogged shut from the inside. You know the trick; every pump hand does, even the ones who have never seen this hatch: the third dog first. The wheel turns. Light, and a red lamp, and warm air that smells of people.

At the bottom the throat turns, and turns again, and becomes the pump run: a concrete pipe a person can crawl, warm and loud and wet, the pipes overhead sweating onto your back. You crawl it on your elbows for longer than you like. At the end of it, a hatch with a wheel, dogged shut from the inside. It takes you a long time in the dark, with your knuckles, to learn its trick: the third dog first. The wheel turns. Light, and a red lamp, and warm air that smells of people.

a3w_pumprun.again: The pump run. The wheel. The red lamp beyond it.

news.text: the designate went inside the Cistern, the first from Knock in living memory

decision.text: I went into the Cistern for the first time in my life, down the grate and along the pump run.

text.text: The door stands open, swung out on its hinges over the white arc it scraped into the concrete, and the warm breath of the Cistern comes out of the dark. At the top of the apron, at the yellow line, the column waits in its grey.

The door: a slab the colour of the rock, three times your height, without a handle on this side. You have known it all your life. Now that you are looking for a way in, you find what nobody in Knock ever looked for, because nobody in Knock ever wanted it open: to the right of the frame, painted the colour of the rock so long ago that the paint has crazed like old glaze, a steel plate the size of a book, held by four bolts. There is stencilling under the paint. You read it with your fingertips. RESCUE ACCESS. MANUAL CYCLE.

again.text: The open door. The column at the line.
The door. The plate under the paint.

passives.text: Along the seam, under the grime, a bead of weld laid from the inside by somebody in a hurry. A bead like that is nothing to rams built to shear rubble off a frame, if you can get pressure into them.

options.text: (Take the plate off and work the manual cycle.)

mods.why: you have bled a windpump's lines
you saw the weld on the seam as a child

a3w_door_no.speaker: narrator
a3w_door_no.text: Behind the plate: a crank socket, a hand pump, a sight glass that should show oil and shows a brown crust, and a valve stencilled CYCLE. You pump until your arms burn. The sight glass stays dry. Somewhere in ninety years of line a seal has perished, and it is not where you can reach it, or not where you know to look. You put the plate back on its bolts, and nobody in Knock is any the wiser.
a3w_door_no.again: The plate, back on its bolts. The glass, dry.

a3w_door_warn.speaker: narrator
a3w_door_warn.text: Behind the plate: a crank socket, a hand pump, a sight glass with a finger of brown oil in the bottom of it, and a valve stencilled CYCLE. You bleed the line the way you would bleed a windpump's, and pump, and the oil climbs the glass. / You know what it will do when you throw that valve. Ninety-year-old rams against a seam welded by hand: the weld will go. The door will open, not for you but for everybody. Maud on her stool will see it. The column at the end of the lane will see it, and the order in its captain's coat says attendance at the door, and you will be standing in the door. Whatever the people inside were going to decide about it among themselves, they will be deciding it with the city on the step.
a3w_door_warn.again: The oil up the sight glass. The valve.

options.text: (Let the pressure off, and put the plate back.)

a3w_door_open.speaker: narrator

text.text: You throw the valve. / For a long moment nothing happens at all, and then the ground does. It is not a sound so much as a change in everything you are standing on, as if something under the apron had taken a breath ninety years ago and held it and was letting it go. The seam splits along its weld with a crack like river ice. A line of dark opens down the face of the rock, and widens, and the door swings out on hinges as thick as a man, slowly, scraping a white arc into the concrete, until it stands open. Warm air comes out of it, smelling of algae and machine oil and people. / Behind you, Knock has come out of its doors. Maud is on her feet on the apron with her stool knocked over and her stick fallen beside it, and she picks up neither. And in the dark of the doorway, at the very edge of the light, as if the light were cold water and they did not know yet whether to step into it, there are faces.

You throw the valve. / For a long moment nothing happens at all, and then the ground does. It is not a sound so much as a change in everything you are standing on, as if something under the apron had taken a breath ninety years ago and held it and was letting it go. The seam splits along its weld with a crack like river ice. A line of dark opens down the face of the rock, and widens, and the door swings out on hinges as thick as a man, slowly, scraping a white arc into the concrete, until it stands open. Warm air comes out of it, smelling of algae and machine oil and people. / Behind you, Knock has come out of its doors. Maud is on her feet on the apron with her stool knocked over behind her and her hand over her mouth. And in the dark of the doorway, at the very edge of the light, as if the light were cold water and they did not know yet whether to step into it, there are faces.

a3w_door_open.again: The door, open. The faces at the edge of the light.

news.text: the Cistern's door at Knock opened from outside for the first time in ninety years, by the designate's own hand

interject.text: Tamsin has stopped dead on the concrete. "That's my door," she says, to nobody. "That's the door." She does not go any nearer it.
Ash takes his hat off. The Choir do it at a grave, and at a birth, and he does not say which this is.

text.text: Up the lane, the column is coming. Not running: Captain Lowe has them walking, four wardens in grey in a line behind him with their rifles slung, the way people walk to a funeral they have been ordered to attend. Knock stands back out of their way into its doorways. At the top of the apron there is a yellow line, painted on the concrete ninety years ago for nobody, and Lowe stops at it, and the wardens stop behind him. He takes his cap off. He looks past you into the dark of the door, at the faces looking out, and for a while he does not say anything at all. / "Designate," he says.

Up the lane, the column is coming. Not running: Sergeant Reyes has them walking, four wardens in grey in a line behind her with their rifles slung. Knock stands back out of their way into its doorways. At the top of the apron there is a yellow line, painted on the concrete ninety years ago for nobody, and Reyes stops at it, and the wardens stop behind her. She looks past you into the dark of the door, at the faces looking out, and her jaw works once. / "Designate," she says.

Up the lane, the column is coming. Not running: the senior warden, Kress, has them walking, three in grey in a line behind him with their rifles slung. Knock stands back out of their way into its doorways. At the top of the apron there is a yellow line, painted on the concrete ninety years ago for nobody, and Kress stops at it, and the others stop behind him. He looks past you into the dark of the door, and swallows. / "Designate," he says.

options.text: Hold them there. Nothing has been attended yet.
(Say nothing. Turn your back on them and go in.)

a3w_door_held.speaker: narrator

text.text: "Held." He says it over his shoulder to the wardens without raising his voice, and they stand. "Attendance is a word, designate, not a door. You have opened the door. I will wait for the word." He does not put his cap back on. "Go in and see them. I would, in your place."
"Held," Reyes says over her shoulder, and the wardens stand. "The captain's clause, designate. Attendance is a word, not a door. I'll wait for it." She looks into the dark. "Go in."

"Held," Kress says over his shoulder, and the others stand. "Line six of the order: residents are not to be frightened." He looks at the faces in the dark. "They look frightened, designate. I'll wait for your word."

a3w_door_held.again: The column, held at the line.

news.text: the designate went inside the Cistern, the first from Knock in living memory

decision.text: I opened the Cistern's door from outside, by a manual cycle nobody in Knock knew was there, and walked in with the column standing at the line behind me.

a3w_door_silent.speaker: narrator

text.text: You turn your back on him and walk into the dark. Behind you he says nothing for a moment. Then, to the wardens, quietly: "Hold." And to your back, not loud, so that only you will hear it: "Silence is not a word, designate. I will wait for one."
You turn your back on her and walk into the dark. Behind you, a pause; then, to the wardens: "Hold." And to your back: "That's not a word, designate. The captain's clause wants a word. I'll wait."
You turn your back on him and walk into the dark. Behind you, a pause; then: "Hold." And, uncertainly, to your back: "Designate? I'll... wait for the word, then."

a3w_door_silent.again: The column at the line, behind you, waiting.

news.text: the designate went inside the Cistern, the first from Knock in living memory

decision.text: I opened the Cistern's door from outside, by a manual cycle nobody in Knock knew was there, and walked in with the column standing at the line behind me.

text.text: The door, shut, the colour of the rock. Somebody has chalked on it, in the guild's green, small and neat at the height of a factor's hand: CLAIMED — SALVAGE — T.G. Somebody else has tried to scrub it off, and it has only gone pale.

The door, shut, the colour of the rock. Along its seam, where the old bead was, a new one, grey as rope and neat as stitching, laid from inside. Children still put their ears to the door. It still hums.
The door, shut, the colour of the rock, as it has been all your life. Children put their ears to it for the hum, and now and then somebody on the other side knocks back, which is new.

The door stands open on the apron, swung out over its white arc, and the hall inside is lit. People go in and out of it as if it had always been a door. Somebody has put a chair just inside it, in the warm, and an old woman from Knock is sitting in it.
The door stands open on an empty hall. Somebody has swept it. Nobody goes in.

again.text: The door, shut.
The open door.

text.text: The hatch, black glass and a scorched tray, and the Grille beside it dark. Nobody has thought what to do with it. Maud still sits beside it at seven.
The hatch's panel, dark, though the hum behind the rock goes on. Bram has chalked on the tray: PAGE 41. ASK ME.
The hatch, its panel lit a dim green again, the tray on its rails. It runs out at seven as it always did, and MOTHER says thank you as she always did, and Maud sits beside it with her book.
The hatch, its panel lit a dim green, the tray on its rails. It runs out at seven. Nobody comes out of it any more, and nobody sends anything in but water and wool.

The hatch, its panel lit, the tray run out and left out, with a cup in it and a jar of somebody's flowers. MOTHER opens it to Knock every morning now, for anybody, and says good morning instead of thank you, which took her a week to learn.
The hatch, its panel lit a dim green. At seven it runs out on its rails with nothing in it, and MOTHER says, to nobody, "The hatch is open," and waits, and then it runs back in.

sign.speaker: narrator
sign.text: A painted board: TOLL ROAD — CARDS SHOWN — FACES UP. Under it, smaller, in a different paint: WATER 1 HERE. And under that, scratched: "the Guild remembers".
sign.again: FACES UP. Somebody has scratched over the scratching, and given up.

take.speaker: narrator
take.text: The watch stool by the hatch lamp. Knock keeps one person awake at the door every night, for sixty years, for nothing.
take.again: The stool, the lamp. The night isn't going anywhere without you.

sat.speaker: narrator
sat.text: The lamp hisses. The wind drops. Stars, more than anyone could count, and the dark road coming down past the stand. Hours. Then, far up the road, something that is not the wind.

stool.speaker: narrator
stool.text: The watch stool, worn to the shape of sixty years of Knock.
stool.again: The stool, empty, waiting for whoever has the watch.

arrive.speaker: narrator
arrive.text: He comes down the road past the dark stand like a man walking into a wind, one hand on the rock, one leg dragging, a dust mask of leather and tin pulled down at his throat. He doesn't look at the shacks or the lamp. He goes straight to the Cistern door and beats on it with his fist, slow, the way you'd knock on a door you'd knocked on before, and slides down it to sit.

face.text: You bring the lamp. He turns his head. His eyes find your face, and widen, and something in them gives way, relief or grief. "You," he says. Just that. "You."

passives.label: Night Watch
passives.text: Under his breath, under the wind, a word you almost don't hear and won't forget: "Larkspur."
Blood to the knee, old and new. A sunburn down one side of his face only.

options.text: Who are you? How do you know me?

mods.why: Pell trained you through the Grille

run_pell.speaker: narrator
run_pell.text: You hammer the Grille until a light comes, shout for Pell, and run back. He hasn't moved.

wound_pell.speaker: npc_c9_02
wound_pell.text: Pell's voice through the holes, a few steps away, steady: "Tell me what you see. Where's the blood coming from? ... The hip. Old wound, gone bad — smell it? Then there's nothing for it with what you have. Hold his hand. Hold his hand and listen to him."

wound.text: A rifle wound in the hip, weeks old, gone bad under a field dressing. And above it a second scar, closed long ago, not stitched: sealed, with a clean line of something like glass melted into the skin. Machine work. You have only ever heard Pell describe it. There is nothing you can do with a needle and water, and you both know it.

wound_fail.speaker: narrator
wound_fail.text: Blood to the knee. You press where it seems to come from and he hisses, and it doesn't stop. It is not the kind of wound pressing stops.

dying.text: His hand closes on yours with more strength than he should have. He presses something into it: a photograph, creased soft. "Don't let them—" A breath that doesn't finish. His eyes are still on your face. Then they aren't on anything.

photo.speaker: narrator
photo.text: It's you. Older — forty, forty-five — on the broad steps of a ruined city of towers, squinting into the wind. On the back, in pencil, a date forty-one years gone.

passives.text: The shadow under your chin falls to the left. The towers' shadows fall to the right.

passives.label: Linnet's print
passives.text: The steps. You know those steps: they are on the cheap print over Linnet's cot.

text.text: He sits against the door as if waiting for it to open. Someone has put a blanket over his knees.

His pack is light: a notebook in tight marks that aren't quite letters, a tin cup, no map, no water. The dust mask at his throat, when you ease it off, has a sign painted on its brow with care: half a sun with no ground under it, or an open hand. On his left forearm, a neat square burn, old and deliberate.

passives.text: Inside the mask's rim, scratched letters, worn almost smooth.

options.text: (Leave him with Knock, and go to Maud.)

arrive.text: Three riders in the square on tired horses, Guild sashes faded to the colour of the road. The one in front is grey at the temples and polite about it. "Brannick Hale, outrider, the Tollmen's Guild. We're after an old man with a dust mask at his throat, carrying stolen Guild property. He came this way. We know he came this way." He looks at you, and at your face, a moment too long. "You found him."

passives.text: He came straight to the post-house. He knew which house.

passives.label: Corin
passives.text: Up on the rise, a glint: Corin, on his belly, with the rifle.

options.text: (Hand over the notebook.) This is what he carried. Take it and go.
He died in the night. We buried him with his things.

mods.why: you know how the Guild talks

options.text: (Say nothing; let him search. The photograph is in your boot.)

mods.why: you've hidden from the watch-bell all your life

options.text: (Raise your arm to the rise.) Knock gives the Guild water. Not its dead.

give.text: Hale turns the notebook over, flicks it, frowns. "This is all?" He looks at you a long time. "This is all." He tucks it into his coat. "The Guild thanks Knock." Then, almost gently: "We'll be taking our due for the trouble."

decision.text: You gave the outriders the stranger's notebook and kept the photograph.

lie.text: "Buried." Hale weighs it. Weighs you. "With his things." He looks at the fresh earth by the door where Amos and Sim worked half the night. "Then the Guild will take its due for the trouble, and the dead can keep what they stole."

decision.text: You lied to the outriders: the stranger was buried with his things.

lie_fail.text: "Buried." Hale smiles for the first time. "With his things. Search the post-house," he says over his shoulder, and his riders go, and you hear Maud shouting, and then something breaking.

hide.text: They search the post-house, the shacks, you. The photograph is flat in your boot under your foot and nobody thinks to look at your boots, because nobody ever does. Hale stands in the square with his hands on his hips. "Knock," he says. "Sixty years of the Guild's good water, and this is the thanks."

decision.text: You hid the stranger's things from the outriders.

hide_fail.text: They search the post-house, the shacks, and then you. Carrow finds the notebook. Nobody finds the photograph in your boot, because Hale is already shouting, because Maud has come at Carrow with the post-book.

due.speaker: narrator
due.text: Their due is the post-house. It goes up in the time it takes to say so: sixty years of letters, the shelf, the table, the cots. Maud goes in after the post-book before anyone can stop her and comes out with it, burning, and with her leg broken under a fallen beam. The outriders ride north without looking back. Knock stands in the square and watches its letters go up in the morning wind.

news.text: Guild outriders burned the post-house at Knock

fight.text: Hale sees your arm, and looks up at the rise, and sighs like a man who expected nothing better. "Corin Asch," he says. "Twenty years." His hand goes to his revolver. Behind you, Dace comes out of the lane with his pipe.

again.text: "We're done talking."
again.again: Hale doesn't look round. He is watching the post-house.

night.speaker: narrator
night.text: Your cot behind the partition, the blanket folded back the way Maud leaves it. The photograph is still in your hand. You don't remember deciding to keep holding it.
night.again: The cot. The photograph, still in your hand. Sleep, or don't.

day.speaker: narrator
day.text: Your cot behind the partition. Not now; there is the day to get through first.
day.again: Not yet. The day isn't done with you.

text.text: You're late, and I need you. Gloves are on the tray. Close the door — they keep coming in to look at him like he's a sermon.
{name}. Good — steady hands. Shut the door behind you; half the ring has been in here to stare at him.

passives.text: The dust mask on the side table has letters scratched inside the rim, worn almost smooth.
Pell keeps tugging the sheet back over the man's left forearm.

menu.text: Nobody we know. Nobody anybody knows. Ask what you like — I've run out of things to do with my hands.
menu.again: What else? He isn't going anywhere, and it seems neither am I.

options.text: Let me look at the wounds myself.

mods.why: Pell trained you

options.text: What are you hiding under that sheet?
The dust mask on the table. What's the sign on it?

cause.text: Thirst, mostly. A rifle wound in the hip that went bad weeks ago. He walked on it a long way — boots worn through on the outer edge, sunburn down one side of his face only. West-bound, into the afternoon sun, for a long time.

wounds.text: Pell steps back and lets you work. Under the rot, the old wound was closed once — not stitched: sealed, with a clear line of something like glass that has melted into the skin. "Machine work," Pell says quietly. "I've only ever read about it. Somewhere out there, someone still has a real hospital."

stitches_q.text: A city, maybe. Somewhere with power and clean hands and patience. He walked away from it with this in him, and kept walking until he reached us. You'd have to want something badly to do that.

wounds_fail.text: Pell catches your wrist before you reopen something. "Watch, don't help." He walks you through it: a rifle wound, a fever, a very long walk.

arm.text: Pell holds your eyes for a moment, then folds the sheet back. On the inside of the forearm, a neat square burn, deliberate and old, and at its edge a few lines of tiny printed marks the fire didn't reach. "He burned something off himself," Pell says. "Carefully. On purpose. Leave it be."

mods.why: Pell trusts you

arm_yes.text: The marks at the edge are the same print as the labels on MOTHER's old crates. I don't know what that means and I would rather not guess out loud. Not here.

arm_no.text: I recognise a man who has been dead since dawn. Help me or go.

text.text: Half a sun with no ground under it — or an open hand, depending how you hold it. Painted with care. And yes, I saw the scratches inside. Initials, maybe. Worn too smooth to read.
Half a sun with no ground under it — or an open hand, depending how you hold it. Painted with care. Somebody loved that sign.

pack.text: Ines took the pack. Except this — it was in his fist when he knocked. He wouldn't let go of it, even after.

photo.text: It's you. Older — forty, forty-five — with a city of broken towers behind you, squinting into the wind. On the back, in pencil: a date forty-one years gone. "I've been staring at it for an hour," Pell says. "It's you. I don't care how."

passives.text: The shadow under your chin falls to the left. The shadows of the towers behind you fall to the right.
Every print you have ever seen has grain in it. This has none — the dust in the air is drawn, not caught.

options.text: It can't be me. I wasn't born.
I need to see the Elder.

photo_denial.text: No. You weren't. Neither was the man who carried it to our door, by the look of him, and yet here we both are. Ines will want to see you.

photo_place.text: Somewhere with buildings taller than anything in our books. Ines reads the old atlases. Ask her — and ask her where she's put his pack.

again.text: Still here? He isn't getting any more talkative.
again.again: You keep coming back to him. So do I.

early.text: Not yet, {name}. Go to the clinic first and let Aurel show you what he showed me. Then come back and we'll talk like people with all the facts.
early.again: The clinic first, {name}. Aurel is waiting, and so is he.

text.text: Sit. You were on the door when he came — you saw him alive, which is more than the rest of us. A man walked across the waste and died with your face in his hand. Tell me what he said.
Sit. No — stand, if you'd rather; I'll be quick, because I can't hold the others for long. A man walked across the waste and died with your face in his hand.

council.again: Go on. I can hold them a little longer.

passives.text: Her eyes go, once, to the sealed Archive door behind her desk — and away.

options.text: He said one word through the grille: "Larkspur." Then he fell.
I'll go. I want to know who he was.

word.text: Larkspur. A flower — we had seeds of it once, in the old hydroponics catalogue. She writes it down, very carefully, as if the pen might break. "Don't say it to anyone else."

word_why.text: Because it's the only thing he said, and I would like it to stay ours until we know whose it was. Indulge an old woman.

why.text: Because a dead man carried your face across the waste on purpose. Whoever sent him wanted you. I'd like to know why before they come for you themselves — and they might, if we sit here and pray about it.

others.text: Bram wants the door welded shut. Half the ring wants a prayer said over the body and the whole thing forgotten by supper. And MOTHER… MOTHER says population variance is unchanged, and thanks us for our continuity.

want.text: I want one person who can keep their head to walk out, look, and come back and tell me the truth. That person has your face. It seems the waste agrees.

pack.text: Here. Waterskin, empty. A notebook full of marks no one can read. His dust mask. Take them; they're more yours than ours.

passives.text: The marks in the notebook repeat in blocks of five. A cipher, not a language.

options.text: (Read the notebook.) This is record shorthand — the same hand as our own record room.

notebook.text: You read a line aloud before you understand it: "Road east of the salt. Sell the map to the dog-men if you must, but keep the face." Ines goes very still. "Where did a stranger learn the hand our records are kept in?"

notebook_deflect.text: I can't. Which is exactly why you're going outside, and I am staying here to keep sixty people calm. Don't read that hand aloud in the ring.

options.text: Back to the matter of leaving.

text.text: Everything, {name}. I'm old; I keep the council minutes. Some of them are dull and some of them are sealed for good reasons, and neither kind will help you on the road.
Everything, {name}. I'm old. Old people are mostly made of things they haven't said.

options.text: The Archive. You looked at it.

hiding_yes.text: She is quiet for a long time. "There are records in there older than me, and MOTHER doesn't like them read. I read one, once, when I was young and certain. I have been less certain since." She smiles without much in it. "Bring me back the truth and I'll show you the door. Not before."

decision.text: Elder Ines promised to open the Archive for you if you return with the truth.

hiding_no.text: Then you'll have to forgive me for the things I keep. Most of them are only sad.

refuse.text: Then I'll send Tamsin. She volunteered before the body was cold, and she'll go whether I send her or not.

refuse_send.text: Ines nods slowly. "I will. And when she doesn't come back, you'll go after her, and you'll have lost a day you didn't need to lose." She is already writing the order.

decision.text: You let Tamsin go outside alone.

options.text: …Give me the order. I'll go after her.

text.text: Then hurry. Take this to Bram — he won't open the door for anyone else. And {name}: write. The caravans carry letters if you pay them in something they want.
Then go with my word, not behind my back. Take this to Bram; he won't open the door for anyone else. And write — the caravans carry letters if you pay them in something they want.

decision.text: You agreed to go outside for the council.

options.text: If I'm going, I'm going armed. Open the armoury.

mods.why: Ines trusts you

options.text: (Hold her gaze.) You know I'll need it.

armed.text: One rifle — the bolt gun, it's the only one that still shoots straight — and twenty rounds. Bring the rifle back. Bring yourself back first.

armed_no.text: We have eleven rifles for sixty people, and nobody has fired one in a generation. No. Find what you need out there — I suspect it's full of rifles.

after.text: Go carefully. Write. And if you find the people who sent him — be polite until you can't.
after.again: You're still inside, {name}. The door won't keep forever, and neither will I.

options.text: Factor Pike at Shale would pay the Cistern a fortune for viable seed.

seed.text: "The bank is the ring's. It is not mine to sell and it is not the guild's to buy." She lets that stand. Then, more quietly: "It is also ninety years old and has never been under a sky. If it went into the ground somewhere with sun on it, I would call that the bank doing what it was built to do."

options.text: The Choir at Shale farms under the open sky. It would go in the ground.

mods.why: she trusts you

seed_yes.text: She unlocks the vault herself and chooses the case the way you choose a word. "Tomato, bean, squash, millet." She puts it in your hands, cold. "For the sky. Not for a ledger. I am trusting you with the difference."

seed_no.text: "No." The word is final in the way doors are. "Not to the guild, and not through you to the guild. The vault stays locked."

meet.text: A woman of twenty-four in Cistern grey, the sleeves cut off at the shoulder, stands at the end of Mags's bar as if the floor might tip. Copper hair hacked short. A chipped front tooth. She knows you by your walk before you are close enough to know her. "Don't," she says. "Don't say anything yet. I want to do this one first." She looks at your face for a long time, the way you would read a page you had only ever heard read aloud. "Your nose is worse than in the picture."
meet.again: She is still looking at your face, as if it might be taken back.

options.text: (Hold the photograph up beside your face.)
Go home, Tam. It isn't safe out here.

meet_photo.text: "It's you." She holds it next to your face and looks from one to the other. "It's you older, and somebody's put you somewhere you'd hate. Look at your shoulders. You never stood like that at the Grille. I could hear you not standing like that." She gives it back.
meet_photo.again: She has given the photograph back. She is still comparing.

text.text: "You asked." She says it fast, like ripping off a bandage. "Eighteen years and you finally asked. So: hatch day, six o'clock, and the hatch just — stayed open, and the panel said VARIANCE, and I climbed. The fridge held the hatch for me. I'll think about what that means tomorrow." She looks past you at the door, the street, the white sky over it. "Today there's a sky."

"I said I was coming out. I don't say things I don't do." She says it fast, like ripping off a bandage. "Hatch day, six o'clock, and the hatch just — stayed open, and the panel said VARIANCE, and I climbed. The fridge held the hatch for me. I'll think about what that means tomorrow." She looks past you at the door, the street, the white sky over it. "Today there's a sky."

meet_out.again: "Today there's a sky," she says again, to make sure.

meet_home.text: "Home." She laughs, once. "You sound like Ines." She doesn't move from the bar. "I'm not going back in. I didn't climb out of a hole to be told to climb back into it by the person I climbed out for."
meet_home.again: She hasn't moved from the bar.

meet_join.text: "So." She drags a pack out from under the stool. It has been packed for a long time; the straps have set in their creases. "I've got a knife, two days' water and no idea what I'm doing. Am I coming with you, or am I sitting at Mags's bar finding out what everything costs?"
meet_join.again: The pack, on her knee. The question, still open.

decision.text: Tamsin came out of the Cistern, the first in living memory, and came on the road with you.

options.text: Stay here a while. Get your feet under you. I'll come back for you.

meet_come.text: "I packed six years ago," she says. "Don't look at me like that. You'd have asked eventually." She is grinning before she finishes, all teeth, the chipped one too.

meet_wait.text: "Left behind again." She says it lightly and it isn't light. "Fine. Nell says there's a cot. I'll be here, finding out what everything costs. Don't take long. I've done enough waiting for one life."

waiting.text: "Well?" Tamsin, at Mags's bar, the pack under the stool.

decision.text: Tamsin came out of the Cistern, the first in living memory, and came on the road with you.

text.text: "Mags says I tip like a Tollman. I'm going to take that as a compliment until somebody stops me."
"Rust it, the sky's still there. I keep checking."

options.text: Go back to Shale. Wait for me at Mags's.

text.text: Tamsin is lying on her back with her hands behind her head, not sleeping. "There's no ceiling," she says. "Anything could just come down."
Tamsin sits too close to the fire, the way people do who grew up without one. "Go on, then."

camp.again: Tamsin pokes the fire with a stick and waits.

options.text: You went somewhere on your own today.
You went somewhere on your own today.

Three orders, the terminal said. Reserve 9.

s1.text: "There's no ceiling." She says it to the sky, not to you. "Eighteen years I asked you what the sky was doing and you said blue, and now I'm under it and it isn't doing anything. It's just — up. All the way." A breath. "Tell me what it's doing. Properly. Like at the Grille."
s1.again: "Properly," she says again. "Like at the Grille."

options.text: (Tell her: the dust high up, the stars behind it, one satellite still crossing, the dark at the edges.)
It's dark, Tam. Go to sleep.

s1_sky.text: "A satellite." She tracks it with a finger until it goes. "Somebody built that and it's still going and they're dead." She doesn't sound sad about it; she sounds like someone handed a present.
s1_sky.again: She is still watching the place the satellite went.

s1_blue.text: "You always say blue." But she's smiling at the dark.
s1_blue.again: She is smiling at the dark.

s1_photo.text: After a while: "The picture. Of you. Do you know who made it?"

options.text: Yes. I know who made it.
No. I'm going to find out.

s1_lie.text: "Huh." She doesn't ask who. She looks at you for a second longer than she needs to, and then back up at the sky. "Okay."
s1_lie.again: She is looking at the sky, not at you.

s1_true.text: "Good. Me too." She puts her hand out on the ground between you, flat, palm up, and after a second you understand it is how her fingertips used to come through the holes. "Partners." Then, too quickly: "I've been sick before, you know. When I was little. The clinic. Forget it. It's boring." She rolls over, and is asleep, or pretending, in a minute.

s1_matter.text: "Everything matters out here. That's the whole thing about out here." She thinks about it. "In there nothing mattered because nothing changed. I've been sick before, you know. When I was little. Forget it. It's boring."

text.text: Tamsin hasn't said anything since Shale, which she never does. "He was braver than me," she says at last. "Jonah. Braver than everybody. It didn't help him at all."

"He's alive." Tamsin says it like she's checking the word still works. "Jonah. You changed the — the conditions. Not him. He was going to be brave right up a tower and off it." She pokes the fire. "I'd have gone up the tower. Rust it. I'd have gone first."

s2.again: She is still looking at the fire, not at you.

options.text: Be careful, Tam. I can't lose you as well.
You're not fragile. You never were.
Brave isn't the point. Being here tomorrow is.

s2_fragile.text: "There it is." She doesn't look up. "Ines's voice. Pell's voice. Everybody who ever stood at the end of a clinic bed." She throws the stick on the fire. "I'm not glass. I climbed out of a hole." It is a long time before she says anything else, and when she does it is about the weather.
s2_fragile.again: She is talking about the weather, and nothing else.

s2_clinic.text: She is quiet a while. Then, fast, before she can stop herself: "I was born wrong. Early. Lungs like wet paper. I lived in the clinic till I was six — Pell's white room — and MOTHER sang to me through the panel every night. Old songs. I thought every kid got sung to." She laughs, badly. "I've never told anyone that. Not even you, at the Grille. Don't make a thing of it."
s2_clinic.again: "Don't make a thing of it," she says again.

s2_end.text: She lies back. "Good. You're good at not making things a thing." She is asleep before you are.

s2_cold.text: "Jonah." She shrugs, and it isn't a shrug. "People die of being brave. I knew that. I just didn't *know* it." She turns away from the fire. Whatever else there is, she isn't telling you tonight.
s2_cold.again: Her back is to the fire.

r1.text: She doesn't sleep. After a while: "Riddle." She doesn't look at you. "I've known you my whole life and I'd never seen you, and now I can't stop looking. What am I?" A pause. "You can say you don't know. That's allowed. That's always allowed."
r1.again: "The riddle's still open," she says to the fire.

decision.text: You answered Tamsin's riddle. Slowly, she said.

options.text: Tam. I don't — not like that.

r1_yes.text: She turns her head. "Yeah?" And then, because she is Tamsin: "That was a terrible answer. Correct. But terrible." She doesn't move closer. She leaves her hand on the ground between you, palm up, the way it used to come through the holes. "Slow," she says. "I want this one slow. I've had eighteen years of talking fast through a wall."
r1_yes.again: Her hand on the ground between you, palm up.

r1_later.text: "Don't know yet." She nods, like it's an answer she can keep. "Riddles keep. I'll ask again one day, and you can not-know again if you like." She doesn't sound hurt. She sounds like someone with time.
r1_later.again: She has time. She says so with her shoulders.

r1_no.text: "Good." She says it quickly and means most of it. "Riddles are better unanswered anyway. And you're still — " she waves a hand at the whole of you. "You're still the Grille. That doesn't go anywhere." In the morning she is exactly herself, and stays it.
r1_no.again: She is herself. She stays it.

r1b.text: "Again?" She grins at the fire. "I've known you my whole life and never seen you, and now I can't stop looking. What am I?"
r1b.again: "What am I?" she asks the fire.

decision.text: You answered Tamsin's riddle, the second time she asked. Slowly, she said.

options.text: Still don't know. Leave it unanswered.

r1b_no.text: "Unanswered. The best kind." She nearly means it. "I won't ask a third time. I don't do that to people."
r1b_no.again: She doesn't ask a third time.

r2.text: Away from the fire the dark is the real kind, and she stands in it with her face up and her eyes shut. It has started to rain, the thin, rare, dusty rain of the flats, and she has never in her life stood in rain. "Tell me what the sky is doing," she says. You tell her: it is raining on her. She laughs, and opens her eyes, and they are on you. "I'm asking," she says. "I always ask. You can say no, and I'll still be here tomorrow, being annoying. Can I?"
r2.again: "I asked," she says, quietly. "You can still say no."

decision.text: Tamsin asked, in the rain, and you said yes.

r2_yes.text: "Good," she says, close enough that you feel it more than hear it, and then neither of you says anything for a long time, and the rain does what it likes. Much later, under the blanket by a fire burned to nothing, half asleep: "That's what the sky's doing. Write it down."
r2_yes.again: She is asleep against you. The rain has stopped.

r2_not.text: "Okay." And it is; you can hear that it is. "Then you ask me. When it is. I'll be here." She tips her face back up into the rain and stays there until she is soaked, laughing at nothing.
r2_not.again: She is still out in the rain, laughing at nothing.

r2_no.text: "Okay." She keeps her face up to the rain a while longer, so you can't see it. "Thanks for saying it to my face. People mostly don't." When she comes back to the fire she is herself again, and she doesn't make you pay for it.

r2_ask.text: "Yeah?" She looks at you across the fire for a long moment. "You're sure. You're asking. Not me." Then she grins, all teeth. "Yes. Obviously yes. I was going to wait a hundred years."
r2_ask.again: She is grinning at you across the fire.

decision.text: You asked Tamsin, when it was time, and she said yes.

r2_ask_yes.text: She meets you halfway, because of course she does. Much later, half asleep: "Next time it rains, you're telling me what the sky's doing. Properly."

quit.text: "Okay." She doesn't argue. If she cries, it isn't where you can see. "Thanks for saying it to my face." After a while: "We're still the Grille. That doesn't stop."

decision.text: You ended it with Tamsin, to her face.

listed_r.text: She doesn't sit down. She has a scrap of paper, folded small and soft with handling, and she unfolds it so you can see: a list of names in her square hand. Ines. Teague. A Tollman whose name she never knew. The last line is fresh, and it is you. "Twice," she says. "I keep a list. I've kept it since I was six." She folds it. "So we're done. The other thing. I'm not leaving the road because of you, but that's done."
listed_r.again: The list is folded away. She doesn't take it out again.

decision.text: You lied to Tamsin twice. You are on her list, and what was between you is over.

I just wanted you to know where you are."
listed.again: The list is folded away. She doesn't take it out again.

s3.text: "I went to the records office." She says it before you have sat down. "On my own. The desk. A person can ask for their own entry, it says on the wall. Twenty for the paper." She holds it out: a strip from the warden's printer. ROE, TAMSIN — RESERVE 9 — NO ENTRY. "No entry." She laughs, and it cracks in the middle. "Sixty people in there and I'm not one of them. The city counts dead people in the Sink. It doesn't count me."
s3.again: The strip of paper is on her knee. NO ENTRY.

decision.text: Tamsin asked Meridian's records office for her own entry. There is none.

s3_ask.text: "Did you know?" She is watching your face the way she watched it at Mags's bar.

options.text: Nine said something about Reserve 9. I didn't understand it.

s3_why.text: "Then *why*?" Her voice goes up. "It hid me. The fridge. It's the only thing in there that keeps the count. It hid me from the count, and the city never noticed, and I've been — what? Not written down. A mistake nobody filed."
s3_why.again: "A mistake nobody filed," she says again.

options.text: Maybe it hid you for your own good.

decision.text: You told Tamsin she was hidden for her own good. She went back to Shale.

options.text: Maybe it hid you for your own good.

decision.text: You told Tamsin she was hidden for her own good. She went back to Shale, and what was between you is over.

options.text: Then we find out why. Both of us.
What do you want to do?

s3_broken.text: "For my own good." She stands up. She is very calm, which is the worst thing you have seen her be. "That's what Ines said, every time I asked about the door. That's what Pell said about the clinic. That's what the fridge would say if it said anything." She picks up her pack. "I'll be at Mags's. Don't come."
s3_broken.again: She is gone down the road.

s3_find.text: "Both of us." She folds the strip and puts it inside her shirt, against her skin, like something she means to keep. "Pell would know. The clinic. He talks through the Grille to anybody who stands there. Or your fridge with legs, if it'll say anything that isn't a clause." A breath. "Rust it. I'm not crying about a piece of paper."
s3_find.again: The strip is inside her shirt.

s3_cold.text: She doesn't look at you. She drops a strip of printer paper on the ground between you: ROE, TAMSIN — RESERVE 9 — NO ENTRY. "I went to the records office. Not written down." She lies down on the far side of the fire. "Don't say anything. I'll find out why on my own."
s3_cold.again: She is on the far side of the fire.

decision.text: Tamsin asked Meridian's records office for her own entry. There is none.

why_nine.speaker: npc_md_nine
why_nine.text: "Clause 40: a person's entry is read to the person." The lens turns to Tamsin and clicks twice. "You are the person. I will read what is not there." It opens neither ledger. "The record has sixty for Reserve 9. The caretaker's ration returns, which come to my desk each quarter, are for sixty-one, and have been for eighteen years. A reserve is kept for relocation; its people are assessed fit, and a child assessed unfit is not carried on the count." A pause. "The caretaker never sent you to be assessed. You were never counted. The record suggests it did that on purpose, every quarter, for eighteen years. I have logged it as an error. It is the only error I have never filed with anyone."

why_nine2.text: "On purpose," Tamsin says. "Every quarter." She looks at Nine a long time. "You knew, fridge. And you never told anyone." "No," Nine says. "Clause 40." It is not the reason, and everyone at the fire knows it.
why_nine2.again: Neither of them is looking at the other now.

choice.text: "So the fridge hid me." Tamsin turns it over like a stone she found. "From a box on a form that said I'd be no use where they were taking everyone. Sang to me so I'd sleep while it did it." She isn't crying; she is past that, somewhere colder. "I could write to it. I could write to Ines and have the whole ring know by supper. Or I could keep it. Keep it till I know what it's for."
choice.again: "Write to it, tell Ines, or keep it," she says. "Go on."

decision.text: Tamsin kept what she learned about her own count. It was hers to decide, and you said so.

options.text: Write to MOTHER. Tell it you know.

decision.text: Tamsin wrote to MOTHER, unsigned, to tell it she knows.

options.text: Tell Ines. The ring should know what was done to you.

decision.text: Tamsin wrote to Elder Ines, and the ring will know what was done.
Tamsin kept what she learned about her own count, until it matters.

choice_yours.text: "Mine." She sits with that a while. "Then I keep it, till I know what it's for. Thanks for not deciding for me. Everybody decides for me." She folds the strip of printer paper smaller.

choice_mother.text: "Thank you for your continuity," she says, trying the words out like a letter. "That's what I'll write. It's all it ever says to anyone. I'll send it from the next town with a caravan and I won't sign it." She looks at the fire. "It'll know."

choice_ines.text: "The whole ring." She thinks about Teague's face. "Yeah. Let them choke on it at supper." She doesn't sound happy. She sounds like someone pulling out a splinter.
choice_ines.again: She is still pulling at the splinter.

choice_keep.text: "Until it matters." She folds the strip small and puts it back against her skin. "That's what Ines would say." A beat. "It's what I'd say, too. Rust it."
choice_keep.again: The strip is back against her skin.

s4.text: "Three orders." She has been thinking about it for days; you can tell by how little she says. "RESERVE 9 — OUTSTANDING — CARETAKER NON-COMPLIANT — ORDERS 3. The city's told the fridge three times to open the door and take everyone, and three times it said no." She looks at you. "It hid me, and it said no. Same machine. Same reason, maybe." A breath. "When they come for the door — and they will — where are you?"
s4.again: "Where are you?" she asks again, quieter.

decision.text: You told Tamsin you would stand at the Cistern's door with her when the city comes for it.

options.text: Wherever keeps the most people alive.
Maybe the city's right. Sixty people can't live in a hole forever.

decision.text: You told Tamsin the city might be right about the Cistern.

s4_with.text: "With me." She nods, once, like signing something. "Then I'll stand in it, and you stand next to me, and the fridge can sing to both of us." She almost laughs. "I'm going to protect a machine that hid me in a cupboard for eighteen years. Rust it. Ines would be so proud."
s4_with.again: She has signed something, in her head. You can see it.

s4_lives.text: "That's an answer for Ines." Not unkind. "Mine's the door. I'll be in it. You work out the most people from wherever you are." She lies back. "I hope it's next to me."
s4_lives.again: "Next to me," she says, to the sky.

s4_city.text: "Then we'll be on different sides of it." She says it simply. "I'll be in it. You'll be wherever the city tells you to be." She turns over, and she doesn't say goodnight, and she has always said goodnight.

s4_cold.text: "Three orders," she says. "The fridge said no three times." She doesn't look at you. "When they come for the door, I'll be in it. I'm not asking where you'll be."

out.text: "Big." She doesn't even have to think. "Everything's further away than it should be, and it's all *on*. The wind. Things move that nobody moved. I followed a lizard for ten minutes yesterday. Don't tell anyone." She thinks. "Ask me tomorrow and I'll say something different. I'll say something different every day for a year."
out.again: She is watching something move that nobody moved.

maud.text: "Maud talked to me through the vent every night for eighteen years. About goats, mostly." She smiles at the fire. "She said the day I came out, one of us would cry. She didn't say which." A beat. "It was Corin. Don't tell him I told you."

nell.text: "Nell's the first friend I ever made with a face." She grins. "She showed me how to pour without spilling and how to tell when a Tollman's lying, which is always. She wants out with the Wheel. I told her the world's big. She said she knows." Tamsin shakes her head. "She doesn't."
nell.again: "She doesn't know," Tamsin says again, with great authority.

fridge.text: "The fridge." She makes a face. "It says thank you for your continuity like it means goodnight. I used to think it was the most boring thing alive." A beat. "It kept the lights on for sixty people for ninety years. I don't know what I think about it."
fridge.again: "I don't know," she says again, and doesn't like not knowing.

meridian.text: "They count everyone." She says it with something like awe and something like disgust. "Everyone. The dead in the Sink get a number. The lens at the gate looked at me and didn't click." She shrugs. "Story of my life."

wren.text: "She reads walls." Tamsin watches Wren across the fire. "I read people. We're both wrong half the time, which is better than most." Lower: "She has dreams. She won't say what about. I can tell."
wren.again: She is watching Wren, who is pretending not to know.

ilya.text: "He's the only grown-up who looks at me like I could hurt him." She sounds pleased. "Everybody else looks at me like I'm about to break. He counts things under his breath. I counted with him yesterday. Forty-one fence posts. He said right."
ilya.again: "Right," she says, in Ilya's voice, and grins.

ash.speaker: npc_of_03
ash.text: "You'll want to go home before the end, child," Ash says, to the fire. "There's a weight to a door you were born behind. It doesn't come off out here."
ash.again: Ash is looking at the fire, and at her.

ash_tam.text: "Don't call me child." Tamsin doesn't raise her voice. "You took a vow so you'd never have to decide anything again. I climbed out of a hole so I would." Across the fire Ash says nothing at all, which from him is an answer.
ash_tam.again: Neither of them gives an inch.

options.text: He's not wrong about home, Tam.

ash_home.text: "Great. Two of you." She goes to sleep on the far side of the fire with her back to both of you, and in the morning she walks ahead.
ash_home.again: Her back is to both of you.

ash_leave.speaker: npc_of_03
ash_leave.text: "As you say, friend." He bows his head over the fire a little. "She'll learn about doors on her own. Everybody does."
ash_leave.again: Ash has bowed his head over the fire.

ash_none.text: The fire does the talking for a while. Neither of them gives an inch, and neither of them gets up.

nine.text: "Got a mother, fridge?" Tamsin asks Nine across the fire, with her chin on her knees.
nine.again: She is waiting for the fridge to answer.

nine2.speaker: npc_md_nine

nine_go.text: "At its desk." She looks at Nine like a riddle with the wrong answer in it. "Fine, fridge. I'll come and be read to." Nine says, "Thank you," and nobody at the fire knows what to do with that.
nine_go.again: Nobody knows what to do with it still.

nine_leave.text: "Deciding for me again." She says it lightly. It isn't light. Nine's lens stays on her a long while after she has stopped looking at it.
nine_leave.again: The lens is still on her.

walks.text: "I'm going back to Shale." She already has the pack on. "Nell's got a cot. Mags'll give me work. I came out to matter somewhere, and I don't matter here, so." She doesn't make a speech of it. She just goes down the road without looking back, which she learned from you.
walks.again: She is gone down the road.

decision.text: Tamsin left the road and went back to Mags's in Shale.

home_walk.text: "I'm going home." She says it to the road, not to you. "Back through the hatch, if the fridge will have me. I came out for one person." She doesn't finish it. She doesn't need to.
home_walk.again: She is gone up the road toward Knock.

decision.text: Tamsin went home to the Cistern. She came out for one person, she said.

left.text: "Oh. It's you." Tamsin, behind Mags's bar with Nell, wiping a glass that is already clean.
left.again: She wipes the clean glass again.

she told you the thing she tells nobody

back.text: "All of it?" She puts the glass down. "That's a lot of wrong." But she is already reaching under the bar for the pack. "Don't make me regret it. I've got a list."

decision.text: You asked Tamsin back, at Mags's bar, and she came.

back_no.text: "You're sorry I left. That's not the same thing." She picks up another clean glass.
back_no.again: She picks up another clean glass.

broken.text: "Not you," Tamsin says, without looking up from the bar. "Not now."

text.text: Tamsin, behind Mags's bar, wiping a glass that is already clean. She knows you are there; she knew from the door. "They came up the track with it," she says, without looking up. "The Cistern's door, open, and the car, and your name on the foot of the paper." She puts the glass down. "I'm not asking you why. I don't want to know what it sounds like when you say it."

"You said carry on." Tamsin does not look round. "And then you didn't. I know. I was there, I was in the door, I heard you not say it." She is quiet a moment. "It doesn't go back in, though, does it. The first thing you said. I heard that too."
"Don't." Tamsin does not look round. "Whatever it is. Don't."

intro.text: There you are. I've been sitting on the clinic stairs for an hour like a dog waiting for its supper. Is it true? Is it you in the picture?
intro.again: Still here. Still on the stairs. Go on, then.

photo.text: She takes it like it might bite. "That's your nose. That's your stupid ear." A long look. "Older, though. Tired. And you're standing like Ines stands — like somebody who gives orders. Where are you going to learn to stand like that?" She hands it back too quickly.

scared.text: Of the outside? Terrified. Of staying in here until I'm Ines's age, counting algae and saying thank you to a machine? Worse.

text.text: Ines told me I'm going alone. I'm not, though, am I? You're here. You came.
Not without me, you're not.

options.text: Stay. I need someone inside I trust — someone who'll tell me the truth when I write.

come.text: She's grinning before you finish. "I packed this morning. Don't look at me like that — you'd have asked."

decision.text: Tamsin came with you.

stay_ok.text: She hates it; you can see her hate it. "Fine. I'll be your eyes. And if you don't write, I'm coming after you anyway." She hugs you hard enough to hurt.

decision.text: Tamsin stayed in the Cistern as your eyes inside.

stay_hurt.text: "Too dangerous for me. Right." She stands. "You sound like Ines." She doesn't look back.

decision.text: You told Tamsin to stay behind. She took it badly.

text.text: Well? The door isn't going to open itself. Well — Bram might.
Write, {name}. I mean it.

Ash has been looking at the hatch all evening, across the dark apron, the way he looks at a grave before he digs it. "Tamsin," he says to the fire. Not child; he has learned that much. "You were born behind that. So were sixty more, and not one of them has ever stood under a sky." He turns his cup. "My brothers are camped out past the apron. They've their own idea about that door. They're wrong about most of it." He looks at her. "They're not wrong about the sky. Open it. Let them out under something that doesn't keep books."

"If they open it, I'll hold it for them. If they don't, I'll stand in it. That's what a door's for. I found out from the wrong side."

"Open it." Tamsin doesn't raise her voice. "Everybody's told me to go home my whole life. Now you want everybody out." She is looking at the hatch too. "It's their door.
