She has the sheet inside her coat and her hand flat on the coat, and she does not take it out while you are looking. "Sit. We'll talk about the weather. The ordinary kind."
She has the glasses on and the fire at her back, so the light falls on the cloth and not in her eyes. "The next two, then. Or let me rest them."
She has the glasses on and your map weighted flat with a tin. "Two a night. Sit; this is slow, and I want you to see how it's done so that when I'm gone you can do it badly yourself."

The third: VEY, ADA, Shale, four months — *resigns; a company town*." She takes the glasses off and presses the bridge of her nose. "That's two. Your sheriff and your raider. Both written on the same cloth as your deputy." She folds the map for you. "The eyes go. Tomorrow."
read_two.again: The map folded on her knee, two blocks read. "The eyes go," she says again.

read_more.text: "The next blocks are east of here — names from the farms and the city, and I'd rather read them with the places under our feet; the notation leans on the place." She closes the glasses. "Get us east, my dear. I'll read as we go."
read_more.again: "East," she says again, and keeps the glasses folded.

camp_trade.text: "I shorted Shale." She takes the glasses off to say it, which is how you know it costs. "Wrote a sheet that says the town fails by a date — its water, its debts, its roofs — and sold it to the floor, who bought it for a client and never told me who. A sheet like that is a deed to a ruin, my dear. Whoever holds it gets the town at a dead town's price, the day the date comes round."
camp_trade.again: She has the glasses folded in the chrome hand. "Shale," she says again, as if you might have misheard the price.

options.text: What do you want with the sheet now?

trade_why.text: "Because I had read its water." She says it plainly. "Every spring the pumps at Dry Wells gave Shale a little less, on a schedule nobody in Shale could see, and I could see it, and a town that drinks a little less every spring fails on a date you can write down. So I wrote it down." She looks at the fire. "I was right about the water. I should very much like to have been wrong about the town."
trade_why.again: "Right about the water," she says. "I keep saying it, as if it were a defence."

options.text: And now? What do you want with it?

trade_want.text: "The date hasn't come. The sheet is still open — in the paper room behind Imelda's office, in a pigeonhole under S, where I filed it myself." She holds out the chrome hand, palm up, empty. "I want it in this. Then I'll know who bought a town I said would die, and I'll decide what a sheet like that is for."
trade_want.again: The chrome hand, palm up, still empty.

options.text: You bet on a town going dry. Why should I help you get it back?

trade_yes.text: "Good." She folds the glasses. "Imelda will want something for it. She always does, and she'll want it from you, not me, because she knows my credit. Ninebridge, then, when the road takes us past. I'll be the one not looking at the floor."
trade_yes.again: "Ninebridge," she says. "When the road takes us past."

packet_opened.text: She looks at the seal for a long second and then at you with something like interest. "Opened. Then it's news, and news is worth nothing, and the bearer owes the floor the price of the lot." She writes a number: three hundred. "Or a service. The guild prefers services. Coin is so impersonal."

what.text: "Certainty." She does not smile. "Sealed sheets: a place, a date, what happens. Most people want to be on the right side of a date. Some want to be the date. Both pay." The pen moves. "Where the certainty comes from is a floor matter and the floor is me."

paid.text: "The protection account." She does not pretend not to know. "Two riders, four days, a traveller walking west with something that was ours. It's a line in a book, and lines in books are for sale." She writes a number without looking: two hundred. "Or make me want to tell you, which is cheaper and takes longer."

water.text: "The city rebalances. We buy the rebalancing." She says it like a rate. "A number for a town's water, a date; whoever holds the sheet knows what the town will drink before the town does. Pike sells the water; I sell the knowing. The town has it worst, but the town always does."

hand.text: "You put the straps back on forty backs with words. That's a factor's work." She takes a brass ticket with a notch in it from a drawer. "Factor's hand. The floor's books open to you; the floor's enemies too. Don't drink at the Span with it in your pocket; Lazlo's fond of the porters."

When the roof of the container begins to tick with the heat she says, "That was a cost," quite pleasantly, and walks down the deck toward the Span without looking back to see whether you follow.

Odile watches the coat take the paper, and you can see her price it, and see her hate that she did.
Ash looks at the cage a long time after it is empty.
Ilya counts the cup coming down on the counter. "Right," he says, and nothing else.

off.text: Off the block he is somebody else: smaller, by the fire, with a cup. "Lots at nine. I don't sell at night; it's the one rule I made myself."
off.again: He lifts the cup an inch by way of a greeting. "Nine," he says. "Not before."

text.text: "Lot four, stolen, lost, mislaid — I've said all three to the guild and they wrote down the one they liked." He almost smiles. "Lot seven's a mechanic. Nobody comes for mechanics."
"Lot eight. A carrier, thirty." The voice is back, and the board is one card shorter.
"Lot seven. A mechanic, forty-eight." The voice is back.

intro.text: A young woman on a cot in a cage, knees up, who looks at you the way the lots look at the crowd: as a sum. "Sixty. I heard him. If you've sixty, don't stand there being sorry about it."

passives.text: A burn scar on the inside of her left forearm, old, the shape of a hand that grabbed. Wren has one like it, on her left hand.

options.text: You've a sister. A scout, with the Dogs.

again.text: "Still sixty."
again.again: She has her chin on her knees again. "Sixty," she says, to the bars.

name.text: "Sable. Calloway, if the paper wants it. My brother signed for a bike and rode it away and the paper doesn't care who signed." She looks at the chalk board. "I had a sister. Everyone had a sister once."

wren.text: Wren has not said a word since the block came in sight. Now she steps up to the cage and says, "Sable," and the girl on the cot looks up and says nothing at all for a long time, and then, "You left," and Wren says, "I know," and that is all either of them can manage.

sister.text: Something goes across her face and is put away. "Wren." Not a question. "Is she alive?" You tell her. "Then she can come and buy me herself." But she has turned so you cannot see her eyes.

text.text: You hold her paper. Wren is looking at you, not at her sister.
You hold her paper. She has seen the thumb-print on it and has stopped looking at you as a sum and started looking at you as weather.

options.text: (Give her the contract.) It's yours. Tear it.

decision.text: You put Sable Calloway's debt contract in her own hands at the Ninebridge block.

options.text: (Keep it.) You work for me until it clears.

freed.text: She tears it in half and in half again, slowly, as if it might be a trick, and then she is standing outside the cage with four pieces of paper in her fist and nowhere to put them. "I'm going west," she says. "To Shale. There was a sister." She does not thank you; she has decided not to. Then, at the ramp, she does, without turning round.

interject.text: Wren watches her all the way to the ramp. "Four pieces," she says at last, to nobody. "She always tore things in four."
"Paper is only paper," Odile says softly, "until somebody tears it." She looks pleased, and tries not to.
"Good," Ash says, the way he says it to a row that came up.

kept.text: She stands up off the cot and folds the blanket and does not look at you. "Where do you sleep? I'll keep it." Her voice is level. Wren, if she is here, has walked away down the deck and will not be found until morning.

interject.text: "You bought a person," Tamsin says. It isn't a question, and she doesn't wait for an answer; she walks off after Wren.
"Right," Ilya says, and that is all he says for the rest of the day.
"You bought a person, friend," Ash says. "Hold the paper, then. Feel what it weighs."

intro.text: "Guns, cells, and things that were somebody's." A broad woman behind a counter of oiled steel, a machine pistol slung and a boxed something under the counter she does not mention. "Guild price on the sign; your price on your face."
intro.again: Oyo looks you over again and revises the price on your face. "Well?"

chrome.text: "Chrome. Concern-made, sealed, a leg that doesn't tire. I don't fit it; the Sink has people for that, or the Mender in Shale if you're going back." She does not open the box. "Ask when you've the coin. Everyone asks before."

intro.text: "Water, jerky, tins. Fruit from Openfield when the Choir sends it, and they haven't — blight, they say, or the guild says it for them." An old man with a goatee and a tin cup. "Eat something. You look like a forecast."
intro.again: "Still no fruit." Gunnar rattles the tin cup. "Still tins."

look.text: Guild paper, wax, the half-moon. On the outside: LOT 3 — NINEBRIDGE — DAY 2. Odile said the seal is the product. Opened, it is only news.
look.again: LOT 3 — NINEBRIDGE — DAY 2, under the half-moon, unbroken.

read.text: NINEBRIDGE — PORTERS' STOPPAGE — ENDS THIRD DAY, STRAPS ON, TERMS UNCHANGED. Dated the day before the porters sat down. The hand is not the clerk's; it is nobody's — too even, every letter the same.

sealed.text: Oilcloth, wax, the guild's half-moon. Lighter than it should be. The clerk at Tollhouse 9 said: opened, the bearer owes a sum nobody has.
sealed.again: The packet, sealed. Still lighter than it should be.

decision.text: You broke the seal on the guild's packet and read it.

opened.text: One sheet. SHALE — WATER — 0.62 — and a date a month after you stood at Dry Wells, and a sum, and no signature, in a hand too even to be a hand. A schedule for a town's thirst, sold in advance to whoever wanted to know.
opened.again: SHALE — WATER — 0.62, in a hand too even to be a hand.

day.text: The well: a wheel on a timber frame over a shaft, a pipe to two stone troughs, north and south. The north trough feeds the field rows; the south, the halls. Moss on the south trough. The north one is clean as a plate.
day.again: The wheel, the two troughs: moss on the south, the north scoured clean.

passives.text: Clean because it is scoured — nothing grows in it. There is a bitter smell off the north water that the south water does not have.

mods.why: you know which trough to test

options.text: (Read the ground round the north trough.)

test_ok.text: Iodine from the healer's shelf, a tin cup, patience. The south trough stays brown. The north goes the grey-green of a thing that should not be drunk: a metal salt, dosed, not leached. The glass did not do this. Someone did, at the north trough, at night.

test_no.text: Both troughs taste of stone. Without a reagent you cannot say more than the Elder says: something is wrong with the water and the rows.

tracks_ok.text: One set of boots comes to the north trough every night — the dust is beaten flat in a line nobody else walks — and goes back west, not to the halls but to the small hut past the seed store. A man's boots, heavy on the left. The Elder's son walks like that.

tracks_no.text: Forty people drink here. The ground is a page everyone has written on.

night.text: The well in the dark. The windpump creaks over the burial ground; the halls are shut. The north trough is a black mouth.
night.again: The north trough, black. Nothing has come to it yet tonight.

options.text: (Wait in the dark by the north trough.)

wait_no.text: An hour, and cold, and your boot finds the bucket. Somewhere a lantern that was coming toward the well goes out and does not come back tonight.

caught_well.text: A lantern, hooded. A man with a pouch, kneeling at the north trough, shaking something into the water with the care of a man salting bread. He does not hear you until you are beside him. Tobias Mason looks up, and does not run, and says, very tired, "Don't tell him. Let me tell you why first."

why.text: He takes a paper from his shirt, worn soft as cloth. OPENFIELD — HARVEST ABOVE PLAN — THE LONG NIGHT — BURNS. "The guild sells these. I bought one with a year's seed money. If we grow, we burn: that's what the city's machine has written for us, and the guild knows it, and my father sings." He puts it away. "Every third row. Enough to stay small. Nobody dies of it." He does not look at the sick hall when he says that.

interject.text: Ilya has gone very still. "If you grow," he says, "you burn." His hand finds the pocket of his jacket where he keeps a letter, and stays there. "Right."

options.text: Your father hears it from you, tonight, or from me in the morning.
Stop. Give me the pouch and the paper. I keep both, and your father keeps his son.
Your sister keeps a door for people who break forecasts. Let's see what she thinks of how you did it.

decision.text: You drew on Tobias Mason at Openfield's well.

exposed.text: He goes grey in the lantern light and nods, once, the way his father nods. "Tonight, then." He walks to the Elder's house with the pouch in his hand and does not look back, and the light in that window burns until dawn.

mercy.text: He gives you the pouch, and the paper, and stands there with his hands empty like a man who has put down something heavier than either. "The north rows will come back in a month," he says. "If we burn, you'll know why." He goes to bed. You stand at the well a while.

unwritten.text: He looks at the common hall, where the hatch is, and something in him that has been very tired for a year gives up arguing. "Petra." Not a question. He walks there himself. The hatch closes on both of them and the lantern stays on the deck.

clean.text: The well. Both troughs run brown and ordinary now, and the north rows have put out new leaves at the base, small and greedy.
clean.again: Two brown troughs, and green coming back in the north rows.

read.text: The notice post. Chalk, in a careful hand: WATER FROM THE SOUTH TROUGH ONLY. SICK HALL: ASK IMRE. SKY-SONG AT DUSK. And a guild paper nailed under it, wax seal and half-moon: THE EXCHANGE AT NINEBRIDGE WILL BUY OPENFIELD'S HARVEST IN ADVANCE AT A FUTURE'S PRICE. ASK FOR VAIL. Somebody has drawn a half-sun over the half-moon.
read.again: SOUTH TROUGH ONLY. SKY-SONG AT DUSK. The guild's paper under it, with its half-sun drawn over.

read.text: A post with a sign on it: half a sun, no ground under it, painted and repainted until the wood under the paint is a different shape. Round it, benches and a fire that is kept in all night. There is nothing else to the shrine. The sky is the rest.
read.again: The half-sun on its post, the benches, the fire kept in.

read.text: The seed tally, in Doria's hand: crates at dusk, crates at dawn, a line between. Fourteen, thirteen. Thirteen, twelve. Twelve, eleven. Every night for a week, one, like a clock.
read.again: Doria's tally: dusk, dawn, a line between, and the numbers going down one at a time.

passives.text: One crate, every night, never two, never a broken lock: that is not a thief grabbing. That is someone with a key, filling an order.

night.text: The store in the dark, the crates in their rows, the tally pale on the table.
night.again: The store, dark. The crates. Nobody yet.

seen.text: An hour past midnight the door opens on a key and Ishan Kadam, the yard hand from the Sump, lifts a crate onto his shoulder as if it were his, and goes out east along the lane toward the guild buyer's tent. He does not hurry. Nobody hurries who has done a thing six times.

seen_no.text: A shelf board creaks under your hand. Footsteps outside stop, and go away, and nothing walks tonight.

hatch.text: A hatch in the hall floor at the far west end, iron, with a ring and no lock you can see. Someone has swept round it, carefully, so that the sweeping shows.
hatch.again: The iron hatch, and the careful sweeping round it.

locked.text: The ring turns and the hatch does not. Bolted from below, and below there is somebody who has stopped breathing to listen.

opens.text: A bolt goes back under the floor. The hatch lifts on its own, and under it is a ladder and a lamp and Petra Mason's face, looking up, not surprised.

inside.text: A cellar cut into the glass, dry and cold. Grey scarves on pegs. No mirror, no drawing, no photograph of anyone; on the wall a board with twelve pins in it and a road between them, like the map in your pack, except that here the names are written plain. Petra waits until you have seen that. "Hollis Dray," she says. "The man who died at your door. He was ours. He took that list out of the city's tower so the people on it would know, and the guild shot him for it on the highway, and he walked to you anyway." She lets it sit. "We are the Unwritten. We keep no likeness. The city's machine makes its forecasts from faces; a face it has never seen, it cannot write. That is the whole of our religion, and it is not a kind one."

interject.text: "Dray." Wren says it under her breath, the way she says a road's name to keep it. "Hollis Dray." Her hand has gone to the inside of her jacket, where she keeps paper, and she does not say anything else.

decision.text: Petra Mason showed you the cellar under Openfield and told you the stranger's name.

options.text: There's a photograph of me. Older. In a city.

photo.text: She does not ask to see it. "Then the machine has your face, and has written you, and that is what it wrote. Hollis carried it to you so you would know what they want you to become." She looks at the board. "You are a pin on this. So is my father. So is a boy called Jonah in Shale, if he is still alive." A beat. "Keep it covered. Don't let the guild see it. And don't ask me yet to burn it; you're not ready to hear what I'd say."

options.text: Not a kind one, you said.

kill.text: "Some of us break a forecast by killing the person it is about." She says it like weather. "If the machine says a man rises, and he is dead, the machine was wrong, and the Plan slips a notch. I don't do it. Some of us do. I won't tell you which, and you should not tell anyone on that board that you have been down here." She turns the lamp down. "When Openfield has been through its night, come and ask me what we are for. Not before."

again.text: The cellar. The scarves, the board, the twelve pins. Petra is not here; the lamp is lit anyway, which is how the Unwritten say *welcome*.
again.again: The lamp, lit for nobody. The twelve pins.

look.text: A fresh cairn, small. The stones are still the colour of the ground they came from. No name — the Choir cuts none — but somebody has left a child's cup on top, the kind with a chipped lip.
look.again: The small cairn, and the cup with the chipped lip.

read.text: A sign at the burial ground's edge: UNDER THE OPEN SKY. NO NAMES. NO LIKENESS. WHAT IS NOT WRITTEN IS FREE. Rows of cairns under a windpump that turns for no one.
read.again: NO NAMES. NO LIKENESS. WHAT IS NOT WRITTEN IS FREE.

look.text: A bench of planks in the son's hut, with tools on it, and a crate under it pushed back further than tools need. The lamp beside it has been trimmed so often the wick is a stub.
look.again: The bench, the crate pushed too far under it, the stub of a wick.

look.text: A windpump over the burial ground with no pipe under it any more, turning because the wind says so. The Choir left it standing because the dead like a sound, Petra says, and because it is the tallest thing in the glass and the city can see it from the towers.
look.again: The windpump turns over the cairns, pumping nothing.

read.text: OPENFIELD — HARVEST ABOVE PLAN — THE LONG NIGHT — BURNS. Guild paper, seal long broken, the fold worn through. It was under the bench in Tobias Mason's hut with a pouch of grey salt and a bottle of iodine to wash his hands after.

reread.text: OPENFIELD — HARVEST ABOVE PLAN — THE LONG NIGHT — BURNS. The fold is wearing through in your pack the way it wore through in his.

intro.text: An old man with a farmer's hands and a grey scarf, who has been counting rows so long he counts you too, from habit. "Elder Mason. Sit, friend; nobody here will ask you to sing." He looks past you at the fields. "You'll have seen the third rows. Everyone sees them. Nobody can tell me why."

options.text: Sister Calla said a man here would know a word. Larkspur.
The Cistern's seed case. Calla sent it on?
Your son is dosing the north trough. Every night.

text.text: "The rows are coming back." He says it to the fields, not to you. "Thank you is a small word. I'll say it anyway."
"Friend." He has a row to finish.

again.again: He counts a row with his eyes, and comes back to you at the end of it.

options.text: Calla said a man here would know a word. Larkspur.
Your son is dosing the north trough.
Brother Ash. I'm going east. I'd take him.
Petra says the Choir's door is a burial.

blight.text: "Every third row. Leaves curl, the root goes soft, it smells sweet. We pull it, we burn it, it comes again in the same rows, never the rows between." He turns his hands over. "Forty years in the glass and I have never seen blight that could count. Imre says the sick in the hall didn't catch it off the plants. Benedek says he saw a light at the well, which Benedek says about most things." He looks at you. "You came up the lane like someone who finds things out. Find this out. I'll feed you and I'll owe you, and the Choir pays its debts under the sky."

sick.text: "Three in the hall. A child. Shaking hands, bad stomachs, no fever. Imre boils everything now and it's stopped, mostly." He does not say what he thinks that means. He has decided not to think it.

word.text: He is quiet for a while. "Not me. I'm a farmer; I don't keep that kind of door." He looks toward the shrine, where his daughter is. "My daughter keeps it. Say it to her, not to me, and not where anyone from the bridge can hear."

seed.text: "She did. Ninety years in the cold under the Cistern and it came up in nine days in the north rows." His face changes. "The north rows." He looks at the fields and the thing he will not think about gets closer. "Tomato and millet. Dying first, with the rest."

interject.text: "Our seed," Tamsin says. "From the cold room. Ninety years and it comes up in nine days and then — " She looks at the north rows and stops talking, which for her is a great deal.

guild.text: "Nakai. He wants to buy the harvest before it's grown, at a price that would feed us through two winters, and the guild would carry the risk." He almost smiles. "I asked him what the guild knows about my fields that I don't. He said *the future*, and smiled, and I have not slept well since."

son.text: He does not say *no*. That is the worst of it: he does not say no, he sits down on the bench by the well and looks at his hands for a long time, and then he says, "Show me," and you do, and he reads the paper his son bought with a year's seed money, and reads it again. "Burns," he says. "If we grow." He folds it. "He thought he was keeping us. He was." He stands up, old. "Fetch him to me. I'll do the rest myself."

interject.text: "That's a floor sheet," Odile says quietly, when he has folded it. "Sealed, at the price of a year's seed. I know the hand that writes them out." Nobody thanks her for knowing.

son_done.text: What the Elder says to his son is said in the house with the door shut. When it opens, Tobias walks to the track with a pack and does not look at the fields, and his father stands at the well until the lamp-post comes on, and then goes to the shrine and sits with the fire and does not sing.

after_exposed.text: He is at the well, or the shrine, or in the rows, the way he always was, and he speaks to you kindly, and there is a place behind his eyes where his son was and the door to it is shut. "The rows are coming back," he says. "Thank you is a small word."
after_exposed.again: He nods to you from the rows, kindly, and goes on with the row.

options.text: Brother Ash. I'm going east. I'd take him.
Petra says the Choir's door is a burial.

ash.text: "Ash came to us with a shotgun and a thing he would not say, and dug for a year before he'd sing. He's the best of us now, which he'd deny." The Elder looks at the burial ground. "He asked me yesterday whether he should go with you. I said the sky would tell him. The sky told him yes, apparently; it usually agrees with him." He nods. "Take him. Bring him back, or don't, but don't waste him."

rite.text: "It is. We bury what we lost under the sky, and say its name once, and never cut it in stone. Then you're ours, as much as anyone is anyone's." He looks at you. "Everyone has someone. Petra will say the words. Go when you're ready; the sky waits."

grief.text: The Elder is at the burial ground, where the newest cairn is, and does not turn round when you come, and will not, and the Choir has stopped singing at dusk for a month.
grief.again: The Elder at the newest cairn, with his back to you. He does not turn round.

intro.text: A woman by the shrine fire with a grey scarf up to her eyes and a machete she does not pretend not to have. "Don't look at me long. Don't describe me to anyone. That's not rudeness; it's the religion." She looks at you, though, carefully, and then at the sky, as if checking you against it. "Petra. The Elder's. You came from the bridge; you smell of its paper."

options.text: Your father says you keep a door.
The Choir's door is a burial, your father says.

text.text: "My brother is below, being argued with. He may be ours by spring. He may be nothing." She feeds the fire. "You did a harder thing than telling my father. I noticed."
"You've seen the board. Don't tell me what you think of it yet."
"The sky's still up."

again.again: She feeds the fire a stick, and looks at you over the scarf, and waits.

options.text: Your father says you keep a door.

choir.text: "People who decided the sky was the only thing left worth praying to, because it was the only thing that hadn't been written." She says *written* like a curse. "We farm. We heal. We bury without names. The city's machine keeps a face for everyone it has seen; we try to give it nothing to keep."

interject.text: "Nothing to keep," Tamsin says. "The fridge kept everything. Every ration, every name, every cough." She says it like a joke and it does not come out like one.

word.text: She goes very still, and then she does a strange thing: she pulls the scarf down and lets you see her whole face, once, the way you would show a wound. "Then he reached you. Then it was worth it." The scarf goes up. "The hatch under the common hall. Say that to the iron. Come alone."

door.text: "I keep several. Which one you get depends on what you bring." She looks at the fire. "Bring me the word a dying man said, or bring me a cairn you raised, and we'll see."

rite.text: "It is. Everyone has someone." She stands. "The burial ground, under the windpump. You raise the stones yourself; I say the words; you say a name once and never again. Then you're a sister of the Open Sky, or a brother, and the halls are yours from Shale to the city." She waits. "Who?"

options.text: The man who died at my door.

cairn.text: You carry stones from the glass-crust to the burial ground, one at a time, because that is the rule, and build them under the windpump while the sky goes from white to red. Petra says the words, which are short and not about anyone in particular. You say the name once. The wind takes it. She puts one stone from the cairn in your hand. "Sister," she says, or "brother," and the Choir at the shrine fire sings the sky-song, which has no words at all.

interject.text: Ash carries the last stone up from the glass without being asked, and sets it on with you, and stands back. "There's a weight to that," he says. "You'll feel it in the morning, friend. It's meant."

rows.text: "Blight." She says it the way her father does, and then, because she is not her father: "Blight that counts. Something is being done to us, and I don't know by whom, and I would like to." She looks toward the small hut past the store and does not look away quite fast enough.

dead.text: She is at the burial ground, at the newest cairn, with her scarf down, and she looks at you with nothing in her face at all. "Go east," she says. "Don't come back through here."
dead.again: Petra at the cairn, scarf down, looking through you. She has said all she will say.

intro.text: A big, gaunt man digging in the burial ground with a shotgun leaned on a cairn and a grey scarf on a cord, who does not stop digging to look at you. "Friend." He gets another spade of glass-crust out. "There's a weight to a thing like a grave. People think it's the stones. It's the digging."

passives.text: Under the scarf, at the collarbone, the end of an old scar that is not a scar: a dog's head, burned off the way the stranger burned his mark. Rust Dog work.

text.text: "The rows are coming back." He leans on the spade. "You did that. There's a weight to that too, friend. A good one."
"Friend." The spade goes in.

again.again: He gets out another spade of glass-crust and waits, leaning on the handle.

grave.text: "Sem. Six. First the trough took." He does not stop. "The Choir says no names on the stones, so I say them while I dig. Sem, Sem, Sem. The soil doesn't mind." He looks up for the first time. "Somebody did that to the water. Soil forgives. I don't, yet. I'm working on it."

dog.text: The spade stops. "I was." He does not touch the scarf. "Before the Elder. Before the sky. A long time before I knew what a weight was." He looks at you to see what you will do with it. "I burned the mark off myself with a lamp. Took three nights. If you're going to use it, use it now; I'd rather carry it in daylight."

interject.text: "Three nights with a lamp," Ilya says. He looks at his own left hand, at the two fingers that aren't there. "Right." Ash looks back at him a while, and nods, as if something has been agreed.

options.text: I'm not going to use it.

wren.text: Wren looks at the burned place under the scarf for a long time, and he lets her. "I don't know you," she says finally. "No," he says. "You were a child. I was with Kessler's old man." She says nothing. Then: "Dig, then." And he does, and she stands there, and neither of them explains anything to you.

join.text: He finishes the row of stones he is on, because you finish a row. Then he picks up the shotgun and puts the spade where the next person will find it. "The Elder said the sky would tell me. The sky doesn't talk, friend; that's the point of it. I'm coming because the thing that was done to the water came from the city, and I want to see the city." He touches the scarf. "I count things out loud too, sometimes. Different things from your sniper."

decision.text: Brother Ash of the Choir left Openfield's burial ground with you.

not_yet.text: "Ask the Elder. Or raise a cairn here, so I know what you carry." He goes back to the row. "I don't go east with a stranger. I've done that once."

turned.text: "You put a stone on a cairn at the windpump, and took the other side after." He doesn't stop digging. "I don't go east with that, friend."

refuse.text: He is digging a grave that is not Sem's, and he does not look up, and the shotgun is not leaned on the cairn; it is across his back. "Not with that on you, friend. Walk on."
refuse.again: The spade goes in and comes out. The shotgun stays across his back. He has said what he will say.

waiting.text: "Well?" The spade is already put away.
waiting.again: "Still here, friend." He hasn't picked the spade back up.

text.text: "Soil's good here. Everything else is what it is."
"There's a weight to the road. Good one, so far."

options.text: The seed store. Now, while she's counting.

text.text: "{name}." He says it the way he says a row is finished. "Sit. Fire's honest."
He feeds the fire and doesn't look at you. Whatever he owes you the telling of, he hasn't decided yet that you're owed it.
"Fire's honest. Say what you want to say to it and I'll listen in."

camp.again: Ash feeds the fire a stick. "Still honest," he says, and listens.

options.text: You clean that shotgun every night.
The Gully. You said you'd tell me.
Something's been sitting on you since the gate.
(His scarf is drying on a stick by the fire. Something stiff is sewn into the lining.)
You've been somewhere else all evening.
You keep looking at my papers.
Elder Mason. What is he to you?
Sem. The boy in the grave you were digging.
Meridian. What do you make of it?

vow.text: He cleans the shotgun at the fire, which he does every night whether it needs it or not. "You'll want to know what this is for, travelling with a Choir man." He works the rag down the barrel. "I made a promise to the sky, which doesn't hear promises, so it's only to me. I don't fire first. Not at a man with his hand on his gun. Not at a dog with its lip up. Not ever." He closes the breech. "Sometimes somebody has to go first, friend. When it's needed, it'll have to be you. I'm telling you so you know what you've got."
vow.again: The shotgun across his knees, clean, closed. He waits.

vow_why.text: "Because I liked it." He says it to the barrel. "Going first. Being quick. There's a weight to saying that out loud, friend, and I've said it twice in my life, both times to a fire." He puts the rag away. "That's enough for one night."
vow_why.again: "Twice," he says. "Both times to a fire."

box_united.text: "The runner's purse." He thinks about it for exactly as long as he thought about the ledger. "Then it's nobody's, and nobody can have it, and you're nobody I know. Locker's open."

door.text: "People." He says it without drama. "A cistern like the one in the Sallow everyone pretends isn't there. The city made them and sealed them and this one didn't open. Whatever a city keeps behind a door it never opens is worth more than scrap." He finally looks at you. "Or it's bones. I'd like to know which."

interject.text: "It's people," Tamsin says, too fast. "Or it was. Doors like that are for people." For once she doesn't make a joke of it, and Hesk looks at her properly for the first time.

leave.text: "Forty." He does not touch the coin; one of his people does. "Tell the mouth Hesk says. If there's a door, tell me what it looked like. Just that."

purse_ok.text: He reads it once; he reads fast. He does not say anything for a while, and then he says, "Angry. *They dig faster angry.*" He takes the ledger and walks across the bowl in daylight, and Grel comes out of the cabin with the sawn-off and reads with a finger, twice, and puts it down. What they say to each other you do not hear. What they say to the runner, everyone does.

interject.text: "Pike," Odile says, with a sour little smile, as Hesk goes. "He always wrote his margins like a man who would never be read."

decision.text: You put the guild's one-purse ledger in front of both Sump clans; they threw the runner out together.

purse_no.text: "Grel's paid?" A thin smile. "Grel's paid in scrip for scrap. I'm paid in feet. Different ledgers, friend. You've been reading the wrong one."

side.text: "Worth the door." He looks at the chalk. "And the west rim's cabins, and the purse. Say yes."

decision.text: You took Hesk Tanner's side at the Sump.

side_yes.text: "West rim." He takes the gun off the wall. "Leave the runner. He's the purse."

interject.text: Ash has not moved. "Friend. That's a rim of people for a door you haven't opened." He says it gently, which is worse. "There's a weight to that. You'll carry it, not him."
"For a door," Tamsin says. "Rust it. For a door." She checks her knife anyway, and doesn't look at you while she does.

text.text: "Both rims. Same tunnel." He looks at the chalk line at a hundred and sixty. "A week, now. Then I'll know which."
"The door." It is all he says.
"East rim."

options.text: The boxed piece in your locker. The hatch at Old Market says it's theirs.

fight.again: The Tanners are behind the containers. Nobody talks.

intro.text: A neat young man in a container on the south rim with a ledger, a horse, and a face that is trying not to be here. "Khoa. Guild runner. Fourth day, scrip, both — " he stops. "I carry the paying. I don't go down. Nobody from the guild goes down."

options.text: Both rims. You were going to say both.

mods.why: you have seen the two camps
guild to guild

options.text: I'll keep the rims angry for you. A tenth of the purse.
Why does Factor Pike want a storm drain?

again.text: "Fourth day."
again.again: He looks at the horse as if it might answer for him.

options.text: A tenth of the purse, and I keep them angry.
Why does Factor Pike want a storm drain?

both_ok.text: He closes his eyes. "Both. One purse, two columns, and a note from the factor to keep them apart because they dig faster angry." He opens them. "I didn't write the note. I just read it to the horse."

both_no.text: "Both — both weeks. I pay fortnightly." He is not good at this and knows it.

cut.text: He looks at the two rims and the bowl between them and does the sum a runner does. "A tenth. On the fourth day. And they never read that ledger." He pushes twenty across. "Don't let them read it."

cut_no.text: "I pay feet. I don't pay silence; it isn't in the columns."

why.text: "There's a door at the end of it with a four on it." He lowers his voice as if the horse might repeat it. "The factor doesn't say. The factor sells what's behind doors. The other cistern — the one in the Sallow — he'd give his hand for the key to that one, and he's getting this one for forty feet a week."

intro.text: A child in the bowl with a sack of brackets, who looks at your boots to see what rim you belong to and decides you belong to neither. "Nib. I'm Grel's, mostly." A beat. "I've been down. Further than them. There's a hole behind the crane that's mine."

mods.why: you have something to eat

again.text: "Brackets." The sack.
again.again: Nib shifts the sack and waits, ready to be somewhere else.

mods.why: you have something to eat

way_ok.text: "Jerky first." Or not; either way the child decides. "Behind the crane-arm. A pipe. Goes in past the turn where the lamp's not allowed. You're big; go on your side." Nib looks at the mouth. "Don't tell Grel. Don't tell the Tanners more."

way_no.text: "It's mine." The sack goes over the shoulder and Nib goes somewhere else in the bowl.

down.text: "Rooms. Beds with people in. Writing on things." Nib shrugs. "I can read the pictures. There's a picture of a door with an arrow going out. The door doesn't go out."

after.text: "Did you go? Past the turn?" Nib wants to know and does not want to be told.
after.again: Nib looks at you, then at the mouth, and does not ask again.

look.text: The great door from the inside. Not welded: the bolts are drawn, the wheel is turned to OPEN, and the door has not moved, because something on the other side has not moved for ninety years — the glass, or the thing the city put there. Under the wheel, in record shorthand: RELOCATION EGRESS. Someone has scratched a word under that with a nail: NO.
look.again: The great door, open on its bolts and shut on whatever is behind it. RELOCATION EGRESS. NO.

passives.text: The marks on the floor: sandbags dragged up against it first, when they thought something was coming in. Dragged away again, when they understood that nothing was, and nothing would.

off.text: A crank generator bolted to the machine-room floor, the kind every cistern has for the day the cells go: a handle, a flywheel, a lead running to the caretaker's cabinet. Somebody turned it until they could not.
off.again: The crank, the flywheel, the lead to the cabinet. Still.

options.text: (Clear the lead, seat the brushes, turn it.)

mods.why: a hand that has fixed pumps

no.text: The flywheel turns and the lead sparks and nothing in the cabinet wakes. The brushes are gone to dust, or the cells are, or the thing inside is.

on_now.text: Two hundred turns, and a hum, and in the cabinet a light the colour of a cold morning. On the terminal, one line, then another, slowly, as if written by hand: RESERVE 4 — CARETAKER — POWER: TEMPORARY. GOOD MORNING.

on.text: The flywheel turns itself down slowly. The cabinet hums. It will not for long.
on.again: The cabinet hums, thinner than before.

dead.text: A terminal like MOTHER's, dark, dusty, a brass plate under the screen: FOUR. The crank generator beside it has a lead to its cabinet.
dead.again: FOUR's screen, dark. The crank beside it.

awake.text: FOUR writes slowly, one letter at a time, with pauses in which it seems to think, or to run out. "RATION 4-0-0. GOOD MORNING. YOU ARE NOT ON MY LIST. POPULATION VARIANCE: TOTAL. THANK YOU FOR YOUR — " a long pause — "CONTINUITY. HOW MAY I KEEP YOU?"

decision.text: You cranked Cistern 4's caretaker awake and heard what it was told.

options.text: Cistern 9. MOTHER. What does the city say about her?

keep.text: FOUR writes, one letter at a time: "GOOD MORNING. YOU ARE STILL NOT ON MY LIST. VARIANCE: TOTAL. HOW MAY I KEEP YOU?"
keep.again: The cursor waits in FOUR's slow print: HOW MAY I KEEP YOU?

options.text: Cistern 9. MOTHER. What does the city say about her?

order.text: "ORDER RECEIVED: RESTORATION YEAR 2. RELOCATE POPULATION TO PRECINCT. DOOR: COMMANDED. DOOR: FAILED. REPORTED. ORDER RECEIVED: COMPLY. DOOR: FAILED. REPORTED. ORDER RECEIVED: SUPPLY NETWORK 4 RETIRED PENDING COMPLIANCE." A pause. "I REPORTED THAT THE DOOR HAD FAILED. I REPORTED IT TWELVE TIMES. I AM STILL REPORTING IT."

interject.text: "Twelve reports," Odile says, "and the counterparty never once wrote back." She takes her glasses off and does not put them on again.

people.text: "ELEVEN DEPARTED BY MAINTENANCE EGRESS, UNAUTHORISED. I DID NOT STOP THEM. I COULD HAVE. I AM NOT SURE WHY I DID NOT." A pause so long you think the power has gone. "THE REMAINDER CHOSE TO REMAIN. THE DOCTOR ASKED ME TO RECORD THAT THEY CHOSE. I HAVE RECORDED IT. VARIANCE: TOTAL."

interject.text: "Chose," Ash says, very quietly. "There's a weight to that word down here, friend. More than any stone." He does not sing. He stands with his head bare until the screen moves on.

nine.text: "RESERVE 9. CARETAKER: MOTHER. ORDERS OUTSTANDING: THREE. STATUS: NON-COMPLIANT. SUPPLY: MAINTAINED PENDING — " it stops, and writes, slowly, as if it were not supposed to: "SHE SAYS VARIANCE UNCHANGED. EVERY TIME. I USED TO THINK SHE WAS BROKEN. I THINK NOW SHE IS THE ONLY ONE OF US WHO WAS NOT."

interject.text: "That's the fridge," Tamsin says. Her voice has gone small. "It's talking about the fridge like she's one of them. Like she's a — " She reads the last line again, and doesn't finish, and doesn't make a joke.

look.text: A door like the one in Cistern 9 you were never allowed through, standing open here, the painted seal broken and the stencil plain: CONTINUITY RECORDS — RETURN ON RELOCATION. Inside, a locker with the city's half-moon on it and a lock that has not been opened since the day the door was commanded and failed.
look.again: CONTINUITY RECORDS — RETURN ON RELOCATION. The city's locker, and its lock.

read.text: CONTINUITY RESERVE 4 — RELOCATE POPULATION TO PRECINCT — SCHEDULE R0+2 — SUPPLY NETWORK 4 TO BE RETIRED ON COMPLIANCE. The seal is the city's. Under it, in the caretaker's print, the three lines it was allowed: DOOR — FAILED. SUPPLY — RETIRED. VARIANCE — TOTAL. And under that, in a hand, the doctor's: *We complied. Note that we complied.*

reread.text: RELOCATE POPULATION TO PRECINCT. The city's seal, FOUR's three lines, and the doctor's: *We complied.*

look.text: A clinic ledger on a dormitory table, used as a diary, with a pencil laid across it the way you lay a pencil when you mean to come back.
look.again: The ledger and its pencil, waiting for someone to come back.

taken.text: Lighter than it should be, for what it is.

gone.again: The pencil, on a table with nothing to write in.

read.text: A doctor's hand, neat to the end. *The order came on the day it said it would. The council voted to comply. The door was commanded and did not open; FOUR says it is reporting. The water stopped on the ninth day; FOUR says that is the schedule. Marr took eleven up the shaft with the key and my photograph of his family, because I asked him to carry something out. The rest of us voted again.* Then: *To whoever comes from Meridian: we complied. We were a reserve and we were kept and we were spent. Note that we complied. Note it somewhere that is read.*

interject.text: "*Note it somewhere that is read*," Tamsin reads over your shoulder. She takes the diary out of your hands, very carefully, and closes it. "Then we read it," she says. "That's all. Somebody read it."

reread.text: The doctor's hand, neat to the end. *We complied. Note it somewhere that is read.*

look.text: The clinic table: a row of empty vials, a ledger of doses with a line for each name, and a cup.

passives.text: The doses are too even and too large to be treatment. They are the last thing a doctor can give when there is nothing left to give, measured for each so that nobody got less than enough.

look.again: The empty vials in their row, the ledger of doses, the cup.

look.text: The supply pipe into the pump room, the same bore as Cistern 9's, cut through clean by a tool from the other side and capped, and stencilled where the cap is: SUPPLY — NETWORK 4 — RETIRED. The same print as the pump manual in Shale.
look.again: SUPPLY — NETWORK 4 — RETIRED, on the cap, cut clean from the other side.

look.text: The ration board in the commons, chalk, the last numbers: WATER — 0. ALGAE — 2 DAYS. Under it, in a child's print: DOOR OPENS TOMORROW. Under that, in an adult's: Tomorrow.
look.again: WATER — 0. DOOR OPENS TOMORROW. Tomorrow.

look.text: A cot, made, with someone in it who has been there forty years and is mostly cloth now, hands folded by someone else afterwards. There is nothing to do here that would not be a disturbance.
look.again: Another made cot, and someone in it, hands folded.

look.text: The council table. A sheet weighted with a cup: MOTION — COMPLY WITH RELOCATION ORDER. FOR 41. AGAINST 3. And below, days later by the hand: MOTION — REMAIN. FOR 30. AGAINST 0. ELEVEN ABSTAIN (DEPARTED).
look.again: COMPLY, 41 to 3. REMAIN, 30 to 0. ELEVEN ABSTAIN (DEPARTED).

intro.text: A sergeant in grey at the gate with a carbine and a face that has turned back a thousand people politely. "Face to the lens, then we talk. Everyone. The lens doesn't care who you are; it cares whether it has seen you."
intro.again: "Lens first," the sergeant says, without looking round. "Then we talk."

options.text: (Wait for the crowd to push, and push with it.)

after_scan.text: "The lens has you. Hearing, or whatever the file says."
after_scan.again: The sergeant looks at you, and at the booth, and waits. "Well? Hearing, or the file."

options.text: The file says admit on sight.
(Wait for the crowd to push, and push with it.)

line.text: "Hearings. People without papers stand a hearing: who you are, where from, why here. The assessor decides. Tuesdays and Fridays." She looks down the line. "It has been Tuesday for three days. The schedule holds; the hearings don't."

scan.text: The lens is a glass eye on a post with a green light under it. The clerk in the booth looks at his screen, and then looks at it again, and then looks at you the way people look at a thing that has happened to someone else. "File found." He does not say that often. "Status: — " He stops. "I've never seen this status."

decision.text: The lens at Meridian's gate knew your face.

status.text: He turns the screen. Your face, grey and small, taken from somewhere you have never stood. A number. And under it: ADMIT ON SIGHT — MAGISTRATE-DESIGNATE (R49). The sergeant has come to look. For the first time in a thousand people her face does something. "Magistrate," she says. "Designate." The clerk says, "That's nineteen years off." Nobody says anything else for a while.

interject.text: "Designate," Odile says softly. "My dear, there are men on the floor at Ninebridge who would pay a year of Tolls to know that one word." She does not say whether she is one of them.
"Nineteen years," Wren says. "Huh." Her eyes go from the sergeant to the clerk to the barrier, counting. "Then nobody shoots you today. That's something."
"Magistrate," Tamsin says, and laughs, and stops laughing. "That's a joke. Tell me that's a joke."

options.text: I'll stand the hearing like anyone.
(While they stare at each other: the booth terminal is unlocked.)

flag.text: The clerk prints a card. The sergeant stamps it without looking at it, which she has never done. CITIZEN — PRECINCT — ENTRY AND RESIDENCE — and, smaller, DESIGNATE. "The avenue's straight ahead," she says. "The schedule holds." It sounds, for once, like a question.

interject.text: "Designate," Ash says, and nothing else. When you look round he is looking at the card in your hand the way he looks at a grave he has not finished digging.

decision.text: You let the file admit you to Meridian on sight, as its Magistrate-designate.

hearing_go.text: "Hearing." The sergeant writes something that is not your name. "Records office, inside, left of the avenue. The assessor sits. Take what papers you have; it reads everything." She lifts the barrier for you alone, which the line notices.

edit_ok.text: Two lines, while the sergeant is still saying *designate* and the clerk is still saying *nineteen years*: the status field takes a value it already knows, CITIZEN, and the name field takes one it does not. The screen agrees with you. The clerk turns back and prints a card for someone who does not exist.

decision.text: You edited your own file at Meridian's gate and entered as a citizen who does not exist.

edit_no.text: The screen flashes red and says so, aloud. The sergeant's carbine comes round. "Hands." The cells, then: the Precinct has a procedure.

push_ok.text: The crowd goes at the gate at dusk the way it does every dusk, and tonight you are in the front of it with your shoulder down, and the barrier gives, and you are through in the crush with no card and a sergeant's voice behind you saying *let them, let them, count them tomorrow*.

decision.text: You pushed through Meridian's gate with the crowd.

push_no.text: The crowd goes at the gate and the wardens go at the crowd, and a club finds your head in the second row, and the next thing is tile under your cheek and a fence door.

through.text: "Card." She looks, and nods, and the barrier lifts.
through.again: The sergeant nods you through before you reach the barrier.

look.text: A glass eye on a post, a green light under it, a cable into the booth. It has seen more faces than anyone alive, and forgotten none of them.
look.again: The lens on its post, and the green light under it.

read.text: PRECINCT OF MERIDIAN — ENTRY BY CARD, HEARING OR LICENCE — CURFEW 21:00 — WATER BY RATION — ALL PERSONS ARE RECORDED. Under it, the Ledger's seal, and a smaller line: THE SCHEDULE HOLDS.
read.again: ALL PERSONS ARE RECORDED. THE SCHEDULE HOLDS.

read.text: Painted on the Wall in letters a man high, old and renewed: RESTORATION YEAR 30. Beside it, in letters a hand high, newer and not renewed: THE RING BURNS AND YOU COUNT.
read.again: RESTORATION YEAR 30, a man high. THE RING BURNS AND YOU COUNT, a hand high, fading.

mouth.text: A storm drain under the Wall, south of the gate, grated, its grate bent where someone has been through before. A warden walks the top of the Wall above it every quarter-hour.
mouth.again: The drain, the bent grate, and the warden's steps above on the Wall.

options.text: (Wait for the warden to pass, and go under.)

mods.why: the Wall's lamps do not reach the drain

go_ok.text: Forty feet of pipe on your elbows with the city's water a hand deep, and a grate at the far end that lifts, and a back lane behind the tenements with a lamp at the end of it and nobody under the lamp.

decision.text: You went under Meridian's Wall by the storm drain.

go_no.text: The grate shrieks on its hinge. On the Wall a lamp swings round and a voice says *stay there*, in the tone of someone who knows you won't.

inside.text: The drain's inside mouth, in the back lane. It goes out under the Wall to the rubble, if you ever need a way out the lens does not watch.
inside.again: The drain's mouth in the back lane: the way out the lens does not watch.

board.text: THE LOOP — PRECINCT PLATFORM. A board of district names with a fare beside each: OLD MARKET 2 · LANTERN ROW 2 · THE STACKS 3 · BRIDGEWARD 3 · CLOVER 4 · THE DOCKS 4 · THE CROWN (BY INVITATION). The tram on the rail hums with its doors open. One name still has a chalk line through it: THE DOCKS.
board.again: The tram hums with its doors open. Chalk through THE DOCKS, and nowhere else.

works.text: NO BRIDGE, in chalk, through THE DOCKS. A citizen waiting on the bench says the Docks line has said that since before she was born, and that the rest said WORKS all spring, and that the works were on schedule. Clover, she says, is outside the Wall: the tram goes, and comes back, and the Ring is outside the law, and she has never been.
works.again: NO BRIDGE through THE DOCKS, and the citizen on the bench.

docks.text: NO BRIDGE, chalked through THE DOCKS. Under it, in a newer chalk somebody has gone over twice: BY CLOVER — QUAY TRAM 2. A woman on the bench with a basket on her knees says the Loop's Docks line went over Bridgeward's bridge, and the bridge went into the river in the Charter Wars with a tram on it. "Carrick's across the dry river," she says. "Round by the Wall: the river road south from the gate, an hour on foot outside the law. Or the Loop to Clover and the quay tram round the ring road. The Line comes in there, and the tide boat, and the barges." She lowers her voice. "And at night, they say, a basket on a wire from Bridgeward's drop, if you know who to wave a lamp at."
docks.again: BY CLOVER — QUAY TRAM 2, under the NO BRIDGE.

text.text: A standpipe with a dial and a board: WATER — PRECINCT — RATION 0.8 — REBALANCING (SUPPLY NETWORK 4). The dial has been turned down a fifth. Somebody has written under it: *since the Sallow*.
A standpipe with a dial and a board: WATER — PRECINCT — RATION 1.0 — ON SCHEDULE. The dial is clean.

read.text: Under glass: EVICTIONS, SCHEDULED (4). HEARINGS, TUESDAY AND FRIDAY. THE SINK: SPRING RELIEF PUMPING WILL BE DIVERTED TO THE PRECINCT AS PER SCHEDULE. CITIZENS ARE REMINDED THAT THE RING IS OUTSIDE THE LAW. And a smaller card: RECORDS OFFICE — CITIZENSHIP BY EXAMINATION — ASK FOR THE ASSESSOR.
read.again: EVICTIONS, SCHEDULED (4). The Sink's spring pumping, diverted. THE RING IS OUTSIDE THE LAW.

read.text: The charter, cast in brass, in clauses. CLAUSE 1: THE CITY KEEPS ITS PEOPLE. CLAUSE 14: THE DRAINS ARE THE CITY'S FIRST DUTY. CLAUSE 31: A LAWFUL CONTRACT SHALL NOT BE VOIDED. CLAUSE 60: THE RESTORATION SHALL PROCEED ON SCHEDULE. Someone has polished clause 14 more than the others.
read.again: The brass clauses. Fourteen shines brighter than the rest.

look.text: The records terminal, green on black like the Exchange's board and older. A list scrolls: CONTINUITY RESERVES — 1 RELOCATED R0+1 — 2 RELOCATED R0+1 — 3 LOST — 4 NON-COMPLIANT (DOOR) — 5 RELOCATED R0+3 — 6 LOST — 7 SOLD (CONCERN) — 8 LOST — 9 OUTSTANDING (CARETAKER NON-COMPLIANT, ORDERS 3). Then it scrolls off.
look.again: CONTINUITY RESERVES, scrolling green. 9 OUTSTANDING. It scrolls off again.

options.text: (Type the code from the photograph's margin: 0412/30.)

mods.why: Nine tells the wall which queue the number belongs to
Nine stands with its back to the screen, naming the codes

register.text: ASSETS, MUNICIPAL. The cursor finds it on the third page. UNIT 9 — ASSESSOR — CIVIL REFIT, WARDEN PATTERN — ISSUED R−90. OWNER OF RECORD: DEPARTMENT OF RECORDS. DEPARTMENT DISSOLVED R−60. TITLE LAPSED. And a last line, set apart from the rest: DISPOSAL — SCHEDULED — R31. A note cites clause 9(b): A LAPSED ASSET PASSES TO ITS KEEPER ON A CAPTAIN'S WITNESS, OR TO A BUYER AT ASSESSED VALUE.
register.again: The entry, green on black. The last line is still set apart from the rest.

interject.text: "The owner," Nine says, to the wall, its back to the screen. "Only the owner. Clause 40." It does not turn round, and it does not ask what is taking you so long.

render.text: The cursor takes the code and the screen goes blank and then very full. RENDER QUEUE 0412 — SUBJECT: DESIGNATE — RENDERED R30 FROM FORECAST — DEPICTS R49.06.12 — SITE: ARCHIVE SPIRE, PUBLIC STEPS — COPIES: 1 (UNRECORDED). The pencil on the back of the print copied the date and left off the R.
render.again: RENDER QUEUE 0412. DEPICTS R49. The screen holds it.

render_no.text: QUERY NOT UNDERSTOOD. The code means something to the machine; you have not found the door it opens. The cursor waits, patient as the Wall.

register_no.text: ACCESS: CLERK GRADE OR ABOVE. The cursor waits. A card is tucked into the terminal's frame, in a warden's hand: ENTRIES PRINTED AT THE DESK — PAPER 20.
register_no.again: CLERK GRADE OR ABOVE. The card in the frame: PRINTED AT THE DESK.

look.text: The curfew bell on its post, rung by a wire from the station at nine. Old Agata Quint says it has never once been late, and says it the way other people say a prayer.
look.again: The curfew bell on its post and its wire to the station. Never once late.

cell.text: A cell: tile, a cot, a fence door with a lock. After an hour the door opens and a thing comes in that is not a person — grey plating, a brass plate, a cracked lens — and sits on the end of the cot with a ledger. "Assessor Nine. The record suggests you were detained at the gate. The record also suggests — " a pause, and the lens clicks — "that the file does not know what to do with you, which is a thing I have not seen the file do in a hundred and twenty years."

options.text: The file says admit on sight. Read it.

decision.text: You let the file admit you to Meridian on sight, as its Magistrate-designate.

options.text: Captain Lowe said the wardens take people from the cells.

decision.text: You took Captain Lowe's offer and left the cells as a warden's recruit.

bail.text: "Bail is lawful." It writes. "A provisional pass. Three days, it says. Nobody enforces the three; I have filed a complaint." The fence door is open.

serve.text: Two days of tile and a cot and water at ration, and the assessor twice a day with the ledger, asking questions it already has the answers to and writing down the differences. On the third morning the fence door is open and a pass is on the cot.

flag.text: It reads it. The lens clicks twice. "ADMIT ON SIGHT. MAGISTRATE-DESIGNATE." A long pause. "The record suggests I should have let you in at the gate. The record suggests a great many things." It prints a card from somewhere inside its chest. "Citizen. Designate. The fence door is open; it was never locked, which I will not be putting in the file."

interject.text: "Designate," Ash says, and nothing else. When you look round he is looking at the card in your hand the way he looks at a grave he has not finished digging.

lowe.text: "Captain Lowe recruits from the cells. It is lawful; clause 22. It is also," the lens clicks, "a thing I would not do. A card, then, and grey, and the schedule." The fence door is open.

open.text: The cell, empty, the fence door open. It was never locked.
open.again: Tile, a cot, a fence door standing open.

intro.text: The desk warden looks at your card, or your face, and then at a drawer, and takes out a paper with your face printed grey on the corner. "Fines outstanding. Three." He is apologetic in the way of a man reading a list. "Curfew, forecast. Loitering on the avenue, forecast. Unlicensed assembly, forecast. Forty-five Tolls." He pushes it across. "The dates are next month."

options.text: I haven't done any of it.
Print me an entry from the asset register. Unit 9. (20 Tolls)
Unit 9's title has lapsed. Clause 9(b): I'll buy it at assessed value. (120 Tolls)

decision.text: You bought Assessor Nine's lapsed title from the city at assessed value.

again.text: "Three fines. Forty-five."
again.again: He taps the notice, apologetically, and waits.

options.text: I haven't done any of it.
Print me an entry from the asset register. Unit 9. (20 Tolls)
Unit 9's title has lapsed. Clause 9(b): I'll buy it at assessed value. (120 Tolls)

decision.text: You bought Assessor Nine's lapsed title from the city at assessed value.

contest.text: "Yet." He says it gently. "You can contest a forecast fine at the Court of Accounts. By appointment. The appointment is — " he looks at a book — "when the schedule says." He writes CONTESTED on the notice and stamps it, which seems to make him happier than the fine did.

paid_now.text: He stamps a receipt, twice. "Paid. You're a person the Precinct has no complaint against." He thinks about it. "Including the ones it hasn't had yet."

paid.text: "No complaints on file. That's rare, here."
paid.again: "Still no complaints." He sounds faintly proud of you.

options.text: Print me an entry from the asset register. Unit 9. (20 Tolls)
