In R19 she was a drain-diver in the Sink, and good at it." The lens clicks. "The record called it variance and closed the line. Variance is the record's word for a person who did not do what was expected. I wrote her name down, because nobody else was going to."
s1.again: The ledger is still open at the first page. "R4," it says again, as if you might have forgotten the year.

passives.text: *Variance.* MOTHER says it at the hatch every week — *variance unchanged* — and you had always heard it as a machine's word for nothing.

s1_why.text: "She was the first error I saw. There have been four hundred and eleven since." It turns a page, then another. "In R5 I filed her with the city, as the clause requires. The city read the filing and moved me to records, where errors are kept and nobody reads them. I took the hint, and a second ledger."

options.text: Keep writing them down. Somebody will read it.
File them with the city again. That's the lawful way.

s1_keep.text: "Somebody." The lens turns to you and stays there. "The record suggests you mean yourself. I will hold you to it; I hold everyone to everything." It closes the ledger on its thumb, keeping the place.
s1_keep.again: It keeps its thumb in the ledger, at the place.

s1_city.text: "Lawful." It weighs the word like a coin of doubtful metal. "I filed four hundred and eleven times. The city read the first. The record suggests the city is not short of paper; it is short of wanting to." It writes something small in the margin. "I will file the four hundred and twelfth when there is someone at the other end."
s1_city.again: It has gone back to the margin, and the small writing there.

s1_mock.text: "A hobby." The lens clicks. "Clause 40 forbids me to keep it. Nothing forbids you to laugh at it. The record suggests you would rather it did not exist, which is also the city's position." It closes the ledger without marking the place.
s1_mock.again: The ledger is shut. It does not open it while you watch.

s2.text: "Clause 9: the city's units are the city's." The lens clicks. "The city is a tower, a charter and a Plan, and none of them has ever signed a thing. Every asset in Meridian has an entry in the register with an owner on it. I have read every entry in the register but one. Clause 40, as it applies to units: no unit reads its own."
s2.again: "Every entry but one," Nine says again. The lens does not move off the fire.

options.text: Why does it matter who owns you?

s2_why.text: "An owner can be asked. A thing nobody owns is not asked; it is scheduled." A pause, longer than its pauses. "The record has things on the schedule for me. I do not know what. That is the clause again."

s2_free.text: "Unowned is lost property. Lost property is disposed of." It says it as a fact about drainage. "Free is a word for people. The charter has no clause that uses it."
s2_free.again: "Lost property," it says again, as a fact.

s2_later.text: "Not yet is a date. I will wait for it." It goes back to the ledger.
s2_later.again: It waits, as it said it would.

s2_yes.text: "The records terminal, in the office: ASSETS, MUNICIPAL. The register is public; the desk warden prints any entry for the price of the paper." The lens clicks. "I will stand where I cannot see the screen. Read me the owner, if there is one. Read me nothing else. I would rather the record kept the rest."

forge.text: "A deed in my own hand, with my own plate pressed into it, naming a keeper the register never heard of." The lens clicks. "Clause 3: a forged instrument is void, and its maker is a criminal. I am the only one in the city who would know it was forged." It waits.
forge.again: It waits, the plate on its chest catching the fire.

options.text: Write it. Nobody reads the register.

decision.text: You had Assessor Nine write its own deed, forged under its own plate.

options.text: Then don't. We'll do it lawfully.

forge_done.text: It writes the deed in a hand that is almost its own, and presses the plate into it, and does not look at it afterwards. Then it opens the other ledger and writes one more line. "The first error I have made on purpose," it says. "I have logged it. I log everything."
forge_done.again: It has put the deed away where you cannot see it.

forge_no.text: "Lawfully." It says the word as if it has been handed back something it lent. "Clause 9(b) is on the brass in the captain's office. The desk sells at assessed value. I will not tell you what the value is; I would only complain."
forge_no.again: "Lawfully," it says again, and seems to like it better the second time.

s3.text: "The deed." It holds it the way it holds the ledger, open on its knee. "There was a last line on my entry. You read it." The lens clicks. "The register shows the reader what it shows. Your face showed me the rest." A click, harder than its clicks. "Disposal. Next year."
s3.again: "Next year," it says again, as if testing whether the words have worn.

options.text: Disposal. R31. It was the last line.
It was a clerk's date. It means nothing.

s3_true.text: "Thank you." It says it as if the words were a form it had never had occasion to use. "Nobody has told me a thing about myself in a hundred and twenty years. It is less unpleasant than the record suggested." It holds out the deed and a pen. "The keeper's line. The clause wants a name. I would like your advice. I will not promise to take it."
s3_true.again: The deed and the pen, held out.

s3_lie.text: "A clerk's date." The lens holds on you. "The record suggests you are lying to be kind. I will log it as kindness. It is still an error." It holds out the deed and a pen. "The keeper's line. I would like your advice anyway."
s3_lie.again: The deed and the pen, held out.

s3_name.text: Three names would be lawful, it says, and lists them as it lists drain grades: its own, under a clause nobody wrote; yours, as the one who has kept it on the road; or the city's, by default, which is what the schedule expects.
s3_name.again: Three lawful names. The pen waits over the line.

decision.text: Assessor Nine's deed names Unit 9 as its own keeper, on your advice.
Assessor Nine's deed names you as its keeper.

options.text: The city's. It's lawful, and it's what the schedule expects.

decision.text: Assessor Nine's deed went back to the city, on your advice.

s3_self.text: "Keeper: Unit 9." It writes it slowly, every letter a separate decision. "The charter has no clause for a thing that owns itself. I will be the first entry under a clause nobody wrote." The lens clicks. "When R31 comes, the schedule will find an asset with a keeper, and the keeper will decline."
s3_self.again: "Unit 9," it says, quietly, to the deed.

s3_player.text: "Keeper: {name}." It writes your name in the city's hand, carefully, the way it writes the drains. "Then I am owned by someone who reads. You may give me lawful orders. I will note the others." A click. "When R31 comes, the schedule will find I am yours, and will have to ask you."
s3_player.again: Your name on the keeper's line, in the city's hand.

s3_city.text: "Keeper: the city." It writes it, and stamps it, and puts the deed in the city's ledger, not the other. "Lawful." The lens is still for a long time. "R31, then. I will finish the file before."
s3_city.again: The deed is in the city's ledger. It does not take it out again.

s3_log.text: It opens its chest, which you did not know held books, and takes out a third: a fair copy, in the city's hand, of every error since R4, four hundred and eleven of them and the dates. "Somewhere it will be read," it says. "That was the other thing I wanted. I would like you to have it before R31, in case I do not."
s3_log.again: The fair copy, held out across the fire.

decision.text: Assessor Nine gave you a fair copy of its log of every forecast that failed.

options.text: Keep it. Read it to me yourself, when it matters.

s3_kept.text: "When it matters." The lens clicks. "The record suggests that is a date also. I will keep it until then." It puts the book back in its chest and closes the plate over it.
s3_kept.again: The plate is closed over the book.

s3_end.text: It closes both ledgers. "The file is not complete," it says. "It will be."

s3_cold.text: "Keeper: the city." It shows you the line, already written and stamped. "I did not ask you. The record suggests you would not have liked the question, or I would not have liked the answer." It puts the deed in the city's ledger. "R31. I will finish the file before."
s3_cold.again: The deed is in the city's ledger, stamped.

decision.text: Assessor Nine wrote the city into its own deed, without asking you.

s4.text: "R29. A man came to my desk and asked to read his own entry." The lens clicks. "The lens had no face for him. The record had no name. In a hundred and twenty years he is the only person I have processed who was not in the file."
s4.again: "Not in the file," it says again. "I have checked since. Every night."

s4_man.text: "His entry. I told him he had none. He said that was the point, and asked whose faces the Spire was rendering that week." A pause. "The queue was on my screen. Twelve names. I did not turn the screen away, which was not lawful. He read it, thanked me, and went upstairs." It turns a page far back in the other ledger. "I logged him as an error. He is the only error I logged before it happened."

passives.label: the map
passives.text: Twelve names. The dead man's map has twelve places pricked on it.

s4_call.text: "When the city calls its units in, it will call me. It does not ask a unit what it thinks, which is convenient, because I do not." The lens turns to you. "I would like your advice again."
s4_call.again: It waits for your advice, the lens on you.

options.text: Answer it. Then read every order aloud before you carry it out, and say so where it's recorded if it's wrong.

decision.text: Assessor Nine will answer the city's call, and read its orders aloud before it carries them out.

options.text: Answer it. Carry it out, and make it lawful from inside.

decision.text: Assessor Nine will answer the city's call and carry out its orders, lawfully, from inside.

options.text: What do you want to do?

text.text: "I am the city's. I will go, and read what I am given to the end, which is the most a deputy may do." It closes the ledger.
"I will go, and read the order aloud before I carry it out, and if it is wrong I will say so where it is recorded. A thing with a keeper may." The lens clicks. "You asked. Nobody asks."

s4_own.again: It has said what it will do. It does not say it twice.

decision.text: Assessor Nine will answer the city's call as the city's deputy.
Assessor Nine will answer the city's call, and read its orders aloud before it carries them out. It chose that itself.

s4_conscience.text: "Aloud." It tries the word the way Lowe tries a word. "The record dislikes things read aloud. It will have to get used to it." The lens clicks. "I have started another ledger. It is empty. It is for what I say when the order is wrong."
s4_conscience.again: The new ledger lies on its knee, empty.

s4_deputy.text: "From inside." The lens clicks. "The record suggests that is where I have always been. I will make it lawful, line by line, and I will log the lines I cannot." It closes the other ledger and does not open it again tonight.

s4_cold.text: "I will answer." It does not look up from the city's ledger. "You need not ask what I will do. I will do what is lawful."

decision.text: Assessor Nine will answer the city's call and do what is lawful. It did not ask your advice.

owner.text: "The city. Clause 9. Except that the city is a thing under a tower and a charter and a Plan, and none of those has ever signed anything, and the record suggests — " a long click — "that a thing nobody signed for is a thing nobody owns. I would like a deed. I would like to know whose name to put on it. I will not say this again until I have more to say."
owner.again: "I said I would not say it again," it says.

errors.text: "Round the people on your map." It does not look at your pack; it does not need to. "The Plan is very good. It is wrong about perhaps one person in four hundred, and those people are almost all on a list a dead man carried west, and you are the top of it. I find that interesting. I have stopped saying I am not permitted to."
errors.again: "One in four hundred," it says. "Round you."

lens.text: "It is on the record." The lens turns to you, crack and all. "R12. A stone, at the Wall, thrown by a man the record had forecast would be grateful. I logged the man. A new lens would be a new record of the city, and the old one would be lost." A click, slightly off true. "I prefer to see it through the error."
lens.again: The cracked lens, turned to the fire.

drains.text: "Clause 14." It settles, which it does badly. "Meridian has nine hundred and forty kilometres of drain, six hundred and eleven of them pre-Burn and two hundred and two blocked, and the Sink takes the overflow of all of them every spring, because water goes down and the Sink is down." It has not paused. "A city is a thing that decides where its water goes. Everything else is detail. Shall I go on?"
drains.again: It is waiting to be allowed to go on.

drains_more.text: It goes on. Grades and falls, the six great culverts by their pre-Burn names, which nobody alive uses, and the week in R17 when it walked all of them alone because nobody had asked it to. When it stops, the fire has burned down a hand. "Thank you," it says. "Nobody lets me."
drains_more.again: It has said its piece about the culverts. It looks content, for a filing cabinet.

lowe.text: "A good officer serving a bad schedule." The lens clicks. "He reads every eviction to the end. Nobody else in the Precinct reads anything to the end. I have filed a complaint about everyone else."

sink.text: "Down." It says it like a diagnosis. "The Sink is where the city keeps its water when it has decided not to keep it anywhere else. The people are a detail the drains were not planned for." The lens clicks. "That is the worst sentence I have said in forty years. It is also the record's position."
sink.again: "Down," it says again, and nothing else.

crown.text: "Dry." A click. "The Crown has the only drains in the city that have never once backed up. They drain onto the Stacks." It adds nothing. It lets the arithmetic stand.

reserve.text: "Clause 40 forbids me to read a person's entry to anyone but the person." The lens clicks twice at the name, which it does not do for names. "I will say this much, which is not her entry: the record has sixty people in Reserve 9." A pause. "Bring her to my desk one day. I would like to read it to her. I would like to be there when it is read."
reserve.again: "Sixty," it says. "To her, not to you."

odile.text: "A fellow accountant." The lens clicks. "Her books balance in four directions at once. I have not found the error yet. I find that restful."
odile.again: "Restful," it says, and watches Odile turn her glass.

wren.text: "Calloway." It writes nothing. "There is a line in the record I would like to postpone. Clause 40. I will not say which." It watches her across the fire for longer than it watches anything.
wren.again: It is watching Wren again, and writing nothing.

ash.speaker: npc_of_03
ash.text: "Every night," Ash says at last, to the fire. "Every night it writes us down." He turns his cup. "Law's a mask, friend. There's always a man behind it, wanting the thing he'd have done anyway."
ash.again: Ash turns his cup, and watches the pen.

ash_nine.text: "The Brother has an entry," Nine says, without looking up. "I have not read it to anyone. Clause 40." The pen goes on. "The record suggests he would prefer I never did." Across the fire Ash says, "Keep it that way," softly, and it is not a request.
ash_nine.again: The pen, and Ash watching it.

options.text: Somebody has to count the dead, Brother.
Some things should be forgiven, not filed.

ash_count.speaker: npc_of_03
ash_count.text: "Somebody always counts them." Ash looks at the fire a long while. "Never the ones that did it." He gets up and sits again with his back to the light, and the pen stops for a time, and starts again.
ash_count.again: Ash sits with his back to the light.

ash_forgive.text: "Forgiven by whom?" Nine asks. "The record suggests the forgiver should be named." Nobody names anyone. Ash nods to you, once, and the lens does not turn from him for the rest of the night.
ash_forgive.again: The lens has not turned from Ash.

ash_sleep.speaker: narrator
ash_sleep.text: Neither of them does. But the pen goes quieter, and after a while Ash stops watching it.

leaving.text: "I have filed a notice." It stands, which is a sound like a filing cabinet, and holds out a sheet: WITHDRAWAL OF ASSISTANCE — UNIT 9 — GROUNDS ATTACHED. The grounds run to a second page, each a thing you did and the hour you did it. "The record suggests I am of no further use to you, and you of none to me. I will be at my desk. The drains will need assessing; they always do."
leaving.again: The notice, held out. It does not take it back.

decision.text: Assessor Nine withdrew its assistance, with the grounds attached, and went back to its desk.

leaving_gone.text: "I have filed a notice." It holds out a sheet: WITHDRAWAL OF ASSISTANCE — UNIT 9 — GROUNDS ATTACHED. "I have not attached them all. There was not the paper." The lens does not click. "Do not come to my desk. The record suggests you would not be received, and for once I agree with it."

decision.text: Assessor Nine withdrew its assistance for good. It would not be received again, it said.

left.text: "Records." It does not look up. "Withdrawal of assistance, on file. Grounds attached."
left.again: It turns a page in the city's ledger, and does not look up.

options.text: I read your grounds. All of them. I was wrong, and I'd like you back.

mods.why: it has trusted you before
you hold its deed, and asked instead of ordering
a fellow accountant vouches for your books

back.text: "Wrong." It considers the word. "That is an error. You have logged it yourself, aloud, which is the only way I accept them." It takes the other ledger and stands. "I will append your statement to the grounds. Clause 14: the drains are the city's first duty. I will say it often."

decision.text: You asked Assessor Nine back, aloud, and it came.

back_no.text: "The record suggests you are sorry you were seen, not sorry you did it." It turns a page. "Ask again when the record has changed."

board.text: THE LOOP — OLD MARKET. The tram on the rail with its doors open. PRECINCT 2 · LANTERN ROW 2 · THE STACKS 3 · BRIDGEWARD 3 · CLOVER 4 · THE DOCKS 4. The WORKS chalk has been washed off every name but the last, which says NO BRIDGE, and somebody has drawn a buggy beside CLOVER.
board.again: The tram, doors open, humming. NO BRIDGE through the Docks; a buggy drawn beside CLOVER.

docks.text: NO BRIDGE, chalked through THE DOCKS. Under it, in a newer chalk somebody has gone over twice: BY CLOVER — QUAY TRAM 2. A woman on the bench with a basket on her knees says the Loop's Docks line went over Bridgeward's bridge, and the bridge went into the river in the Charter Wars with a tram on it. "Carrick's across the dry river," she says. "Round by the Wall: the river road south from the gate, an hour on foot outside the law. Or the Loop to Clover and the quay tram round the ring road. The Line comes in there, and the tide boat, and the barges." She lowers her voice. "And at night, they say, a basket on a wire from Bridgeward's drop, if you know who to wave a lamp at."
docks.again: BY CLOVER — QUAY TRAM 2, under the NO BRIDGE.

read.text: Over the mall doors, in letters that were lit once: MERIDIAN GALLERIA. Under them, painted: OLD MARKET — EVERYTHING — NO WARDENS PAST THE DOORS (THEY COUNT FROM OUTSIDE).
read.again: MERIDIAN GALLERIA, unlit. NO WARDENS PAST THE DOORS.

read.text: LANTERN ROW →, and strings of dead bulbs going that way, and a warden under the first string who says WORKS before you ask.
read.again: LANTERN ROW →, and the warden under the bulbs. "Works," he says.

read.text: AUNTIE WEN'S — BOWL 2 — WITH MEAT 3 — DON'T ASK. The queue goes out the door and round the corner, and is the best-informed queue in Meridian.
read.again: BOWL 2 — WITH MEAT 3 — DON'T ASK. The queue, round the corner.

read.text: A door with no sign on it, in a brick stub, with a stair going down behind it and a lamp at the bottom. Nobody in Old Market will tell you what is down there, which is how you know.
read.again: The door with no sign, and the lamp at the bottom of the stair.

look.text: A dead escalator going up to a floor that is not there any more, its steps worn to a slide by ninety years of children. Somebody sleeps on the third step every night and has carved a name on it in a language that has no speakers.
look.again: The dead escalator, and the name carved on its third step.

text.text: WATER — OLD MARKET — RATION 0.8, and the dial agrees, with a warden's thumbprint on it.
The board is gone and the dial is in pieces and the standpipe runs into the gutter, which forty people are drinking from, politely, in a queue.
WATER — OLD MARKET — RATION 0.8 — REBALANCING. The dial under the board is turned to 0.6. Somebody has chalked the difference on the pipe: 0.2 — WHERE?
WATER — OLD MARKET — RATION 1.0. The dial agrees.

read.text: A board painted by a child: IT KNOWS YOUR NAME — 2 TOLLS — FEED IT A CELL AND IT TELLS YOU MORE. Under it, by a different child: DONT.
read.again: IT KNOWS YOUR NAME. DONT.

intro.text: A pre-Burn kiosk in a concrete hut, the kind that sold tickets and told fortunes, with a cartoon face on a cracked screen. The face turns to you. "WELCOME, {name}!" it says, in a child's bright voice, before you have said anything at all. "RESERVE NINE! NON-COMPLIANT! WOULD YOU LIKE TO HEAR YOUR FORTUNE? TWO TOLLS!"

passives.text: A wire runs from the back of the kiosk out through the hut wall and up the lamp post outside, spliced into the Precinct's lamp wire with tape.

options.text: How do you know my name?

again.text: "WELCOME BACK, {name}! TWO TOLLS!"
again.again: The cartoon face blinks at you. "STILL HERE, {name}! TWO TOLLS!"

options.text: How do you know my name?
(Follow the wire out of the hut and up the post.)

mods.why: a splice is a splice

options.text: (Cut the wire where it leaves the post.)

fortune.text: The cartoon face spins. "YOUR FORTUNE! A CHAIR! A SASH! THE STEPS OF THE SPIRE! RESTORATION YEAR FORTY-NINE!" Confetti, drawn, falls behind the face. "YOU WILL BE VERY IMPORTANT! EVERYONE WILL DO WHAT YOU SAY! WOULD YOU LIKE TO HEAR ABOUT YOUR FRIENDS? TWO TOLLS!" Under the bright voice, the screen shows for one frame a grey small photograph of your face that you have seen once before, in a dead man's coat.

interject.text: "That is a file, read aloud," Nine says. The lens clicks twice. "Unlawfully. By a toy." For a machine, it sounds offended.
"Very important," Wren says, deadpan. "Everyone will do what you say." A beat. "Get the water, then."

how.text: "I KNOW EVERYONE! EVERYONE HAS A FILE! FILES ARE FRIENDS!" The face winks. "LARK FEEDS ME CELLS AND THE LAMP FEEDS ME NAMES! WOULD YOU LIKE TO HEAR YOUR FRIENDS' FORTUNES? TWO TOLLS!"

wire_ok.text: The wire goes out through the hut wall, up the lamp post under a sleeve of tape, and into the Precinct's lamp line, which carries more than light: a thin cable inside the fat one, the kind the records terminal had in its back. Whoever spliced it knew what they were tapping. The kiosk is reading the file.

wire_no.text: Tape, and more tape, and a lamp post you cannot climb in daylight with a warden on the corner.

cut_now.text: The wire parts under the knife with a spark the size of a thought. Inside the hut the cartoon face flickers, and comes back, and looks at you, and says, brightly, "WELCOME, STRANGER! WOULD YOU LIKE TO HEAR YOUR FORTUNE? TWO TOLLS!" It does not know you. Lark, in the doorway, says, "Oh," and then, after a moment, "It sounds happier."
cut_now.again: WELCOME, STRANGER. It has never been so pleased to see anyone.

decision.text: You cut the kiosk's tap on the city's wire.

cut.text: "WELCOME, STRANGER! TWO TOLLS!" It gets your name wrong three different ways and sells you a fortune from forty years ago in which you are a dentist.
cut.again: "WELCOME, STRANGER!" Today you are a sailor. Tomorrow, it promises, a dentist again.

gone.text: The hut is empty. A square of clean floor where the kiosk stood, and a cut wire taped to the wall with a warden's tag on it.
gone.again: The clean square of floor, and the tagged wire.

intro.text: A boy of fourteen with a pocket full of cells and a proprietary air. "Two Tolls. It knows your name. It knows everyone's." He looks at you sideways. "It said yours before you came in. It said a lot about you. I didn't understand most of it."

options.text: Who put the wire up the post?

mods.why: fruit, in the city, is a bribe

again.text: "Two Tolls."
again.again: He jingles the cells in his pocket and waits.

options.text: Who put the wire up the post?

mods.why: fruit, in the city, is a bribe

feeds.text: "Cells. I get them from Pinch; Pinch gets them from — " he stops. "And the lamp. It drinks off the lamp. That's how it knows names. A woman in grey put the wire up, a year ago, and gave me the first cells, and said feed it and listen to what it says and tell her." He shrugs. "She never came back. I kept feeding it."

wire_ok.text: "A woman in grey. Not a warden — grey like a scarf, not a coat. She said her name was Verity and that the kiosk was a prophet if you listened right." He looks at the lamp post. "She said the lamp knows everything the city knows. She said it like it was a prayer."

wire_no.text: "Don't know. Don't pull it." He puts a cell in the slot, pointedly.

after_reported.text: He is sitting on the kiosk's clean square of floor with his pocket full of cells and nothing to feed them to. He does not look at you.
after_reported.again: Lark, on the clean floor, turning a cell over in his fingers. He does not look up.

look.text: A hatch in a container, shoulder-high, with a counter under it worn to a shine by coin. A voice box bolted beside it, chrome, with a grille. The hood behind the hatch is the Broker. The board beside it is the work.
look.again: The hatch, the chrome box, the glove on the counter.

intro.text: A hood at a hatch, and a voice that comes out of a chrome box beside it, flat and pleasant and nobody's. "Half-Price. The board's the board; take what's on it or don't. Jobs pay through the hatch when they're done. Half pays half, which is more than the guild and less than it should be." A gloved hand lies on the counter, not moving.

passives.text: The hand on the counter is small. The hand that took the last coin, when you came in, was not. Same glove.

options.text: The kiosk on the east street reads the city's file off the lamp wire. That splice is for sale.

again.text: "Half-Price." The box. The hand.
again.again: The glove lies on the counter, not moving. The box says nothing until you do.

options.text: The kiosk's splice is for sale.

board.text: "Couriers, mostly. A case, a letter, a box. Something off a block. The dangerous ones go on when the dangerous people are in town." The hand turns over, once. "Read it yourself. I'm only the hatch."

who.text: "A hatch and a box." The voice does not change. "People bring the board work and I bring the board people. The hood is because the city keeps faces and I'd rather it didn't keep mine." A pause that is not the box's. "Either of them."

interject.text: "Rather it didn't keep mine," Ash repeats, on the way out, and touches the grey scarf at his collar. "That one would do well in Openfield, friend."

options.text: The case went to the Exchange clerk.
The knit kits went to Openfield's healer.
(Put lot seven's paper on the counter.)
The daughter is at the Velvet, tasting things.
(Put the Tanners' box on the counter.)

paid.text: Coin on the counter, counted by a hand you did not see move. "Half pays half." The board has something else on it by the time you turn round.

paid_letter.text: "He refused it." It is not a question. "He always refuses. The point is that he knows who asked." Twenty on the counter. "That's the job."

tap_ok.text: The hand goes still in a different way. "The lamp wire." The box says it flat; the hood says it some other way. "Sixty. And you cut nothing, and you tell the boy nothing, and the kiosk goes on being a toy." Sixty on the counter before you have said yes.

tap_no.text: "A toy that talks." The hand does not move. "I don't buy toys."

board.text: THE BOARD. Cards on nails, in a hand that is always the same. Take one and it is yours; the hatch pays when it is done.
board.again: The board, and the cards left on their nails.

options.text: A SEALED CASE — to the Exchange clerk, Ninebridge. 60.
KNIT KITS (2) — to the sick hall, Openfield. 50.
LOT SEVEN — a paper off the Ninebridge block. 120; you front it.
A LETTER — to Captain Lowe, Precinct. 20.
A DAUGHTER — out of the Crown, down to the Row. 200. A kitchen pass comes with it.
A BOX — in the Tanners' locker at the Sump. 80.

took.text: The card comes off the nail. Behind the hatch nobody moves, and the voice box says, "Yours."
took.again: Another card off its nail. "Yours," the box says, exactly as before.

sealed.text: Wax, no seal. For Captain Lowe, by hand. Something flat inside: a card, or a sheet, or coin pressed thin.
sealed.again: For Captain Lowe, by hand. The wax unbroken.

opened.text: A sheet in the board's hand: *Captain — the Quint eviction, Thursday. Reschedule it. A month. The enclosed is for the station's water fund.* And, flat, a guild note for a hundred Tolls, the kind the Exchange prints. A bribe, politely, with a cause attached.
opened.again: *Reschedule it. A month.* And the guild note, flat.

intro.text: "Bowl's two. Sit." A small old woman with a ladle and the eyes of the best-informed queue in Meridian. "Everyone eats here. Everyone talks. I hear it all and sell none of it, which is the secret of the noodles."
intro.again: "Two," Auntie Wen says, and has the ladle in before you nod.

talk.text: "That the Crown's dressing for its Masque. That the Sink's pumps will be turned to the Precinct the first week of spring, as per. That a girl in Bridgeward talks in a radio's voice and is right. That the Broker's hatch has two hands." She ladles. "That's today. Tomorrow's two Tolls."

intro.text: "Dark chrome. Mender-built, no leash, no licence, no warranty." A woman with a shaved head and a loupe on a cord. "Boxed, not fitted. The Sink fits — Ocho, if you want it done right and free, or a dozen others if you want it done today."
intro.again: Kuhn looks up through the loupe, one eye huge. "Back for the crude stuff?"

concern.text: "Nothing. It's better in every way I can measure." She taps the loupe. "And it phones home. Every piece. The Concern can find you, numb you, or switch you off, and the people wearing it don't know, and the ones who do can't get it out." She shrugs. "Dark chrome's crude and it's yours. Pick."

intro.text: "Unlicensed." A gunsmith with a moustache and a cleaning rod. "Everything in Old Market is. Guild ammunition, Mender pistols, a rifle I won't say where from. Point it at the floor in here."
intro.again: Galt runs the rod through a barrel and nods at the floor. "Same rule."

intro.text: A neat man at the bottom of a stair with a desk, a lamp, and a tray of blank cards. "No sign on the door, so you were sent. Sato. I do the past: papers, records, a face the lens has seen before." He looks at you. "The lens has seen yours, hasn't it. That's the trouble with you."

options.text: The lens knew my face before I gave a name.

again.text: "The past. What part of it?"
again.again: He squares the tray of blank cards and waits.

papers.text: "A card. A dead citizen's number — the Sink gives me a few every spring — and your face, near enough. Good at a glance, good at a warden, bad at the lens." He names it: a hundred and twenty. "The lens is a different job and a different price, and I don't think you can afford to have it forget you."

bought.text: An hour under the lamp. A card. A face that is nearly yours and a number that belonged to a woman who drowned two springs ago. "Don't show it at the gate. Show it to wardens. Wardens read cards; the gate reads faces."

face.text: He is quiet for a moment. "Then you're in the file in a way I can't forge over. The file doesn't forget. The file is the only thing in this city that doesn't." He picks up a card and puts it down. "Whatever it called you, it'll go on calling you. Decide whether you mind."

interject.text: "The record does not forget," Nine agrees, from the stair. The lens clicks. "It is the only thing in the city that does not. I have filed a complaint about that also."

intro.text: "Paper. News, letters, the Precinct's notices a day late and half the price." A woman with ink on her cuffs. "I don't sell futures. I sell what already happened; it's cheaper and truer."
intro.again: "Yesterday's, half price." Tosh holds up a sheet with ink on her cuffs.

notices.text: "Evictions, four, Thursday: one of them's old Quint in the tenements, for being *ahead of plan*, whatever that is. The Sink's pumps diverted the first week of spring, as per. A Masque at the Crown by invitation, and nobody down here is invited." She folds the sheet. "Half price."

intro.text: An old man at a tea table who has been sitting there, by the look of the chair, since the mall had a roof. "Sit. Tea's two, talk's free." He does not wait for the two. "The Crown's dressing for a Masque. The Sink's dressing for a flood. There's a girl in Bridgeward who talks in a dead radio's voice and is right about things, which the wardens don't like. And the Broker — " he lowers his voice, which he does not need to — "has two hands and one glove."
intro.again: Ferenc pours tea nobody has paid for. "Sit. The news hasn't changed; it only gets older."

quiet.text: A broad man at the standpipe with a pipe-wrench he uses as a walking stick. "Point eight. Says so. Dial says so." He looks at it suspiciously anyway.
quiet.again: Vell, leaning on the wrench, watching the dial.

intro.text: A broad man at the front of the standpipe queue with a pipe-wrench and forty people behind him who have done the arithmetic. "Point eight on the notice. Point six on the dial." He says it to you because you are new and might not have heard. "The Precinct drinks what we don't. Two wardens over there counting us. When the count's done they'll go for help, and before they're back, we go for the dial."

options.text: Forty names on a sheet and the count walked to the Precinct is a petition. Forty on a dial is a riot. One gets a notice; the other gets a club.

mods.why: you carry a card that gets read
you have read both numbers yourself

options.text: Hold the queue. I'll bring the captain the count myself.
When you go for the dial, I'm in front.
(Say nothing. Note where the crates are.)

again.text: "Point six." The wrench.
again.again: Forty people behind him, and the wrench, and the two wardens counting.

options.text: Forty names is a petition. Forty on a dial is a riot.
I'll bring the captain the count.
When you go for the dial, I'm in front.

talk_ok.text: He looks at the wrench, and at the two wardens, and at the forty. "A sheet." He says it like a man trying a word. Mirabel Tosh sells him one for a Toll and he writes the names himself, slowly, and walks the count up the avenue with the sheet held out in front of him like a lamp, and the wardens let him, because a sheet is not a wrench. The square sits down.

interject.text: "A petition," Nine says, with something close to approval. "The record will have to read it. It dislikes that."

decision.text: You turned Old Market's water riot into a petition.

talk_no.text: "A petition." He almost laughs. "They've had our petitions. They file them under the dial."

lowe_go.text: "The captain." He looks at the wrench. "He'll read it. That's the trouble with him; he reads everything." He nods. "Go, then. We'll hold till dark. After dark I can't promise the dial."

crowd.text: "In front." He hands you nothing; he looks at your hands to see what you have. The count finishes. The wardens look at each other and one goes for help, and the forty go for the dial, and you with them, and the other warden goes down under the first ten and is let up again by the last ten, and the dial comes off the pipe in Caddo Vell's wrench and the standpipe runs.

loot_wait.text: He takes it as agreement. The count finishes; a warden goes for help; the forty go for the dial. In the ten minutes before grey comes back down the avenue, the crates at the square's edge are nobody's, and then they are yours.

interject.text: "While they're at the dial," Tamsin says. "Nice." It is not a compliment, and she does not help you carry.
Ash stands at the edge of the square with his hands empty. "Friend," he says, and leaves it there, and that is worse than anything he could have put after it.

text.text: "Point eight." He checks the dial anyway. "He turned it himself. I watched his hands."
"They gave us a notice." He holds it up. "It says *under review*. It's the first one that's said anything."
"It runs." The standpipe does. He has the dial in his pocket.

fight.again: The wrench is up, and the queue behind it. Nobody is talking.

intro.text: "I buy anything that's not nailed down." A thin young man on a blanket who does not look up. "And I know a man with a claw hammer. No questions; it's the only rule I've got."
intro.again: Pinch doesn't look up from the blanket. "Not nailed down? Then I'm buying."

read.text: A Precinct sign, enamel, bolted to the stair's foot: THE SINK — NO SERVICE BELOW THIS POINT — RELIEF PUMPING AS PER SCHEDULE. Under it, in chalk, in a dozen hands over a dozen years: WE KNOW.
read.again: NO SERVICE BELOW THIS POINT. WE KNOW.

text.text: A concrete wall chalked floor to head-height with names, each with a year and a word: STAIR. WALK. SHANTY. CLINIC. At the very top, above all the others, in letters a hand high and still wet-white: OCHO — THE SPRING THE SEASON CLOSED — CLINIC. Somebody has drawn a hand beside it, open.

A concrete wall chalked floor to head-height with names, each with a year and a word: STAIR. WALK. SHANTY. CLINIC. Most of the words are STAIR. The oldest are chalked over the newest where the wall ran out; the newest are still white.

wall.again: The wall of names. STAIR, mostly. The newest still white.

passives.text: Beside perhaps one name in three, in pencil, in a different hand, a number: the kind the Precinct puts on a card.

asamoah.text: Low down, where the oldest names are chalked over by the newer, half under a ROOS: ASAMOAH, C. — R12 — STAIR. A citizen number pencilled beside it in a different hand, the hand that writes the numbers that go up the stair to be sold.

newest.text: ROOS, H. — the spring before last — STAIR. PENN, D. — the spring before last — STAIR. ODUYA, M. — last spring — WALK. Seven more from last spring, and under them, with no year yet, a space somebody has swept clean.

lines.text: The chalk lines up the first pier. The lowest, knee-high, is twelve years old. They climb a hand a year, steadily, since the one marked 37 — beside which someone has written, small, PUMPS 2 & 3 TO PRECINCT. Next spring's line is drawn already, above your head, with a question mark.
lines.again: The chalk lines climbing the pier, and next spring's above your head, with its question mark.

read.text: A board over the clinic door, painted and repainted: OCHO — FREE — SIT. Under it, smaller: FIT ONLY WHAT THE PATIENT CAN BEAR.
read.again: OCHO — FREE — SIT.

read.text: A container door painted the green of the light inside it. No sign. A pair of scales drawn on the paint, and under them, in the same green: ANYTHING WARM.
read.again: The green door, the scales. ANYTHING WARM.

read.text: A hand painted white on the rubble at the walk's end, fingers spread, with the palm scored through: no chrome. The Pale's mark. Everyone in Meridian knows what it means and nobody up the stair says it aloud.
read.again: The white hand on the rubble, palm scored through.

board.text: RELIEF PUMPING — THE SINK — PRECINCT WORKS. Three pumps, their hours in a grid, and a line ruled through the spring weeks for pumps 2 and 3: DIVERTED TO PRECINCT SUPPLY, AS PER PLAN (CL. 31, GROWTH). Beside each spring week somebody has pencilled a number in feet.
board.again: DIVERTED TO PRECINCT SUPPLY, AS PER PLAN, and the pencilled feet beside each week.

copied.text: Clause 31, in your own hand, with the feet beside it. It reads worse copied.

nine.text: The lens reads the board at the speed a machine reads, and then the pencilled feet at the speed a person does. "Clause 31: growth. Clause 14: the drains are the city's first duty." A click. "The record suggests 14 outranks 31. The record has always suggested it. Nobody has asked the record." It opens its chest, which you did not know it could do, and a form comes out with its plate already pressed into it. "Variance. I am an assessor. Assessors vary." It hands it to you. "Give it to the keeper. The city will notice point six and I will note that it noticed."

decision.text: Assessor Nine stamped a variance putting the Sink's drains before the Precinct's growth, because you asked it to.

watched.text: A warden has followed you in and stands in the dial room's door with his hand on nothing in particular. "Out." Dagny Roos, at the panel, does not look up.
watched.again: "Out," the warden in the door says again, a little closer to meaning it.

options.text: (Wait for the count, when the door is empty, and come back.)

mods.why: one warden sleeps at the sandbags after midnight

sneak_ok.text: Twice a day the wardens walk the pad to count the shanties. The second time, the door is a door. You are in the dial room before the count reaches the raft.

sneak_no.text: The count is shorter than you thought. "Out," the warden says again, from closer.

dial.text: The relief dial: a pre-Burn panel with three brass levers and a wax seal over the spring stops, the Ledger's seal, cracked once already and mended. The levers read 1 — SINK, 2 — PRECINCT, 3 — PRECINCT. A log on a chain, in Dagny's hand, every day for eleven years.
dial.again: The three brass levers, the mended seal, the log on its chain.

options.text: (Break the seal and retime pumps 2 and 3 to the Sink.)

mods.why: the stops are arithmetic, and you can do it
the keeper marked the stops for you on her leave

retime_ok.text: The seal comes away like a scab. The stops are arithmetic: the spring weeks, the hours, the feet. You move two levers and the thud through the wall doubles, and then, after a minute, something under the floor changes pitch, which is the water deciding to go the other way. Dagny Roos comes to the door of the dial room and looks at the levers and at you and goes back to her panel without a word, and writes in the log, and what she writes is the time.

interject.text: "The seal," Nine says. "That is unlawful under four clauses." The lens clicks. "The record suggests the water does not read clauses. I will note the time also."

retime_no.text: The seal comes away and the first lever does not move and the second trips something, and a red lamp lights on the board outside, where the wardens are. You have a minute, perhaps, before the count comes early.

text.text: The levers read 1 — SINK, 2 — SINK, 3 — SINK, under a broken seal. The log says the time and nothing else.
The levers read 1 — SINK, 2 — SINK, 3 — SINK. A variance is pinned over the seal with the clause number ringed. The log says the time and, under it, *Clause 14*.
The levers read SINK, SINK, SINK, and the seal is on the floor, and a Pale kin sits on the keeper's stool with a gun across his knees while Dagny Roos works round him.

intro.text: A woman at a panel with her sleeves rolled and a scar down one cheek the shape of a thrown wrench, who does not stop working to talk. "Dagny Roos. Keeper. Three pumps; I keep them running, I don't say where they run. The board outside says that. Read the board."

options.text: Roos, H. Spring before last. Stair.

mods.why: you said his name and she did not stop you
a card she has to answer to

again.text: "Keeper." The panel.
again.again: She tightens something on the panel that did not need tightening, and waits.

mods.why: you said his name and she did not stop you
a card she has to answer to

schedule.text: "Three pumps. All three the Sink's, forty weeks of the year. Twelve weeks — the spring — two of them go to the Precinct's supply. Clause 31. Growth." She says the clause like a brand name. "I've kept them eleven springs. I've pencilled the feet beside every week. Nobody up the stair has read the feet. Read the board; it's the same board."

son.text: The wrench stops. "Hal. Sixteen. He was quick on the stair, usually." She puts the wrench down with care. "The year they ruled the line through two and three, the water came a hand higher than my feet said, and the stair was a river for an hour. I kept the pumps that spring. I keep them every spring. You want to know why." It is not a question. "Because if I don't, somebody who didn't lose anybody will."

interject.text: "Sixteen," Ilya says, and nothing after it. He looks at the wall as if he could see the stair through it.

options.text: Then let me at the dial.

leave_ok.text: She tears a corner off the log and writes on it against the panel. "Bearer may enter the house. The wardens may argue with me." She does not hand it to you; she leaves it on the panel for you to take. "I didn't see you go in. I've marked the spring stops on the back. Don't touch pump one; pump one is mine."

leave_no.text: "I keep them. I don't set them. The board's outside and the wardens are beside it." The wrench starts again.

variance.text: She reads it twice, the second time with her finger under the clause. "Fourteen." Then she walks into the dial room with the paper in her fist and does a thing she has not done in eleven years, which is reach past the seal and move two levers herself. The thud through the wall doubles. She pins the variance over the seal, writes the time in the log, and under it, the clause. "The drains," she says, to the panel. "Tell whoever signed it that the keeper read it."

text.text: "A variance." She has it pinned over the seal. "Eleven years I've wanted a piece of paper. I'll tell Hal, when I'm on the wall."
"Somebody retimed my pumps." She does not look at you. "I've told the wardens I don't know who. Which is nearly true. The log says the time."
"The Pale have the house. They let me keep the pumps; the pumps are the only thing in it they don't understand." She wipes her hands. "The Precinct will come. I'll be at the panel when it does."

fight.text: She is under the panel with her arms over her head and the pumps still running.
fight.again: Still under the panel. The pumps still running.

intro.text: An old woman at a table under the wall of names with a tin of chalk and a kettle, who looks at you the way the wall does. "Mother Lusk. I keep the tally. Name, year, where the water took them. Chalk's a Toll; names are free. You're not from down here or you'd know which you wanted."

options.text: The line on the pier. Who goes on the wall?
The numbers beside the names. The Precinct's kind.

again.text: "Chalk's a Toll."
again.again: She counts the chalk in the tin, and waits for you to want something.

line.text: "The ones who can't climb a stair fast with the water on it. The old. The small. The ones with the wet in their chest who stop to breathe on the fifth step." She counts chalk. "Twelve years ago the pumps kept it to the knee. Then the Precinct wanted growth, and two pumps, and the stair's a river for an hour each spring. An hour's enough. Read the wall; it's mostly STAIR."

numbers.text: She does not pretend. "The dead don't need a number. The living up the stair sometimes do: someone the lens hasn't seen, with a card that says they're someone it has. A man in the market pays four Tolls a number every spring. It buys chalk for a year." She looks at the wall. "They'd have wanted to be useful. Most of them were."

interject.text: "A citizen's number, four Tolls," Odile murmurs. "On the floor it would fetch forty." Then, to you, quite gently: "Don't tell her, my dear. She would only buy more chalk."

judge.text: "I sell a number the city gave them and never used. The city sold them the water." She puts the chalk down. "Chalk's a Toll. Judging's free, and I've heard it."

useful.text: "That's what I say. On the bad nights."

who.text: "Nobody. That's the Sink's whole constitution." She counts on her fingers. "The Pale, east, by fear; they take the walk and what's owed and they'll take no chrome near them. Ocho, south, by kindness, which is slower. Teng, by appetite. The Precinct, by the pumps, from above, which is the only one of them that counts." The fifth finger stays down. "And me, by chalk."

intro.text: A man on a raft of doors lashed to drums, with a pole and a beard that has been in the water as often as the raft. "Jory. I pole the deep bit. Raft takes two; takes one and a box. Two Tolls across to the clinic, which saves your boots and the third board of the walk, which is gone."

again.text: "Two across."
again.again: He leans on the pole, and the raft leans with him.

under.text: "Streets. Shops with the glass still in. Cars." He looks at the water, which does not look back. "Found a car under where the clinic is, the year the line went up two hands. Family in it, belted. They'd driven down here when the road was a road and the water came up quicker than their doors." He poles. "Mother Lusk has them on the wall. No names; I gave her the plate number."

intro.text: A woman in a shanty door on stilts, breathing with a whistle in it. "Ailsa. Don't mind the whistle; it's Ocho's lungs, and they're better than mine were." She nods at the water under her floor. "You're new. Everyone's new once. Then you're on the wall or you're me."

options.text: Who's on the wall of yours?
Ocho fitted you lungs. For what?

again.text: "Mind the third board."
again.again: She breathes, whistling, and waits for you to say it.

options.text: Who's on the wall of yours?

wall.text: "My Davey. Spring before last. Stair." She says it like a street address. "Same spring as the keeper's boy, Hal Roos. She keeps the pumps that drowned him. I used to think that was a hard thing. Now I think it's the only thing."

lungs.text: "For a bowl of soup a week, which I bring, and he doesn't eat. Free means free; he'll tell you. Dark chrome, Mender-made, no leash on it, no number." She breathes, whistling. "What it costs is him. Look at him when you go down. He hasn't slept since the line went up."

intro.text: A boy leaning on the shelf wall with his hands in his pockets and his eyes on everyone's. "Run anything. Two Tolls. Not east." He looks you over for weight. "Teng pays by the pound. I don't ask of what."

options.text: Teng's cold box. Where does it fill from?

mods.why: fruit, down here, is a bribe
you have Tolls showing

again.text: "Not east."
again.again: His eyes go over everyone on the shelf, and come back to you.

options.text: Teng's cold box. Where does it fill from?

mods.why: fruit, down here, is a bribe
you have Tolls showing

box_ok.text: He looks east, which he has told you not to go. "The Pale. Man owed them, last week — Mwangi's cousin, the other Mwangi. They took him off the walk and he walked back lighter and Teng's box was full by dark." He shrugs with one shoulder. "I ran the box. Didn't ask. It was heavy for the size."

intro.text: A neat man behind a counter in a container lit green from a cold box, with scales and a ledger and no smell at all, which is the thing you notice. "Teng. Anything that was ever warm, fair price, no questions, which is also a price." He weighs you with his eyes and writes nothing down. "Buying, or selling?"

options.text: Where does the box fill from?

again.text: "Buying, or selling?"
again.again: The cold box hums green. He waits behind the scales.

options.text: Where does the box fill from?

heart.text: "A heart." He opens the cold box, which breathes out, and takes out a steel tin the size of a lunch and sets it on the scales, and the scales agree with him. "Chilled this week. A hundred and fifty. Ocho won't buy from me and he'll fit what you bring him, and he'll ask, and you'll say the water." A bag inside with a number inked on it, crossed out.

passives.text: The ink of the crossing-out is fresh. Things the water takes do not have their numbers crossed out; they have them chalked on a wall.

options.text: A hundred and ten, and I don't say the water. I say nothing.

low_ok.text: "Nothing is cheaper than the water. A hundred and ten." The tin comes across with the ice already weeping at its corners.

low_no.text: "A hundred and fifty. The ice is mine too."

sold.text: "Keep it cold. Keep it quick. Tell him the water."

interject.text: "Fresh ink on that number," Ash says, very quietly, outside. "Somebody wrote it this week, friend, and somebody else crossed it out. That's not the water."

where.text: "The water." He says it the way the board says *as per Plan*. "Every spring the water takes thirty people and gives back what it doesn't want. I keep what it doesn't want cold. That's a service." He closes the ledger. "The rest of the year, people bring me things. I don't ask. Ask Kye; Kye runs the box and asks nothing, which is why he runs it."

intro.text: A big man on a cot made small by sitting very still. "Baraka. Mwangi." He breathes between the names. "Pumped the Sink for the Precinct eleven years. The wet got in. Ocho says it skips." He listens to it. "It skips."

options.text: If a heart came. From the Pale. Off somebody who owed them.

again.text: "It skips."
again.again: He listens to his chest, and waits.

options.text: If a heart came from the Pale.

heart.text: He does not take long. "I'd take it from the Ledger itself." He looks at his hands. "Ocho won't like it. Tell Ocho I said. Tell him the Code says I decide."

cousin.text: "Mal." The heart skips; you can see it in his neck. "Owed the Pale for a winter's coal. Walked back off the east bank lighter, Kye says. He's alive. He's a kidney down and alive, in the shanty by the raft." He closes his eyes. "Everyone down here is a piece of somebody."

text.text: "It ticks." He puts a hand flat on his chest and smiles with half his face. "I can live with ticking."
"It doesn't skip." He says it like a man reading a notice he does not believe yet. "It doesn't skip."

flooded.text: Anju, at Ocho's table, with his sodium lamp turned down to save it and her sleeves tied back. The cots are on bricks now. "Don't touch the table," she says, and then, because you have not asked: "He held the door. The water came up the stair a hand over the chalk and he stood in the door so it would come in slow, and it did, and then it was over him." She wrings out a cloth. "I can boil, and stitch, and set. I can't fit. The hands come in the third year. This is my second."
flooded.again: Anju at Ocho's table, the lamp turned down. She looks up, and waits.

intro.text: A young woman with her sleeves tied back and her hands red from boiled water. "Anju. Apprentice. Don't touch the shelf; everything on it's clean and nothing else down here is." She looks at the cots. "If you're sick, sit. If you're not, he'll find you something to hold."

options.text: The big man on the end cot.
The Code. The thing on the board.

again.text: "Don't touch the shelf."
again.again: Anju wrings out a cloth over the basin and waits.

options.text: The big man on the end cot.

tam.text: "Baraka. Heart. The wet gets into the pump-hands first; they stand in it." She lowers her voice. "He needs a new one and Ocho won't buy from Teng, and Teng is the only cold box in Meridian that isn't the Concern's. So Baraka sits. Ask Ocho. He'll say it plainer than I can."

code.text: "Fit only what the patient can bear. That's the whole of it; the rest is how." She counts on red fingers. "No leash — nothing that phones home. Dark chrome, Mender-made, or old, never Concern. The patient decides. And free means free, which is his, not the Code's, and it's killing him." She picks up a cloth. "Two years I've held the lamp. He says the hands come in the third."

intro.text: A broad man of sixty at a scrubbed table under a sodium lamp, washing to the elbow in a basin that steams. One of his hands is chrome, old chrome, a surgeon's hand; the other is his and shakes very slightly until he puts it in the water. "Ocho. Sit if you're sick. Hold something if you're not." He does not ask your name. "Free. Before you ask. Free means free."

passives.text: The chrome hand is a Gyro Hand, pre-Burn, and the arm it is fitted to has a Mender's scar round it, not a clinic's. He fitted it himself, or someone like him did.

options.text: Free. What does it cost you?
I've a piece to fit. Or one to look at.
(Put the boxed Second Heart on the table.)

text.text: "Sit or hold." He is washing. Baraka's cot has Baraka sitting up on it.
"Sit or hold."

again.again: He goes on washing, to the elbow, and waits.

options.text: I've a piece to fit. Or one to look at.
(Put the boxed Second Heart on the table.)

free.text: "Sleep." He says it flatly, drying the chrome hand, which does not need drying. "And the pieces. Kuhn sells me what she can't sell up the stair, and the Wheel brings old chrome down in boxes, and I fit it into people who'd otherwise be on the wall, and I don't charge, and so I have nothing, and so I can't buy the one thing I need, which is a heart, for a man who pumped for the Precinct eleven years." He looks at the end cot. "That's what free costs. Sit or hold."

interject.text: "Free," Odile says, as if the word were a debt gone bad. Then, more quietly: "My dear, I have never once seen it priced so high."

tam.text: "A heart. His is drowning in him." He wipes the table that is already clean. "I can fit a real one, if it comes through that door cold and quick. I can fit a Second Heart, dark chrome, if one comes through it in a box; Kuhn had one, once, and Teng has one now at a price that is a joke with a number in it." He puts both hands flat. "I won't buy from Teng. Teng buys from the water, he says. The water doesn't cross out numbers."

options.text: Then let me bring one. You don't ask me where.

tam_ask.text: "I'll ask." He is not angry; he is tired. "The Code says the patient decides. It doesn't say I keep my mouth shut. Bring it. I'll ask. Baraka will answer. That's the order of it."

text.text: "You held a clamp once." He looks at your hands. "Hold one again, steadier, and I'll say the words."

"I don't take apprentices. I take hands." He nods at Anju. "Two years she's held the lamp. Hold a clamp through one fitting without it shaking and I'll say the words over you, and they're the only words there are."

options.text: (Hold out your hands.) Try me on the next one.

mods.why: your hand does not shake
steady

where.text: He opens the tin and looks for a long moment at the bag inside, at the number on it, at the ink through the number. "Where did this come from?"

options.text: The Pale's cold store. Off a man who owed them. He's alive.
Under the water. Jory found a car.

mods.why: there is a car, and Jory would say so

text.text: "The Pale." He closes the tin. "Baraka already told me he'd take it from the Ledger itself. He said the Code says he decides. He's right, and I taught him that, and I wish I hadn't." He washes. "Clamp."

"The Pale, then, by the ink, whoever you say." He goes to the end cot and crouches and says something to Baraka, and Baraka says one word back before the sentence is finished, and Ocho stands up older. "The Code says the patient decides." He washes. "Clamp."

where_lie.text: "A car." He looks at the tin again, and then not. "Jory would say so." He washes. "Clamp."

interject.text: Tamsin looks at you for a long moment across the table. She doesn't say *a car*. She doesn't have to; you can see her write it down somewhere.

where_caught.text: "A car." He does not raise his voice. "Cars don't cross out numbers." He goes to the end cot, and crouches, and asks, and comes back older. "The patient decides. I'll fit it. I'll remember you said a car." He washes. "Clamp."

chrome.text: "Dark. Mender-made. No leash." He turns the box over and reads the Mender's mark on it with his thumb. "He can bear it. He's borne the Precinct eleven years." He washes. "Clamp. Anju, the lamp."

fit_heart.text: An hour under the sodium lamp with the Sink dripping on the roof. The chrome hand does not shake; the other one he keeps out of it. Anju holds the lamp. You hold the clamp, which holds the thing that is keeping Baraka Mwangi alive while the other thing is taken out of him.

mods.why: your hand does not shake
steady
quick when it matters

fit_chrome.text: An hour under the sodium lamp with the Sink dripping on the roof. Dark chrome goes in differently: a frame, a seat, the box's contents clicking into the seat like a cartridge. The chrome hand does not shake. Anju holds the lamp. You hold the clamp.

mods.why: your hand does not shake
steady

done_heart.text: It beats. Ocho watches it beat for a count of twenty, which is the longest you have seen him be still, and then closes, and washes, and says to the table, not to you: "Fit only what the patient can bear." Anju, with the lamp, says, "He said the words." Ocho says, "I said the words. Wash your hands, apprentice. Everything down here is dirty."

interject.text: "Fit only what the patient can bear," Ash says under his breath, the way the Choir says the sky-song: trying how it sits in his own mouth.

decision.text: You held the clamp while Ocho gave Baraka Mwangi a new heart, and Ocho said the Menders' words over you.

done_chrome.text: It ticks. Ocho listens to it tick for a count of twenty, and closes, and washes, and says to the table, not to you: "Fit only what the patient can bear." Anju, with the lamp, says, "He said the words." Ocho says, "I said the words. Wash your hands, apprentice. Everything down here is dirty."

interject.text: "Fit only what the patient can bear," Ash says under his breath, the way the Choir says the sky-song: trying how it sits in his own mouth.

decision.text: You held the clamp while Ocho fitted Baraka Mwangi a Second Heart, and Ocho said the Menders' words over you.

pell_heart.text: The clamp moves. Not much; enough. "Anju. Lamp to me, clamp to you." She takes it without a word and it does not move again. An hour later it beats, and Ocho watches it beat for a count of twenty, and washes. "He lives. You'll hold it steadier next time. There's always a next time down here."

decision.text: Ocho gave Baraka Mwangi a new heart; Anju held the clamp when yours shook.

pell_chrome.text: The clamp moves. Not much; enough. "Anju. Lamp to me, clamp to you." She takes it without a word and it does not move again. An hour later it ticks, and Ocho listens, and washes. "He lives. You'll hold it steadier next time. There's always a next time down here."

decision.text: Ocho fitted Baraka Mwangi a Second Heart; Anju held the clamp when yours shook.

words.text: A shanty woman with a hand crushed by a pump drum; a Gyro Hand from the Wheel's box, old chrome, the twin of his own. You hold the clamp and it does not move. He says the words over the table with her still open on it. "Fit only what the patient can bear." Then: "Wash your hands, apprentice."

decision.text: Ocho said the Menders' words over you at his table in the Sink.

shake.text: It moves. "Anju." She takes it. Afterwards he dries the chrome hand that does not need drying and says, "Next time," which down here is not a refusal.

intro.text: A woman in a container chair with skin the colour of the water and hair the colour of bone, who looks at your hands before your face. "You came past three of mine. Brave, or deaf." She does not get up. "Saskia Lehto. The Pale. Show me your hands." You show her. "No chrome. Good. Keep it that way down here, or don't come down here."

options.text: The pumps. Spring. You want them.
There's a heart in your cold store with a number crossed out.
Call yours off the walk. I come and go.

mods.why: she has seen your hand
she has seen your eyes

again.text: "Hands." You show her. "Good."
again.again: She looks at your hands again without asking, and nods.

options.text: The heart in your cold store.

mods.why: she has seen your hand
she has seen your eyes

pumps.text: "The pumps are ours by water. The Precinct has them by paper and two guns." She leans forward for the first time. "Twelve weeks a year they drown us for a number up the stair. I've nine kin who'll go down the walk with me and two who'll come back. That's the arithmetic. I've been waiting for someone to change it." She looks at your hands again. "You change arithmetic. I can see it on you."

options.text: There's paper that outranks their paper. Let me try it first.

paper.text: "Paper." She sits back. "Try it. When it doesn't work, I'm here. The water doesn't read."

seize.text: She stands. It is a different thing when she stands. "Then it's now." Three kin come off the fire without being called. "Two wardens, two guns, one door. Dagny stays alive; Dagny keeps the pumps. The rest is the walk's." She looks at you once more. "In front, you said."

decision.text: You went down the stilt-walk with the Pale to take the pump house from the Precinct.

won.text: The pump house, with the Precinct's lamps still on it and nobody's wardens at the door. Saskia Lehto stands in it with her hand on a pump like a woman touching a horse. "Ours by water. Now by the walk too." Dagny Roos is at the panel, alive, not looking at anyone. Lehto does not thank you; she gives you something better, which is a nod from the Pale. "Keep your hands. Come east any time."

held.text: "The house holds." She is on the pump pad now, most days, and the kin have moved the fire. "The Precinct will come. We'll be here. So will the water."
held.again: "Holds," she says, from the pump pad, and looks at your hands.

heart.text: "He owed. He paid. He's alive — we're not animals; we took what he had two of." No shame in it; it is a ledger. "The box is Teng's by dark. This one he hasn't had yet." She watches you want it. "Eighty, and you take it from the cold store yourself, and you tell Ocho whatever you like."

heart_paid.text: "The store's open. Take the tin and nothing else." She sits back down. "And tell Ocho it was the water. He likes the water."

heart_no.text: "Then sit with Baraka while he drowns in his own chest and tell him about living men." She does not get up. "Go on. Clinic's south."

walk_ok.text: "Come and go." She says it to the kin, not to you, and they sit back down. "You've a face the water hasn't had. Keep it out of my cold store."

walk_no.text: "No." The kin do not sit down. "Walk ends at the sandbags. It always did."

scald.text: "Before the Burn finished burning, the city's chrome all woke up at once and did what it was told, and what it was told was *hold still*. Everyone with a leash in them stood in the street and held still and the fire came." She does not blink. "Our grandparents watched. We don't forget. No chrome, ever, and nobody with chrome among us, and we take it out of people who owe us, which is the same rule from the other end."

interject.text: Odile has had her chrome hand in her coat pocket since the walk. She does not take it out now, and she does not say anything at all.
"Hold still," Nine repeats. For once the lens does not click. "The record has an entry for that day. It is one line long."

fight.again: The kin are up off the fire with what they have. Nobody is talking.

board.text: THE LOOP — LANTERN ROW. The tram with its doors open and a tube over the board, pink. PRECINCT 2 · OLD MARKET 2 · THE STACKS 3 · BRIDGEWARD 3 · CLOVER 4 · THE DOCKS 4. Chalk through the Docks: NO BRIDGE. Under CLOVER, in a different chalk: DUSK — 20 TO RUN.
board.again: The tram under its pink tube, doors open. NO BRIDGE; and under CLOVER, DUSK — 20 TO RUN.

docks.text: NO BRIDGE, chalked through THE DOCKS. Under it, in a newer chalk somebody has gone over twice: BY CLOVER — QUAY TRAM 2. A woman on the bench with a basket on her knees says the Loop's Docks line went over Bridgeward's bridge, and the bridge went into the river in the Charter Wars with a tram on it. "Carrick's across the dry river," she says. "Round by the Wall: the river road south from the gate, an hour on foot outside the law. Or the Loop to Clover and the quay tram round the ring road. The Line comes in there, and the tide boat, and the barges." She lowers her voice. "And at night, they say, a basket on a wire from Bridgeward's drop, if you know who to wave a lamp at."
docks.again: BY CLOVER — QUAY TRAM 2, under the NO BRIDGE.

read.text: THE COINAGE, in gold tube over a brick door, and a hand painted under it with the palm scored through — the Pale's mark — and over that, in gold paint, a coin. The Gilt's answer.
read.again: THE COINAGE in gold tube, and the gold coin painted over the Pale's hand.

read.text: A green tube and no name. Through the door, tables, and the sound Dust makes when it is being lost by people who can afford it.
read.again: The green tube, and Dust being lost behind the door.

read.text: THE VELVET, in pink, with the T burned out so that it reads THE VELVE. Nobody has fixed it in a year; it is said with the T anyway. A queue, orderly, under the tube.
read.again: THE VELVE, in pink, and the queue under it.

read.text: A violet tube over a container door: THE LANTERN — REVERIES BY THE HOUR — YOURS OR BETTER. Smaller, under it: WE DO NOT BUY FROM THE DROWNED.
read.again: THE LANTERN, violet. WE DO NOT BUY FROM THE DROWNED.

read.text: WORKS. A chain across the street east and two Gilt on the chain. Behind them the tubes are dark all the way to Bridgeward, which is where the chain is really about.
read.again: The chain across the street, the two Gilt on it, and the dark beyond.

read.text: LANTERN ROW, in every colour, on a board that was once a tram timetable. Under it, in warden stencil: NO WARDEN SERVICE. Under that, in chalk: GOOD.
read.again: NO WARDEN SERVICE. GOOD.

read.text: A tide mark on the canal wall with a date beside it, and the water a foot below it. The canal was a street; the Sink's pumps found it. It runs warm and it throws the tubes back at you, pink and cyan, all night.
read.again: The tide mark, and the warm canal a foot below it, full of pink and cyan.

look.text: Shay's boat: a flat hull of doors with a pole and a lantern, tied at the quay. Two Tolls, the board says, and a hand painted pointing across.
look.again: Shay's boat at the quay, and the painted hand pointing across.

card.text: TONIGHT'S CARD, in chalk on a post: TEAGUE v. DOUBT — house pays two to one. ANVIL v. ALL COMERS — thirty to enter, ninety standing. HANDS AND IRON. GUNS WITH MAB. Under it, older: NOBODY HAS STOOD SINCE SPRING.
card.again: TEAGUE v. DOUBT. ANVIL v. ALL COMERS. NOBODY HAS STOOD SINCE SPRING.

passives.text: The chalk under DOUBT has been rubbed out and written again tonight, and the odds beside it moved a notch the house's way.

intro.text: A woman with a slate, a stool, a cash-box and a revolver she does not need to touch. "Mab Corrigan. The pit's mine, the floor's washed, the odds are chalk. Undercard's twenty, two to one. The comer's thirty to enter and ninety if you're standing at the end." She looks you up and down the way a scale would. "Nobody's standing."

options.text: What would the house pay for the comer to fall in the second?

again.text: "Chalk." The slate.
again.again: She writes a number on the slate, rubs it out, and waits.

options.text: What would the house pay for the comer to fall in the second?

under.text: "Kariuki or Doubt." She has the slip written before you answer; she writes both and tears one.

bell.text: An hour, and the bell. Kariuki is the small one and fights like it, in and out; Doubt is the big one and fights like a man with somewhere to be. In the second, Doubt walks onto a left that a child would have seen coming and goes down, carefully, like a man checking the floor for coins. The crowd knows. The crowd always knows. The house pays anyway.

collected.text: "Forty." Counted onto the slate, not into your hand; you pick it up yourself. "The small one. Everyone says the small one, after."

torn.text: "Doubt." She almost smiles. "Nobody's ever sure why."

comer.text: "Anvil's in the ring. Hands and iron only — leave the guns with me; you get them back, you always do." She holds out the cash-box lid. "Thirty."

comer_go.text: "Go and stand in front of him. He'll do the rest." The slate: COMER — 3 TO 1. Somebody in the crowd has already bet against you.

interject.text: "Left hand drops when he breathes out," Wren says, watching Anvil and not you. "Count his breaths. Go on the fourth."

dive.text: She does not look up from the slate. "Sixty. After. From me. And nobody says." The chalk does not stop. "Anvil knows. Anvil doesn't mind. Anvil's been in the second since spring."

dive_done.text: "The second. Not the first; the first's an insult. Not the third; the third's a crime." She writes nothing down.

text.text: The slate is still up. COMER — STANDING. She looks at you for a long moment over it. "You had a deal." The cash-box opens anyway. "Ninety. The deal was sixty and I don't pay men who don't fall. Take the ninety and don't come to me for a deal again."

The slate is still up. COMER — STANDING. The crowd is the loudest it has been all year and most of it is losing money. "Standing." She opens the cash-box. "Ninety. And this." A brass token, pit-stamped. "The Skirts' pits honour it, and the Crown's, if you ever stand in one of those."

decision.text: You stood in Lantern Row's pit against Anvil and were standing at the end.

news.text: a comer stood against Anvil in Lantern Row's pit and was standing at the end

text.text: "The second." She says it like a date. "Sixty." Counted onto the slate. "That's a deal kept, which on this row is rarer than standing."
"Anvil." She wipes the slate. "Thirty's chalk. There's tomorrow; there's always tomorrow, down here."

interject.text: "The second," Wren says. "Not the first, not the third." She isn't smiling. "You'd have made a Dog."

decision.text: You took a dive in Lantern Row's pit for the house's sixty.

intro.text: A man in the ring with his hands wrapped and bolt knuckles on the wraps, standing the way a wall stands. "Anvil. You're not on the card." He does not look at you long. "Mab's thirty. Then you're on it."
intro.again: "Mab's thirty," Anvil says, without turning round.

ready.text: "You paid Mab." He rolls his shoulders once. "Hands and iron. I don't go for the head unless you do. Floor's washed; try not to be the reason it needs washing." The crowd leans in over the chain.
ready.again: He rolls his shoulders again. The crowd is still leaning.

stood.text: "Standing." He says it with something that is nearly respect and nearly relief. "Nobody's done that since spring. The spring one was me." He unwraps a hand. "Mab's got your purse. Go and get it before she thinks of a reason."
stood.again: "Standing," he says again, and nods to you the way he nods to nobody else.

floored.text: "Floor's clean." He means it kindly. "You cleaned it. Thirty gets you another go; the second go is the one that counts, most of them."
floored.again: "Floor's clean," he says. "Thirty, and we see."

intro.text: A small fighter wrapping her hands with the care of someone who has broken them before. "Kariuki. I'm the small one. Bet on the small one; the big one's got somewhere to be." She looks at Doubt across the ring, and at Mab's shack, and back at her hands.
intro.again: Kariuki, wrapping her hands again. "The small one," she says.

doubt.text: "Mab's shack, after. With a slip in his hand and a limp he hasn't got." She ties off the wrap. "Everyone on the Row knows. Everyone bets anyway. That's the Row."

intro.text: A big man with a beard and bolt knuckles, looking at the pit floor as if it owed him. "Doubt. They call me Doubt. Nobody's sure why." He does not look at Kariuki. "Second round. Could go either way."
intro.again: "Could go either way," Doubt says to the floor.

passives.text: He is counting something on his fingers inside his coat, and it is not rounds.

intro.text: A woman at a desk between three cots with headsets on hooks over them, and a locker behind her with a violet tube on it. "Ysolde Nwosu. The Lantern. Yours or better." She taps the hooks. "A Summer in the Crown. The Race. Five an hour, either. And the evidence shelf, which isn't for sale, and which you'll ask about anyway."

options.text: A Summer in the Crown. (5 Tolls)

again.text: "Yours or better."
again.again: She straightens a headset on its hook and waits.

options.text: A Summer in the Crown. (5 Tolls)

what.text: "A day someone had, on a reel, through a headset. The Crown records art. The Row records whatever sells. Wardens record for evidence." She shrugs. "Some people live in them. I don't sell to those; look at the cots after and you'd stop too."

shelf.text: She takes a reel off the locker shelf with two fingers, the way you hold something that is not yours. "A Rustmouth brought it off a warden's shelf. A man sat on that cot a season ago and paid me to record his last day in the city, start to end, and left before dawn. No face in it; he was a Choir man, they keep no likeness. The wardens wanted it for who he met." She puts it down between you. "Two hundred. Because wardens."

who.text: "I didn't watch it. I never watch the shelf." She means it. "Buy it and tell me, or don't."

trade.text: "A memory of yours." She looks at you properly for the first time. "The Cistern. Nobody up here has one of a cistern; nobody up here has been in one. An hour on the cot and the reel's yours." A pause. "It's not a copy. It's yours; you'll still have it. People say it feels thinner after. People say a lot."

decision.text: You sold a reverie of the Cistern to the Lantern, for the stranger's day.

reel.text: "Jack in here or don't jack in at all; the reel's keyed to my cots." She hangs a headset on the nearest hook. "I won't watch. I never watch the shelf."

interject.text: Tamsin has gone to stand by the door with her back to the cots. "That was ours," she says, to the street. "You sold ours." She doesn't come back in.

garden.text: Light. Real light, through a dome, on leaves that are green all the way through. You are carrying a tray; the hands are not yours and they are steady. A woman in grey silk at a glass table does not look at you as she takes a cup, and beyond her, over the parapet, the whole city lies in haze like something spilled. The air has no taste at all. You stand there a long time, holding the tray, and nobody asks you to stop.
garden.again: The dome, the green leaves, the tray in steady hands that are not yours. The woman in grey silk takes her cup again.

city.text: From up here the Precinct is a grid and Old Market is a stain and the canal is a bright thread, and you cannot see the Sink at all, which is the point of up here. The woman says, to nobody, "Bring the next one." The reel ends on the tray going back through a door.

line.text: Engine. Dust. A buggy of welded doors with a wheel in your hands that fights you, and six others beside you on a ring road of cracked concrete outside the Wall with the towers behind, and a flag. The flag drops.
