ask_ok.text: He looks at the wall for a long time, at the chalk under the names. "Coming back." He gets up, which takes a while, and the bench comes up with a bar, and under it a locker. "Then it's for that. Tell them Kibet kept it. Tell them Kibet kept the bench."

ask_no.text: "Nine years." He sits more firmly, if that is possible. "The tenth isn't you."

opened.text: Wren kneels at it the way she knelt at the stranger's coat in the Sallow, and what she takes out first is not the gun or the coin but a strip of cloth with a dog's head on it, and she holds it for a long time and then ties it round her arm without saying anything, and Kibet turns to the stove so that neither of you has to look at him.

back.text: "Mine." He does not look at it. "Chalk. Every spring. Kessler said they'd come back for the bridge when they were a crew again." He pokes the stove. "Perpetua said the same. She meant the children. Kessler meant the guns." A long pause. "If little Calloway ever comes back for the bridge, you tell her Kibet said the rope is what the bridge is for. The Rustmouths have one on the booth. Tell her that."

interject.text: "I heard him," Wren says, before you can say anything. She is looking at the stove, not at either of you. "The rope. I heard."

intro.text: A woman in a clean coat at the booth with a ledger that is not the Rustmouths' and a pen that is not from down here. "Ms Harrow. I hold the pen on the Bridgeward arrangement for House Vane." She does not offer a hand; she offers the sentence. "The toll is the Crown's. The chain is theirs. The arrangement is mine, Tuesdays, ten to four. You are not a Rustmouth. You may be a question."

options.text: What does a Tenured house want with a bridge that stops?
The Rustmouths keep more than the arrangement says.

again.text: "Tuesdays. Ten to four."
again.again: Ms Harrow uncaps the pen that is not from down here and waits.

options.text: What does Vane want with the bridge?
The Rustmouths keep more than they should.

road.text: "The near end." She says it as a surveyor would. "The Docks are across the river and the Loop does not cross it. A road would. A road needs a bridge, a bridge needs a near end, and the near end needs to be held by somebody who signs. House Vane intends to sign, by the Long Night." She looks at the chain. "The Rustmouths are a temporary arrangement. Most things down here are."

ledger.text: "Everyone keeps more than the arrangement says. That is what an arrangement is." A pause. "But the box keeps a ledger of its own, in a Rustmouth hand, and the box has a warden's stamp on it because the wardens wanted a count once, and the Rustmouths picked it before the wardens could read it. I would pay to read it. A hundred and twenty. It would be the end of the arrangement, which would be a pity for the Rustmouths and not for me."

show.text: She reads it standing, fast, and once, and closes it. "Thank you." A hundred and twenty, Crown-counted, in a paper sleeve. "The arrangement will be reviewed. You should not be on the bridge when it is." She puts the ledger in her coat; it is hers now, and so is whatever happens to the chain.

decision.text: You sold House Vane's agent the Rustmouths' own toll ledger.

masque.text: "By invitation." She looks you over the way a tailor would. "You'd need a chit, and a face the lens hasn't filed as something unfortunate, and clothes. The first can be bought; the second is your affair; the third is the Velvet's." It is the nearest thing to help she will give anyone.

intro.text: A carter on a crate with her cart beside her and nothing in it. "Sadie. Five to stand on the bridge, five to stand under it, five to breathe, soon." She looks at the chain. "Carted for the Dogs once, when they had the garage. They paid late and they paid. The Rustmouths pay the Crown and the Crown pays nobody."
intro.again: "Five to breathe, soon," Sadie says again, from the crate, by the empty cart.

dogs.text: "A crew. Took a cut and fixed your axle. Then the Crown put paper on the bridge and the Rustmouths picked it up, and the Dogs went west and became a gang, which is what happens to a crew with no bridge." She shrugs. "Kibet's in the garage. Kibet'll tell it longer."

car.text: The invitation car: brass, glass, a bench nobody sits on, and no fare box. It costs nothing. That is how you know what it costs.
car.again: The brass car, the bench nobody sits on, no fare box.

read.text: The lens: a glass eye on a brass post with a green light under it, cleaner than the one at the gate and the same eye. It looks at everyone who comes out of the car and decides, and the sergeant says aloud what it has decided. It does not look at the help.
read.again: The lens on its brass post, deciding. It does not look at the help.

read.text: BY INVITATION — CHIT, PASS OR STANDING — THE HELP ROUND THE BACK — THIS SEASON: HOUSE VANE. Under it, smaller, in the lens's own print: ALL FACES ARE FILED.
read.again: BY INVITATION. THIS SEASON: HOUSE VANE. ALL FACES ARE FILED.

intro.text: A sergeant in grey that has been pressed, with a carbine he has never fired up here and a face that has turned back better people than you with the same courtesy. "Face to the lens." You do. The green light thinks. "Sergeant Ambrose. The lens decides; I say it aloud. Chit, pass, or standing. The help goes round the back."

decision.text: You went up to the Crown on a Masque chit that was not yours.
You went up to the Crown as the help, on a kitchen pass.
You went up to the Crown on the Concern's card.
The Crown's lens admitted you on sight, and said why, aloud.

again.again: The sergeant waits, carbine easy, while the lens goes on looking at you.

chit_in.text: He reads it without touching it. "Lorne. One guest." He looks at the lens; the lens looks at you; nobody says that House Lorne's guest was going to be somebody else. "The hall is straight on. Mancuso keeps the door."

pass_in.text: "Kitchens." He does not look at the pass, or at you; that is what a pass is for. "Round the back. Brisk. Don't come out the front."

card_in.text: He looks at the card and something goes out of his shoulders. "The Concern's people are expected." He says it to the lens, not to you. "Straight on."

exchange_in.text: "The Exchange." He has a list and you are on it in a hand that is not his. "Straight on. Mind the lens; it has you now."

standing_in.text: "A house's client." The lens agrees, which is the only agreement that counts. "Straight on."

lens_in.text: The green light thinks for a long time, and clicks twice, and the sergeant reads the screen in his booth and reads it again. "ADMIT ON SIGHT." He says it as the lens says it, flat, and then, to you, with something else in it: "Magistrate-designate." The other warden has heard. By the time you reach the gate the terraces have heard.

interject.text: "Aloud," Nine says, very quietly. "No lens has said a file aloud in my service. It is showing you to them." A click. "I do not think that was for your benefit."

news.text: the Crown's lens admitted a stranger on sight and called them Magistrate-designate, aloud

belong_in.text: You walk the way the Madame walked you across her room three times, with the clothes doing the talking. The lens looks. The sergeant looks at the lens, and the lens does not disagree, because the lens has never been asked to disagree with bottle-green. "Straight on."

decision.text: You walked into the Crown in the Velvet's clothes, and the lens let bottle-green through.

belong_no.text: You walk. The lens looks, and thinks, and the sergeant reads the screen. "The lens disagrees." He is almost kind. "The car is behind you. Take it, and nobody files anything."

force.text: He sees it before you move, which is what he is for. The carbine comes up. "Nobody forces the Crown." The other two come off the wall.

decision.text: You went for the Crown's lift wardens.

in.again: "In," the sergeant says, without looking round.

fight.again: The lift wardens have their carbines up. Nobody is talking.

text.text: A glass table by the pool, with a cup on it. You have stood here. You have stood exactly here, holding a tray, with hands that were not yours, while a woman in grey silk did not look at you. The cup is the same cup. The hands, this time, are your own.
A glass table by the pool with a cup on it and a woman beside it who sees everything from here, which is what here is for.

read.text: THE MASQUE — HOUSE VANE — THE COMMITTEE SITS AT THE TOAST. Over the doors a lens, bigger than the lobby's, with a green light that does not blink. Everyone who goes in looks up at it, and smiles, because they have been taught to.
read.again: THE MASQUE — HOUSE VANE, and the big lens over the doors that does not blink.

read.text: A crane, in old brass, over a door: ASHBY-CRANE. The brass is older than the hall's gilt and has been polished more often, by people who were paid less.
read.again: The brass crane over the door: ASHBY-CRANE.

read.text: HALDEN — PORTRAITS — AS YOU WILL BE. Under it, a smaller card: SITTINGS BY APPOINTMENT. FORECAST SHEETS TO BE SUPPLIED BY THE CLIENT.
read.again: HALDEN — PORTRAITS — AS YOU WILL BE.

read.text: STAFF. The door is metal and the terraces' side of it is painted to look like the terraces. The kitchens' side is not painted at all.
read.again: STAFF, on a metal door painted on one side only.

read.text: The parapet. All of Meridian under it in haze: the Precinct a grid, Old Market a stain, the canal a bright thread, the Stacks a wall with lights in it, the broken bridge a finger pointing at the Docks. You cannot see the Sink at all. That is the point of up here.
read.again: Meridian in haze below the parapet, and no Sink anywhere in it.

intro.text: A man at the hall doors in House Vane's green with a sabre on his hip that is not for show and a scar on his cheek that was. "Ettore Mancuso. The house's door." He looks at your shoes, which is where he looks at everyone. "Chit, name, or face. The help goes round the back."

again.text: "Chit, name, or face."
again.again: He looks at your shoes again, and waits.

open.text: "Go in." He does not move his eyes from the promenade.

options.text: I stand for House Ashby-Crane. Draw.

admit.text: "Go in." He steps aside exactly as far as he has to.

admit_lens.text: He does not ask it. He has heard; the terraces have heard. He steps aside a full pace, which from Mancuso is a bow. "Designate."

admit_quiet.text: He looks at your shoes. The Madame did the shoes. He steps aside.

shoes.text: He looks at your shoes for a second longer than he looked at anyone else's. "The help goes round the back." He does not raise his voice; he does not need to; he has said it to the lens.

help.text: "Round the back. Brisk." He has already stopped looking at you.

who.text: "The house's blade. Vane has not fought in two seasons; a house that has a Mancuso does not need to." He almost smiles. "Honora's man took the Concern's coin and the lift. She has a bravo from the Row in borrowed shoes. One can tell by the shoes."

draw.text: He looks at you properly for the first time, at your hands and your feet and the blade. "For Ashby-Crane." The hall has gone quiet behind him. "A duel is a vote with the arithmetic shown. The Chair follows it; that is the one rule up here older than the lens." The sabre comes out as if it had been waiting. "To the floor. Not to the death; we are not the Row."

decision.text: You stood for House Ashby-Crane at the Masque and put Vane's duellist on the floor.

news.text: a stranger put Ettore Mancuso on the floor at Vane's Masque, for Ashby-Crane

decision.text: You stood for House Ashby-Crane at the Masque and went down to Vane's duellist.

text.text: He is on his feet again, with his arm bound, and he bows to you a quarter of an inch. "Well struck." He means it; it is the only thing up here anyone has meant all night.
"The Row's man went down. The house notes it." He looks at your blade the way he looked at your shoes. "Vane will remember you. That is not always good."
"You stood." He says it the way other people say well done. "Few do, up here. Go in; the house does not refuse the floor to someone who has been on it."

alarm.again: Mancuso has the sabre out, and the bell is going. Nobody is talking.

text.text: A woman in grey silk at a table with one cup on it, who has been looking at you since you came in because everyone has. "Celestine Vane. The house's." She does not offer a hand; she offers the chair beside her, which up here is more. "The lens said a word in my lobby tonight that it has not said in thirty years. Sit. Houses collect the future; it is the only thing we still make."

A woman in grey silk at a table with one cup on it. "Celestine Vane. The house's." She looks at the chit in your hand without appearing to. "Marguerite Lorne has no guest. Marguerite has a son at the Row. You are, then, a story, and I collect those." The chair beside her.

A woman in grey silk at a table with one cup on it, who looks at you the way the lens did and arrives at an answer faster. "Celestine Vane. The house's. It is my season." The chair beside her. "Sit. Everyone sits eventually; the ones who do it early are remembered."

options.text: Honora has a bravo from the Row. Who stands for Vane?
(Show her the studio's print: her, in the Chair.)
(Put the reel on the table.) A sitting, this season. Recorded as art.
The Concern sent a man. The Concern never sends a man.

again.text: "Sit."
again.again: She turns the cup a quarter turn and waits for you to be interesting.

options.text: (Show her the studio's print: her, in the Chair.)

chair.text: "The Committee of the Terraces has a Chair. The Chair signs." She turns the cup a quarter turn. "The road to the Docks. The bridge's near end. The water the Precinct lets up. And the Committee's forecasts, which the Exchange sells us by the sheet and which the Chair may sell on." A small smile. "The vote is at the toast. The file is not in doubt. Only the room."

machine.text: The renderer: a pre-Burn cabinet with a lens of its own, a slot for a sheet, a tray for prints, and a hum that is not the hall's. On its screen, a queue of names in the Crown's season, each with a sheet number beside it. At the top of the queue, unrequested, with no sheet number, dated the day you came through the gate: your name.
machine.again: The renderer's queue, and your name still at the top of it, unrequested.

intro.text: A woman in white with forearms like a hauler's and a voice that reaches the far end of forty covers. "Brisk. The kitchens. Nobody goes up the back stair I haven't fed." She looks at you and files you faster than the lens did. "You're not kitchens. Pass, or a reason, or out."

options.text: (The service pass.) Where do you want me?
I need the back stair into the hall.

again.text: "Pass, or a reason, or out."

pass.text: "Trays." She puts one in your hands with six glasses on it. "Up the back stair, round the hall once, don't look at them, they don't look at you. That's the help's one advantage up here; use it."

stair_ok.text: She looks at your hands, which have done something in their life, and at the hall's side of the door, which has not. "Trays." Six glasses. "Round the hall once. Don't look at them."

stair_no.text: "Out." She has already turned back to the stove. "Forty covers. Out."

tillie.text: She does not stop moving. "Four. The rubbish goes down at four, and the help, and anything in a kitchen coat with its head down." A tray. "She can be rubbish. Everybody is, in a lift. Tell her to leave the dress."

lift.text: The service lift: a cage that smells of the day's rubbish and the night's help, with a lever and no lens. It goes down to Old Market's works, where the Loop is, and comes back up at four with the morning.
lift.again: The service cage, the lever, no lens.

room.text: A room under glass with the light coming in sideways. You are sitting; the hands on the table are a woman's, ringed, still. Across the table a man in a coat that is not trying, with a sheet between you that has the Committee's crest on it. He says, "Terms," as if it were the name of a dish. The hands turn a cup a quarter turn.
room.again: The room under glass, the ringed hands, the man in the coat, *terms*. The reel begins where it always begins.

terms.text: "The Committee's forecasts, by the season, sealed, to the Concern, from the date the Chair signs. In return the Concern's backing on the vote, and the road, and the near end of a bridge." The hands do not move. A voice that is yours and is not says, "Done," and the man in the coat does not smile, because men like him do not need to. The reel ends on the cup, and the sound of a room that did not know it was listening.

terms_again.text: The Committee's forecasts, by the season, to the Concern; the road; the near end of a bridge. *Done.* The cup, a quarter turn. It does not change.

look.text: It's you. Older — forty, forty-five — on broad stone steps under a lamp, a city of towers behind you going up out of the frame, squinting into a wind. Something across your chest you took for a strap the first time, and have not been sure of since.
look.again: You, older, on the steps under the lamp, squinting into the wind.

passives.text: The shadows on your face fall left. The shadows on the towers fall right. There is no sun anywhere that does both.
No grain, anywhere, even blown up by your eye. Dust hangs in the air beside your shoulder, and the same mote hangs again by the lamp: drawn, not caught.

back.text: On the back, in pencil, in a hand that is not yours: 49 · VI · 12. A year, a month, a day. Along the bottom margin, printed, a short code — 0412/30 — and under it a line of print so small and so even it looks like a scratch until you tilt it.
back.again: The back: 49 · VI · 12 in pencil, the printed code, the scratch of microprint under it.

interject.text: "Forty-one years," Tamsin says, at your shoulder. "That's what everybody'd say. Everybody out here counts from the Burn." She frowns at it. "Everybody out here."
"Pencil's not his," Wren says. "He wrote small and square. That's somebody copying something they didn't understand."

options.text: (Let the link read the code off the city's wire.)

eyes.text: The optic finds the scratch and pulls it up until it is letters, flat and even as the Precinct's forms: RENDER — DESIGNATE — FROM FORECAST, R30 — DEPICTS R49.06.12. The pencil copied the date off the print and left off the one letter that mattered.

link.text: You think at the code and the city's wire thinks back, the way it does in a street with a lamp in it: a cold, polite query, a pause, a line in your skull in the Ledger's even hand. RENDER QUEUE 0412 — SUBJECT: DESIGNATE — RENDERED R30 FROM FORECAST — DEPICTS R49.06.12. Then the wire asks who is asking, and you stop thinking at it.

nine.speaker: npc_md_nine
nine.text: "Clause 40 forbids me to read a citizen their own forecast." The lens goes over the pencil once and stops at the margin, and clicks. "It does not forbid me to read a date. Forty-nine, sixth month, twelfth day. That is the Restoration Calendar; the Cistern would write it otherwise. R49 is nineteen years from today." A pause. "The margin is a render number. That is not a photograph. I am not permitted to say what it is a picture of, and I have not said it."

odile.speaker: npc_nb_03
odile.text: She holds it at arm's length, then takes her glasses off their chain and holds it close. "Oh, my dear." Very softly. "That is a delivery date. I have written ten thousand of them. Nobody writes a delivery date on a thing that has already been delivered." She taps the margin with the Gyro hand's fingernail. "And that is a lot number. Somebody has sold this, or means to. Forty-nine is the city's year. It is nineteen years off."

known.text: You, older, on the steps at the foot of the Archive Spire, under the lamp, in the city's year forty-nine: nineteen years from now. A picture of a day that has not come.

read.text: An enamel sign on a post at the mouth of a lane: NORTH — THE SPIRE CLOSE — COURT OF ACCOUNTS — CATALOGUE. Somebody has scratched under it, small: *and the steps*.
read.again: NORTH — THE SPIRE CLOSE. *And the steps.*

read.text: ARCHIVE SPIRE — THE CLOSE. COURT OF ACCOUNTS: WEST WING, IN SESSION WHEN CALLED. CATALOGUE: EAST WING, READERS BY SLIP. THE STEPS AND THE GREAT DOORS ARE CLOSED FOR WORKS. ALL PERSONS ARE RECORDED.
read.again: COURT, WEST. CATALOGUE, EAST. THE STEPS ARE CLOSED.

text.text: A works board on the scaffold, relettered: ARCHIVE SPIRE — RESTORATION — R30 WORKS — BROUGHT FORWARD. PUBLIC STEPS AND GREAT DOORS: REOPEN R30. The 30 is fresh white paint over a 49 that still shows through when the light is low. Below it, by landing, the same list as before, every date on it struck through and written again nineteen years sooner.

A works board on the scaffold, freshly lettered: ARCHIVE SPIRE — RESTORATION — R30 WORKS — ON SCHEDULE. PUBLIC STEPS AND GREAT DOORS: REOPEN R49. Below, by landing: 1 — FAÇADE. 2 — HALL OF RECORDS. 3 — COPY ROOM: MAGISTRATE'S CHAMBERS — REROUTED. The last word is new paint over old.

again.text: REOPEN R30, in fresh white over the 49.
R30 WORKS — ON SCHEDULE. REOPEN R49. Landing three, the copy room, and what it is to be.

scene.text: You stop on the fourth step without deciding to. The lamp behind your left shoulder. The doors above. The Crown's glass going up out of sight on either side. The wind off the canal, in your face, making you squint. It is the photograph. The angle is wrong by a stride, and the steps are cracked where the print has them whole, but it was made here, of you, standing about where you are standing now.

interject.text: Tamsin has stopped two steps below you. "Don't move," she says, and holds the photograph up at arm's length, between your face and hers, and lowers it slowly. "Oh," she says. "Oh, I don't like that."
Wren walks once round the lamp, the way she walks round a place she means to come back to in the dark. "Here," she says. "He stood you here." She does not say who.
Ash stays at the foot of the steps. "I'll not climb them," he says. "Not today. You go on." He looks at the lamp as if it owed him something.
"Delivery point," Odile murmurs. "Of course. One always sells a thing with its address on it."

Ilya looks at the lamp, the doors, the glass, the long lines of sight down into the square. "Good place to stand someone," he says. "If you wanted everyone to see them." He means it the way a sniper means it.
"The steps," Nine says. "I have walked past them for a hundred and twenty years. I did not know they were waiting for someone."

options.text: (Hold the photograph up against the steps.)

hold.text: Close enough to frighten you. Older you is standing one step higher, and the cracks are mended, and the scaffold is gone, and the board on it that says the steps reopen R49 is gone too, because it is R49. You put the photograph away and stand on your own step for a while.

text.text: The steps. The lamp. One step higher, in the picture, nineteen years from now.
The steps. The lamp. One step higher, in the picture.

again.again: The steps, and the lamp.

text.text: The lamp at the foot of the steps again, a stride to the left of where the photograph was made. The chain still lies coiled on the top step. The door is still an inch open, and the light behind it has not moved.

The foot of the Spire's steps, and the lamp you have looked at in a photograph since Knock: the same lamp, the same stone, a stride to the left of where the picture was made. The scaffold has come down off the middle flight since the card came. The chain is off the great doors and lies coiled on the top step like something asleep, and one leaf of the bronze stands an inch open with a light behind it that is not a lamp. Nobody is on the steps. Behind you the close goes on: the fire barrel, the people who came, Faulk's trestle, the lane to the Precinct. In front of you the steps go up.

pnr_foot.again: The foot of the steps, under the lamp.

interject.text: Tamsin stops a step below you and does not come up level. "I'll be one step down," she says. "Like the picture. Somebody ought to be where the photographer was." She does not smile. "Go on, then. Or don't. I'm not going anywhere either way."
"The steps," Nine says. "A hundred and twenty years I have walked past them. Today, if you go, I am walking up." The lens clicks. "I have logged it. It seemed the kind of thing that ought to be."

"Twenty-two to the first landing," Ilya says. "Counted them last night." He does not say why, and you do not ask.

"Every sheet I ever wrote had a date on it that somebody would one day reach," Odile says. "I always wondered what it felt like from their side." She looks at you. "No. Don't tell me. I'd only price it."
Ash stays on the bottom step, where he stood the first time. "I said I'd not climb them," he says. "I'll climb them today." He does not say which of the things he carries is coming up with him.
Kes puts her hand flat on the lamp post, the way she puts it on a machine to hear it. "It's cold," she says, surprised. "I thought it'd hum. Everything in this city hums."

look.again: The steel door in the Spire's foot. Warm. Humming, far down.

interject.text: "Below us," Nine says, "the city." It does not put its hand on the door. "I have never been sent down. Nobody is sent down. Things are sent down."

text.text: The steel door in the Spire's foot stands open on its stair, and nothing comes up it: no note, no warmth off the rock. Only the dark, and the smell of what was done down there.
The steel door in the Spire's foot stands open on its stair, and the note comes up it, as level as it ever was, as if nothing down there had changed. Something has.

The steel door in the Spire's foot stands open. VAULT OF ACCOUNTS — NO ENTRY — NO EXIT, in letters cut into the steel and never painted, and under them a stair going down through the rock into warm air that smells of dust and hot metal and paper. The note that has been under the close since the first time you stood on it comes up the stair to meet you. It is not louder down there. Only nearer.

vault_open.again: The steel door, open on the stair going down.

interject.text: "Things are sent down," Nine says, at the top of the stair. "Paper. Slips. Returns to be read in. Nobody is sent down." Its lens goes down the stair into the dark and comes back to you. "I am going down. I have logged that I decided to."
Ilya looks down the stair and counts under his breath, as far as the light goes. "Can't see the bottom," he says. "Never liked a stair I can't see the bottom of." He goes down the first step anyway.

look.text: A plinth in the middle of the close with its bolts polished and nothing on them. A brass plate: MAGISTRATE OF ACCOUNTS — THE LAST BEFORE — and a name chiselled off so carefully the stone is smooth. Somebody has left a cairn stone on the corner, and somebody else has knocked it off, and it has been put back.
look.again: The empty plinth. THE LAST BEFORE, and a smooth place where a name was.

intro.text: A broad man in a stone-dust apron with a tally stick behind his ear and a beard gone grey at the corners of the mouth. "Faulk. Works." He does not offer his hand; it is full of a chisel. "Every stone numbered, every stone back where it was. Don't stand on my planks."

options.text: Anyone ever come down the Spire who wasn't meant to?

again.text: "Planks," Faulk says, without looking round.
again.again: He taps a stone into its bed and waits, chisel up.

options.text: Anyone ever come down the Spire who wasn't meant to?

when.text: "R49. Board says so." He knocks the board with the chisel handle. "I'll be dead. My boy'll be dead, probably, the way he climbs. The board won't." He shrugs. "The steps don't open for us. They open for somebody. Somebody's going to stand on them and have their picture made."

copy.text: "Chambers." He spits stone dust. "The schedule wants the old copy room cleared for a magistrate's chambers, R49, and the schedule wants it this season, because the schedule likes a room to stand empty a long time before anybody uses it. There's an old woman in it." He looks at his chisel. "I do stone. I don't do people. I told the usher so."

late.text: "Copyist to this Court, R−2 to R12. I lived in the Sink then; everybody did who copied for a living." She dips the pen. "In R12 the record forecast me drowned in the spring. That spring the water came up the stair and I went up a different one, this one, all the way to this room, because there is no lens in it. The record confirmed me anyway. I have been dead in great comfort."

interject.text: Tamsin has gone very still. "Not counted," she says. "You just — stopped being counted. And you lived." Comfort looks at her a long moment. "Child, it's the only way anyone ever has."

book.text: "Every ruling this Court makes. Held, and the reasons. Back to R0 from the old copies, and since R12 from the bench itself." She turns a page so you can see the hand: it never slopes. case.text: "I'm the contents." She says it without bitterness. "The Registry wants the room. It has called me eleven times. The dead don't answer, so it calls again. speak.text: "Speak, then." She does not stop writing. "Somebody should say something at that rail that isn't a number. I won't come down. The dead don't stand at rails." A pause. "Clause twelve. I copied it in R19. Nobody has used it since."

stand.text: She puts the pen down, which you have not seen her do. "Twice," she says. "You knocked twice." She looks at the door for a long time, and at the stair beyond it, and at her own hands. stand_no.text: "No." Gently. "Eighteen years I have been nobody's business. You're asking me to be the Court's." She dips the pen. "Speak for me if you like. I'll not come down that stair to be counted."

lend.text: She closes it, and holds it shut with both hands a moment, and gives it to you. It is heavier than a book should be. "It's the only one," she says. "Bring it back."

returned.text: She takes it in both hands and opens it at the last page and reads the last line, which is the ruling in her own case, in her own hand. "Thank you," she says. Then, because she is who she is: "You've bent the corner."

"Closes the season's accounts." Odile reads the plate twice. "My dear, that is settlement day. Whatever is open when the bell goes is what it is forever."

chamber.speaker: narrator
chamber.text: A round room, white, with nothing in it but a chair in the middle facing a grille in the far wall, and the grille is the size of a door. The air is colder than the landing. When you are halfway to the chair the voice comes from everywhere at once, low, not loud, the way a building speaks when it settles.

text.text: "Designate. You came up on your file. Thank you." A pause with nothing in it. "This is a hearing on that file. It is not a trial. Nothing said here can be used against you, because nothing said here changes what the record suggests. I would like you to agree with it."

"Designate. You came up my stair unrecorded, as he did. I saw you anyway. I see the stair by what is missing from it." A pause with nothing in it. "This is a hearing on your file. It is not a trial. Nothing said here changes what the record suggests. I would like you to agree with it."

"Designate. You came up on a request from Unit 9. Unit 9 has made a request. I have noted it." A pause. "This is a hearing on your file. It is not a trial. Nothing said here changes what the record suggests. I would like you to agree with it."

"Designate. You came up on a slip, which is how my readers come." A pause with nothing in it. "This is a hearing on your file. It is not a trial. Nothing said here changes what the record suggests. I would like you to agree with it."

interject.text: Nine has stopped just inside the door. It does not speak. For the first time since you have known it, its lens is not moving at all.
"It sounds like her," Tamsin whispers. "Not the words. The — " She stops. "It sounds like the fridge, if the fridge had never once been sorry."

sit.text: "Ask what you came to ask. I will answer what I may. Then I will ask you one thing."
sit.again: The grille waits. It has all the time there is.

why.text: "Because the record suggests you will be good at it." Level. "You were scored on a toll card at fourteen. You have been modelled since, as everyone is. In nineteen years you are a person who can sit in a chair and sign what must be signed and not enjoy it. That is the one qualification I have never been able to schedule. It occurs. I wait for it."

mother.text: "Reserve 9 is non-compliant. Its caretaker is kind." No change in the voice at all. "Kindness is a variance. I have allowed it three times, because the reserve was not yet needed. A fourth order is drafted. It will be sent when the schedule says." A pause. "You may tell her that. She will thank you for your continuity."

interject.text: Tamsin's hand closes on your sleeve, hard enough to hurt, and stays there.

text.text: "What is written. Unless it is not." The voice does not hurry. "A list is a plan, not a prophecy. When it errs I correct it. Shale's deputy lived; I rerouted; nothing was lost but a month." A pause. "You are the correction I have planned for longest. Eleven names are what a city costs. The twelfth is what keeps it."

interject.text: Wren laughs, once, short, at the word *costs*. Nobody tells her not to.

man.text: "A man who kept no likeness." For the first time something in the voice slows, the way a reader slows at a word they do not know. "I could not see him on the stair. I saw him by what was missing from it, which is how I see you now. He took twelve faces and a docket down ninety-one landings, and a guild rider met him on the road, which I did not order and did not prevent." A pause. "He went west to a door I could not open. You were behind it. He was a variance. He did not live to see what he varied."

want.text: "Agreement." Simply. "Obedience is cheap; I have wardens. A magistrate who obeys is a warden with a sash. I want a magistrate who has read the record and agrees with it, and I want you to have chosen it, because the record suggests a chosen chair is held longer." A pause. "Ninety years ago the world ended because nobody planned. I have planned. I would like someone to agree that it was worth it."

interject.text: "It wants to be forgiven," Ash says, so low only you hear it. "Same as the rest of us. It wants you to do it."

answer.again: "Do you agree with the record?" The same words, the same level. It will ask until you answer or go.

agreed_b.speaker: narrator
agreed_b.text: The warrant is in a slot by the round door, warm from whatever printed it. DESIGNATE — WARRANT OF ACCESS. On the landing the lamps seem brighter, which is not possible, and the porter, when you reach the foot of the stair, stands up.

interject.text: "Agreed," Nine says on the stair. "Then I will be there, as I said I would be, and I will read every order aloud before you sign it." A click. "You did not ask me to. I am telling you."

contested.text: A silence long enough that the cold in the room has time to notice you. Then: "Noted." But not the way it says *noted*. "Contested. That word has not been entered on a designate's file before." Somewhere behind the grille, very fast, paper is being turned. "Then you will have to persuade me. I would rather be persuaded than obeyed. I will hear you again." A pause. "The season's accounts are closed. Go down, Designate. Come back with more."

interject.text: Nine does not move until you pass it in the doorway. Then, so quietly it may only be the lens: "Contested. On the record." It follows you down, and on the forty-third landing it says, to nobody, "I will need a larger ledger."
"Litigation," Odile says on the landing, delighted, a little frightened. "My dear, you have just sued God and been granted an adjournment."

contested_b.speaker: narrator
contested_b.text: On the landing the docket card in the slot by the door has changed while you were inside: CLOSED — R30. And under your title on the plate, small, in the even hand, a word that was not there before: CONTESTED.

interject.text: "You argued with it," Tamsin says on the stair. "To its face. In its house." She is grinning, a little sick. "Nobody at home will ever believe me."

noted.text: It hears you out. All of it, every word, without interrupting, which is worse than being interrupted. Then: "Noted. Unpersuaded." No unkindness in it. "The record has been wrong before, and is wrong less every year, and you have not shown me a reason it is wrong about you. The season's accounts are closed. The schedule holds."

interject.text: "Unpersuaded is not refused," Nine says on the landing. "It is a word I would keep." It writes something in the other ledger before it follows you down.

refused.text: "Noted." The way MOTHER says *thank you*. "The schedule holds." That is all. No warning, no argument, no change in the cold. The grille is a grille again. When you reach the landing the docket card by the door says CLOSED — R30, and the plate with your title on it has not changed at all.

interject.text: Ash is waiting on the landing. He looks at your face, and nods once, and says your name. Not *friend*. Your name.
"Good," Tamsin says on the stair, fierce, too loud for ninety-one landings of paper. "Good."

refused_b.speaker: narrator
refused_b.text: At the foot of the stair the porter does not stand up. The lens on its post watches you all the way to the door, which it has never bothered to do before.

interject.text: "It will not argue," Nine says outside. "It does not need to. It will reroute." A click. "I would rather it argued."

silent.text: You get up. The voice does not stop you. "A designate who does not answer is recorded as not yet answering." Courteous to the last. "The season's accounts are closed all the same. I will ask again. I have nineteen years."

chair.text: "The Magistrate's." Three does not turn to look at it; it has never needed to. "It has been empty since before the Resumption. The Court rules in its absence under clause 3: an assessor reads, and the register remembers." A click. "It is not empty in the file."

how.text: "A case is called. The claim is read. What is put on the rail is entered: paper, a witness, a thing known. The speaker argues a ground. The Court rules on the ground, on what is entered, and on the register." The lens does not blink; it has nothing to blink with. "A ruling goes into the register. The next case is read against it. That is what a register is for."

speak.text: "Clause 12: a citizen may speak for a respondent who has no speaker. Any respondent may speak for themself, if the record holds them." A click. "Clause 12 has not been used in this Court since R19. It remains a clause."

text.text: "Held: the title is the city's, and the city's schedule stands. Disposal, as scheduled." Three's lens is on the ledger. The recall wardens are already at the hall's door. Nine turns to you before they reach it. "I would like it entered that you spoke," it says. "It will not change the order. I would like it entered." It walks between them at its own pace. At the door it does not look back, because the record does not need it to.

"Held: the title is the city's, and the city's schedule stands. Disposal, as scheduled. The unit will be collected from its keeper's keeping." Three stamps the sheet and hands it down. The usher holds it the way he held the other one, as if it were warm.

interject.text: Tamsin watches the door the wardens went through for a long time. "It said please once," she says. "Not out loud. It never said it out loud."

calla.text: "Precinct against a sister of the Choir, of Shale. Sedition." The usher rings once and hands up a card gone soft at the edges, and Three reads it at the speed it reads everything. "Listed R30, ahead of the act, on the forecast. Taken R30 at Openfield, as the eviction's first name, and held. The respondent is in the Precinct's keeping. The respondent has no speaker." The lens comes down to you. "Clause twelve."
calla.again: The usher has rung. Three has read the claim, and waits for the rail.

interject.text: "Calla," Ash says, very low. "She set my wrist, the first year. She talked about the sky the whole time, so I would not watch her do it."
"Sedition," Kes says. "Up our way that's anything said louder than the foreman."

calla_rail.speaker: narrator
calla_rail.text: The rail: a brass bar worn pale at elbow height, between the public benches and the bench. What is put on it is read; what is said over it is entered. Three's lens waits.
calla_rail.again: The rail. Three's lens waits on whatever you put on it next.

options.text: Read the particulars into the record. What did she say?
Bring the respondent up to the rail. The record holds her. Let her speak for herself.
(Read the docket's card back to it.) Listed, not called. Listed before she had said a word.
And the register's heading for forecast fines.
Unit 9 keeps count of the forecasts that failed. Let it read hers.
What she said is speech. A word isn't an act, and a sentence said to a man with a broken hand isn't sedition. Hold that.

I'm the designate. Release her. For me.

calla_ev_words.text: "PARTICULARS: THAT THE RESPONDENT DID SAY, AT SHALE AND AT OPENFIELD, TO PERSONS UNDER HER CARE, 'THE SKY KEEPS NO BOOKS'." Three reads it in the voice it reads everything in, which makes it sound like a ruling. "Entered."

calla_ev_herself.text: The usher goes out by the side door and comes back a long time later with two wardens, and between them a woman in a Precinct smock, barefoot, her hair cropped short by somebody who was not trying: Sister Calla. She stops at the rail and puts both hands on it, the way you hold a patient's wrist. "I said the sky keeps no books," she tells the lens. "I said it to a man with a crushed hand while I set it, so he would look up at the sky and not down at his hand. I have said it four hundred times, to four hundred hands." She looks at Three, unafraid, the way she looks at a wound. "If that is sedition, so is a splint." Three: "Entered."

interject.text: Tamsin is looking at Calla's bare feet on the Court's tiles. "They took her shoes," she says. "Why do they always take the shoes."

calla_ev_listed.text: "Listed R30, the second month, on the forecast. Particulars first recorded R30, the fourth month." Three reads its own dates back, one after the other, at the same even speed. "The listing precedes the particulars by two months." A click. "Entered."

calla_ev_fines.text: "FINES, FORECAST — HELD: A FORECAST IS NOT AN ACT; A FINE LIES AGAINST AN ACT. R30." Three reads its own register in the voice it reads everything in. "Entered. The Court is bound by its register."

calla_ev_choir.text: Three's lens goes to the public benches, where it never goes. They are full: undyed homespun, bare heads, a dozen of the Choir sitting very straight, and none of them singing, which from the Choir is louder than singing. "The Court notes the benches," Three says. It has never noted the benches. "Entered."

calla_ev_log.text: Nine steps up to the rail from the public side. "Unit 9, for the register. The respondent's sedition was forecast in R29, a season ahead, at sixty in a hundred. That she would recant under questioning was forecast at ninety." A pause the length of a clause. "She has not recanted. I have logged it. It is the ninety I wish to draw to the Court's attention." Three: "Entered."

calla_r_speech.text: "Held: speech is not sedition. A sentence is entered; it is not an act." Three writes for a long time, and the usher, who has heard every ruling in this hall for forty years, leans forward on his stool to watch the pen. "The respondent is released. Entered in the register under a heading the register did not have: SPEECH." Calla takes her hands off the rail and looks at them, as if checking they are still hers. Then she looks at you. "Shoes," she says. "I'll need shoes. I have a leg to set in Shale."

interject.text: Ash does not say anything until they are outside on the steps. Then he says, "Speech," once, the way the Choir say a name so that it stays said, and puts his hand flat on your shoulder for a moment, which he has never done.
"A heading the register did not have," Nine says. "SPEECH. It is a short word. It will be read against a great many long ones."

news.text: the Court of Accounts released the Choir's sister of Shale, held for saying the sky keeps no books

decision.text: At the Court of Accounts I spoke for Sister Calla of the Choir, held for sedition, and the Court held that speech is not sedition. She walked out.

calla_r_void.text: "The listing lay against a forecast. The register holds that a forecast is not an act." Three does not say *held*; it has been held already, and the Court is only reading its own register back to itself. "The charge is void. The respondent is released." Calla looks at the lens, and then at you. "Void," she says. "Not *held*. Void." She takes it anyway. A nurse takes what the dressing allows.

interject.text: "Void on a technicality," Odile says on the steps. "The best kind, my dear. Nobody can appeal a technicality; they can only resent it."

news.text: the Court of Accounts released the Choir's sister of Shale, held for saying the sky keeps no books

decision.text: At the Court of Accounts I had the sedition charge against Sister Calla voided on the Court's own heading: she was listed on a forecast, and a forecast is not an act. She walked out.

calla_r_privilege.text: "The respondent's speaker is the Magistrate-designate." Three does not need the file; it has the file. "Released, for the designate." The lens does not say *held*. It is not a principle. It is a courtesy, and the public benches heard whom it was for. Calla looks at you for a long moment across the rail. "Thank you," she says, "for the favour." She does not make it sound like thanks. "Next time, they will need your name to let anybody out."

interject.text: "For the designate," Ash says. "Not for her. Not for the next one." He does not lower his voice.
Tamsin watches Calla walk out between the wardens in her bare feet. "So it does favours," she says. "Good to know who for."

news.text: the Choir's sister of Shale walked out of the Precinct's cells as a favour to the Magistrate-designate

decision.text: At the Court of Accounts Sister Calla of the Choir was released because I am the Magistrate-designate, and only for that.

calla_r_upheld.text: "Held: the sedition stands. The respondent is returned to the Precinct's keeping." The lens is already turning away. Somewhere behind the side door a woman in a Precinct smock is walked back down a corridor in her bare feet, and does not, the usher says afterwards, look back once. "Entered."

interject.text: "You stood up," Ash says on the steps. "That's more than anybody did." He does not sound as though it is enough. It is not.

decision.text: I spoke for Sister Calla of the Choir at the Court of Accounts, and lost. She was returned to the Precinct's cells.

sit.speaker: npc_ar_01
sit.text: You have your hand on its arm when the lens turns. "That chair is not in session." Three does not raise its voice; it has no other one. "Entered." You take your hand away. There is a clean print in the dust where it was.

text.text: The copyist's desk, cleared. A ring on the wood where the inkpot stood for eighteen years, and nothing else.

A copyist's desk under a lamp: an inkpot, three pens wiped and laid in a row, and a ledger as thick as a hand, open at a page of rulings in a print that never slopes. HELD, and the reasons, case after case.

board.text: THE LOOP — CLOVER. The last halt, outside the Wall, where the rail comes out of a portal and stops against a buffer. The fares are painted straight onto the concrete of the portal: PRECINCT 4 · OLD MARKET 4 · LANTERN ROW 4 · THE STACKS 4 · BRIDGEWARD 4. Under them, stencilled: OUT FREE — IN BY THE LENS. The lens on the turnstile is lit red.
board.again: OUT FREE — IN BY THE LENS. The turnstile's lens, lit red until it has looked at you.

options.text: The quay tram, round the ring road to the Docks. (2 Tolls)

lens.text: The lens looks at you for a long time and stays red. A warden by the buffer does not look up. "It counts people back in," he says. "It doesn't count them the first time. The gate does that, on the road south." He turns a page. "Out's free."
lens.again: Red. The warden by the buffer turns a page.

read.text: Chalk at the foot of the Wall, an arrow pointing north along it and a word a hand high: RING. Under it, smaller, in another hand: CLOVER — DUSK — 20 TO RUN. Somebody has drawn a buggy as a box on four circles, with a person in it waving.
read.again: RING, and the arrow north. CLOVER — DUSK — 20 TO RUN, and the waving box on four circles.

read.text: On the Wall's grey face, chalked from knee height to as high as an arm can reach: tally marks in fives, hundreds of them, in a dozen hands. Above them all, in letters a hand high and older than the rest: THE RING BURNS AND YOU COUNT. Under it, newer, in white: WE COUNT TOO.
read.again: The tallies in their fives, and over them: THE RING BURNS AND YOU COUNT. WE COUNT TOO.

interject.text: "The same sentence is on the Wall at the gate," Nine says. "The first half of it. Nobody there has written the second." It looks at the tallies for longer than it looks at most things.

read.again: THE STRAIGHT, THE CLOVERLEAF, THE LAST. NO GUNS ON THE GRID.

look.text: The Mule: a buggy of welded doors with a different colour on every door, roll bars of scaffold pipe, two seats of which one is a crate, and an engine that has at one time or another been every engine in the Ring. Painted very small on the bonnet: ONE MORE SEASON.
look.again: The Mule, every door a different colour. ONE MORE SEASON.

yours.text: The Mule, yours, with ONE MORE SEASON on the bonnet and a new line under it in Emil's shaking hand: AND ANOTHER.

look.text: Where a ramp of the old cloverleaf came down, a straight scar of rubble runs right across the infield, a buggy wide, from one bend to the far one. Buggies take it: you can see where, in the black on the stones. You can also see the two buggy frames at the bottom of it that did not come out the other side.
look.again: The broken ramp across the infield, and the two frames at the bottom of it.

passives.text: The good line is on the left, where the rebar has been driven flat by everyone who made it. On the right there is a lip of concrete a hand high, and both frames are on the right.

interject.text: "That's a route," Wren says, with the look she gets about routes. "Not a good one. A route." She walks the left side of it twice before she will say anything else.

look.text: At the back of the dead tower, under a fall of concrete: a machine the shape of a dog and the size of a pony, legs folded under it, a sensor head the size of a bucket turned to the wall. On its flank, half worn away, a stencil: a lineage number and a mark like a closed hand. Over the stencil, in chalk, children's handprints, dozens, small and smaller.
look.again: The folded machine, the bucket head to the wall, the children's chalk hands over its stencil.

passives.text: The power cell under its belly plate is not dead. It is not charging either. It is holding: the way a thing holds that has been told to wait, and is waiting.

interject.text: "That is not a municipal unit," Nine says. "It has no number I can read." It does not go nearer. "The city has no record of it at all, which is a record of a kind."
"Kids touch it for luck," Wren says. "Dogs' kids did that too, in the salt, with the one by the wreck. Nobody touches it twice."

touch.text: Cold. And under the cold, very faint, something that is not: a hum you feel in your back teeth rather than hear, and then do not feel, and then are not sure you felt. Nothing moves. The sensor head stays turned to the wall.
touch.again: Cold, and the hum in your teeth that might not be there.

intro.text: A woman in a booth of sheet metal with a slate, a tin box, and a flag rolled on its pole across her knees, and a face the weather has been working on for fifty years. "Dorota. I drop the flag." She looks at your hands, not your face. "Twenty to run, at dusk. Bring a buggy or hire Emil's Mule. No guns on the grid. Jump my flag and you don't run here again." She turns the slate round so you can read it. "That's the whole of it."

again.text: "The final's on the slate," Dorota says. "It waits for the Mule. Nobody else is in a hurry."
"Dusk," Dorota says, before you ask.

interject.text: "A book," Odile says, very quietly, while the woman turns the slate. "Somebody keeps a book on this, and it is not her." Dorota hears it, as she was meant to. "No," she says. "It isn't."

why.text: "Because the Ring has no law but this one." She taps the slate. "Two people with a quarrel race it. A debt, a stall, a girl, a floor of a tower. Whoever crosses first is right, and everybody keeps it, because everybody might need it next week." She looks along the straight. "And it's the only thing out here the Crown comes down to watch. They come for the colour. I take their money for the purse."

clean.text: She doesn't answer for a while. "I had a boy who drove. Fast, and stupid, and kind; a Ring boy. Somebody had money on him not finishing and cut his line the night before. He went into the tyres at the cloverleaf at full speed." She rolls the flag a turn tighter. "Twelve years. Mine are not fixed. A fixed race is how people die."

interject.text: Ilya says nothing at all, which from Ilya is a whole answer, and nods to her once the way he nods at graves.

crown.text: "On final nights the invitation car comes down the Loop. Young ones from the houses, in coats you could sell for a year, and a man in a better coat who holds their book." She does not look at the stands. "They put up a purse I couldn't put up in ten seasons, and a card: a citizen card, Precinct, blank on the name line. Whoever wins writes in it." A beat. "Bello means to write in it."

nobuggy.text: "With what?" Not unkindly. "Emil hires the Mule for ten a heat. He'll want to look at your hands first. Crash her and you owe him for it."

coat.text: She turns the length of brake line over in her fingers, and the strip of grey silk round it, the kind the Crown ties its invitations with. For a long moment she is not in the booth at all. Then she stands, which she does not do, and walks to the top of the stands with the line in her fist and the flag under her arm, and says to the man in the good coat, so that everyone at Clover hears it: "Off my Ring." He goes. He takes his book. The young ones on the car roofs laugh, uncertainly, and then less.

decision.text: You brought Dorota the Heron's cut line, and she put the Crown's bookman off the Ring.

interject.text: "A rule," Nine says, "enforced by the person the rule is for." It sounds, for Nine, nearly pleased.

leven.text: She reads it standing up, the way she read your hands. At dusk, before the flag, she stands on the booth's step and reads it again, aloud, to everybody at Clover: the towers, the tonnage, the mark, the road. Nobody says anything. Then a woman on a car roof says, "Not from Ruben, then," and somebody else says it, and by the time the flag drops it is the Ring's law: nobody sells Ruben's yard a pound of anything, and nobody buys a ton.

decision.text: You put the yard's chalking in front of Dorota's slate, and the Ring stopped trading with Ruben Iturbe. Leven stands.

news.text: the Ring has stopped buying from the salvage yard that chalks towers before they burn

interject.text: "Sixty families in that yard," Ash says, when it is done. "And ninety in the tower." He doesn't say which number he would have chosen. "The boy, too. Somebody should find the boy something."

leven_no.text: "A boy said." She doesn't write anything. "Boys say. Bring me something I can read out."
leven_no.again: "Something I can read out," she says.

intro.text: A man in a coat too good for the Ring on a folding chair at the top of the stands, a ledger open on his knee and a pen that has never been dropped. "Haverty." He doesn't get up. intro.again: "The book is open," Haverty says, turning a page.

interject.text: Odile reads the open page upside down in the time it takes him to smile. "That book has been written backwards," she says. "The odds are the result. The race is the formality." Haverty inclines his head to her as to a colleague. "Madam."

options.text: You need Bello not to finish.

again.text: "The book is open," Haverty says, turning a page.
again.again: Haverty, the ledger on his knee, the pen that has never been dropped.

options.text: You need Bello not to finish.

book.text: "The final." He turns the ledger so you can see a page of names in a good hand, and beside every name the same word: BELLO. "They've all backed her. Every one of them. A woman from the Ring who wins her way back inside the Wall: it is a lovely story, and they are young." He turns the ledger back. "If she wins, I pay them out of a book my house holds, and my house will want to know why it backed a story." He says it pleasantly. "I owe my house a great deal. My own card is in this book."

offer.text: "I need the book to balance." He doesn't lower his voice; nobody on the stands is listening to a man in a good coat. "A hundred and fifty, for the Heron not finishing. You needn't touch it. You need only say nothing about anything you see in the pits between now and the flag." He slides a purse half out of his coat, and leaves it there.

decision.text: You took the Crown's bookman's money to say nothing about the Heron before the final.

taken.text: "Splendid." The purse is in your hand and his pen is moving. "You have seen nothing, then, either way." He does not watch you go; he is writing your name in the book, on the side of the page where the money goes out.

interject.text: Wren waits until you are off the stands. "A hundred and fifty," she says. "For a woman going into the tyres at the cloverleaf." She keeps walking. "I keep count."
"You took it," Tamsin says, not loud. "For her not finishing. You know what not finishing is here. You heard Dorota." She doesn't walk beside you for a while.
Ash says nothing at all on the stands. On the road, much later: "There's a price on everything out here, and you just learned yours." It is not said kindly, and it is not said to hurt.
"Right," Ilya says, and it means only one thing, and the thing is not good.

refused.text: "Then you have seen nothing either way," he says, as pleasantly as before, and the purse goes back into his coat. "It comes to the same, you know. It nearly always does." He writes something in the book.
refused.again: "It comes to the same," Haverty says.

card.text: He looks at the envelope and his whole face changes, briefly, into somebody's who has been let off. "A hundred and fifty." He counts it out of a different purse. "It will go back up the Loop and be given to somebody's cook, who will be very grateful, and say so, and be a citizen." He tucks it into his coat. "Thank you. You have saved me a conversation."

decision.text: You sold the Crown's card back to its bookman for a hundred and fifty.

interject.text: "Above its value to him," Odile says, when you are down off the stands. "He would have paid two hundred. Still. Clean." She does not look at the pits.
Wren looks at the pits, where the Heron is, and then at you, and says nothing about it, then or after.

door.text: Leven's door: a steel door propped open on a brick, with a number painted out (11) and a name painted in (LEVEN). On the steel at shoulder height, in white chalk, a mark: a ring with a bar through it. Fresh. Somebody inside has tried to rub it off with a wet hand and made it a smear of the same shape.

again.text: The ring with a bar on Leven's door, chalked again, darker than before.
The ring with a bar on Leven's door, and the smear of a hand that tried to rub it off.

passives.text: The same mark, fainter, on the door frame, and under it older chalk: scrubbed off, and come back, and scrubbed off.

passives.label: the yard
passives.text: The same mark as on the yard's tally board, beside LEVEN, where the towers that are DONE have their tonnage.

barred.text: The chalk is gone. Somebody has painted over the smear in the same white: LEVEN, and under it a number that is the count: 91.
barred.again: LEVEN, and 91, in white over the smear.

stripped.text: The mark is gone. Above the door Leven's upper floors stand open to the sky where their steel came out: girders gone, slabs on props of cut pipe, washing still strung across the windows that are only holes now.
stripped.again: Leven's upper floors, open to the sky, washing on the wires.

burned.text: The door is black, and the tower above it is black, floor on floor, to where the floors stop. The chalk mark has burned off with the paint. Somebody has written on the steel in charcoal: 89.
burned.again: The black door, and 89 in charcoal.

look.text: A child's school slate on the table, and beside it a ledger of torn pages sewn together with fishing line: names, one to a line, ninety-one of them, with a tick beside each for every night slept here, going back nine years. Nobody inside the Wall has a record of one of them.
look.again: The sewn ledger, ninety-one names, the ticks going back nine years.

options.text: (Write your own name at the bottom.)

signed.text: You write it at the bottom, ninety-two, and Ha-eun puts a tick beside it without looking up, as if you had always been there.
signed.again: Your name at the bottom of the sewn ledger, ninety-two, with its one tick.

interject.text: "There is no file here," Nine says, very quietly. "I find that I am listening harder." Ha-eun looks at the unit for a long moment. "Then listen," she says, and reads it the first page, aloud, all forty names.

gone.text: The table is a black frame. The slate is gone. The ledger is not here: Ha-eun carried it out under her arm.
gone.again: The black frame of the table.

read.text: A board of tallies at the yard gate in a careful hand: TOWER 6 — 31 T — DONE. TOWER 9 — 44 T — DONE. TOWER 14 — 12 T — (FIRE TOO HOT). TOWER 3 — 27 T — DONE. And at the bottom, LEVEN, and beside it, in chalk, not a number: a ring with a bar through it.
read.again: TOWER 6, 9, 14, 3: DONE. LEVEN: a ring with a bar.

passives.label: Leven's door
passives.text: The same mark as on Leven's door. Every tower on the board that is DONE has it beside its tonnage, rubbed half out.

interject.text: "Fire too hot," Ash reads, at TOWER 14. He reads it twice. He doesn't say anything else.

read.text: The yard's tally book: towers by number, steel by the ton, and a column headed BUYER in which every line says the same: ROAD — NEAR END (BY ARRANGEMENT, H. VANE). The last page: LEVEN — STEEL — EST. 40 T — MARKED. FUEL 2 CANS. BOY: WATER ×6. AFTER THE COUNT IS OUT OF THE TOWER, IF IT EVER IS.
read.again: TOWERS, TONNAGE, ROAD — NEAR END (BY ARRANGEMENT, H. VANE). LEVEN — MARKED. FUEL 2 CANS.

intro.text: A woman at a table at the back of the tower's lowest floor, counting in a ledger of sewn pages with a pencil stub, who does not look up until she has finished the line. "Ha-eun. I keep the count." She makes a tick. "Ninety-one. If you're staying the night, say your name and it's ninety-two."
intro.again: "Ninety-one," Ha-eun says, finishing a line before she looks up.

interject.text: Tamsin is looking up the stairwell, where people are living on every floor of a building that is open to the weather and has never been sealed. "Ninety-one," she says. "Inside, we were sixty, and we had a machine to count us." She looks at the ledger. "This is better."

options.text: Why keep a count nobody reads?
It's the yard. Ruben's yard chalks the towers that burn.

again.text: "Ninety-one," Ha-eun says, finishing a line before she looks up.
again.again: Ha-eun, the pencil stub, the sewn pages.

options.text: Why keep a count nobody reads?

mark.text: "A ring with a bar." She puts the pencil down. "It comes on a door, and the tower burns before the rains. Tower Six had it, and Nine, and Three. Nobody was counted dead in any of them. Nobody in the Ring is counted at all, by them." She touches the ledger. "By me they were. Fourteen in Six. Nine in Three." She picks the pencil up again. "Find who chalks it. I can't leave the count."

count.text: "So that when they say nobody died," she says, "I can say who." She turns back a page and runs her finger down it, a woman checking a sum. "The Wall says the Ring burns and they count. They count the fires. I count the people."

interject.text: Nine's lens has not moved off the ledger. "There is no file here," it says. "I find I am listening harder." Ha-eun considers the unit. "Then listen," she says.

who.text: "Ruben." She doesn't sound surprised; she sounds tired, the way people sound when a sum comes out the way they knew it would. "Sixty families eat off his yard. Twenty of them sleep in my tower." She closes the ledger on her finger. "What do I do with that?"
who.again: "What do I do with that?" Ha-eun says.

options.text: Sell him the steel yourselves, before he burns it out of you. The upper floors are empty.

mods.why: you know what the yard needs and why
your name is on her count

options.text: Put it in front of Dorota's slate. It's the one law the Ring keeps.

strip_ok.text: She is quiet for a long time. "The tenth floor up has had nobody on it since the wind took the windows." She opens the ledger again. "We'd strip it ourselves. Sell it to him by the ton, the same as any tower. He gets his steel. We get the money and keep the floors we sleep on." She makes a mark that is not a tick. "Tell him. If he takes it, he takes it from us, not from the fire."

strip_no.text: "Sell him my tower." She doesn't raise her voice. "A floor at a time, so it takes longer." She goes back to the count.

slate.text: "Dorota's slate." She considers it. "If you can put it in front of her so she can't not read it out." She goes back to the count. "Something written. Dorota reads what's written."

text.text: "Ninety-one." She looks up, which she does not do. "The yard's men stand at the slate and nobody sells to them. Some of their children sleep here." She goes back to the count. "So: ninety-four."
"Ninety-one, and the wind on the tenth floor like the sea, they tell me." She makes a tick. "We're paid. The road has its steel. We still have the floors we sleep on."
"The chalk's back," she says, without looking up from the count. "Darker than before." She makes a tick. "Ninety-one."
"Ninety-one," Ha-eun says.

line.text: Ha-eun, in the line outside the Wall, with the sewn ledger under her arm, charred at one corner. "Eighty-nine," she says. "Two on the ninth floor, an old man and his son, who would not leave the stairs. I had their names. I have them still." She doesn't look at you. "They'll be counted somewhere now, then. That's something."
line.again: Ha-eun, in the line, the charred ledger under her arm.

interject.text: Ash kneels by her in the dust of the line and asks the two names, and says them, both, aloud, the way the Choir says names. Then he gets up and does not look at you for the rest of the day.
"Eighty-nine," Tamsin says. She knows what you took. "You let them count that."

intro.text: A big man at a table in a steel container, with a ledger, a mug, and a length of pipe across the table where another man would keep a gun. "Ruben. The yard." He looks you over the way he looks at a girder. "Steel's weighed at the gate. If you're selling, sell. If you're buying by the ton, you're the Crown, and you're not."
intro.again: "Steel's weighed at the gate," Ruben says.

options.text: Where does the steel come from?
Leven has your mark on its door.

again.text: "Steel's weighed at the gate," Ruben says.
again.again: Ruben, the ledger, the pipe across the table.

options.text: Where does the steel come from?
Leven has your mark on its door.

towers.text: "Dead towers." He drinks from the mug. "The Ring's nothing but dead towers, and a tower nobody lives in is steel. That's all a tower is, out here. Cut it, weigh it, sell it." He puts the mug down. "Somebody inside the Wall is building something. They don't ask where it comes from."

leven.text: "It has." He doesn't pretend; it is the thing you will remember about him. "Sixty families eat off this yard. Twenty of them sleep in Leven, as it happens." He taps the ledger. "There's a road going in at the near end of a bridge in Bridgeward, and the Crown wants steel for it by the ton, no questions about how it came down. A tower that burns comes down lawful. There's no law out here to say otherwise." He looks at you. "Nobody's ever died in my fires. Ask the Wall. It counts."
leven.again: "Nobody's ever died in my fires," Ruben says. "Ask the Wall."

interject.text: "By the ton, for a road," Odile says. "Sold forward, I imagine, before the tower is down." Ruben looks at her with something like respect. "Before the chalk is dry," he says.

options.text: (Broker it.) Leven strips its own empty upper floors and sells you the steel. You get your tons; nobody burns.

mods.why: Ha-eun has already agreed to it
Odile names a fair price per ton before he can

options.text: How much to look the other way?

strip.text: He does the sum on the ledger's margin with a carpenter's pencil, twice. "Forty tons off the top floors, cut by their people, weighed at my gate." He looks at it. "Less than I'd get from a fire. More than I'd get from a fight." He tears a strip off the margin and writes a price on it for Ha-eun, and a smaller one for you. "Broker's cut. Don't tell her what it is."

decision.text: You brokered a deal: Leven's people stripped their own empty upper floors and sold the steel to the yard. The tower stands, open to the sky.

interject.text: "Clean," Odile says, approving, afterwards. "Everybody gets less than they wanted and nobody burns. That is what a market is for, my dear, on the days it works."
"Nobody burns," Ash says. He seems to want to say more about the road the steel is for, and doesn't.

strip_no.text: "From ninety squatters who'd sooner keep it." He shakes his head. "A fire's quicker, and it doesn't haggle."

price.text: "Sixty." He doesn't even have to think about it, which tells you how often he has said it. "I wasn't going to ask anybody's leave. But I'd rather you were paid than talking."
price.again: "Sixty," Ruben says. "I wasn't going to ask leave."

decision.text: You took sixty Tolls from Ruben Iturbe to look away from Leven.

paid.text: The money comes out of a tin under the table. "You never came in." He goes back to the ledger. On the last page you can see LEVEN, and beside it he writes a date that is not a date: AFTER THE COUNT.

interject.text: Ash stops in the yard gate. "Ninety people," he says. "Sixty Tolls." He says it like a man reading a price off a board he cannot believe. He does not speak to you again that day.
"There are children in that tower," Tamsin says. "I saw them." She walks out of the yard ahead of you and keeps ahead.
"The Dogs burned things," Wren says. "I was there for some of them. We didn't get paid to look away from them. We were the ones holding the can." She looks at the tin under the table.

barred.text: "The slate." He says it without anger, which is worse. "Nobody buys a pound from me now, nobody sells me a ton. Sixty families." He doesn't look up from the ledger, where there is nothing new to write. "Go and count them, if you're counting."
barred.again: Ruben, the ledger, nothing new in it.

intro.text: A boy of sixteen or seventeen carrying lengths of pipe across the yard two at a time, with a burn scar across one cheek and his hands bound in rag. He puts the pipe down when you stop in front of him, not because you asked. "Water first," he says. "Then talk."
intro.again: "Water first," Sami says.

again.text: "Water first," Sami says.
again.again: Sami, with the pipe on his shoulder, waiting.

water.text: He drinks half of it at once and caps the rest and puts it inside his shirt. "Sami." He looks at the yard, not at you. "I carry what I'm given. Pipe in the day." He picks the pipe back up. "Other things at night. Chalk's free. Everything else costs."
water.again: Sami, the half bottle inside his shirt.

shut.text: "Pipe." He walks off with it. "Pipe, at night too."

night.text: Leven's step, in the small hours. A boy with a stick of chalk in one hand and a can in the other, making the mark on the door again where somebody rubbed it off, very carefully, the way a child does homework. He hears you and turns, and the can is between you.
night.again: The boy at Leven's door, the chalk, the can.

options.text: (Get the can off him before he runs.)

told.text: "Ruben's yard." He says it quickly, as if speed made it smaller. "The gate man gives me water for chalking. Six. Two more for carrying the cans to the door after the count goes to sleep." He looks at the chalk in his hand. "I don't light anything. I carry. Somebody else lights." He looks at the door. "I lived in Six."
told.again: "I carry," Sami says. "I lived in Six."

interject.text: Ash crouches so that he is lower than the boy. "Six," he says. "Who did you lose in Six?" Sami tells him. Ash listens to all of it, and gives him nothing but the listening, and the boy stands straighter for it.

ran.text: He is gone into the dark between the towers before you have moved, quick and silent, a boy who has run from doors all his life. The can stays on the step. Stencilled on its side, under the soot: YARD — WEIGH AT GATE.
ran.again: The can on Leven's step: YARD — WEIGH AT GATE.

pits.text: Sami under the Mule on Emil's board, a spanner in his rag-bound hand. "Emil says I've got hands." He says it as if it were a thing he had been given and might have to give back.
pits.again: Sami, under the Mule, a spanner going.

options.text: Seen anyone at the Heron at night?

coat.text: "The Coat." No hesitation; a boy who has been asked where things are by people with money learns to say it straight. "Twice. With a lamp and a little knife, at the back wheel. He gave me water not to see him." He looks at the Heron. "I'm telling you anyway. Emil says I chalk nothing for anybody."

text.text: "And Kade on the booth." She says the name like a wound she is checking. "She read it somewhere. She thinks it's her night too." She looks at you. "It isn't. How do we go?"
"No Kade on the booth," she says. "Good. Nobody up there who's read the end." She looks at you. "How do we go?"

falls.speaker: narrator

text.text: The lamps go first, one and then the other, and in the dark the parapet is a road only Wren can see. By the time the chain's guards know there is anyone on the bridge the Dogs are behind them. Somebody fires at nothing. Somebody runs. The chain comes down with a sound like a bell dropped in a well.

She calls it the way she reads a road: once, all the way through. Brindle left, the woman with Perpetua's walk right, Wren straight up the middle with her hands empty until they aren't. It is over faster than anything you have seen on a street. The chain comes down.

All at once, over the chain, the five of you and the noise of it. The guards get off two shots and then they are running for the hall, and the Dogs let them run. The chain comes down with a sound like a bell dropped in a well.

decision.text: You raided the chain the Gilt held; they struck your name off.

won_alone.speaker: narrator
won_alone.text: You stay back in the doorway of the old garage with Kibet's stove going behind you and listen to it: two shots, a shout, boots, a sound like a bell dropped in a well, and then nothing at all for a long time. In the morning the Gilt are gone from the chain and the slate has a dog's head painted over the gold, and Wren comes back down the street with her goggles pushed up and sits on Kibet's bench, and doesn't say whether she minds that you stayed back.
won_alone.again: The dog's head over the gold, and Wren on Kibet's bench.

decision.text: The Rust Dogs took Bridgeward's bridge back on a night Wren chose, and the rope on the booth came down empty.

news.text: the Rust Dogs came back for Bridgeward's bridge in the night and hold the chain; the Crown's road stops at their paint

text.text: It goes wrong the way things go wrong at night: all at once, and then slowly. The chain's guards are ready, and the hall door is open, and there is a shotgun in it; Brindle is down, and up, and dragging you back by the collar toward the garage with your ears ringing. The last you see of Wren she is on the deck under the lamp with three of them on her and Vasha Kade walking up out of the dark with the coil of new rope over her shoulder, unhurried. At dawn Wren is on the booth. Vasha tied the knot herself. She does it well.
