text.text: THE LINE — TWO-TWELVE. DEPARTURES DAILY 07:00: EAST HALT, FOUR WAYS, YARD NINE, WEST HALT, MERIDIAN. FARE 25. Under it, in fresh chalk: CAR DOWN. NO CONTRACTS UP. SHIFT HOLDS FOOTGATE.

THE LINE — TWO-TWELVE. DEPARTURES DAILY 07:00: EAST HALT, FOUR WAYS, YARD NINE, WEST HALT, MERIDIAN. FARE 25. Arrivals — none. The letters are lamps behind glass, and every few minutes one of them flickers as if somebody somewhere had touched it.

look.again: The Line board. Departures at seven. Fare twenty-five.

options.text: (Buy a ticket west at the window under the board.)

hail.text: For a long minute nothing. Then, small, in the corner where the fare is: STILL HERE? LODGE. AFTER DARK. And the fare again.

board.text: A board of brass pegs outside the lamp room, two hundred of them, a tag on every peg for every man or woman who came up. At the end, eleven pegs with their tags hung back on them by somebody's hand, and chalk under each: STILL DOWN. Beside it a notice in clean print: SIX EAST — CLOSED — GEOLOGICAL — RECOVERY NOT ECONOMIC. DEBTS OF THE DECEASED TRANSFER TO NEXT OF KIN PER CONTRACT §9. — THE WINDOW.
board.again: Eleven tags hung back on their pegs. STILL DOWN. GEOLOGICAL.

interject.text: "Geological," Nine says. "A finding with no surveyor's name under it. The record would send it back." Its lens stays on the word. "Here there is no record to send it to."
"Eleven," Wren says. "And the debt walks down the road to whoever's left." She looks at the pegs a long time. "Same as the block."
"Paragraph nine," Odile says, and takes her glasses off. "Debts pass to kin. I have seen that clause sold on the floor as a feature."

options.text: (Read the names someone has pencilled under the tags.)

names.text: Under the tags, in pencil, in several hands: Yusuf Rasul. Joran Haber. Ivo Ansel. Kwame Asare. Lidia Moss. Hamid Sayegh. Ewa Kowal. Dilan Arslan. Marek Szabo. Obinna Nwankwo. Tess Varga's boy, no name on the tag but the number.
names.again: Eleven names in pencil, in several hands.

up.text: The eleven tags are off their pegs. Somebody has written under the empty pegs, in the same pencil: UP. And under that, smaller: BURIED.

won.text: Every peg on the board is empty: the lamps are down the pit. The Window's notice is gone. Somebody has nailed eleven tags along the top of the board, in a row, where everybody going down will touch them.
won.again: Every peg empty. Eleven tags along the top of the board.

broken.text: Lamps down the pit again, on new pegs with new numbers: the men off the Line. The eleven tags are gone and nobody will say where. The Window's notice is still there.
broken.again: New numbers on the pegs. The Window's notice.

revolt.text: The board is bare. Nobody is going down Six, and nobody is going up the hill. Somebody has written across the board in coal: WE STOPPED THE CAR.

text.text: The cage hangs at the top of the shaft with its gate chained. Nobody is going down Six while there is a war on the slope.
The cage at the top of the shaft, its gate open, the winch warm. Six is working.

The cage at the top of the shaft, gate shut, a brake lever as long as your arm. One of the Clean is asleep on a crate against the cage house wall with his chin on his chest. The other is somewhere you can hear but not see.
The cage at the top of the shaft, gate shut, a brake lever as long as your arm. The Clean stand either side of the cage house door. "The pit is closed," one says. "Unsafe ground."

cage.again: The cage, and its brake lever.

options.text: (Kes puts two fingers on the brake housing. "Ten seconds. Nobody saw that.")
(Slip past the sleeping guard and work the winch yourself.)
The Concern will want the pillar log before the Shift gets it. Let me go down and bring it.

mods.why: the Contract Office has your name: the Clean have heard it
their lens reads Concern chrome in you

options.text: (Fold forty Tolls into the nearer one's glove.)

winch.text: Past him, close enough to smell his soap. The gate opens on oiled hinges. The brake is a long lever and a winding wheel, and the cage is yours if you can let it down without dropping it.
winch.again: The brake lever under your hands.

slip.text: The brake bites, slips, bites. The cage drops a yard and stops with a clang that goes down the shaft and comes back up it, and the sleeper on the crate lifts his head. You are outside the cage house before he has found his lamp.
slip.again: The sleeper on the crate, awake now.

woke.text: A board under your boot. He is awake and on his feet with a hand on his weapon before you have taken the next step. "Pit's closed," he says, without any interest at all. "Go home."

no.text: "Unsafe ground," he says again, as if you had not said anything, and the other one has not moved at all.

text.text: Eleven graves on the slope between the pithead and Nursery, in a row, filled, with a lamp tag nailed to a stake at the head of each. Somebody has planted cabbages between them. In the Skirts, nobody wastes ground.

Eleven graves on the slope between the pithead and Nursery, dug and left open, with water in the bottom. A stake at the head of each and nothing on the stakes. The Shift dug them the day the gallery came down, and the Window has never said what for.

again.text: Eleven graves, filled. Cabbages between them.
Eleven graves, open, waiting.

interject.text: Ash stands at the end of the row the way he stands at every grave, a little too long. "They dug them first," he says. "Before anyone said they could fill them. That's a people who mean it."

text.text: The strike board, with the three demands crossed through one by one in Maren's hand, and under them: WON. WE WENT UP TOGETHER. The eleven names, and under the names, every name of the Shift who stood the picket.
The strike board has been taken down and used for a barricade. Where it hung, a list in coal of who has a rifle and who has a pick, and who is dead.
The strike board is still up. Nobody has had the heart to take it down. Somebody has hung Maren's rag on the nail at the top of it, folded.

The strike board: NO LAMPS DOWN UNTIL — 1. SIX EAST OPENED AND THE ELEVEN BROUGHT UP. 2. THE DEAD'S DEBTS VOID. 3. A STEWARD WITH A STOP. Under it the eleven names, and a column of who has stood the picket and how many days. And pinned at the bottom, in Maren's hand: THE VOTE WHEN THE CONCERN ANSWERS. NOT BEFORE.

look.again: The strike board.

intro.text: A woman sitting on an upturned lamp crate with a rag in her fist. She coughs into it, folds it, puts it away, and looks at you as if she had been expecting you for some time. "You're the one off the Line with the Concern's card in your pocket." She does not say how she knows. "Maren. The Shift. You'll want the car up the hill, and the car's stopped. No lamps down, no car up."
intro.again: Maren folds the rag and puts it away.

interject.text: "Okafor, Maren," Nine says, very quietly, only to you. "The twelfth line." Its lens does not leave her. "The record has never been inside this place. I would like to watch it be wrong."
"You run all this?" Tamsin says. "Nobody runs it," Maren says. "I hold the pen."

options.text: The Concern sent for me. I didn't come for them.

text.text: The Lodge at night: soup, wet wool, the stove. Maren at the end of the long table with a ledger of who has eaten. "Sit. Eat something. Then tell me."
Maren at the head of the picket, coughing into her rag. "Still here."

again.again: Maren waits, the rag folded in her fist.

options.text: Your name is on a list in Meridian. The city's list.
I've seen what happened in Six East. It wasn't geological.
The claim. Let's take it to the Contract Office.
Bring the eleven up. I'll go down with you.
Pim Rasul says "geological" because the Window pays his mother's ration for it.
Rafe has six cases of powder out of the magazine. He means the car.
There are twenty men on the platform with Concern paper.
(Put the Weighhouse book on the table in front of her.)

six.text: "Eleven days ago the east gallery came down with eleven in it." She says it the way you say a thing you have said every day since. "Orrin on the winch heard her talk before she went: you don't get a roof talking in good ground. The Window says geological. The Window shut the gallery, docked eleven lamps, and sent the dead's paper down the hill to their kin. That's the Concern's whole answer, on a notice."

leave.text: "Orrin runs the cage for the Shift. Tell him I said." She coughs. "The Clean sit on it by day. At night one of them sleeps; he's been sleeping eleven nights. If you see the pillars, you'll know what I know. Tell me what you see."
leave.again: "Orrin. At night. Tell me what you see."

demands.text: "Three things." She counts them on her fingers, which are black at the knuckles from twenty years of coal. "The eleven brought up and buried. Their debts void: a dead man's paper doesn't go to his children. And a steward with a stop: the right to say this ground's bad and walk off it without the Window doubling your paper." She puts the hand flat on her knee. "We go up together, or we don't go up."
demands.again: "Up. Void. A stop. We go up together."

card.text: "Nobody comes up here for the Concern. They come for something the Concern has." She looks at you a while longer than is comfortable. "You can have the car when it runs. It runs when Six does."

list.text: You tell her the line: OKAFOR, MAREN — THE SKIRTS — STRIKE BROKEN; HANGED (THE CONCERN). She listens all the way through, then coughs, folds the rag. "Hanged. By the Concern." Something nearly a smile. "They'd have to want me that much." She thinks about it the way she thinks about a roof. "Nobody in Meridian has ever been up here. How would they know what we'll do?"
list.again: "How would they know what we'll do?"

text.text: You tell her what Pim Rasul told you at the spoil heap: a man from the office with a surveyor's chalk, RETREAT on fourteen to twenty-two, the pillars cut back a bit a week, the roof talking on the Tuesday. Maren listens with the rag in her fist. "Robbed," she says. "Retreat mining. You take the legs out from under the roof on your way out. You don't do it with men still in the gallery." A long breath. "Unless you've a tonnage."

You put Dysart's order on the table: PILLARS 14–22 — RETREAT MINING AUTHORISED. Maren reads it twice. She doesn't cough. "Steward's objection noted," she reads out. "That was Ivo. Rafe's brother. He said no, and they reviewed his paper, and he went in anyway so his crew wouldn't go in without him."

You tell her what you saw: pillars fourteen to twenty-two cut back to a waist, fresh pick marks, RETREAT chalked on them, and a long D. She listens with the rag in her fist. "Robbed," she says. "Retreat mining. You take the legs out from under the roof on your way out, for the last of the coal. You don't do it with men still in the gallery." A long breath. "Unless you've a tonnage."

decision.text: You gave the Shift the proof that Six East was robbed, not fallen.

proof_given.text: "Then it's a claim." She says it slowly, as if the word were new and she wanted to see what it weighed. "Clause eleven. Every one of us signed it and none of us read it: THE CONCERN WARRANTS THE WORKINGS. The Concern keeps its word, they tell us. It's the one thing it sells." She stands. "The Letter at Footgate takes claims. For the kin. When you're ready, I'll walk there with you."

claim.text: "Now, then." She puts her coat on. "I'll do the talking. You do the paper." She stops at the door. "If the Letter says no, it says no as written, and then we're where we were, and you've lost nothing but a walk."
claim.again: "I'll do the talking. You do the paper."

options.text: (Go to the Contract Office with her.)

dig.text: "Tonight." She doesn't argue; she has been waiting for someone to say it. "Orrin on the winch, six of us, you. A pick each. The Clean sleep or they don't." Night comes down on Number Six. The cage, the dark, the heading, and at the end of it the fall, and seven people taking it apart with their hands and a jack, an hour, two, five, propping as they go; the roof talks twice and everyone stops breathing. Then the first boot. Then the rest of them, one at a time, wrapped in the Shift's coats, up the cage in the grey before dawn and onto the slope, into the graves the Shift dug eleven days ago.
dig.again: The eleven, up the cage in the grey before dawn.

decision.text: You went down Number Six with the Shift at night and brought the eleven up from Six East to be buried.

news.text: the Shift brought the eleven up from Six East in the night and buried them on the slope

passives.text: You find the safe line through the fall: the stone that holds, the stone that doesn't. The roof talks once less than it would have.

interject.text: Ash digs without stopping, as he digs at Openfield, and when the first one comes out he says the man's name off the tag before anyone else can. Nobody asks him how he knew to.
Wren goes in front with the lamp and reads the roof the way she reads a road. Twice she puts her hand up and everyone stops, and twice she is right.

dug.text: Maren stands at the end of the row with her coat open and says the eleven names, slowly, and then the Shift says them back. Then she hands you a lamp tag of your own, blank. "That was a shift in the mine," she says. "You're Shift now, if you want it. The tag says so."
dug.again: The row of graves. A blank tag in your hand.

pim.text: "The Rasuls." She nods slowly. "Yusuf was his brother." She writes something in the ledger of who has eaten. "Tell his mother the Shift's soup is hers. Tell Pim he can say what he saw." She looks up. "The Window can cut a ration. It can't cut the soup."

rafe.text: For a moment she says nothing at all. "Six cases." The rag goes into her fist. "Rafe lost Ivo under that roof. I'd want the car too." She stands up. "But the car has a crew in the cable house, Shift people, and the Clean will come down Cascade with rifles the morning after. I'll take the powder off him. He won't thank either of us."

decision.text: You told Maren about Rafe's powder. She took it off him.

scabs.text: "Twenty of them." She knew. "Off the guild's block at Ninebridge, on Concern paper. Debtors, same as us." She folds the rag. "We don't beat debtors off a platform. We feed them, if they'll sit down. If they go down Six, holding is starving, and the vote goes to Rafe." She looks at you. "Turn them, or buy their paper at the Letter's counter. Then call the vote."
scabs.again: "Turn them, or buy their paper. Then the vote."

book.text: She reads the book page by page, with her finger an inch above the paper the way people do who learned to read late. At Dawit Mekonnen's line she stops. At Nils Haber's she shuts it. "Joran's boy," she says. "His father's paper put him over their line. Our dead are feeding their scale." She stands. "The Skirts should see this. Today."
book.again: Maren, with the book shut under her hand.

options.text: Then put it on the wall on Cascade. All of it.

book_out.text: By noon a page of it is on the wall on Cascade beside Saba Mekonnen's notice, and by two there are three hundred people outside the Weighhouse who have read it, and the Clean at its door are looking at each other.
book_out.again: Three hundred people outside the Weighhouse.

decision.text: The Shift put the Weighhouse book on the wall on Cascade. The Skirts shut the Weighhouse.

news.text: the Skirts shut the Concern's Weighhouse after its book went up on the wall: the debtors it sent up the hill were weighed for parts

vote_ask.text: "Tonight." She doesn't ask whether you are sure. "Everybody, the Lodge, after the lamps would have come up. Then it's theirs, not mine and not yours." She looks at you. "Say what you think when it comes to you. Or don't. Either's allowed."

text.text: The Lodge, full to the doors and out of them, wet wool and breath and the stove. Maren stands on the bench: hold, she says. No lamps down. The Window can starve us slower than we can starve its tonnage, if nobody else digs. Then Rafe stands on the table: they ride over our heads every day in that car. Stop the car and the hill eats what it's got. Six cases says it stops tonight. The room turns its head from one to the other, and then, one by one, to you.

The Lodge, full to the doors and out of them, wet wool and breath and the stove. Maren stands on the bench: hold, she says. No lamps down. The Window can starve us slower than we can starve its tonnage, if nobody else digs. Rafe stands at the back with his arms folded and says nothing; whatever he had, he hasn't got it now. The room turns its head, one by one, to you.

vote_carried.text: You say it as well as you can, and it isn't enough. Rafe says one word back, CAR, and the Lodge says it with him, and Maren steps down off the bench without a word and sits.

vote_hold.text: Hands go up, slowly and then all at once. Maren counts them out loud without needing to. "Hold," she says. "No lamps down." Rafe goes out into the dark without a word. The stove ticks. Nobody goes home.

dawn_won.speaker: narrator
dawn_won.text: At dawn Corwin Dysart knocks on the Lodge door with his hat in his hand and a paper in the other. Nobody else has dug Six for eleven days and twenty men on the platform would not; the quarter's tonnage is a number with nothing in it. The Concern's terms, as written: Six East opened by the Concern's crew and the dead returned to kin; the debts of the eleven void under Clause 11; a steward with a stop. Maren reads it twice, and signs, and gives him back his pen. He takes the noon car up the hill and does not come down.
dawn_won.again: Dysart at the Lodge door at dawn, with the Concern's terms.

decision.text: The Shift voted to hold, and with nobody to dig Six the Concern gave the Shift its three demands. Maren Okafor lives.

news.text: the Shift won its strike at Number Six in the Skirts: the dead's debts void, the lamps going down again

interject.text: "Strike broken; hanged," Nine says, to nobody in particular. "Variance." It says the word the way someone else would say a prayer they had stopped believing in and found they still knew.

dawn_broken.speaker: narrator
dawn_broken.text: At dawn the cage goes down with the men off the Line in it, past the picket, with the Clean either side of them, and the winding engine starts for the first time in eleven days. By noon the Window has cut the strikers' ration to nothing. By evening the Clean have come up Cascade for Maren Okafor, as the leader of an action in breach of every contract on the slope. She goes with them without a word. In the morning she is on the post at Footgate, and the Concern's notice is nailed under her feet.

decision.text: The Shift voted to hold while the men off the Line still dug. The strike broke, and the Concern hanged Maren Okafor at Footgate.

news.text: the strike at Number Six was broken; the Concern hanged the Shift's leader from the post at Footgate

vote_car.text: "Car," Rafe says, and the Lodge goes out behind him into the dark with the six cases carried between them like a coffin. Maren goes too, last, because it is hers whether she wanted it or not. Footgate. The cable house behind the station, its drums the size of rooms and two of the car's own crew asleep beside them.
vote_car.again: The cable house, the drums, the crew asleep beside them.

car_clean.speaker: narrator
car_clean.text: You wake the crew and walk them out past the Clean's lamps before you set the fuse, and the drums come off their mountings with a sound the whole slope hears. Rafe goes back in for the last case, which is not set right, and does not come out. Two of the Clean die at the fence when the shooting starts. The car hangs on its track with its cable lying down the station like a dead snake.
car_clean.again: The car, hanging, the cable down the station.

car_dirty.speaker: narrator
car_dirty.text: Your fuse is a minute too short. You get one of the crew out. The other one is still in there when the drums come off their mountings with a sound the whole slope hears. Rafe dies at the door going back for him. The Clean fire down Cascade until morning. The car hangs on its track with its cable lying down the station like a dead snake.
car_dirty.again: The car, hanging, the cable down the station.

car_dirty_done.speaker: narrator
car_dirty_done.text: Rafe sets it fast and badly. The drums come off their mountings with a sound the whole slope hears, and with them the cable house and both the car's crew, and Rafe, who was still at the door. The Clean fire down Cascade until morning; three more die. In the grey Maren walks up and down the Lodge counting who is left, and does not stop coughing.

text.text: Maren at the head of the long table with the Lodge's ledger, and for once nobody waiting to be fed. "Clause eleven." She still says it as if she can't believe it held. "As written. The Letter put her stamp on it like it was a delivery note."

Maren at the head of the long table with the Lodge's ledger, and for once nobody waiting to be fed. "Lamps going down," she says. "Eleven up. A stop." She coughs, folds the rag. "We went up together."

won.again: Maren, with the ledger and nobody waiting to be fed.

options.text: The city wrote that you'd hang.

won_line.text: "Then the city was wrong about one thing." She considers it. "Or it was right and we weren't here yet." She almost laughs, which makes her cough. "Tell it Maren says hello. And that she's busy."

won_next.text: "Now they remember us." Flat. "The Concern doesn't forget a claim. They'll be cold to you at Footgate; you stood next to us. And the Shift will want rifles, because the next time they won't send a notice." She looks at you. "The car runs. Bell will have your name. Go up the hill if you have to. Come back down."
won_next.again: "Go up if you have to. Come back down."

revolt.text: Maren in the Lodge with a rifle across the table that she has not touched, and a list of the dead pinned where the strike board was. "We have guns now," she says. "I never wanted guns. I wanted a stop." The rag, folded. "The hill's shut. The car's down. Nobody's hanged. Ask me in a year if it was worth it."
revolt.again: Maren, and the rifle she has not touched.

intro.text: A big man with coal in the creases of his knuckles, standing where he can watch the Clean watch the cage. "My brother's under Six East," he says, before you have said anything. "Say 'geological' to me and see what happens."
intro.again: Rafe, watching the Clean.

text.text: "You took it." He knows. He doesn't raise his voice. "Out of the cellar. You or her, it's the same thing." He looks at the cage. "Fine. Hold, then. See how long holding lasts."
Rafe, arms folded. "What."

again.again: Rafe, arms folded.

options.text: Don't. People ride that car, and Shift people run the cable house.

mods.why: Ivo is in the ground now, not under it

decision.text: You talked Rafe Ansel out of blowing the car. He gave you the powder.

options.text: I'm with you. Stop the car.
There's a door in the Concern's chrome. Kes can switch every piece on the slope off at once.

decision.text: You told Rafe Ansel about the door in the Concern's chrome, and who could open it.

brother.text: "Ivo. Steward of the east crew." He says it to the cage, not to you. "Dysart wanted pillars fourteen to twenty-two taken back for the tonnage. Ivo said no. The Window reviewed his paper the same day: doubled. He went in anyway, because his crew was going in, and he wouldn't send them in without him." He breathes out. "That's Ivo. That's what geological means."

want.text: "The car." He doesn't lower his voice; he has said it in the Lodge. "They ride over our heads every day in it, up to their orange trees. Six cases out of the magazine and the cable house comes off its mountings, and the hill eats what it's got. A week. Then they come down and talk." He looks at you. "Maren says hold. Holding is starving slower."

stood.text: He looks at the cage a long time. Then he goes down into the Lodge's cellar and comes up with six greasy cases and puts them at your feet, one at a time, like a man paying a debt. "If the Letter says no," he says, "I know where the magazine is."

door.text: Rafe goes very still. "Every piece," he says. "The Clean's lenses. Their rifles' sights. The car's brakes." He is already moving. "She's been sitting on that? Kes!" He goes off down the slope shouting her name, and you remember, too late, that she told you it was a timetable.

You tell her: a dormant channel in every Concern piece, and a way to turn it round, and the one person in the Skirts who has done it. She writes nothing down. When you have finished she says, "Four hundred. And a contract, offered, when the car runs." A pause. "And Ms Oyelaran is reviewed."

A post with a crossbar beside the gate, in sight of every door on Cascade, and a notice nailed to it in clean print: ACTION IN BREACH OF CONTRACT BY ANY PARTY ON THIS SLOPE IS SABOTAGE. SABOTAGE IS ANSWERED AT FOOTGATE. Nothing on it now. Old rope marks on the crossbar.

Fresh pick marks, bright on the black. Chalk on each: a number, and RETREAT, and a long D. Above them the roof has sagged into a belly, and somewhere in it, very quietly, something ticks.
look.again: Pillars cut to a waist. RETREAT — D. The roof ticking.

passives.text: Retreat mining: you take the pillars on your way out of a worked gallery, last thing, for the coal in them, and you let the roof come down behind you. You never do it with a crew still working the face beyond. Whoever cut these knew there were people past them.

interject.text: "Somebody did that with a plan," Ilya says. He touches a pick mark with one finger. "A bit a week. Right."
Wren listens to the roof with her head on one side. "Don't talk," she says, very quietly. "It's talking."

look.text: The fall: the roof come down across the gallery from wall to wall, slabs and slack and broken props, piled to where the roof used to be. At its edge, half in the rubble, the glass of a lamp. Then another. Eleven people are on the other side of this, and none of them are waiting any more.
look.again: The fall, and the lamps at its edge.

options.text: (Dig carefully to the lamps at the edge.)

mods.why: Wren reads the roof for you
Kes holds the lamp where you need it

tags.text: An hour on your knees with the roof ticking over you. The lamps first, then the belts they hung from, and on each belt a brass tag with a number. Eleven. You leave everything else where it lies. Bringing them up is for more than one pair of hands.
tags.again: The edge of the fall, dug back.

talks.text: You get one slab off and the roof answers: a crack like a door slamming, a shower of slack down your collar. You are back at the pillars before you know you have moved. Nobody digs that alone.
talks.again: The fall. The roof still ticking.

open.text: The fall dug back to a passage the width of a man, propped with new timber. Beyond it the gallery is empty. The Shift took everything they found up the cage, and chalked on the last prop: UP.

text.text: The wall on Cascade, three deep in paper. In the middle of it, nailed through all four corners so nobody can take it down, a page of the Weighhouse book: NAME — DEBT — YIELD — SERVICE. Somebody has written beside the yield column, in big letters, what K L C H stand for.

The wall on Cascade, three deep in paper: lost, found, for sale, a room, a goat, a pair of boots in good condition. NO LAMPS DOWN in red over all of it. And one notice newer and neater than the rest, pinned at eye height by somebody who comes back every day to straighten it.

options.text: (Nail a page of the Weighhouse book to the wall beside it.)

saba.text: DAWIT MEKONNEN, MINER, NUMBER FOUR, WENT TO THE WEIGHHOUSE TO CLEAR HIS PAPER. THE WINDOW WROTE DISCHARGED IN SERVICE. HE HAS NOT WRITTEN. IF YOU HAVE SEEN HIM UP THE HILL TELL SABA, NURSERY, THE SECOND ROW. HE IS TALL AND HE HUMS.
saba.again: HE IS TALL AND HE HUMS.

rest.text: A goat, two scrip a day for its milk. A room on Nursery, no cough. CONTRACT FOR SALE, TEN YEARS LEFT, GOOD TERMS, ASK AT THE POND. A child's drawing of an orange tree. And small, in the corner, chalk: THE LEDGER CAN'T SEE US. GOOD.
rest.again: A goat, a room, a contract for sale, an orange tree.

pin.text: You nail the page up beside Saba's notice and stand back. It takes an hour. First one person stops, then four, then the whole of Cascade is reading it over each other's shoulders, and somebody who can read the letters says them out loud, and somebody else says what they stand for. By dark there are three hundred people outside the Weighhouse. By midnight there are none inside it.
pin.again: The page, nailed up beside Saba's notice.

decision.text: You nailed a page of the Weighhouse book to the wall on Cascade. The Skirts read it, and shut the Weighhouse.

news.text: the Skirts shut the Concern's Weighhouse after its book went up on the wall: the debtors it sent up the hill were weighed for parts

interject.text: "There's a weight to that," Ash says, watching them read. "Now it's everyone's."
Tamsin reads it with them and then turns round to you with a face like a slammed door. "Bits," she says. "They weigh them for bits."
"That's a block," Wren says. "With a doctor at the counter." She doesn't say anything else for an hour.

hc_home.text: Saba is not at the wall. Her notice is gone; there is a nail where it was. You find her outside the shack on Nursery with a bowl of beans to shell, and Dawit beside her on a crate with a patch over one eye, humming. She looks at you for a long time. "They carried him up Cascade on a door," she says. "Nobody would let me help. They said I'd drop him laughing." She goes back to the beans. "I would have."

hc_dead.text: Saba at her wall, straightening a notice that has no reason to be straight any more: the Weighhouse is shut and nobody goes up. "You've been up the hill," she says. "Everybody says. Did you see him? Dawit. He's tall. He hums."

options.text: (Tell her what you found on floor nine.)

hc_told.text: You tell her: a cold room, a column of labels with his number on every one, and what the Clinic floors did when the Skirts stopped sending. She listens with her hand flat on the notice. When you finish she takes it down, folds it in four, and puts it in her apron. "So it was us," she says. "Shutting the Weighhouse. That's what did it." She doesn't cry. "I'd shut it again. I want you to know that. I'd shut it again."

hc_lied.text: "No." She straightens the notice. "No, well. It's a big hill." She will be standing at this wall for years. You know it, and you walk away anyway.

intro.text: A woman straightening a notice on the wall that does not need straightening. "Have you been up the hill?" she says, before anything else. "Dawit. He's tall. He hums when he works. He went to the Weighhouse to clear his paper and they wrote that he's in service."
intro.again: Saba, straightening her notice.

again.text: "Anything?" Saba says. She already knows the answer from your face.
again.again: Saba waits.

what.text: "His paper crossed the line after the winter. The cough took two months' tally. You go to the Weighhouse when you cross the line; they weigh you and offer you service, and service clears it all, and the family gets a settlement." She says it like a lesson. "He went on a Tuesday. On the Friday the Window gave me forty scrip and his boots, cleaned. Nobody comes back from service. Everybody says they're in the gardens." She looks at the notice. "He would have written."

boots.text: She brings them out of the shack: a miner's boots resoled twice, cleaner than any boot on the slope. "Take them," she says. "Find out. I can't look at them." Inside the left tongue there is a printed tag. You read it twice: 9-1182 — EFFECTS — RETURN TO KIN.
boots.again: The boots, and the tag in the tongue.

tell.text: You tell her as gently as it can be told, which is not very. She doesn't sit down. She straightens the notice on the wall one more time, very carefully, and then she takes it down, and folds it, and puts it in her apron. "He hummed," she says. "Nobody up there will know what he hummed."
tell.again: Saba, with the notice folded in her apron.

exposed.text: Saba on the step of her shack with Dawit's name chalked on the door. "They shut it," she says. "Three hundred people. I didn't know there were three hundred people who would." She looks up the hill. "It won't bring him down."

text.text: The Weighhouse door, kicked in and nailed shut again from the outside with planks. WEIGHED written across the planks in somebody's blood or somebody's red paint, and under it a list of names that keeps getting longer.

A sign by the Weighhouse door in clinic-white enamel: WEIGHING — VOLUNTARY. SERVICE DISCHARGES ALL PAPER IN FULL (CLAUSE 31). SETTLEMENT TO KIN. And the iron deck of the old ore scale still set in the floor inside the door, so that everyone who comes in stands on it.

intro.text: A woman in clinic white at a table by the scale deck, with a board of names and a pen she uses like a scalpel. "Sit. Breathe." Then she sees you are not from the bench. "Fittings are by appointment. Weighing is for paper that has crossed the line. Which are you?"
intro.again: Dr Lisle, with her board of names.

text.text: Dr Lisle looks up and, for the first time, puts the pen down. "You've been reading," she says.
"Sit. Breathe," Dr Lisle says, to the bench, and then, to you: "Yes?"

again.again: Dr Lisle, with her pen.

mods.why: a pair of boots with a tag in the tongue

options.text: (Put Dawit Mekonnen's boots on her table.) 9-1182.
K, L, C, H. Kidney, liver, cornea, heart. You grade them.

what.text: "When a contract's paper crosses the line, the holder is weighed: what they can still carry, what the contract can still yield." She says it the way she would say a dose. "Most go home with a schedule. Some are offered service. Service discharges the whole of the paper under Clause 31 and the family is settled. It is the only door out of the Skirts that opens." She caps the pen. "Nobody is made to walk through it."
what.again: "The only door out of the Skirts that opens."

interject.text: "Yield," Nine says. "A term of assessment." Its lens holds on her board. "I would like to see the schedule it is assessed against." Dr Lisle does not answer it.

service.text: She looks at the bench, at the queue on it, and lowers her voice. "Service is on the Clinic floors. Floor nine. They go up on the freight car at two, asleep; it is kinder. I have never been up." She says the last part as if it were a defence. "I weigh. I don't ask what the scale is for. Someone has to stand between this bench and the Clean collecting the old way, and that someone is me."
service.again: "I weigh. I don't ask what the scale is for."

service_no.text: "Service is service." She uncaps the pen. "Next."

boots.text: She looks at the tag and her face does something small and quickly put away. "Effects return to kin," she says. "That is in the contract. It is a kindness. Most contracts don't send anything back."

nils.text: "Haber. Twenty-two, a miner's lungs, no cough yet, a father's paper by transfer." She reads it off the board without needing to. "Queued. He's a good weight." She hears herself say it. "The paper decides. Not me."

yield.text: She doesn't deny it. She closes the board. "Do you know what the Clean did before the Weighhouse?" Quietly. "They collected. Paper over the line, a family on the slope, and a cart in the morning. Now there is a bench, and a settlement, and the boots come home." She looks at you steadily. "Put it on the wall, if you like. They'll stop coming. The paper will still be over the line. And the cart will come back."

options.text: What's it worth to you that nobody reads it?
I'll keep it quiet. Take one name off your board: Nils Haber.
You pay for names, don't you?

pay.text: "A hundred and fifty." Out of a drawer, in clean Halcyon notes. "For the book, and for the Skirts not to read what it wouldn't understand."

decision.text: You took a hundred and fifty from Dr Lisle to keep the Weighhouse book off the wall.

favour.text: A long silence. Then she rubs one name off the board with her thumb. "Haber walks," she says. "He was never weighed." She looks at you. "And you owe the Weighhouse a silence, and I owe you a door, when you go up. The Clinic floors know my name."

decision.text: You kept the Weighhouse quiet for Dr Lisle, in exchange for Nils Haber's name off her board.

fee.text: "A finder's fee." She doesn't blush. "A hundred, for a name that comes to the bench of its own accord. People do find each other. The Skirts is full of paper over the line."

decision.text: You took the Weighhouse's finder's fee: a name for a hundred Tolls.

fee_done.text: She writes it on the board, and pays you, and turns back to the bench. "Sit," she says to the next one. "Breathe."
fee_done.again: A new name on the board.

interject.text: Wren is gone from the door before the notes are counted. You find her later on the platform, and she does not turn round.
Tamsin looks at you as if she has never seen you before. "Bits," she says. "You sold someone for bits."
Ash says nothing. It is the loudest thing he has ever said to you.
"I sold paper on people for thirty years," Odile says. "I never once sold the person to the doctor." She buttons her coat.

covered.text: "Thank you." She means it, which is the worst part. "Sit," she says to the bench. "Breathe."

read.text: NAME — DEBT — YIELD — SERVICE. Two hundred lines in a clean hand. The yield column is four letters with a grade under each, K L C H, 1 to 3, and a dash where there is nothing to grade. MEKONNEN, D. — 212 — K2 L2 C1 H1 — CLINIC 9, R30. Under the last ruled line, in pencil, the queue: HABER, N. — 90 (TRANSFER, §9) — K1 L1 C1 H1 — QUEUED. And four more, each with a father or a mother under Six East.
read.again: NAME — DEBT — YIELD — SERVICE. K L C H.

passives.text: K, L, C, H: kidney, liver, cornea, heart. Graded the way a surgeon grades an organ for a recipient. A dash under H means the heart is no good. This is not a ledger of debts. It is a donor list.
Four letters, four grades, a dash for the unusable: an inventory, not an assessment. Of four things a body has one or two of. Kidney, liver, cornea, heart.

interject.text: Kes reads over your shoulder and stops breathing for a second. "K L C H," she says. "I thought it was a pay grade." Her hand goes to the back of her neck. "My mother was on a board like this once. I thought it was a pay grade."

intro.text: A young man on a cot in the Weighhouse ward with his boots on, as if he might be leaving. "Haber," he says. "My father's under Six East. His paper came to me; that's the contract. Ninety over the line." He tries a smile. "They say service is up in the gardens. Orange trees."
intro.again: Nils, on the cot, with his boots on.

options.text: What do you think service is?

again.text: Nils sits up on the cot. "Still here."
again.again: Nils, sitting up.

options.text: What do you think service is?
I've read the book. Service isn't the gardens.
Walk out with me. Now, while the door's asleep.

mods.why: Kes blinds the ward's lens for a minute

decision.text: You walked Nils Haber out of the Weighhouse ward at night.

service.text: "Work. Up the hill. Clean work, gardens, orange trees." He looks at his boots. "Nobody writes back. They say that's because it's good up there and they forget us." He laughs. "I wouldn't forget."

truth.text: He listens, and when you have finished he takes his boots off, very slowly, and puts them side by side under the cot as if somebody would come to collect them. Then he puts them on again. "Get me out," he says. "Please."

walked.speaker: narrator
walked.text: Past the sleeping cots, past the scale deck, past the Clean at the door who is looking at Cascade, and out into the cold. He doesn't stop until he is on Nursery among the shacks, and then he sits down in the mud and shakes.

caught.text: "Back on your cot." The Clean at the door, without looking round. Nils lies down again with his boots on.
caught.again: Nils, lying down with his boots on.

free.text: Nils Haber on Nursery, splitting kindling for somebody else's stove. "Joran's boy," people call him. "My paper's nothing," he says. "First time in my life." He doesn't know what to do with his hands.

day.text: A gate in the fence at the top of the freight lane, and a board on it: FREIGHT — 02:00 — CONCERN CREW. The Concern runs its own freight on its own crew, strike or no strike. Crates on the dock behind the station, stencilled MEDICAL — COLD.

two.text: Two in the morning. The freight car comes down its track with no lamps lit and stops at the dock. Out of the Weighhouse's back door and up the lane come two of the Clean with a stretcher between them, and on it someone asleep under a white sheet with a tag on their wrist. Then another. They go into the freight car with the cold crates. A bag comes down off the car the other way and is put inside the Weighhouse's back door: a coat, a pair of boots.
two.again: The freight at two: stretchers up, a bag of effects down.

interject.text: "I have watched the Precinct's carts take people who would not be counted," Nine says, very low. "They did not send the boots back." It does not say which is worse.

intro.text: A shack with a surgeon's table in it, a good one, with a lamp on an arm and a tray of tools that are clean. The man at it is big and bearded and grey, and his hands are the steadiest thing on Nursery. "Lev. Dark work: no channel, no warranty, no Window." He looks at the back of your neck before he looks at your face. "What are you carrying?"
intro.again: Lev at his table.

again.text: "Sit still or I charge double," Lev says. "What?"
again.again: Lev waits.

options.text: What does "yield" mean, on the Weighhouse's board?
Can you take a Concern port out of somebody's neck without killing them?

who.text: "Nine years an orderly on the Clinic floors. Carrying holdfast, mopping, holding things still." He turns a clamp over. "I left the week I understood what I was holding still. Now I fit what people can bear and drink less than I did." He looks up. "Most weeks."

yield.text: He doesn't need to look at the book. "K, L, C, H. Kidney, liver, cornea, heart, graded one to three for match and wear." He sets the clamp down. "Nobody up there needs a whole Skirts body. They need it in pieces, and fresh, and the pieces go to the people who can pay to stay the age they are." He wipes his hands although they are clean. "I don't know whose. I carried holdfast. I didn't read the charts."
yield.again: "Nobody up there needs a whole Skirts body."

interject.text: Ash puts a hand flat on the shack wall as if the floor had moved. "They take the dead for the sky at Openfield," he says. "This is the other thing."

kes.text: Lev looks at Kes the way he looked at the back of your neck. "Lattice port. Window issue." He touches the cable at her nape with one finger and she doesn't flinch, which costs her. "It's in the top of the spine. Cut a live channel and it takes the person with it: that's the Scald's lesson, and the Pale's, and anyone who's held a hand while it went." He sets out the tray. "Somebody holds the channel quiet while I cut. If they hold it, she walks out blind on the grid and free. If they don't, she walks out and has fits. I don't lose people on this table."
kes.again: Lev, with the tray set out.

mods.why: Ash's word: burn the channel first, then cut
holdfast in the pack

decision.text: Lev Ostrander cut the Concern's port out of Kes's neck at his table, with you holding the channel. She walked out free.
Lev Ostrander cut the Concern's port out of Kes's neck. The channel slipped in your hands; she lives, and has fits now.

cut.text: An hour. Her hand on your wrist the whole time, hard enough to bruise. Then a small wet sound and Lev drops something the size of a coin into a dish, with a tail of fine wire. Kes sits up. She puts her hand to the back of her neck, where there is a dressing now and nothing else. "It's quiet," she says, astonished. "It's so quiet."
cut.again: The dish, and the coin in it with its wire tail.

fits.text: Halfway through, the channel jumps under your hands and her whole body goes rigid on the table, and Lev says something you don't catch and keeps cutting. The port comes out. Kes lives. That night at the fire she has her first fit, and you hold her head off the ground until it passes. "Worth it," she says after, with her teeth still chattering. "Obviously. Ask me again tomorrow."
fits.again: The dish, and her hand shaking.

intro.text: A woman on the platform beside the changer's booth with two children asleep on the bags and a tea tin held in both hands. "Two years," she says, not to you exactly. "A hundred scrip. The Line to Meridian is twenty-five a head, Tolls, and there are three of us." She opens the tin to show you: tens, tied with string. "He changes at six. That's sixteen." She closes it. "Meridian has schools. That's all I know about Meridian."
intro.again: Ama, the tin, the children asleep on the bags.

interject.text: "Six to one," Odile says, mostly to herself. She is looking at the booth's board the way she looks at a sheet. "My dear, I priced that spread on a slate at Ninebridge in the year the bridge had eight spans."

options.text: Let me see what the changer can do.

decision.text: You paid the difference on Ama Owusu's fares yourself. Her family went down the Line.

again.text: "Anything?" Ama says. The children are awake now and watching you.
again.again: Ama waits with the tin.

decision.text: You paid the difference on Ama Owusu's fares yourself. Her family went down the Line.

paid.text: She looks at the Tolls for a long time before she takes them. "I'll pay it back," she says, which you both know she won't be able to. "Seven o'clock." She wakes the children.
paid.again: Ama and the children, waiting for seven.

cut.text: Ama, on the platform with the tin. "Sixteen," she says. "I'll save for another year." She doesn't look at the booth, or at you.

intro.text: A man in a booth with a counter, a cash box and a board, and a guild ticket pinned to his coat. "Six to one, scrip to Tolls. Four to one the other way." He taps the board. "I don't set it. I read it."
intro.again: Vulpe, and his board.

text.text: "Docked a week," Vulpe says, without looking up. "For one change at par. The guild doesn't miss a thing." He reads the board. "Six to one."
"Six to one," Vulpe says.

again.again: Vulpe, and his board.

mods.why: Odile knows what a changer's book looks like

options.text: Change Ama Owusu's tin at par.

mods.why: you know his book has a par column
his own ledger, open on his counter
Odile reads him his own par column, line by line

decision.text: You made the changer at Two-Twelve change Ama Owusu's savings at par. Her family went down the Line.

news.text: the changer at Two-Twelve changed a miner's savings at par for once; the guild docked him for it

options.text: Change it at par, or the Shift reads your par column on the wall on Cascade.

mods.why: the Shift has just won a claim against the Concern
the Shift is broken and he knows it

decision.text: You made the changer at Two-Twelve change Ama Owusu's savings at par. Her family went down the Line.

news.text: the changer at Two-Twelve changed a miner's savings at par for once; the guild docked him for it

options.text: What would you pay me to send travellers your way?

who.text: "The board comes up the Line every week from Ninebridge, under the Exchange's seal." He turns it so you can see the wax. "Scrip is the Concern's; Tolls are the guild's; I'm the hole in the fence between them." He shrugs. "I'm on a guild ticket. I owe them more than you'd think."

book.text: He hesitates, then opens it, because nobody has asked him in two years and it is a beautiful book. Every change, scrip in, Tolls out, at the week's rate. And down the margin, ruled in red, a column headed PAR that never moves: one to one. "That's what the guild takes it at," he says, quietly, "from the Concern. On the floor." He shuts it. "Six to one is what the Skirts gets."
book.again: PAR, one to one, in red.

book_no.text: "Ledgers are private." He puts his elbow on it.

par.text: He changes it at par: a hundred scrip, a hundred Tolls, out of the cash box, slowly, as if every Toll were a tooth. "The guild will dock me the difference," he says. "A week. Maybe two." He doesn't look at Ama when she takes it. She looks at him, though, for a long time.
par.again: A hundred Tolls, counted out like teeth.

interject.text: "Par," Odile says, and puts her glasses back on. "My dear, I have waited a long time to see someone say that word at a booth and mean it."

par_no.text: "Six to one." He doesn't move. "Take it up with Ninebridge."

cut.text: "One in ten." He says it without looking up, like the rate. "Anyone you send me with scrip to change, I give you one Toll in ten of what I take. Thirty now, for the woman with the tin, if she changes with me today."

options.text: (Take it. Send Ama to change at six.)

decision.text: You took the changer's cut and sent Ama Owusu to change her savings at six to one.

cut_done.text: Thirty Tolls across the counter. In the afternoon Ama changes her tin at the booth, and counts sixteen, and sits back down on the bags.

interject.text: Odile watches the woman count sixteen. "That is how I started," she says. "One in ten." She does not say anything else.

ruined.text: The booth is shut. A guild man came up the Line and took the board, the box and Vulpe's ticket. Vulpe sits on the platform's edge with his ledger on his knees. "One day at par," he says. "Everyone on the slope changed everything they had. I'll be paying it back to the guild till I die." He almost laughs. "Best day the booth ever had."
ruined.again: Vulpe, with his ledger, on the platform's edge.

text.text: The rate board is gone. A rectangle of cleaner wood where it hung, and chalk: PAR. ONE DAY. WE REMEMBER.
THE CHANGE — THIS WEEK — SCRIP TO TOLLS 6:1 — TOLLS TO SCRIP 1:4. Painted on a board under glass, with the Exchange's wax seal on a ribbon across the corner: the Grand Factor's office, Ninebridge.

board.again: The rate board.

options.text: (Kes: "Obviously the glass is a screen. Give me the night.")

decision.text: Kes re-sealed the changer's board at par for a day. Everyone on the slope changed everything they had.

news.text: the rate board at Two-Twelve read PAR for one day under the Exchange's own seal; the guild sent a man up the Line

options.text: (Lift the glass, and the seal with it, and re-paint the rate at par.)

decision.text: You re-sealed the changer's board at par for a day. Everyone on the slope changed everything they had.

news.text: the rate board at Two-Twelve read PAR for one day under the Exchange's own seal; the guild sent a man up the Line

forged.speaker: narrator
forged.text: In the morning the board says PAR under the Exchange's own seal, and by noon there is a line from the booth to the Lodge. Ama Owusu changes her hundred first. Vulpe changes until the box is empty and then sits down. The next Line brings a guild man with a cane, who takes the board, the box and Vulpe's ticket, and goes back down on the seven o'clock. Provision's prices go up the same afternoon.
forged.again: A line from the booth to the Lodge.

forge_no.text: The seal's wax cracks under your thumb in the wrong place. You put the glass back before anyone looks. It will not take a second try.

text.text: Provision's price board: a lit screen of what things cost in scrip. And over it, faint, an overlay you were not meant to see: every price shifts by a few points as each customer steps up to the counter, a little higher for the ones whose Window balance is deep. The deeper the paper, the dearer the bread.
Provision's price board: a lit screen of what things cost in scrip, and every price on it higher than last week. Somebody has scratched UP into the frame.
Provision's price board: a lit screen of what things cost in scrip. The prices flicker now and then, by a point or two, as people step up to the counter.

board.again: Provision's price board.

interject.text: "I keep that board running," Kes says. "Obviously I know what it does. Everybody pays the board. The board reads your paper." She looks at the counter. "Mercy pays it too."

intro.text: A woman behind Provision's counter in a company apron, who looks as tired as the people she sells to. "Provision. Prices on the board." She glances at your hands. "Outsiders pay in Tolls, at the outsider's price. Don't look at me like that. I pay the same board."
intro.again: Mercy, behind the counter.

text.text: "Up again," Mercy says. "Don't ask me why. You know why."
"Provision," Mercy says.

again.again: Mercy waits.

options.text: The board reads everybody's paper and prices them by it.

board.text: "Course it does." She doesn't lower her voice. "Twelve years behind this counter. You think I can't see the numbers jump when Ewa Kowal's widow steps up?" She stacks tins. "I'm two years from clear. Then I'll say it at the Lodge. Not before."
board.again: "Two years from clear."

intro.text: A container fitted out as a bar, coal dust in every crease, a stove, a counter, and a woman behind it with a long plait and forearms like a miner's. "Lampblack. Coal dust and a door that shuts." She pours before you ask. "Strike pours are half. You're not on strike. The Dust table's open if you've something you'd miss."
intro.again: Rosa, pouring.

again.text: "Back," Rosa says. "Pour, play, or talk?"
again.again: Rosa waits with the bottle.

talk.text: "Strike. Always the strike." She wipes the counter. "Maren says hold. Rafe drinks here less than he did and talks less than that, which with Rafe means something. And the Weighhouse had a busy month." She doesn't say anything about the Weighhouse. She doesn't need to.

rafe.text: "Six cases out of the magazine." Very quietly, wiping the same place on the counter. "Orrin counts them every night; he told me, and I'm telling you, and now it's three of us and that's too many." She looks at the door. "Rafe means the car. He says it in here when he's had two."

kes.text: "Kes?" Rosa laughs. "The Window's girl. Fixes their lenses and their boards. Drinks here at six, sits in the corner, says 'obviously' at everybody. If she's writing on the Line board she likes you." She pours. "Or she wants something. With Kes it's both."

intro.text: A man in the middle of the dry pond with his shirt off and his knuckles taped, and on his right arm, from the elbow down, a company limb in grey composite with a lamp-tag number on it. He sees you look. "No chrome in the Pond. The Pond's rule." He holds the arm up. "This one they switch off for me, when I'm behind on the Window. Saves me the trouble." He grins with a split lip. "Twenty on yourself, forty-five back if you win."
intro.again: Baek, in the middle of the pond.

text.text: "You again." Baek rolls his good shoulder. "Lucky. Again?"

arm.text: "Hauler arm, company issue. Fitted at the Weighhouse when I was nineteen, against the paper." He flexes the fingers; they move, slow. "Fall behind on the Window and one morning it's dead to the shoulder. Pay the Window and it wakes up. Nobody touches it. Nobody has to." He shrugs. "Everybody in the Skirts with company chrome knows. Nobody says. What would you say?"

kes_prices.text: "Provision reads your Window balance off your lamp tag when you step up to the counter and moves the price a few points. Deeper paper, dearer bread." She says it flat. "I keep it running. If I don't, they send someone who'll keep it running worse."

kes_dark.text: You go in beside her, or she takes you in; there is no telling. The Window's grid like a field at night, and in it a single channel, lit, running up the hill: hers. She takes it in both hands, so to speak, and turns it round, and the light goes out of it. When you are back in the cabinet's hum she is crying without noticing. "Nobody," she says. "Nobody's looking. For good." Then: "Obviously I'm not crying."

kes_citizen.text: "Citizen." Kes's fingers go into the cabinet's guts. "Face. A number nobody's got. Fitted last spring at the gate, very brave, no complications." The printer under the counter hums for a long time and gives you forty pages, warm, the Window's own print on the Window's own stock. "Every lens on the hill will believe that," she says. "Obviously don't let a person read it."

kes_dark_fail.text: Halfway round, something on the hill notices. Kes rips out of the cabinet so fast she cuts her hand on its edge. "Bricked," she says. "They've put a watch on the Window. That door's shut." She sucks the cut. "Other doors."

intro.text: A young woman sitting cross-legged on the highest thing within reach, with a cable running from the back of her neck into a box on her knee, goggles pushed up into short coils of hair, a miner's jacket cut down to fit. She doesn't look up from the box. "You read my board." Then she does look up, and grins. "Obviously you did. You're lit up like the gardens. Every lens on the slope turns when you walk past it." She unplugs the cable with a click. "Kes. I keep the Window's eyes working. Mostly."
intro.again: Kes, the cable coiled on her knee.

hail.text: "Every board on the slope is mine. The Line board's the only one with a view." She brags it, then shrugs. "The Window doesn't read its own boards. Nobody does. I could write the Board's birthdays up there and nobody'd notice but the goats."
hail.again: "Nobody reads the boards but the goats."

why.text: "Because the Letter has your name on a list I keep the lens for, and the list says THE BOARD'S GUEST, and the Board doesn't have guests." She swings her legs. "The Board has the Skirts. Contracts, scrip, the Weighhouse, the car. When it wants a thing it hasn't got, it sends for it. So: what are you, that it hasn't got?" She waits, and when you don't answer she nods as if you had. "Fine. Here's a trade. The Shift's eleven under Six East. Help with that, and I'll get you places the car doesn't go. I can open things. You can walk past things. Obviously we should be the same person."

Kes sits cross-legged by the fire, winding a length of cable round her fingers and off again. "Fire's a terrible light source," she says. "Obviously I love it."

s1.text: She winds the cable round three fingers and off again. "Maren took me in when my mother died. Eighteen. I had a port in my neck and a debt on my paper and I thought organising was a word for tidying." She laughs at herself. "She sat me at the long table and made me count who'd eaten. Every night. Two years. Then one night she said: right, you know who everybody is, now we can start." She looks at you. "So. What's the strike for? Your words. Not Maren's."

options.text: So you go up together, or nobody goes.
It's for whatever the Shift decides it's for.
The city has Maren on a list. Strike broken; hanged.

s1_together.text: "Her line." She grins. "You stole her line. Good. It's a good line; it should get around." She winds the cable on. "It's also true, which is rarer."

s1_theirs.text: "Huh." She considers you. "Most people from outside come up the Line with an answer. You came up with a question." She looks pleased and annoyed about it. "Fine."

s1_hanged.text: "Everybody's forecast's hanged. That's the Skirts." She doesn't look up. "That's why you organise. So it takes them longer, and costs them more, and they have to do it in front of everyone."

s1_list.text: She listens all the way through with the cable gone still in her fingers. "It can't see in here," she says at last. "The Window's grid is Halcyon's; the Ledger's lenses stop at the Line. And it can't see me." She almost laughs. "Obviously it got it wrong. It's guessing from outside the fence." Then, quieter: "Unless it isn't."

s2.text: For a while she pretends not to have heard. Then she puts the cable down. "There's a door in every piece of their chrome. A channel nobody's supposed to know about, that runs up the hill. Through it they can see you, wherever you are. Numb you. Switch you off. Ask Baek about his arm." She touches the back of her neck. "I found it in mine when I was nineteen. And I turned it round. For an hour a night it looks the other way, and nobody on the hill can see me." She shrugs, too hard. "That's when the Shift meets. That's why the lenses go blind at the Lodge. That's me."

options.text: Then it's yours. Nobody hears it from me.
I'm wearing their chrome. Can you do it for me?

s2_keep.text: "Good." Something in her shoulders comes down an inch. "Nobody ever says that. They say, think what you could do with it." She looks up the hill. "Rafe would switch off every Concern piece on the slope at once, including Baek's arm and half the Shift's spines. Somebody up the hill would switch them off one at a time, on purpose." Very level: "If you ever give it to anyone, I'm gone. That's not a threat. It's a timetable."

s2_show.text: She touches the back of her neck and does something you can't see, and the night gets a degree quieter, the way a room does when a machine you hadn't noticed stops. "There," she says. "Nobody's looking. For an hour." She lies back by the fire with her hands under her head. "This is the best hour of the day. Obviously."

s2_weapon.text: "It's a door." Sharp. "People keep calling doors weapons. It's a door they put in me without asking, and I found the handle." She picks the cable up again. "If you ever give it to anyone, I'm gone. Remember I said."

s2_me.text: "Yours is lit up like the gardens." She gets behind you and puts two fingers on the back of your neck, light, and does something. "There. An hour a night. Mine and yours." She sits back down. "Don't tell anyone. Obviously."
s2_me.again: "An hour a night. Mine and yours."

s3.text: "One day." She says it to the fire. "That's all. One whole day without the hill in the back of my neck, not an hour I have to steal." She turns the cable over. "It's in the top of my spine. Cut it wrong and it takes you with it; that's what the Scald was, mostly. The Pale cut theirs out with knives and half of them died." She makes herself look at you. "Lev on Nursery might. Somebody who's cut their own and lived might know how. Or I go into the Window at night with someone holding the other end, and turn the door on myself for good." A breath. "I'm scared of it. Obviously. Help me anyway?"

options.text: Keep it. It's too useful to lose.

s3_way.text: "Right." She wipes her face with the heel of her hand, fast, as if it had been smoke. "Right. Good." She doesn't say anything else for a while, and doesn't need to.

s3_risk.text: "I don't know." Honest, which costs her. "Ask me on the day. Ask me twice."

s3_use.text: "Useful." She tests the word. "Yes. To everybody but me." She turns round to face the dark.

link.text: "Lev's table. The Window at night. Or I keep it." She has obviously been over it a hundred times. "Tell me what you think. I'll still choose."

options.text: It's yours. If you want to keep it, keep it.

decision.text: Kes decided to keep the Concern's port in her neck, and her sight on the grid with it.

options.text: The Shift needs your sight. Keep it for them.

decision.text: Kes kept the Concern's port in her neck, because you said the Shift needed her sight.

options.text: I'm still looking. Lev, or the Window.

kept.text: "I'll keep it." She sounds surprised to hear herself. "I know what it is now. That's different from not knowing." She touches the back of her neck. "An hour a night's mine. The rest I'll fight for."

kept_use.text: "Everybody needs my sight." She plugs the cable back into the box, click. "Fine. I'll keep it." She doesn't look at you again tonight.
kept_use.again: The cable, plugged into the box.

text.text: "Before Lev cut it I recorded the door. Everything that came through it, a year of it." She has a notebook, which you have never seen her use. "It talks old. Their channel. It's not the Window's grid; it's older. The same tongue the dead machines in the Ashlands answer to, if you know how to say it." She turns a page. "And it's signed. Every order down it is signed, and the signatures carry dates. Ninety years dead. More. Somebody up there signs their orders in a hand from before the Burn."

"I've been listening to the door." She doesn't look up from the cable. "It talks old. Their channel. It's not the Window's grid; it's older. The same tongue the dead machines in the Ashlands answer to, if you know how to say it." She winds the cable tighter. "And it's signed. Every order down it is signed, and the signatures carry dates. Ninety years dead. More. Somebody up there signs their orders in a hand from before the Burn."

s4.again: "Somebody up there signs in a hand from before the Burn."

options.text: What does that mean you can do?

s4_lineage.text: "Talk to it." Simply. "In its own language. The house on the hill has been talking down that door to everybody wearing its chrome for ninety years, and nobody's ever answered back." A grin, not much fun in it. "I could. Obviously."

options.text: Then when we go up, we answer it.
Then keep quiet. Let them think nobody can.

s4_after.text: "After." She tries the word. "Nobody up here plans an after; the Window plans it for you." She draws in the dirt with the end of the cable: a pithead, a road, a hill with a dome on it. "The Shift. The road. Or up there, in the gardens, with the orange tree, just to see if it still smells like nothing." She looks up. "Say what you think. I'll still choose."
s4_after.again: A pithead, a road and a hill, drawn in the dirt.

options.text: The gardens. You've earned an orange tree.

s4_end.text: She rubs out two of the three drawings with her boot and leaves one, and doesn't tell you which until you look. "Nobody's ever let me say before," she says. "Obviously I'm going to be insufferable about it."
s4_end.again: One drawing left in the dirt.

r1b.text: "Asking again." She holds up two fingers. "Second time. Like you said. Still allowed to be no."

options.text: It's a no. Not because of you.

r1_yes.text: "Oh." She looks genuinely startled, then extremely pleased with herself. "Good. Good. I had a whole second speech." She sits next to you instead of across the fire, and talks about the gardens for an hour, and you let her.
r1_yes.again: Kes, beside you instead of across the fire.

r1_later.text: "Fine. Asking again later. I'm very good at asking." She goes back to the cable, and the cable is somehow cheerful about it.

r1_no.text: "Right. Good. Clear." She nods several times. "That's fine. Obviously that's fine." In the morning she is exactly as she always is, which she has clearly decided to be.
r1_no.again: Kes, exactly as she always is.

text.text: She pulls her collar down. Where the port was there is a puckered scar and Lev's neat stitches. "Touch it," she says. "Go on." You do. "There's nothing there now," she says, "and I still feel it twice. Once in the skin, once where their log was." She turns round. "I don't have to steal an hour any more. I'd still like to spend one with you. Say if you don't want to."

She shivers. "I feel that twice. Once in the skin and once in their log. Somewhere up the hill it says where your hand is." She touches her own neck and the night goes a degree quieter. "There. t_gardens.text: "I saw them once. Sixteen, at my fitting." She doesn't need asking twice. "Glass over everything, and under it trees, real ones, in rows, with fruit on, and grass you could walk on in your boots. Rain came out of pipes in the ceiling at ten and at four, and it smelled of nothing. Nothing at all. And an orange tree, by itself, in a pot, with a bench, and an old man on the bench who didn't look old." She stops. "You let me go on."
