decision.text: You talked the guild's press off a Sink boy on the dike road: the paper was his mother's.
You cut a Sink boy loose from the guild's press on the dike road.

boy.text: The boy looks at you as if you might be another one of them. "My mam's," he says. "Not mine. She owes the post at the Sink for medicine. They came for her and she was sick, so." He shrugs, and the rope pulls. "Ishmael," he says, though you did not ask, as if somebody ought to know.

bought.text: The older man counts it twice and hands you the paper and cuts the rope himself, with a care that is almost courtesy. "The guild's obliged." To the boy: "You're lucky." The boy does not look lucky; he looks at you. "Gull Stilts," you tell him. "Down the dike. Ask for Paz at the Netlofts." He goes, running, then walking, then running.

talked.text: The younger one looks at the paper again, properly this time, and then at the older one, and the older one swears softly and folds it away. "Mother's name," he says. "Should've been the mother." He cuts the rope. The boy stands there rubbing his wrists until you tell him: Gull Stilts, down the dike, ask for Paz at the Netlofts. He goes.

no.text: "His mark's his mother's mark. That's debt." The older man puts the paper away. "Stand aside."

decision.text: You bought a Sink boy's paper off the guild's press on the dike road and sent him to Gull Stilts.
You cut a Sink boy loose from the guild's press on the dike road.

walked.text: You stand aside. They go past you along the dike toward the city, the boy between them, and at the bend the older one puts the sack over his head, gently, like a man putting a hood on a falcon.

read.text: Chalk on the Wall's foot where the rubble road turns south along it: an arrow, and DOCKS — CARRICK — NO BRIDGE — THIS WAY ROUND. Under it somebody has drawn a crane, carefully, the way a child draws a horse, and a box hanging from it.
read.again: DOCKS — CARRICK — THIS WAY ROUND, and the careful crane.

read.text: Chalk on a bollard where the river road comes down off the Wall's shoulder: GATE ↑ 1 HR — PAPERS. Under it: CLOVER BY THE QUAY TRAM. And under that, small, in a child's hand: KOBBY'S ROPE AT NIGHT.
read.again: GATE ↑ 1 HR — PAPERS. CLOVER BY THE QUAY TRAM. KOBBY'S ROPE AT NIGHT.

through.speaker: npc_dk_12
through.text: "The through doesn't sell tickets." Femi nods down the shed, where a second road runs straight past the platform and out through the far end into a fenced cut toward the Bond. "Comes in at the throat at two in the morning, nineteen cars sealed, goes into the Bond without stopping, comes out empty or not and goes back east at four. Nobody gets a look." He shrugs. "Nobody weighs it, either. That's not my department. That's Hruska's, and it isn't his."
through.again: "Nobody gets a look. Nobody weighs it."

text.text: You wait on the platform for the seven o'clock. It comes in under its own smoke: Sixty, square-nosed and plated, pulling a pre-war coach with steel riveted over its windows to the height of a seated man, so that you look out over a rim of plate at the country going by. The guard punches your card and sits down opposite with a carbine across his knees. For the first hour you watch the land go past at the speed of a fast cart the way you would watch someone sleeping. Then, somewhere, you sleep too, and wake to West Halt.

The seven o'clock, and at every halt the train stops for a pilot in faded orange who climbs into the cab with a red flag rolled under his arm, rides the section and gets down at the next, while the halt sells water on the platform and somebody sells bread through the coach's slots. West Halt.
The seven o'clock: the coach, the plate at the windows, the guard and his carbine, the country going by at the speed of a cart. West Halt.

interject.text: Tamsin has her face to the slot over the plate the whole way. "It's moving and nobody's pushing it," she says, three times, and then, without looking round: "Don't tell anyone I said that."
"Two cars, one key," Wren says, watching the ditch go by. "Somebody knew which ones. That's not robbing. That's shopping."
"The token for each section is drawn at its end and surrendered at the next," Nine says, watching the signals. "A system with no memory but the register. I admire it."

It comes in under its own smoke: Sixty, square-nosed and plated, pulling a pre-war coach with steel riveted over its windows to the height of a seated man, so that you look out over a rim of plate at the country going by. The guard punches your card and sits down opposite with a carbine across his knees. For the first hour you watch the land go past at the speed of a fast cart the way you would watch someone sleeping. At Kettle Cut the train slows for the curve, and in the ditch under the window two cars lie on their sides, opened like tins. The guard watches them go by and says nothing at all. Then, somewhere, you sleep too, and wake to Yard Nine.

The seven o'clock, and at every halt the train stops for a pilot in faded orange who climbs into the cab with a red flag rolled under his arm, rides the section and gets down at the next, while the halt sells water on the platform and somebody sells bread through the coach's slots. At Kettle Cut the train slows for the curve, and in the ditch under the window two cars lie on their sides, opened like tins. The guard watches them go by and says nothing at all. Yard Nine.

The seven o'clock: the coach, the plate at the windows, the guard and his carbine, the country going by at the speed of a cart. At Kettle Cut the train slows for the curve, and in the ditch under the window two cars lie on their sides, opened like tins. The guard watches them go by and says nothing at all. Yard Nine.

interject.text: Tamsin has her face to the slot over the plate the whole way. "It's moving and nobody's pushing it," she says, three times, and then, without looking round: "Don't tell anyone I said that."
"Two cars, one key," Wren says, watching the ditch go by. "Somebody knew which ones. That's not robbing. That's shopping."
"The token for each section is drawn at its end and surrendered at the next," Nine says, watching the signals. "A system with no memory but the register. I admire it."

text.text: The window cut into the shed's brick at the Line's end. Femi Adebayo looks at your pass, and at you, and punches nothing. "All sections. Seven o'clock, east."
The window in the shed's brick. "Thirty a leg." Femi taps a card pinned to the grille: KETTLE LEVY — BY ORDER OF THE GUILD. "Don't look at me. I've never seen Kettle."

The window in the shed's brick, and two of the guild's riders on the platform behind you with carbines, watching who buys. "Seven o'clock, east," Femi says. "Twenty-five a leg. They're on every train now. Smile for the card."

A ticket window cut into the brick of the freight shed at the very end of the Line, with a grille and a young man behind it with a card punch and a pencil, who draws your face on a toll card in four quick lines before you have said where you are going. "The Line, east. Seven o'clock. Twenty-five a leg; the guild sets it, not me."
The window in the shed's brick. "Seven o'clock, east," Femi says. "Twenty-five a leg."

board.again: Femi Adebayo, behind the grille, with the punch.

options.text: (West Halt, one leg. 30 Tolls, with the Kettle levy.)
(Yard Nine, 2 legs. 60 Tolls, with the Kettle levy.)
(Four Ways, 3 legs. 90 Tolls, with the Kettle levy.)
(East Halt, 4 legs. 120 Tolls, with the Kettle levy.)
(Two-Twelve, 5 legs. 150 Tolls, with the Kettle levy.)
(Show Femi the guild's letter: a seat on the through.)
(Look at the map of the Line.)

text.text: The tide boat at the water stairs, flat and tarred, with salt sacks and a crate of smoked fish coming off it hand to hand, and Mele Tui at the tiller watching the water before she watches you. "Down the delta on the ebb at five," she says. "Stilts, six. Rigs, twelve. Mind your hands on the gunwale."

The water stairs: worn granite down into the Basin, green to the third step, iron rings in the wall for boats. A slate on the ring post, chalked: TIDE BOAT — IN ON THE FLOOD — DOWN THE DELTA AT 5 — STILTS 6 — RIGS 12 — M.T.

stairs.again: The water stairs, and the slate on the ring post: DOWN THE DELTA AT 5.

interject.text: Tamsin sits on the top step and watches a crate of fish go up the stairs and a sack of salt come down. "Everything in the Reach ends up here," she says. "Fish, oil, copper, people. It's a drain with cranes."

options.text: (Down the delta to Gull Stilts. 6 Tolls)
(Down the delta and out to the Rigs. 12 Tolls)

stop.text: THE QUAY — CARRICK. A single tram car off the Loop's old Docks line, its trolley pole bent up to a wire that still carries something, and a board with one name on it: CLOVER 2. The far bank's half of the Loop, running north round the ring road and over the old ring bridge to the Loop's last halt, outside the Wall.

interject.text: "The Loop's Docks branch," Nine says. "Its far half. The drawings show a single line from Clover over the ring bridge to this terminus; the bridge at Bridgeward carried the other half, with a tram on it, the day it fell." The lens clicks. "The timetable for that tram is still in the record. It is very punctual."

day.text: Crane One, dead on the bank above the river wall, its jib out over the dry bed like an arm held out for balance. From the jib's end a cable runs out into the air over the Hulls, sagging, to the torn end of Bridgeward's bridge on the far bank. At the crane's foot a winch with a drum of cable as thick as a wrist, and a steel basket chained to the bank. By day it does not move.
day.again: Crane One's jib, the cable to Bridgeward's drop, the basket chained.

night.text: Night, and the cradle working: the winch's brake squealing, a lamp on the basket going away over the bed toward Bridgeward with two people crouched in it, and Kobby Ofori at the drum with his sleeves rolled. "Over?" he says. "Five. Sit in the middle and don't look down; there's nothing to see but the bed."
night.again: The winch, the lamp going out over the bed, Kobby at the brake. "Over?"

interject.text: Ilya climbs into the basket last and holds the rim with both hands. "I've been shot at from further than this," he says. "I've never hung."

options.text: (Ride the basket over the dry river to Bridgeward's drop. 5 Tolls)

cut.text: Crane One, dead on the bank, its jib bare. The cradle's cable has been cut at the drum and lies in coils on the bed below, already half buried in silt, and the winch is padlocked under the guild's seal.
cut.again: The bare jib, the cut cable in the silt.

text.text: Sixty under the shed, drinking from the water column, and the through's road beside her empty: no through has come in since the wreck east of East Halt, and the Bond's yard is half dark. The dockers on the platform are playing cards on a crate.

Sixty under the shed, drinking from the water column, and on her footplate a pilot in faded orange with a red flag rolled under his arm, drinking tea out of the driver's can: the halts' men ride every section now, even the last.

Sixty under the shed, drinking from the water column, with two of the guild's riders on her step and a third walking the platform, looking at faces. The guild holds the Line end to end, and it wants you to see it holding.

Sixty under the shed: square-nosed, plated, steaming gently at the buffer stop with the water column swung over her tank and a fireman on her roof with a hose. The Line's last ten feet of rail, and a lamp on the buffer that is lit day and night.

read.again: Sixty at the buffer, drinking.

text.text: GUILD FLOOR — CARRICK — FREIGHT BY THE TON — DUES BY THE BERTH. The Concern's notice is gone; four drawing pins hold a square of cleaner paint where it was.

Notices on the guild floor's door: GUILD FLOOR — CARRICK — FREIGHT BY THE TON — DUES BY THE BERTH — THEFT FROM THE QUAY: THE HOOK. And pinned over the guild's, in the Concern's clean type on clean card: RETURNABLE LOST FROM BOND — ONE — REWARD 60 — APPLY THE BOND OFFICER. Somebody has written under it in chalk, small: IT WASHES POTS.

read.again: FREIGHT BY THE TON. RETURNABLE LOST FROM BOND — ONE — REWARD 60.

read.text: THE BOND — CONCERN — UNDER SEAL. Below it, in smaller letters cut into a steel plate as if somebody expected to be argued with: BONDED PREMISES UNDER THE HARBOUR ACT, s. 19. THE HARBOUR MASTER'S AUTHORITY DOES NOT EXTEND WITHIN. The lights on the fence posts are on at noon.
read.again: THE BOND — UNDER SEAL — s. 19. The lights on at noon.

read.text: HARBOUR NOTICE — THE RIVER BERTHS — LEASED TO HOUSE VANE FOR WORKS UNDER THE ACT, s. 41 — OCCUPIERS TO QUIT ON COMMENCEMENT — H. DAHL, HARBOUR MASTER. Somebody has chalked under it, in capitals that go downhill: WE ARE NOT OCCUPIERS WE ARE CREW.
read.again: LEASED TO HOUSE VANE. WE ARE NOT OCCUPIERS WE ARE CREW.

text.text: Crane Two, Constance's, with a strip of red cloth tied to the cab's rail that nobody has taken down since the morning on the Stand.

Crane Two: the other crane on the quay that still works, older than Six and slower, its cab windows patched with tin. CONNIE painted on the counterweight in letters a yard high, and under it, smaller, older: NO BOX DOWN — 22 YEARS.

read.again: Crane Two, and NO BOX DOWN on the counterweight.

text.text: The barge goes at six, flat-bottomed and black with tar, a deckhouse aft and the cargo under tarps, and you sit on a coil of rope and go up the river behind the guild's tug, an old diesel launch that burns the Rigs' oil and coughs it out black, towing three barges on a cable like a string of beads. Everything is wet. Nothing is in a hurry. Herons stand in the shallows and watch you go by as if they had seen barges before and expected better. At Ashby the barges go one at a time into the lock's grey chamber, and the gates close behind, and the water lifts you up between the walls until the Water lies level and grey ahead, while a young woman with red hair walks along the top with a key on a cord and calls the marks. Sawtown.

The barge at six, full-loaded and low in the water, up the river behind the guild's tug, an old diesel launch that burns the Rigs' oil and coughs it out black, towing three barges on a cable like a string of beads, on a river that runs high and steady between its banks. At Ashby the barges go one at a time into the lock's grey chamber, and the gates close behind, and the water lifts you up between the walls until the Water lies level and grey ahead, while a young woman with red hair walks along the top with a key on a cord and calls the marks. Sawtown.

The river does what the city's card says this week: brown and fast and over the meadows, the farms along it under water to the doorsteps. Sawtown.

The barge at six, half-loaded because the river is low, up the river behind the guild's tug, an old diesel launch that burns the Rigs' oil and coughs it out black, towing three barges on a cable like a string of beads, with the bargemaster sounding the bottom with a pole at every bend. At Ashby the barges go one at a time into the lock's grey chamber, and the gates close behind, and the water lifts you up between the walls until the Water lies level and grey ahead, while a young woman with red hair walks along the top with a key on a cord and calls the marks. Sawtown.

interject.text: Tamsin lies on her front on the tarp with her chin on her hands and watches the water go by under the gunwale for an hour without saying anything, which is a record. "It's all going somewhere," she says at last. "All of it. On its own. Nobody pumping." She rolls over. "Rust it, I want one."
"A road that moves," Wren says, watching the bank. "Leaves no tracks either." She almost smiles. "I could get used to it."
Ilya counts the bends aloud, under his breath, and then the herons, and then stops counting anything and sleeps sitting up with his rifle across his knees.

sweeps.speaker: narrator
sweeps.text: The bargemaster looks at your arms. "Sweeps take two and the river takes everybody. A turn on the oars and you ride free, if you can keep a stroke."

sweeps_ok.speaker: narrator
sweeps_ok.text: "Good enough." He spits over the side. "Next six o'clock, either way. You're on the bow sweep."

sweeps_no.speaker: narrator
sweeps_no.text: You catch a crab on the first stroke and go over backwards into the cargo. "Pay the fare," he says, not unkindly. "The river's safer with you sitting down."

text.text: The barge quay: timber staging along the Basin's edge where the Wet's barges tie up, black with tar and white with gull. A long flat barge lies against it with timber stacked on her deck and a family living under a tarp at her stern. A slate on a post: THE BARGES — LOW LANDING — ASHBY — SAWTOWN — UP AT SIX — 10 A REACH — ASK ABOARD.

board.again: The barge quay. UP AT SIX — 10 A REACH.

options.text: (Low Landing, one reach up. No fare.)
(Look at the map of the river.)

read.text: GRIGOR'S STEPS — MULLET — LINES AT DAWN 2 — BRING THEM BACK. A painted fish beside it, smiling, which nobody who has eaten a Basin mullet would do.
read.again: GRIGOR'S STEPS — LINES AT DAWN 2.

text.text: The fuel berth: a tank on the quay stencilled LINE ACCOUNT in the guild's neat letters, and a gauge on its side reading a quarter. The night barge from the delta that used to fill it does not come any more. The guild's men have started buying Hum's diesel off the tide boat, a drum at a time, at Hum's price.
The fuel berth: a tank on the quay stencilled LINE ACCOUNT, and alongside it the Rigs' own launch, low in the water, pumping across a hose with HUM painted on it, at a price somebody on Hum set.

The fuel berth: a tank on the quay stencilled LINE ACCOUNT in the guild's neat letters, a hose coiled on the staging, and a slick on the water round it, purple and gold. The night barge from the delta ties up here with no lamps, every few nights, and nobody on the quay is awake to see it.

read.again: The tank, LINE ACCOUNT.

read.text: THE HARBOUR ACT, framed under glass on the long room's wall, its pages pinned open side by side and gone the colour of tea. Section 19: BONDED PREMISES — the Harbour Master's authority does not extend within. Section 41: IDLE BERTHS — may be leased by the concession for works. Schedule 2, GOODS: cargo, livestock, mails, ship's stores, ballast. Schedule 3, VESSELS IN PORT: a vessel in port shall not be moved, broken or removed while she has a crew aboard, save by her master's leave or the court's order on proof of abandonment.
read.again: The Act under glass: s. 19, s. 41, Schedules 2 and 3.

interject.text: "Schedule 2 has no persons in it," Nine says, reading with its lens almost on the glass. "Schedule 3 has no definition of a vessel's being afloat." It reads both again. "The drafters were thorough about everything except the future. That is the usual way."

text.text: The box Six dropped, empty now: the copper went over the weighbridge in barrows, bar by bar, with the whole quay watching the needle. The dockers have started using it as a windbreak.
The box Six dropped, emptied by the Bond's men in the night and left where it fell. The stain where the tarp was is being worn out of the concrete by boots.

A forty-foot box on its side, the closed eye on its doors and the Concern's seal whole on its wire. Stencilled on the end: MACHINE PARTS — 14.0 T — 7-2390. One end has gone into the concrete and burst along the seam, and through the seam, stacked as neat as loaves on a baker's board, red-brown bars as long as a forearm, each one stamped with the closed eye. Beside it, the tarp, and the boots.

look.again: The box on its side, the copper in the split.

passives.text: Cast copper. A bar that size is thirty kilos if it is a gram, and a box like this holds a thousand of them packed like that. Thirty tonnes, on a bill of fourteen; under a crane whose plate says twenty-five.
The spreader's twistlocks are still in the box's corner castings, sheared clean through. They did not come unlatched. They broke.

interject.text: Kes crouches at the split and turns a bar over with her boot. "Copper," she says. "Halcyon pulls it out of the Teeth by the trainload; the whole arcology's wired with it. They're selling it west." She reads the stencil. "And lying about it, obviously."
"A man under a load," Ilya says quietly. "You don't unlatch wrong after eleven years. You get tired. Or somebody tells you to hurry."

ladder.text: Crane Six's ladder goes up inside a cage on the crane's leg, forty feet to the cab: a steel box with its glass gone dark. A chain across the ladder's foot with a padlock, and a guild guard on the quay who looks at the chain every time he turns.
ladder.again: The ladder in its cage, the chain, the guard turning.

options.text: (Unhook the chain and climb, as Connie's relief.)
(Climb the outside of the cage while the guard's back is turned.)

mods.why: you know when a man is not looking

night.text: At night the cab is dark, the guard is up at the Customs House steps, and the chain is still on the ladder with its padlock.
night.again: The dark cab, the chain, the padlock.

caught.text: "Off the leg." The guard has not raised his voice or his shotgun; he has only turned round at the wrong moment. "Ten Tolls for the climb, or the Harbour Master hears about it."

locked.text: The padlock is older than it looks and better. It does not give, and something in it bends that should not. Better come back by day with somebody's leave.
locked.again: The padlock that would not give.

cab.text: The cab: a seat with the stuffing out, two levers worn bright as cutlery, a pre-war panel with a dial for the load and, under a glass lid, a recorder with a strip of waxed paper hanging out of it like a tongue. Beside the dial, a key switch: OVERRIDE. The quay below is a map of hats.
cab.again: The cab: the dial, the recorder's tongue of paper, the key switch.

interject.text: "Pre-war and unnetworked, no Concern board anywhere in it," Kes says, rapping the panel with a knuckle. "Dumb as a fencepost and about as honest. It said no." She looks at the key switch. "Somebody made it shut up."

mods.why: the printer's codes are an old standard
Kes reads it over your shoulder

tape.text: You tear the strip off and read it against the light. 02:06 LIFT 31.2 T — OVERLOAD — CUTOUT. 02:07 KEY 6/N — OVERRIDE. 02:08 LIFT. 02:10 SPREADER — LOCK FAULT. Then nothing at all: the box was on the quay, and the recorder had nothing more to say.

tape_no.text: Codes in faded purple on waxed paper, times and numbers and abbreviations in a pre-war standard you cannot read. The strip tears off in your hand anyway. Somebody who weighs things for a living would know what it says.
tape_no.again: Codes you cannot read on a strip of wax.

keyswitch.text: The override is a key switch beside the load dial, its brass collar polished by thumbs. Round the slot the brass is scratched bright in a ring: a key that did not quite fit, turned hard, many times over many nights. A factory key does not do that.
keyswitch.again: The scratched ring round the key switch.

done.text: Crane Six's cab, where you tore the tape off the recorder. Somebody has fitted a new roll.
done.again: Six's cab, a new roll in the recorder.

text.text: The tally board on its post: every gang ON, Gang Nine among them, all eight names. Chalked across the top, in letters a hand high, by somebody who has never written so big: WE STOOD.
The tally board: GANG NINE — OFF — BY ORDER. Somebody chalked BLACK across the board once; it has been washed off, and the wash left a grey cloud the shape of the word.
The tally board: every gang on it chalked BLACK — BOND, and under the board, on the concrete, a ring of boots where people have been standing all night so that nobody can say the Stand was empty.

notice.text: "One of our sureties came west in a box she should not have been in." He says it as if a crate of tins had gone astray. "A minor under contract, on her mother's, from the terraces. A returnable: a surety goes back to its contract when the contract's behind. Sixty to whoever brings her to the fence, no questions asked, and she goes home on the through, the way she came but in the coach." He considers. "Well. In a box. But a clean one."
notice.again: "Sixty, no questions; she goes home on the through."

interject.text: Wren has gone very still. "A box," she says. "For a girl." She looks at Roux the way she looks at a road with riders on it.

who.text: "The consignee, which on the westbound through is mostly the Crown." He ticks them off on clean fingers. "Chrome, for the houses that can afford to have it fitted. Medicine. Copper, for terraces. Controllers." He spreads his hands. "The Crown is a very good customer, and the Line is the only road the Crown has to us. Until it builds its own."
who.again: "The Crown is a very good customer."

offer.text: He looks at what you put on his desk without touching it, the way a man looks at a hand of cards he has already seen. "You'll want to take this to the Harbour court," he says, "and she'll rule, because she always rules. The guild will bill us two years of back-freight and win, the dockers will learn that one of their own sold a cutout, and the widow will be the widow of a thief." He opens a drawer. "Who is better off? A hundred and fifty, and the papers stay in my drawer. The widow is not forgotten. The Bond can be generous where it is not obliged."
offer.again: "A hundred and fifty, and the papers stay in my drawer."

interject.text: Odile reads the slip upside down across the desk. "Thirty-one on fourteen," she says, "for two years. He is offering you a hundred and fifty against a bill of several thousand." She looks at Roux almost fondly. "That is not a bribe. It is a discount."

decision.text: Lucien Roux paid you a hundred and fifty for what you had found about Crane Six, and it stayed in his drawer.

options.text: Pay the widow what you'd pay me, and keep your papers.

mods.why: Odile names a figure first

decision.text: You let Lucien Roux keep what you had found about Crane Six in his drawer, for the price of it paid to Dmytro's widow.

took.text: He counts it out on the desk in new Tolls, squares the stack and pushes it across, and puts your papers in the drawer, and locks it, and puts the key in his waistcoat. "A pleasure," he says, and means it.

widow.text: He looks at you with real interest for the first time. "How unusual." He writes a chit, signs it, and blots it. "A hundred and fifty to the widow Lysenko, from the Bond, for her loss, through the guild's floor. She'll think it's the guild's conscience." He puts your papers in the drawer. "Let her."

widow_no.text: "No, I don't think so." He closes the drawer. "Generosity is a thing I offer. It is not a thing I'm told."

refused.text: "Pity." He means that, too. "Take it to the steps, then. She'll rule." He goes back to his ledger.

return.text: "Ah." He writes something down. "At the back of the cookshop, I expect. They always choose the cookshop." He counts sixty onto the desk. "My men will collect her tonight, quietly; nobody need see anything. She goes east on the through at two." He pushes the coins across. "Thank you. People think the Concern is cruel. It is only exact."
return.again: "She goes east on the through at two."

decision.text: You told the Concern's bond officer where Mirela Stan was hiding, for sixty Tolls.

returned.text: You take it. Roux has already gone back to his ledger, and does not see you go.

price.text: "A surety is valued at the outstanding balance of the contract it secures." He does not need to look it up. "A hundred and fifty, in her case. Paid, the surety is discharged and the contract stands whole: her mother keeps her terrace, and the girl is nobody's." He tilts his head. "It is an unusual way to spend money. I find I approve of it."
price.again: "A hundred and fifty. Paid, the girl is nobody's."

mods.why: Odile does the arithmetic of a discharge out loud
you know what his boxes really weigh, and he knows you know

price90.text: He looks at you for a moment, and laughs, quietly, through his nose. "Ninety," he says. "The terraces' interest is somewhat aggressive. I'll write it down."

price_no.text: "The balance is the balance." He smiles. "I didn't set the terraces' interest. I only read it."

discharged.text: He takes the money, writes DISCHARGED across a copy of the girl's paper in the Concern's clean hand, and blots it, and gives it to you. "Her mother's contract is whole. The surety is nobody's." He looks at the copy as you fold it. "Tell her to burn the other one. Paper has a way of being found."
discharged.again: "Tell her to burn the other one."

decision.text: You bought Mirela Stan's surety off the Concern's Bond; her mother's contract stood whole and the girl was nobody's.

news.text: somebody bought a runaway surety's paper off the Concern at the Docks and the girl stayed on the quay

day.text: Roux's desk, clean as a plate, and Roux behind it, or his guard in front of it. Not by day.

night.text: The Bond at night: every light on, the boxes' shadows hard as walls, one guard at the gate with his back to the yard and the office dark. The office door is shut and not locked. The desk's drawers are.
night.again: The dark office, the locked drawers.

mods.why: proper picks

slip.text: Loading slips, filed by through and by night, in a stack as square as a brick. You take the top pair: BOX 7-2390 — CAST COPPER, INGOT — 31.4 T — SEALED, from Two-Twelve, and clipped behind it the guild's freight bill for the same seal: MACHINE PARTS — 14.0 T. Under it, a hundred more pairs, and every one of them says two things.
slip.again: Two weights for one seal, a hundred times.

caught.text: A light in your face. The guard from the gate, not hurrying, with his pistol at his side. "Under bond," he says, as if it were a reason, which here it is. "Hands where I like them."

options.text: I was looking for the girl you lost. I thought she might be in here.

let_go.text: He looks at you for a long time. "She isn't," he says at last, and walks you to the gate, and does not mention it to anyone, which tells you something about how much the Bond's guards like the Bond.

ran.text: You are through the gate and into the dark between the Boxes before he has finished saying stop. Behind you the Bond's lights do not change at all. In the morning there is a new notice on the gate with a good likeness of you on it.
ran.again: A likeness of you on the Bond's gate.

barred.text: He walks you to the gate with the pistol in your back and puts you out on the quay. "Don't come inside the line again," he says. By morning there is a likeness of you pinned to the gate.

empty.text: Roux's drawer. The lock is new.

intro.text: A woman at a desk under the only glazed window on the quay, writing in a ledger with a steel pen. She finishes the line before she looks up. "Henrike Dahl. Harbour Master, by the Act, for the guild, which holds the concession." She caps the pen. "You'll want something. Everyone who climbs my steps wants something. Say it plainly and I'll tell you plainly whether the Act gives it to you."
intro.again: Factor Dahl, writing; she finishes the line before she looks up.

interject.text: "The Harbour Act of the old Port Authority," Nine says. "Still in force. Here the Ledger enforces the concession and nothing else; it cannot see past the dry river." Dahl looks at the cracked lens with professional interest. "It can see the dues," she says. "It always sees the dues."

options.text: How does a thing come before your court?

text.text: "The Stand has blacked the Bond, and the Bond has blacked me, and the through is standing at the throat costing the guild by the hour." Dahl does not look up. "I have sent to the Ring for hands. It's within the Act. So is a stoppage. The Act is not on anybody's side."

"The Concern settled." Dahl turns a page. "Through me, without admitting anything, at a figure I would not have got in court. Every box over the plate." She looks at you. "I don't like a stoppage. I like a quay that knows what it can do even less. It's bad for the dues."
Factor Dahl, writing; she finishes the line before she looks up.

again.again: Factor Dahl, writing.

options.text: I want to bring something before the court.
(Give her Dmytro's tin, here, with the door shut.)
How does a thing come before your court?
A girl off the through, who the Bond calls goods.

act.text: "The Harbour Act: the old Port Authority's, from before the Burn." She taps the framed pages on the wall behind her without turning. "It gives the concession-holder the port: berths, dues, labour, order. The guild bought the concession from the city ninety years ago, and I keep it. Theft from the quay: the hook. A fight: a fine. A killing: the hook. A grievance: the steps, at the change of shift, before me, with the Act open on my knee." She uncaps the pen. "The Ledger enforces the concession. That is all it does here, and it does it perfectly."
act.again: "Theft, the hook. A grievance, the steps."

verdict.text: "Docker's negligence. The spreader's locks failed under a load, and the hooker-on said lift." She does not look at the window, where you can see Six. "The board says what the facts in front of me said. If there are other facts, bring them to the steps, and I'll hear Gang Nine's appeal whenever somebody stands up with it." She writes a line. "I don't like a board that's wrong. It's bad for the dues."

court_how.text: "At the change of shift, on the steps. You speak; whoever is party to it speaks; you put on the table what you have." She lays her pen flat. "I rule on what is on the table. Not on what anyone feels about it, including me. Especially me."
court_how.again: "I rule on what is on the table."

hulls.text: "Idle berths. Section forty-one lets the concession lease idle berths for works, and House Vane pays four hundred a year for them. The occupiers quit on commencement." She does not blink. "There is nothing in the Act about people living on a riverbed. There wasn't a riverbed when it was written."

girl.text: "If she is goods under bond, she is the Bond's, and my writ stops at the fence." Dahl turns the pen in her fingers. "If she is a person landed on my quay, she is a passenger, and she owes her fare. The Act's schedule of goods doesn't list persons. Nobody has ever asked me to read it that way." She looks at you. "Ask me on the steps, and I'll read it."

private.text: She opens the tin and looks at the key, the blue caps, the white card, for a long time, and closes it. "Thank you." She means it. "This stays in this room. The board stays as it is: the board was right, and a guild does not publish that its own weighbridge has been blind for two years. The Concern will receive a bill." She counts a hundred out of a drawer. "A finder's fee. The Act allows one."

decision.text: You gave the Harbour Master Dmytro Lysenko's tin in private. The guild billed the Concern quietly; the tally board still says docker's negligence.

news.text: the guild sent the Concern's Bond at the Docks a bill nobody will talk about

private_done.text: She writes in the ledger with the steel pen, and the tin goes into a drawer under it. "Gang Nine can stand on the line again in a season, when it has learned its business," she says, without looking up. "Good day."

call.text: "Which?" She picks up the pen. "The steps at the change of shift. Six o'clock."

options.text: Mirela Stan: a girl the Bond calls goods.

c_open.speaker: narrator
c_open.text: Six o'clock, the change of shift. The day gangs come off and the night gangs come on, and between them, for a quarter of an hour, the quay stops and climbs the Customs House steps to watch. Dahl sits at the top with the Act open on her knee. Constance stands with Gang Nine; Platt stands with his clipboard; Oksana stands at the back with her arms round herself. Roux has sent a clerk, who stands outside the line of the bottom step as if it were the Bond's fence. "Gang Nine's appeal," Dahl says. "Put on the table what you have."
c_open.again: "Put on the table what you have."

options.text: (The box: thirty tonnes of copper on a bill of fourteen.)
(Platt's order: five hands on a crane that wants eight.)
(The weighbridge register: NOT WEIGHED, two years.)
(Dmytro's tin: the key, the caps, the Bond's pass.)
Dmytro turned the cutout himself, at the Bond's pay, so the Bond's boxes would never be weighed.

decision.text: You laid the whole of Crane Six before the Harbour court: Dmytro Lysenko had overridden the cutout at the Bond's pay, and the guild's weighbridge had been blind to the through for two years. Every Concern box goes over the plate now.

news.text: the Harbour court at the Docks found the Concern's Bond paid a docker to switch off a crane's cutout; every through box is weighed now

options.text: Nine was five where Six wants eight, by the guild's own order. A short gang is the master's fault, not the hand's.

decision.text: You argued Gang Nine's appeal at the Harbour court on the short gang, and kept Dmytro's tin out of it. The negligence was struck and the guild paid for his funeral.

news.text: the Harbour court at the Docks struck a dead docker's negligence: his gang had been worked short by the guild's own order

ev_dk_ev_box.speaker: narrator
ev_dk_ev_box.text: A docker carries a copper bar up the steps in both arms and puts it at Dahl's feet, and the stencil off the box's end after it: MACHINE PARTS — 14.0 T. Dahl looks from one to the other and writes a number.
ev_dk_ev_box.again: The bar at Dahl's feet, and the stencil.

ev_dk_ev_tape.speaker: narrator
ev_dk_ev_tape.text: Dahl reads the tape aloud, in her flat clear voice, the times and the codes: KEY 6/N — OVERRIDE. The steps go very quiet. At the side, without being asked, Platt pulls his key out on its chain and holds it up so that everybody can see it is on his neck.
ev_dk_ev_tape.again: KEY 6/N, and Platt's key held up on its chain.

ev_dk_ev_order.speaker: narrator
ev_dk_ev_order.text: Platt's order is read out: GANG NINE — FIVE HANDS — BY ORDER. Platt says, to nobody, "I wrote the eight in." The Harbour Master's clerk, beside Dahl, looks at his shoes.

ev_dk_ev_register.speaker: narrator
ev_dk_ev_register.text: Tomas Hruska comes up the steps with the register under his arm without being called, opens it at the place, and stands there holding it open until Dahl has read two years of NOT WEIGHED.

ev_dk_ev_slip.speaker: narrator
ev_dk_ev_slip.text: Roux's clerk takes a step toward the line of the bottom step and stops himself. Dahl reads both weights, and the seal number on each, twice, and then a third time.
ev_dk_ev_slip.again: Two weights, one seal, read three times.

ev_dk_ev_tin.speaker: narrator
ev_dk_ev_tin.text: The key cut by hand, the blue caps, the white card with the closed eye on it. Oksana makes a small sound at the back of the steps. Constance turns round and looks at her, and then does not.
ev_dk_ev_tin.again: The tin, open on the step.

c_bond.speaker: npc_dk_01
c_bond.text: Dahl closes the Act on her knee. "Finding. The hooker-on Lysenko overrode Crane Six's cutout with a key he had cut, at the Bond's pay, to lift a box billed at less than half its weight. The spreader failed under the load the cutout was there to refuse. That is not negligence. It is a sale, and the seller is dead." She looks at the Bond's clerk below the line. "The Bond's fence stops my writ. It does not stop my weighbridge. From tonight every box off the through goes over the plate, and the guild will bill the Concern for two years of short weight." To Constance: "Gang Nine stands on the line from the next call-on." And to the steps: "A man who sold the cutout is owed no funeral tally by the Act." She waits. Nobody says anything at all.
c_bond.again: "A man who sold the cutout is owed no funeral tally."

interject.text: "The court is right," Ash says, quietly, to you, "and it isn't enough. It never is." He is looking at Oksana.

options.text: (Put thirty on the step for his funeral.)
The Act gives the court relief for a dead hand's kin.

mods.why: Nine has the clause: relief to dependants, at the court's discretion
you have read the Act

c_bond_tally.speaker: narrator
c_bond_tally.text: You put thirty on the step. Oksana comes up from the back and picks it up and holds it and does not look at you. He goes under the Star in the morning, from the Hulls, the river people's way, with the whole night gang standing on the wall above with their hats off.
c_bond_tally.again: He went under the Star, with the night gang on the wall.

c_bond_mercy.speaker: narrator
c_bond_mercy.text: Dahl turns three pages. "Relief to the dependants of a hand dead in the port's service, at the court's discretion." She reads the clause for a long time. "He was in the port's service when he died, whatever else he was doing in it." A funeral tally from the guild's box. Oksana does not look up.
c_bond_mercy.again: A funeral tally from the guild's box.

c_bond_end.speaker: narrator
c_bond_end.text: "The Act says what it says." Dahl closes it. The court rises; the shift changes; the quay goes back to work. Oksana is the last off the steps.
c_bond_end.again: The court risen, Oksana last off the steps.

c_gang.speaker: npc_dk_01
c_gang.text: Dahl reads the order twice. "Finding. Crane Six was worked five hands where its complement is eight, by the master's order. Under the Act a gang below complement is the master's charge, and what befalls it is the master's fault, not the hand's." The steps breathe out. "The negligence is struck. Gang Nine stands on the line from the next call-on, and the guild pays the funeral tally." She closes the Act. "And from tonight Six works at complement, through or no through, and the guild will argue its demurrage with the Concern." Constance is looking at you. So is Oksana, from the back of the steps; and Oksana looks away first.

interject.text: Nine says nothing at all on the steps. Afterwards, walking away, it says: "The record of this hearing is true in every line and false in its sum. I have filed a great many like it." It does not say whether that is a complaint.

c_adjourn.speaker: npc_dk_01
c_adjourn.text: "Not enough." Dahl closes the Act. "I have a box, a dead man and a quarrel. Bring me something I can hold." The court rises; the shift changes. The board stays as it is, and so does Gang Nine, and the appeal can come up the steps again whenever somebody brings it.

c_withdraw.speaker: npc_dk_01
c_withdraw.text: "Withdrawn." Dahl writes it down. "The steps are here every evening." The quay goes back to work.

g_open.speaker: narrator
g_open.text: Six o'clock on the steps. Roux comes himself this time, in his clean grey, and stands just outside the line of the bottom step. Espe stands with the girl, who keeps her hands in her sleeves. "The Bond holds that the minor Stan is a surety under contract, consigned in error, returnable, and so under bond," Roux says, pleasantly. Dahl looks at the girl. "Put on the table what you have."
g_open.again: "Put on the table what you have."

options.text: (Her paper: RETURNABLE ON DEFAULT OR FLIGHT.)
(Schedule 2, the goods: cargo, livestock, mails, stores, ballast.)
A person is not goods. On this quay she is a passenger, and a passenger owes her fare, not her body.

ev_dk_ev_paper.speaker: narrator
ev_dk_ev_paper.text: The paper is read out on the steps: SURETY — ONE MINOR — RETURNABLE ON DEFAULT OR FLIGHT. And the back, which Dahl reads too, without being asked: GO. The girl's face does not move. Espe's does.
ev_dk_ev_paper.again: RETURNABLE ON DEFAULT OR FLIGHT. GO.

ev_dk_ev_act.speaker: narrator
ev_dk_ev_act.text: Dahl turns to Schedule 2 and reads it out, all of it, slowly, to the steps: cargo; livestock; mails; ship's stores; ballast; and their forty definitions. It takes a long time. Nobody leaves.

g_ruled.speaker: npc_dk_01
g_ruled.text: "No persons," Dahl says, closing the schedule. "Finding. A person landed on this quay is a passenger. A passenger without a ticket owes the fare from her port of embarkation." She looks at Roux. "Two-Twelve to Carrick is a hundred and twenty-five Tolls on the guild's own tariff. Your paper is a contract between you and her mother, in the Skirts. It is not a bill of lading, and it is not mine to enforce." Roux bows very slightly, as if he had lost a hand of cards he had not much wanted. "And the fare?" Dahl says, to the steps.

options.text: She'll work it off on the quay.

g_paid.speaker: narrator
g_paid.text: You count it onto the step. The clerk writes PAID beside a name the guild's ledger has never had before. Mirela looks at the coins, and at you, and says, as if trying the word: "Passenger."

decision.text: At the Harbour court you had it found that a person cannot be goods under bond: in Carrick Mirela Stan is a passenger, and you paid her fare.

news.text: the Harbour court at the Docks ruled that a person landed on the quay is a passenger, never cargo, whatever the Concern's paper says

g_work.speaker: narrator
g_work.text: Espe says she will stand for it: the girl washes pots for wages and the guild takes the wages until a hundred and twenty-five is paid. The clerk writes it down. Mirela looks at the Bond's fence, white-lit across the quay, and then deliberately turns her back on it.
g_work.again: Mirela, her back to the fence.

decision.text: At the Harbour court you had it found that a person cannot be goods under bond: in Carrick Mirela Stan is a passenger who owes her fare.

news.text: the Harbour court at the Docks ruled that a person landed on the quay is a passenger, never cargo, whatever the Concern's paper says

g_adjourn.speaker: npc_dk_01
g_adjourn.text: "The Bond's paper names her a surety under contract," Dahl says. "Nothing on my table says what else she is, and the court cannot find what is not put before it." The girl does not cry. Espe does, angrily. "Adjourned," Dahl says. "Bring me the rest." The steps empty.

h_open.speaker: narrator
h_open.text: Six o'clock on the steps. Imogen Thrale at the foot of them with a roll of drawings under her arm; beside her, a head taller, Kwabena Ofori with his hat in his hands; and behind him, filling the quay to the Bond's fence, more people out of the Hulls than you have seen in daylight. "The river berths are leased," Dahl says. "What is before the court?"

options.text: (The Benguela Star's crew book: ninety years of Sundays.)
The Hulls are vessels in port, with crews aboard. A lease can let the berths. It cannot move a crewed ship.

ev_dk_ev_sched3.speaker: narrator
ev_dk_ev_sched3.text: Dahl reads Schedule 3 aloud. A vessel in port shall not be moved, broken or removed while she has a crew aboard. Somebody at the back of the Hulls' crowd starts to cheer and is hushed by everybody round them.

ev_dk_ev_books.speaker: narrator
ev_dk_ev_books.text: Abena Ofori brings the crew book up the steps in both arms and opens it at the first page, and Dahl turns the pages herself, all of them, slowly, ninety years of Sundays, while the steps wait and the light goes.

h_crewed.speaker: npc_dk_01
h_crewed.text: "Finding." Dahl closes the book gently and hands it back to Abena. "These are vessels in port, and they are crewed. The lease stands for the berths and cannot touch the vessels in them; the marks already made are a master's leave for three hulls, and a leave is not abandonment while the crew is still aboard. House Vane may treat with their masters." She looks at Imogen. "Or build where nobody is." Imogen writes something in her book with the silver pencil. Kwabena puts his hat back on.
h_crewed.again: "These are vessels in port, and they are crewed."

decision.text: At the Harbour court you had the Hulls found to be crewed vessels in port: House Vane's lease cannot move them.

news.text: the Harbour court at the Docks found the old ships on the dry river are crewed and cannot be moved for a Crown bridge

h_adjourn.speaker: npc_dk_01
h_adjourn.text: "A lease of idle berths," Dahl says, "and people in them. That is what is in front of me." She looks at Kwabena, and not unkindly. "Bring me what makes them more than people in a berth. Adjourned." The Hulls go back down the river stairs in silence.
h_adjourn.again: "Bring me what makes them more than people in a berth."

intro.text: A container with its end cut open to the quay, a stove made from a drum, a counter made from a door, and a pot on it the size of a child. A woman behind it with her sleeves pushed up and a ladle in her fist. "Espe's. Soup, bread, rice when there's rice, a bunk next door. Pay first, then I like you." At the back of the box a girl is washing pots in a tin bath and does not look up.
intro.again: Espe, with the ladle.

"Pay first, then I like you." Espe ladles. At the back of the box the girl is singing under her breath over the pots, something with a terrace in it.
"Pay first, then I like you." Espe ladles, and then, not looking up: "I miss the pots being washed properly."

girl.text: "My niece." Espe does not blink. "From the Hulls. Washes pots." She ladles soup into somebody else's cup. "Next."

shown.text: Espe looks at you for a long time over the pot. Then she puts the ladle down. "Mirela," she says, without turning round. "Come and look at this one. Tell me what you think."

denied.text: "My niece," Espe says again, in exactly the same voice, and ladles soup for somebody else, and does not look at you again today.

text.text: "Twelve off a stock car on the Line walked south to the Choir by night and got there, every one. A guild clerk told a docker who told me." She looks at the back of the box, at the girl, and away. "Some people get where they're going."

"Twelve off a stock car on the Line hid in a water tower and somebody sold them to the Concern at fifteen a head. Fifteen." She stirs. "That's what a person's worth on the Line this year. Write it down."
"Bridgeward's fallen to a crew with a dog on its jackets, and the Crown's near end with it. Vane's lady still comes down to the Hulls with her stakes, every day, like a woman visiting a grave."
"A box fell. Gang Nine's off. The Crown's drawing lines on the Hulls. The Bond lost something it calls a returnable." She ladles. "Same as last week, but worse."

read.text: ESPE'S — SOUP — PAY FIRST, chalked on the container's side in letters as big as the container allows, and under it a painted bowl with three lines of steam coming off it, like a drawing of a bowl that is pleased with itself.
read.again: ESPE'S — PAY FIRST.

offer.text: The container next to Espe's, with a door cut in its side and a bed in it that somebody has made with a corner tucked: a locker, a hook, a lamp, a square of window cut in the steel and glazed with something that was a windscreen. A card on the door: BUNK — TWENTY — ASK ESPE.

mine.text: Your bunk in the Boxes: the bed with its tucked corner, the locker, the windscreen window with Crane Six's red light in it, and through the wall Espe's stove ticking as it cools and somebody next door snoring in a language you do not know.

pots.text: A girl washing pots in a tin bath at the back of the cookshop, who goes very still when you come near, the way a hare goes still in a field. "I'm washing pots," she says.

mods.why: Kes says the name of a terrace, and the girl looks up
Connie has spoken for you on the quay

still.text: She goes on washing the same pot, round and round, until you go away.
still.again: The same pot, round and round.

intro.text: "Mirela." She dries her hands on her shirt. Fifteen, maybe, thin the way the terraces make you thin, the Teeth's sun still on the back of her neck, and a coat far too heavy for the quay that she does not take off. "I came in a box. Six days. You count by the stops: you feel it slow, and men talk outside, and then it goes on. They never open the spares." She looks past you at the Bond's white lights across the quay. "Are you going to tell him?"
intro.again: "Are you going to tell him?"

interject.text: Kes looks at her for a long moment. "Which terrace?" she asks. "Nine," the girl says. "The pear houses." Kes nods as if that explains everything, and to her it does. "Then you got further than anyone I knew," she says.

options.text: Why won't you take the coat off?
Where do you want to go?
No. I'm not going to tell him.

again.text: Mirela, at the pots, with her coat on.
again.again: Mirela, at the pots.

options.text: Why won't you take the coat off?
Where do you want to go?

why.text: "Because I'm fifteen." As if that were an answer, which on the terraces it is. "At fifteen a surety goes to the Weighhouse for intake, if the contract's behind. Ma's behind. Everybody's behind; that's what the terraces are." She looks at the fence. "She told me to go. She said, get in a box going west, they never open the spares. So I did."
why.again: "She told me to go."

interject.text: Wren has gone very quiet. "A box going west," she says. "Her mother put her in a box." She looks at the girl for a long moment. "Good," she says, and it costs her something to say it.

coat.text: She puts a hand flat on the lining. "It's sewn in. Ma sewed it." She unpicks three stitches with her thumbnail and lets you see: a Concern paper, folded small and soft with handling. SURETY: ONE MINOR (M. STAN, 15) — RETURNABLE ON DEFAULT OR FLIGHT. On the back, in pencil, in a woman's hand, one word: GO. "If I'm not returned, she's defaulted," Mirela says. "I know. She knew. She wrote that anyway." She folds it back.

options.text: Let me carry it. If they find you, they'll look in the coat first.

keep.text: She looks at you for a long time. Then she unpicks the rest of the stitches and puts the paper in your hand, and closes your fingers over it with hers, which are cold from the washing water. "Don't lose it," she says. "It's the only thing she ever wrote me."
keep.again: "It's the only thing she ever wrote me."

where.text: "Somewhere they don't read it." She thinks. "Somewhere it's just paper."

options.text: The tide boat goes down the delta to Gull Stilts. The water keeps no paper. (6 Tolls for her passage)

decision.text: You put Mirela Stan on the tide boat down the delta to Gull Stilts, with the Concern's paper still on her.

options.text: The seven o'clock east to West Halt, and the track south to Openfield by night. The Choir takes anyone. (25 Tolls for her ticket)

mods.why: the twelve walked it from West Halt, and West Halt will see her down the track
Ash draws her the way and the names to ask for

decision.text: You bought Mirela Stan a ticket east to West Halt and the way south by night to Openfield, where the Choir takes anyone.

options.text: Stay hidden a while. I'll find a way to make the paper go away.

shore.text: Mele's boat goes down on the evening ebb. Mirela goes down the water stairs with Espe's bread inside her coat, and sits in the bottom of the boat between two sacks of salt, and does not look back at the Bond's lights, and then does, once, as the boat clears the Basin's mouth.
shore.again: The tide boat clearing the Basin's mouth.

interject.text: Tamsin watches the boat until it is a dot. "The sky lying down," she says. "She'll like it. You can't box the sea."

choir.text: She goes east on the seven o'clock with a ticket you bought her and the way south drawn on the back of one of Espe's bills, and Espe's bread, and her coat. At the platform's end she turns round to say something, and the guard shouts, and she gets on instead.
choir.again: The seven o'clock, going east with her on it.

interject.text: "Openfield," Ash says, watching the train go. "Ask for the seed store. Say my name." He pauses. "It won't help. Say it anyway."

choir_no.text: You try to draw her the way south from West Halt in the dust with a finger, and get it wrong twice, and she watches you get it wrong. "I'll get lost," she says, very reasonably. "In the dark, in the Flats, by myself." She is right. Not that way; not yet.

wait.text: "All right." She goes back to the pots. "I'm good at waiting. I did six days in a box."

text.text: "Passenger." Mirela tries the word again, as if it might have worn out since. "I owe a fare. I've never owed anything that was mine before." She goes back to the pots, and she has taken the coat off, and hung it on a nail where she can see it.
Mirela at the tin bath, washing pots for wages, singing under her breath something with a terrace in it. She has burned the paper in Espe's stove; she says it took a long time to catch.

after.again: Mirela, at the pots, without the coat.

intro.text: A woman in a coat that cost more than the Hulls, kneeling on the old bridge's stump with a theodolite, writing numbers in a book with a silver pencil. She looks up and smiles as if you were a pleasant surprise. "Imogen Thrale. House Vane's engineer." She waves the pencil at the blue stakes in the bed below, among the ships. "I'm building the far end of a bridge. Or I will be."
intro.again: Imogen at the theodolite, writing.

interject.text: Tamsin looks from the stakes to the washing on the ships' rails and back. "There are people in those," she says. "Yes," says Imogen, kindly. "That's the difficult part."

options.text: And the people in the ships?
Where is the steel coming from?

text.text: Imogen at the theodolite, writing, though the near end across the river is held by a crew with a dog painted on their jackets who do not sign anything. "Bridges are patient," she says, without looking up.
Imogen at the theodolite, writing.

again.again: Imogen, writing.

options.text: And the people in the ships?
Where is the steel coming from?
I'll carry your purse to the masters who haven't signed.
Buy all nine hulls together, at a price that means something.
There's a survey plate on the wall with the old tram bridge on it.
Build on the tram bridge's footing instead.

why.text: "Because the old bridge's far pier stood here, and its footing is still here, eleven metres down on good rock." She taps the stump with the pencil. "A bridge is a sentence with two ends, and the far end wants rock. Anywhere else on this bank I'd have to go looking for rock, and rock is the expensive part."
why.again: "The far end wants rock."

road.text: "Freight." She says it the way other people say a lover's name. "The Line ends here; the barges end here; the Concern's through ends here. Everything Carrick takes in goes into the city round by the Wall, a day for a cart, through the gate, past the lens, and is counted." She smiles. "House Vane would like its goods to arrive without being counted. So would every house in the Crown, which is why they'll all pay the toll."
road.again: "House Vane would like its goods to arrive without being counted."

interject.text: "Past the lens," Nine repeats. "A road to the Crown that never passes the gate." The lens clicks twice. "The Ledger's charter has no clause for a road it cannot see. It will have one by the morning after this opens."

people.text: "Nobody is going to be thrown off a ship." She says it as if she has said it before, often, to people who did not believe her. "The Harbour Master leased us the berths, and the Act says the occupiers quit on commencement. But I would rather they left with something. So I'm buying the masters' marks: a paper of abandonment, forty Tolls a hull. Three have signed." She turns a page. "Forty Tolls is a season, down there. I checked."
people.again: "Forty Tolls a hull. Three have signed."

text.text: "Leven: a tower in the Ring whose squatters stripped their own top floors and sold us the steel. Good steel." She points with the pencil at the quay, where girders lie stacked under a tarp with LEVEN chalked on the ends. "Already here."

"Leven: a tower in the Ring that burned, I'm told." She does not look up. "Good steel. It came down very cleanly." She points with the pencil at the girders stacked under a tarp on the quay, LEVEN chalked on the ends.
"Late." For the first time she sounds less than pleasant. "The Ring stopped selling to our yard. Something about a mark on a door. It will start again; the Ring is always hungry."
"The Ring. Its dead towers are good steel, and there is a yard out there that cuts them by the ton however they come down." She makes a note. "I don't ask how they come down. I'm an engineer."

"Held by a crew with a dog painted on their jackets, who don't sign anything." She sighs. "It will change. The Crown is patient, and dogs get hungry, and there is a great deal of money on the far side of a bridge."

"Bridgeward." She looks across the dry river at the torn deck. "A temporary arrangement with the Rustmouths, who hold the chain for us. Ms Harrow manages the near end. I manage the far one. We meet in the middle eventually; that's the idea of a bridge."

help.text: She counts out two hundred and forty Tolls into a soft leather purse: forty for each of six. "The marks on the papers. And Mr Ofori's, if you can manage it: the Star's the oldest, and the others follow her." She hands you a sheaf of papers, printed, with a line at the bottom for a mark. "Keep twenty for your trouble. I'd rather it was somebody they don't know."

options.text: (Go down the river stairs and buy the marks.)

mods.why: they know your face on the bed
you know they need not sign, and it shows

decision.text: You got House Vane the masters' marks on the Hulls: the old ships on the dry river were abandoned on paper, for the Crown's bridge.

cleared.text: You go hull by hull, a mark and forty Tolls, a mark and forty Tolls, and the masters do not look at you while they make them. Kobby makes his last, on the Star's gangway, slowly, a K and an O, and gives you the paper and turns his back. By the time you climb the stairs the word is all over the bed. The Harbour Master's men will be down at dawn.
cleared.again: Nine marks, and the word all over the bed.

marks_no.text: Kobby's word has gone down the bed ahead of you: on every gangway somebody shakes their head before you have opened the purse. You bring it back up the stairs heavy. Imogen counts it and writes something down. "Well," she says. "That's data."

price.text: "All nine?" She puts the pencil down. "Go on."

options.text: A hundred and twenty a hull, all nine together, paid to the masters on the steps, or nobody signs at all.

mods.why: the Act gives the masters a veto, and you say so
Odile names the figure first, and higher
the crew book on her table

decision.text: You made House Vane buy all nine of the Hulls together at three times its price; the masters walked up the river stairs with the money.

news.text: the old ships on the dry river at the Docks were sold to a Crown house all together, at a price that made the Hulls' masters rich for a season

sold.text: She works it out on a page, twice, and then laughs. "Three times. My mother will be appalled." She signs a draft on House Vane for a thousand and eighty and gives it to you to carry down. On the steps at the change of shift the nine masters take it in turns to count it, and then walk up the river stairs with it in a sack between two of them, and the Hulls follow them up with their bedding.
sold.again: Nine masters and a sack, up the river stairs.

price_no.text: "No." Pleasantly. "Forty is generous for a hull that cannot float. A hundred and twenty is sentiment." She picks up the pencil. "I can afford sentiment. I am not paid to."

plate.text: She comes to the wall with you and reads the plate, crouching, with her nose almost on the brass. "The tram bridge. I had the road bridge's drawings; nobody had these." She traces the line downstream with the silver pencil. "A hundred and twenty metres. Footing to rock." She stands up and looks down the quay at the Bond's fence and its lights, and goes rather quiet.
plate.again: The tram bridge's footing, under the Bond.

move.text: "Under the Concern's yard." She says it carefully. "House Vane and the Concern are partners in a great many things." She looks at the Hulls, the washing, a child on a gangway, and back at the drawings. "Convince me the load works and I'll take it to the house."

options.text: (Work the old tram bridge's loads with her, footing by footing.)

mods.why: you can read the old load tables
Nine has the tram bridge's drawings in its memory, to the bolt

decision.text: You worked House Vane's far end onto the old tram bridge's footing under the edge of the Concern's Bond; the Hulls stay, and the Crown and the Concern want the same ground.

news.text: House Vane moved its bridge's far end at the Docks onto the Concern's bonded yard; the Hulls stay

moved.text: It takes the afternoon, on the stump, in the silver pencil and then in yours. When the last footing comes out right she looks at it for a long time and then laughs. "Sound rock. Under the Concern's yard." She stands. "This will be very expensive for someone, and not me." On her way back along the bed she pulls up a blue stake as if it were a weed, and then, after a moment, all of them.
moved.again: The stakes pulled up like weeds.

move_no.text: The numbers do not come out: the old pier's footing will carry a tram and not a road, and she shows you where with the pencil. "Close," she says. "Close is a bridge that falls down." She goes back to the theodolite.
move_no.again: "Close is a bridge that falls down."

text.text: At the dead crane's foot, a winch with a drum of cable as thick as your wrist, and a big grey man on its brake with a lamp hooked to his belt, who looks at you the way a ship's master looks at weather. "Kwabena Ofori. Kobby, on the bed. The cradle's mine, and the Benguela Star, which is the oldest hull on the river and the only one with her name still on her. Five a head, if you're going over."

A big grey man on the Benguela Star's gangway with his sleeves rolled, mending a block and tackle, who looks at you the way a ship's master looks at weather. "Kwabena Ofori. Kobby, on the bed. Master of the Star, which is the oldest hull on the river and the only one with her name still on her."

intro.again: Kobby, looking at you like weather.

options.text: Master of a ship on dry land?

text.text: "Crew." Kobby says it with great satisfaction, to nobody. "Ninety years of Sundays, and the court read every one." He goes back to his block and tackle, humming.
"Vane's lady pulled her stakes up like weeds." Kobby laughs, deep. "Now she and the Bond can fight over the quay, and we'll sell them both rope."
"A Crown man now, God help me." Kobby at the winch, on a wage from House Vane until the bridge comes. "Five a head, and I give it to the girl in the coat at the far end. Different coat. Same five."
Kobby, looking at you like weather.

again.again: Kobby, at his work.

options.text: Master of a ship on dry land?
(Ride the cradle over to Bridgeward. 5 Tolls)
Sign Vane's paper. Take what she offers while it's offered.

mods.why: he knows the Act is on his side, because you told him

decision.text: You got House Vane the masters' marks on the Hulls: the old ships on the dry river were abandoned on paper, for the Crown's bridge.

hulls.text: "Nine ships on the river the day the river stopped." He waves the block at the bed. "The crews stayed aboard, because where else would they go? Ninety years. Three hundred of us now. We fish the Basin off the wall, we stand on the call-on when Platt will have us, which is never, and we run the cradle." He looks up at the Star's rust. "My great-grandfather was her third mate. He used to say she'd float again. She won't. She's full of people."
hulls.again: "She won't float again. She's full of people."

cradle.text: "A basket on a wire." He points up at Crane One's jib, at the cable running off it into the air over the bed, west, to where Bridgeward's torn deck stands up out of the far bank like a broken tooth. "Before the bridge fell there was a bridge. After, there was nothing, and my grandfather said a rope's a bridge if you're brave. Five a head, at night: people who want into the city without the gate looking at their faces. Letters. Goods. The Rustmouths take two of every five at their end." He shrugs. "You come at night, you pay, Abena takes you over. From their side: swing a lamp twice at the drop, wait, and once. We'll see it."
cradle.again: "Swing a lamp twice, wait, and once."

interject.text: Wren is looking up at the cable with an expression you have not seen on her before. "A road nobody drew," she says. "That's the best kind."

stakes.text: "Vane's." He does not look at them. "Their lady buys our masters' marks. Forty a hull. Three of my cousins took it: a season of rice, for a ship." He puts the block down. "She's polite about it. That's the worst part. You can't hit polite."

books.text: He grins for the first time, all the way across his face. "The articles. A ship's crew signs on in her book. When the river stopped, my great-grandfather said: we're still a crew, so we'll sign on. Every Sunday since." He shakes his head. "Ninety years of Sundays. Abena keeps them now, all nine hulls' books. Ask her; she'll show you. She shows everybody."

signed.text: He looks at the Star for a long time, at the washing and the smoke and the child on the gangway. "All right," he says at last. "All right. Better forty than the river stairs with nothing in our hands." He makes his mark, a K and an O, and goes down the bed with the paper, and the other masters follow the Star, as they always have.

sign_no.text: "No." Not loud. "The Star's a ship. I'm her master. She has a crew." He picks the block up again. "Forty Tolls is what they pay for a thing that's finished. We're not."

text.text: A young woman crouched in the steel basket at the cable's end with a lamp between her knees, who looks up at you with her grandfather's exact face. "Abena. Over?"
A young woman sitting on the Benguela Star's rail with a fat ledger open on her knees, writing names in a careful hand. "Abena. Sunday's tomorrow," she says. "I'm getting ahead."

intro.again: Abena, with the book or the lamp.

options.text: What is it like, over there?

again.text: Abena, with the book or the lamp.
again.again: Abena.

options.text: Could I take the Star's book up the steps to the Harbour court?
What is it like, over there?

book.text: She holds the ledger up so you can see the spine: BENGUELA STAR — ARTICLES, in gold that has mostly gone. "Every hull has one. Every name. Every Sunday, signed or marked." She turns to the first page, where the ink is brown. "The first one's the week the river stopped. Grandad's great-grandfather. Third mate." She closes it carefully. "Grandad says it's a joke we kept telling until it was true."
book.again: "A joke we kept telling until it was true."

borrow.text: She looks at you, and at the book, and at the Star. "Bring it back," she says, and puts it in your hands. It is heavier than it looks. "It's the only one with all ninety years in it."

signed.text: "The Orinoco, the Hope and the Saint Kilda." She does not have to look it up. "Forty each. The Hope's master has seven children; I don't blame him. The Saint Kilda's master drinks; I do." She shrugs. "They're still crewed. Everybody's still aboard. The marks are just marks, till somebody comes to move us."
signed.again: "The marks are just marks, till somebody comes."

city.text: "Loud. Counted." She thinks about it. "They look at your face at the gate and decide if it's a face. I go over twice a night and I've never been further than the end of the bridge." She grins suddenly, exactly like her grandfather. "The Rustmouths give me sweets. They think I don't know they're skimming."
city.again: "They look at your face and decide if it's a face."

interject.text: "I've been counted," Tamsin says. "It's overrated." Abena laughs, and the two of them look at each other like people who have just found out they speak the same language.

look.text: Blue stakes in a straight line across the dry bed between the ships, each with a brass tag: VANE — WEST ABUTMENT — and a number. The line runs through a cookfire, a washing line, and the Saint Kilda's stern, and does not bend for any of them. On the stump above, a theodolite on its tripod, looking at the far bank.
look.again: The blue stakes, straight through the Saint Kilda's stern.

moved.text: The stakes are gone from the bed. A new line of blue runs along the Bond's fence downstream, and the Bond's guards pull them up every morning as fast as House Vane's men drive them in at night.
moved.again: Blue stakes along the Bond's fence, and the guards pulling them.

empty.text: The stakes stand in a bed with nothing round them but rust, the black rings of ninety years of cookfires, and a child's shoe.
empty.again: The stakes, the fire-rings, the shoe.

plate.text: A brass plate let into the river wall's coping, green with ninety years, its letters cut deep: MERIDIAN PORT AUTHORITY — RIVER CROSSINGS — SURVEY DATUM. Under it, engraved, the river in its banks with water in it, and two bridges across it, ROAD and TRAM, their piers marked with depths to rock.
plate.again: The survey plate: ROAD and TRAM, their piers, depths to rock.

mods.why: you have read survey work before

read.text: The road bridge's far pier: rock at eleven metres, right under the stump. The tram bridge's far pier, a hundred and twenty metres downstream: rock at nine. Shallower, and sound. You look down the quay to where the plate's line would land, and it lands inside the Bond's fence, under its white lights.
read.again: Rock at nine, under the Bond.

read_no.text: Numbers, a scale, a north arrow, two lines of piers. Somebody who reads surveys for a living would know what it says. Somebody on this bank does, and kneels on the stump all day with a silver pencil.

books.text: On the Star's mess table, nine ledgers in a row with their spines out, each with a ship's name in faded gold: BENGUELA STAR, ORINOCO, CAPE HOPE, SAINT KILDA, and five more. Each one open at this week, with a pen beside it.
books.again: Nine crew books, open at this week.

intro.text: An old man on the fish steps with a beard like a hedge and a hand line in each fist, who does not look up from the water. "Grigor. Mullet: small, grey, alive, which is three things more than the river. Lines at dawn, two Tolls, bring them back."
intro.again: Grigor, a line in each fist.

options.text: Who brings the oil to the fuel berth?

text.text: "Dawn." Grigor holds a line out without looking round. "Two. Bring it back."
Grigor, a line in each fist.

again.again: Grigor, watching the water.

options.text: (Rent a line and fish off the Basin wall. 2 Tolls)

mods.why: you see them turn under the slick

options.text: Who brings the oil to the fuel berth?

caught.text: Three hours on the wall with your legs over the Basin and the line round your finger, and two small grey mullet in the bucket for it, and a sunburn on one side of your neck. Grigor looks in the bucket and grunts, which from him is applause.

nothing.text: Three hours on the wall with your legs over the Basin, and the line goes slack every time you look away. Grigor takes it back and coils it. "They're down there," he says. "They just don't like you yet."

river.text: "It stopped." He spits into the Basin. "My grandfather said: the Burn, and the dams upriver, and then the city took what was left for the Precinct, and one spring it was a river and the next it was a road for rats. They left the ships where they sat." He jerks his head at the Basin. "This is the sea's. The sea doesn't stop. The sea doesn't take orders from anybody."

interject.text: "The upper river was diverted into the north channel in the Burn's second year by the city's own works," Nine says, looking at the bed with something like fondness. "The drawings are in the Vault. Eleven sluices." Grigor looks at the lens. "Eleven," Nine says again, as if that settled something. "Drainage."

text.text: "There was a night barge from the delta, low in the water, no lamps, every few nights, to the fuel berth. Not since the spring." He coils a line. "Somebody burned it, the tide boat says. Somebody on the shore. Good." He does not explain the good.
"The Rigs' own launch, now, once a month, with a hose that says HUM on it, and a price somebody on the Rigs set." He spits. "The guild hates it. Good."

"A night barge from the delta, low in the water, no lamps, every few nights. Unloads at the fuel berth for the Line's engines." He coils a line. "Nobody on the quay is awake to see it. Nobody asks. The water round the berth's purple in the morning."

intro.text: A woman behind a counter of crates in the cut-open side of a hull, with a split lip that healed crooked and a pistol on the counter where she can reach it. "Nadia. What comes over the rope and what falls off the boxes." She smiles with half her mouth. "Don't ask which."
intro.again: Nadia, behind her crates.

again.text: Nadia, behind her crates, the pistol where she can reach it.
again.again: Nadia.

boxes.text: "Inhalers, lately. Blue caps." She sets one on the crate between you: clean white plastic, the closed eye on the cap. "Somebody on the night gang had a box a week of them for a while and sold me what his girl didn't need, and then he didn't." She looks at you. "Concern medicine at Concern prices. I'm not a charity. The Bond is, apparently, when it wants something."
boxes.again: "Somebody on the night gang had a box a week."

desk.text: At a junior clerk's table in the Customs House's long room, copying berth dues into a ledger in an exact hand, a man in a good coat gone shiny at the elbows. Cyprian Thorne looks up, and for a moment has no expression at all. "Ah," he says. "You." He dips the pen. "I was a factor. Now I copy. The guild sends you back to a desk when the water won't have you." He goes back to the ledger. "Nobody has to be unreasonable."
desk.again: Thorne, copying dues, not looking up.

text.text: "You were on the line that morning." A nod, and something more than a nod. "Stand by me at the call-on any time."
They look at you, and at the Bond, and go back to what they were doing.
"Mind the tarp." Not unfriendly. "That's Dmytro. Nobody's moved him; nobody's allowed."
"Off the Line?" Not unfriendly. "Mind the hooks. Mind the gang-masters more."

options.text: How do I get into the city?

a0.text: "Espe's bunk, twenty, next to the soup. Or the Hulls, if Kobby likes you. Or the Stand, if you like the cold."
a0.again: "Espe's bunk, twenty, next to the soup. Or the Hulls, if Kobby likes you. Or the Stand, if you like the cold."

a1.text: "Dahl, by the Act. The Bond, past its fence. The Crown, whenever it wants a box. Us, on the line, for about four minutes at dawn."
a1.again: "Dahl, by the Act. The Bond, past its fence. The Crown, whenever it wants a box. Us, on the line, for about four minutes at dawn."

a2.text: "River road from the north end, round by the Wall to the gate: an hour, and papers. The quay tram to Clover. Or at night, Kobby's rope." They grin. "You didn't hear the last one from me."
a2.again: "River road from the north end, round by the Wall to the gate: an hour, and papers. The quay tram to Clover. Or at night, Kobby's rope." They grin. "You didn't hear the last one from me."

text.text: "Crew," they say, and grin, and tap a ship's rail as if it were a friend's shoulder.
"You're not from the bed." A look up and down. "Mind the stakes. They're only paint, but the paint's the Crown's."

options.text: How long have you lived down here?
