give.text: "Who?" She has the pencil in her hand, ready to write a name. You can give her the girl. You can give her the reason too, or not.

decision.text: I gave the boom-keeper the mark-cutter, Sigrun Brandvold, and not the reason. Sawtown's law is the Water.

caught.text: Berit writes it in the book, and sits looking at it. "His girl." She puts the pencil down. "Well. The Water is wide." She counts sixty Tolls out of a tin and pushes them over. "That's the boom's, for the marks. It'll be at dawn." She does not ask why. Nobody in Sawtown will ask why.

interject.text: "One oar," Tamsin says outside, very quietly. "They give her one oar and a lake." She looks at you. "You didn't ask why she did it. I would have asked why."

meeting.speaker: narrator
meeting.text: Berit rings the mill bell at dusk, and they come, because she has never rung it before: the Ridge down the hill in a body with Arvid at their front, the Bottoms up the shore with Rufino, the mill hands, the cookhouse, a dozen children, and Wayra Huaman at the back with a bundle in her arms. Two crews and a gap between them on the sawdust floor exactly as wide as a felled tree. Everybody is looking at you.
meeting.again: The two crews on the sawdust, and the gap between them.

options.text: (Say it all: the marks, where the money goes, and the morning in the rain.)

mods.why: you know what happened on the boundary
Sigrun stands up beside you
the tally in Berit's hand
Ash, who says the dead's names

news.text: Sawtown's two crews have ended their feud; the Ridge's foreman gave up his crew and went up the hill

decision.text: At the crews' meeting in Sawtown's mill, Mikkel Brandvold's death was said aloud for what it was: his father sent him up in the rain. Arvid Brandvold gave the Ridge to Cillian Moss and went up the hill alone. The marks stopped. Mikkel's child eats at the Ridge's table.

said.speaker: narrator
said.text: You tell it, and Sigrun Brandvold stands up beside you and tells the part that is hers, and the mill is so quiet you can hear the race under the floor. When you come to the morning in the rain, Arvid Brandvold does not argue. He looks at the bundle in Wayra's arms for the first time in two years, and says, "Yes." Just that. Then he takes his axe off his shoulder and gives it to Cillian Moss, haft first, and walks out of the mill and up the hill in the dark, and Rufino Huaman, after a long moment, walks across the gap and puts the baby into Sigrun's arms.

interject.text: "Mikkel Brandvold," Ash says, aloud, to the mill, the way the Choir says a name at a burial. Nobody tells him not to.
Ilya watches the old man go up the hill until his lamp is gone. "Right," he says, and nothing else, and it is not the word he usually means by it.

shouted.speaker: narrator
shouted.text: You start, and the Ridge start shouting before you are halfway, and Arvid Brandvold walks out with his crew behind him before you can come to the morning in the rain. The gap on the sawdust is wider when they have gone.
shouted.again: The gap on the sawdust, wider.

worked.speaker: narrator
worked.text: Four hours on the walkways with a pike pole, walking logs into their pens by the marks on their butts while Berit calls them: crow's foot, hook, crow's foot. Your arms ache and your boots are full of the Water.

wet.speaker: narrator
wet.text: A log rolls under your pole on the second hour, and you go into the pen after it, and the sorters fish you out laughing. Berit pays you three for the morning and tells you the Water does that to everyone once.

look.text: The boom's tally book open on the desk by the window: a column of crow's feet and a column of hooks, a count a day, and the boom's pay beside each.
look.again: The tally book.

interject.text: Odile turns three pages and runs a finger down the hooks. "Four saws on the flats, my dear, if I read the payroll. They are being paid for six." She closes it. "Somebody is cutting hooks, yes. But somebody on the Bottoms is also not asking why they are suddenly rich."

mods.why: quick with numbers

sum.text: The Bottoms have four saws on the flats and the flats are slow ground. This season the boom has paid them for half again what four saws can fell, a log or two a night more than they can have cut, every night, for months. Whoever is cutting hooks over crow's feet, the money is real, and it is going somewhere.
sum.again: Half again what four saws can fell.

muddle.text: Crow's feet, hooks, and numbers. It comes out different each time you add it.

look.text: The north pen: logs afloat shoulder to shoulder in black water, their butts toward the walkway, each with a mark cut into its end grain. Crow's foot, crow's foot, hook.
look.again: The north pen, crow's feet and hooks.

interject.text: Wren crouches on the walkway and runs her thumb round the hook on a butt. "Fresh. And under it—" she tilts the log to the light, "—a crow's foot, shaved off with a knife. Somebody with a punt and a lamp, at night." She looks along the pen. "Seven like it. Same hand."

mods.why: you know a fresh cut

marks.text: On a dozen butts in the north pen the hook is new, pale wood, cut with a scribe's bent blade; and round it, if you tilt the log, the ghost of a crow's foot shaved away with a knife. All in the pen nearest the dark end of the walkway, where nobody stands at night.
marks.again: The new hooks over shaved crow's feet.

logs.text: Logs, water, marks. They all look alike to you, which is presumably the point.

caught.text: A punt in the north pen, nosed in among the logs, a lamp with its shutter almost closed, and a young woman kneeling in it over a log's butt with a scribe in her fist. She freezes in your light. Then she sits back on her heels and does not try to run. "Well," says Sigrun Brandvold. "Now somebody knows."
caught.again: Sigrun in the punt, the scribe in her fist.

options.text: Why cut your own family's marks?
(Hold out your hand for the scribe.)

why.text: "Because my father won't." She puts the scribe in her lap. "Mikkel was going to marry Wayra Huaman. My father said a Brandvold doesn't marry hooks. Then Mikkel was dead, and Wayra had his baby, and my father has never looked at either of them." She looks at the hooks. "Ridge timber. Ridge money. A log a night to Rufino, and Rufino gives it to Dorit for Wayra's board and the baby's milk." She laughs, shakily. "It's the only thing the Ridge has ever given Mikkel's child. It just doesn't know."
why.again: "It's the only thing the Ridge has ever given Mikkel's child."

interject.text: Tamsin sits down on the walkway with her boots over the water. "You're stealing from your dad to feed your brother's baby," she says. "Rust it, I like you."

scribe.text: She looks at your hand, and at the Water, and puts the scribe in it, handle first: a bent marking knife with a crow's foot burned into the handle. "It was his," she says. "Mikkel's."

intro.text: A young faller with a sun-bleached braid, sharpening a saw chain on her knee outside the Ridge's bunkhouse. "I'm busy." She does not look up. "Ask my father. Everyone asks my father."
intro.again: Sigrun, at the saw chain.

text.text: Sigrun with a baby on her hip and a saw chain in her other hand, looking like someone who has not slept and does not mind. "She bites," she says. "Like Mikkel did."
"My father went to the cookhouse," Sigrun says. "He sat with her an hour. He hasn't said a word to me about it." She almost smiles. "I stopped cutting."
"I'm busy," Sigrun says again.

again.again: Sigrun.

options.text: You're the one cutting your own family's marks.
Will you stand up at the mill and say it, if I say the rest?

why.text: She stops sharpening. "For Wayra Huaman, and my brother's baby. My father won't look at them. The Ridge won't feed them. So the Ridge feeds them anyway, a log a night, and doesn't know it." She starts sharpening again, harder. "Tell Berit if you want. The Water's wide."
why.again: "The Ridge feeds them anyway."

stand.text: "If you've got the rest of it." She looks up the hill at her father's house. "If you can make him hear it. He never hears it from me." She puts the chain down. "I'll stand."

intro.text: A big grey-bearded man with a scar down one cheek, sitting on the step of the foreman's house with an axe across his knees, honing it with long strokes. "Brandvold." He does not stop. "The Ridge cuts the Ridge. The Bottoms cut mud. If you're here to buy timber, see Berit."
intro.again: Arvid, honing the axe.

text.text: Arvid on the step, the axe across his knees, not honing it. "I sat with her," he says, before you can speak. "She has his chin." He says nothing else.
"They're gone," Arvid says. "Down the river. All of them." He hones the axe. "The Ridge cuts the Ridge."
"Mm." Arvid does not stop honing.

again.again: Arvid, on the step.

options.text: You sent him up to fell that leaner in the rain.

mods.why: his daughter has said she will stand
Mikkel's scribe, in your hand
Ash, gently
you know where the money goes

news.text: Sawtown's Ridge and Bottoms are cutting side by side again, and nobody will say why

decision.text: I told Arvid Brandvold alone what I knew about the morning his son died. He walked down to the cookhouse and asked to hold the child. The feud ended, and nobody else in Sawtown knows why.

mikkel.text: The honing stops for one stroke, and starts again. "Don't say his name in my house." He is not in his house; he is on its step. You do not point this out.

bottoms.text: "They dropped a tree on my boy." He says it flat, the way you say a thing you have said every day for two years so you would not have to hear yourself think anything else. "From the flats. A big leaner on the boundary. They wanted it before we got to it. They got it." The axe goes on. "Mud and money, the Bottoms. Always were."
bottoms.again: "They dropped a tree on my boy."

quiet.text: The axe stops. For a long time he only sits, looking at the stumps on the hill. "I told him the Bottoms would have it by noon," he says. "It was raining. He said it was leaning wrong. I told him to fell it anyway." He puts the axe down on the step, carefully, as if it might break. "I've been saying it was them for two years so I wouldn't have to hear that." He stands up. He goes down the hill, not fast, to the cookhouse, and through the cookhouse door. Through the window you see him stop in front of Wayra Huaman, and hold out his hands.

interject.text: Ash watches through the cookhouse window and does not say anything at all. When he turns away he is smiling, which he does not do often.

out.text: He is on his feet with the axe in his hand before you have finished, and you are off his step without being entirely sure how. "Get off the Ridge," he says. "Get off it before I forget I'm a foreman."

intro.text: A red-headed faller with a black eye a week old, kicking a stump on the Ridge path as if it had done something. "Somebody should do something," he says, to you, to the stump, to the hill. "Mikkel was my friend. And they cut hooks on our timber and Berit pays them for it, and Arvid just hones that axe." He kicks the stump. "Somebody should do something."
intro.again: Cillian, kicking the stump.

text.text: Cillian with Arvid's axe on his shoulder, looking as if it is far too heavy. "Foreman," he says. "Me." He shakes his head. "I'd have burned them. I'd have burned them, and it was him."
"Well?" says Cillian.

again.again: Cillian, on the Ridge path.

options.text: Who sent Mikkel up to fell that leaner?

mods.why: you have read the stump

options.text: Do it, then. I'll keep watch.

decision.text: I kept watch while Cillian Moss went down to the Bottoms' skid camp with a can of the Rigs' oil.

options.text: Put the oil can back under your bunk, Cillian.

what.text: "Their skid camp's all dry tarp and old oil." He says it fast, as if he has been saying it to himself all week. "One can. Two in the morning. Nobody hurt; they sleep in the tents, not the shed. Then they'd know." He looks at you sideways. "I'd need somebody to watch the path."

morning.text: He stops kicking the stump. "Arvid," he says. "Who else. I was there, I held the wedge. It was pissing down and the leaner was wrong, you could see it was wrong, and Mikkel said so, and Arvid said the Bottoms'll have it by noon, fell it." He wipes his face with his sleeve. "It split. It came back on him." He looks at you, horrified, as if you had made him say it. "It's the Bottoms' fault. They'd have had it by noon."

burn.text: He grins, a terrible bright grin. "Two in the morning," he says. "Watch the shore path." He goes off up to the bunkhouse at a run, and you hear him laughing.

interject.text: Ash puts his hand on your arm, very hard. "There's a baby in that camp," he says. "Did you know that? There's a baby."

calm.text: He glares at you, and at the hill, and then all the fight goes out of him at once and he sits down on the stump. "Fine," he says. "Fine. It's under my bunk." He puts his face in his hands. "He was my friend."

shut.text: "What do you care?" He kicks the stump again and walks off up the hill.

intro.text: A broad man with a weathered face and cropped black hair, splitting kindling at the Bottoms' fire on the shore with neat, unhurried strokes. "Huaman. The Bottoms." He nods at the flats. "Slow ground. Slow ground never killed anybody." He splits another stick. "Whatever the Ridge told you, it was before breakfast, and we were at breakfast."
intro.again: Rufino, splitting kindling.

text.text: Rufino at the fire, not splitting anything. "My granddaughter eats at the Ridge's table," he says. "I never thought I'd say that sentence." He laughs. "I'll have to get used to it."
"Mm?" Rufino splits another stick.

again.again: Rufino, at the fire.

options.text: The boom's paid you for half again what you can fell this season.

morning.text: "We were on the flats, all twelve of us, eating, when we heard it go." He puts the hatchet down. "I ran up. The tree had split up the middle and come back over its own stump. Mikkel was under it." He picks the hatchet up again. "He was a good boy. He used to come down to our fire and eat with us, when his father wasn't looking. He was going to marry my girl." He splits a stick. "Arvid doesn't know that. Or he does, and it's why."
morning.again: "He was going to marry my girl."

money.text: He looks at you for a long moment, and then he looks up the hill at the Ridge, and something in his face gives. "I don't ask where it comes from," he says. "I know where it comes from. I give every Toll of it to Dorit at the cookhouse, for my girl's board and the baby's milk, because that's whose it is." He goes back to the kindling. "Mikkel's child. Ridge timber. The Ridge just doesn't know it's being generous."
money.again: "The Ridge just doesn't know it's being generous."

intro.text: A young woman at the end of the cookhouse table with a baby asleep in a sling on her chest and a bowl of potatoes she is peeling round it. "Shh." She does not look up. "She's only just gone down. Mika." The baby has a fist up by her face. "If you're from the Ridge, you can go back up it."
intro.again: Wayra, peeling round the baby.

interject.text: Ash sits down across the table, a long way from the baby, and looks at her the way he looks at seedlings. "Mika," he says. "That's a good name." Wayra looks at him, and after a moment, nearly smiles.

text.text: "He came in and held out his hands," Wayra says, astonished, still. "Arvid Brandvold. I gave her to him. He held her an hour and didn't say anything and gave her back." She looks down at the baby. "He comes every evening now."
"Sigrun says I'm to eat at the Ridge now." Wayra shakes her head. "Ridge on one side, Bottoms on the other, and me in the middle with the baby." She smiles. "Like a wedding nobody had."
Wayra glances up from the potatoes, and down again.

again.again: Wayra, at the end of the table.

mikkel.text: "Mikkel's." She peels. "We were going to tell his father at the midsummer fire. Then he was dead, and I was showing, and his father looked at me in the street like I was a hook on the wrong log." The knife stops. "Dorit lets me work for the board. My father pays the rest. I don't ask where he gets it." She starts peeling again. "I'd rather not know."

intro.text: A dark-haired woman with her sleeves rolled at a range the size of a cart, stirring three pots at once. "Avraham. The cookhouse." She points with the spoon. "Ridge on the left, Bottoms on the right, and nobody in the middle. Eat, you look like the rain's been at you. The room upstairs is twenty-five a week, and dry, mostly."
intro.again: Dorit, at the range.

again.text: "Eat," Dorit says, without turning round from the range.
again.again: Dorit, at the range.

room.text: "Twenty-five, the week. A bed, a locker with a key, a window on the Water, and you'll hear the mill all night." She shrugs. "You get used to it."

rented.text: She takes the money without counting it and gives you a key on a string. "Up the back stair. Don't bring your boots in."

wayra.text: "Wayra." She lowers her voice. "Mikkel Brandvold's girl, and his baby. She works for her board and Rufino pays the rest, every week, in Ridge money." She tastes the stew. "Don't ask me how I know it's Ridge money. Berit pays in marks, and I can count."

let.text: A bed under the cookhouse eaves, a locker, a window over the Water. Dorit's, to let.

mine.text: Your room under the cookhouse eaves: the bed, the locker, the mill thudding through the floor, the rain on the shingles, and the boom's lamps on the Water.

look.text: On the boundary between the Ridge's ground and the flats, a stump as wide as a table, grey with two years' weather, and beside it the split trunk, still lying where it came down, moss on it now. Somebody has driven a stake into the ground at its foot and tied a faded strip of cloth to it.
look.again: The stump on the boundary, the cloth on its stake.

interject.text: Ilya walks round the stump once, and kneels at its uphill side. "Cut from here," he says. "The Ridge side. Back-cut too low. Hurried." He touches the split. "Wet wood. Rain." He stands up. "Nobody dropped this on him. He was under his own tree."

read.text: The face cut on the uphill side, the Ridge's side; the back-cut far too low under it, the hinge too thin; and the trunk split up its middle where it went over, the way a tree splits when it is felled leaning wrong in wet weather by someone in a hurry. Nobody on the flats felled this. It came back over its own stump onto whoever was standing at it.
read.again: A barber chair, felled from the Ridge.

wood.text: A stump, a split trunk, two years of moss. You are not a faller.

text.text: Where the Bottoms' skid camp stood: a black square on the shore, the shed's iron roof crumpled in the ash, a child's shoe, and the tents' poles standing in a row with nothing on them.
The Bottoms' skid camp: a shed of scrap iron and tarp full of old oil and dry timber, tents in a row on the shore, a fire, and children's washing. A hook painted on the shed door, very large.

look.again: The Bottoms' camp.

text.text: The great saw in the mill, running fast on a race that comes in full and loud now, the turbine under the floor singing. The mill hands say the Water has never run so steady.

The great saw in the mill: a pre-war band saw the height of a house, driven off a turbine under the floor by the race from the lake. It runs slow. "Race is half what it should be," a mill hand shouts over it. "The dam keeps the Water low, and the city keeps the dam."

look.again: The great saw.

drive.text: The drive: where the race comes out under the mill, logs that have been through the saw's pen go out down a chute into the Water in a long rush, and the young ones ride them, standing, from the chute's foot to the boom, for a bet. Twenty Tolls to anyone who rides one all the way in without going under.
drive.again: The drive, logs going out down the chute.

options.text: (Ride a log down the drive. 20 Tolls if you stay up.)

up.speaker: narrator
up.text: Down the chute, the log rolling under your boots, the Water coming up white, a moment of flying, and you stay up all the way into the boom with your arms out like a fool and the whole bank cheering. Berit pays the bet out of the boom's tin without comment.

under.speaker: narrator
under.text: Halfway down, the log rolls, and you do not. The Water is colder than anything you have ever felt. They fish you out with a pike pole, and give you five for the entertainment.

night.text: The drive's chute, still, the race running under the mill in the dark.
night.again: The drive, still.

cast.text: "First light," Magda says. "The river's highest at first light, when the dam lets the noon water down overnight." She hands you the bow sweep. "Pull when I say pull. Don't when I don't."

chute.speaker: narrator
chute.text: Below the Landing the river goes into a gorge and down a long fall of water over rock, the Chute, and the Patience goes into it nose first with Magda at the stern oar shouting. Rock goes by close enough to touch. "Pull!" she shouts. "Now! Pull!"
chute.again: The Chute, the rock going by.

interject.text: Tamsin is holding on to the deckhouse with both arms and laughing so hard she cannot breathe. "AGAIN," she shouts at the river. "DO IT AGAIN."

options.text: (Read the water and call the rocks for her.)

through.speaker: narrator
through.text: Through, and out into the long flat reach below with the gorge behind you and the Patience turning slowly in the eddy as if she were pleased with herself. Magda lets go of the oar and laughs out loud. "Twenty years," she says. "Never once dull."

rock.speaker: narrator
rock.text: A rock you did not see comes up under the bow with a sound like a door slamming, and the Patience slews and ships water, and for an hour after the Chute you bail with a bucket while Magda swears at you and the river by turns. She is not hurt. Neither is the load.

night.speaker: narrator
night.text: The night reach: a long slow river through reed beds higher than the barge, no moon, Magda's stern lamp the only light, and then other lamps, low on the water, shuttered, coming out of the reeds on both sides. Two flat boats. A woman with a rifle stands up in the first. "Evening, Patience," she calls. "Bryony. You know me, Magda." Magda does, by her face. "Guild load, is it? Let's have a look at what the guild doesn't write down."
night.again: The reed boats in the night reach.

options.text: It's Magda's mooring in those cases. Let us by.

mods.why: you have met her on the bank
Wren, who knows a brand when she sees one

options.text: (Pay her twenty to let you by.)

kennel.text: You prise up the lid of the nearest case with Magda's knife. Straw, and in the straw a board potted in black resin with the Concern's closed eye etched on it, a tag wired to it, KENNEL 7, and on its underside a socket shaped for something's neck. Bryony looks at it a long time in her lamp. "A kennel board," she says. "The brain for a hound. One of the machine dogs." She looks at the eleven other cases. "Somebody means to wake dogs in the city."
kennel.again: "Somebody means to wake dogs in the city."

interject.text: Kes has gone very quiet. "Concern lineage," she says. "Fresh off the line. You put one of those in a sleeping hound and say the word, and it's a hound again." She looks down the dark river toward the city. "Twelve. That's a pack."

options.text: Let us by. I haven't decided what to do with them.

by_kennel.text: Bryony looks at you, and at the case, and sits down in her boat. "Decide well," she says. "We'll hear." The boats go back into the reeds.

by.speaker: narrator
by.text: Bryony looks at Magda a long moment and then sits down in her boat. "Go on, then, Patience," she says. "Tell the guild the river was asking after it." The reed boats go back into the dark as quietly as they came.
by.again: The reed boats going back into the dark.

warned.speaker: narrator
warned.text: The shot goes off over the reeds like a door slammed in a cathedral, and every heron in the night reach goes up at once. When it is quiet again the reed boats are gone. Magda lets her breath out. "They'll remember that," she says.

toll.text: "No." Bryony does not raise her rifle; she does not need to. "Something from the cases, or twenty for the river, or we sit here till morning and the guild's tug finds you in the reeds." Magda is looking at you.

options.text: (Open a case and show her what she's asking for.)

one.speaker: narrator
one.text: Two of the reed people lift a case down into their boat between them as if it were a coffin, and Bryony touches her hat to Magda, and they are gone. "That's a twelfth of my mooring," Magda says. "I hope it was worth something to somebody."
one.again: One case gone into the reeds.

deep.speaker: narrator

text.text: The deep reach above the city, before dawn: the river wide and black and slow, forty feet of it under the keel, the city's lamps on the horizon and the Wall's lens-towers blinking. Magda at the oar, not looking at the cases. "Your call," she says. "I carry what I'm paid to carry. But your call."

The deep reach above the city, before dawn: the river wide and black and slow, forty feet of it under the keel, the city's lamps on the horizon and the Wall's lens-towers blinking. The cases sit under their tarp, sealed, ticking a little as they cool.

deep.again: The deep reach, the city's lamps.

options.text: (Put the cases over the side, here, where it's deep.)

news.text: a guild load bound for the city's Docks went into the river from the Patience

decision.text: I put the Patience's sealed load over the side in the deep reach above the city: twelve cases of the Concern's kennel boards, in the mud for good. Nobody was paid for them.

drowned.speaker: narrator
drowned.text: One by one, over the gunwale, and each goes down with a sound like a stone into a well, and the river closes over it and goes on being the river. Magda watches every one go and does not help and does not stop you. When the last is gone she says, very quietly, "That was my mooring." Then the city's basin, at dawn, and she ties up, and does not say goodbye.
drowned.again: The cases going down one by one.

interject.text: "Dogs in the city," Ash says, watching the black water. "And children in the city." He looks at Magda. "We'll find her mooring. We have to."

city.speaker: narrator
city.text: The city's canal basin outside the Wall at dawn, a grey square of water among warehouses, and on the quay a man in guild green with a cart and two porters, waiting, with a paper he holds out for the waybill. Beyond the warehouses, a hundred yards up the gate road, the wardens' post at the Wall with its lens.
city.again: The basin, the guild's man with his cart.

options.text: (Hand the load to the guild's man.)

decision.text: I saw the Patience's sealed load to the guild's man at the city's canal basin. Magda Kowal has her mooring and her barge. The guild has twelve cases of the Concern's kennel boards.

options.text: (Take the load and the waybill up the road to the wardens instead.)

news.text: the wardens seized a guild load of Concern machine parts at the city gate, off the Patience

decision.text: I took the Patience's sealed load and the guild's waybill to the wardens at the city gate. The record has twelve cases of the Concern's kennel boards, and the guild's name on the paper.

options.text: (Push off again into the deep reach.)

delivered.speaker: narrator
delivered.text: The guild's man counts the cases onto his cart, and signs the waybill, and counts a hundred and fifty Tolls into Magda's hand without looking at her. She gives you half, and a copper ring off her finger stamped PATIENCE. "Ride on my account," she says, "anywhere on the river." The cart goes off toward the Docks' bridge with its tarp down.
delivered.again: The cart going toward the Docks.

interject.text: Kes watches the cart all the way to the bridge. "That's twelve dogs," she says. "Twelve. In a city." She does not look at you for the rest of the morning.

wardens.speaker: narrator
wardens.text: The guild's man says something sharp and then, seeing where you are pushing the cart, nothing at all. At the wardens' post a sergeant reads the waybill twice and lifts the lid of a case and looks at the closed eye on the board for a long time, and sends a runner in through the gate. "The record thanks you," he says, and means it, and gives you the record's bounty, which you halve with Magda. Magda gives you a copper ring stamped PATIENCE. "Ride on my account," she says. "I'll not be carrying for the guild again for a while."
wardens.again: The sergeant and the closed eye.

interject.text: "The record will want to know who ordered twelve hound controllers into a city it keeps," Nine says. "So will I."

intro.text: A woman with a weathered face and a chin with a scar across it, sitting on the Patience's deckhouse roof mending a sweep with wire, a black barge under her with nothing on it. "Kowal. The Patience." She pats the roof. "My father's, then mine. Then the guild's, if I'm not careful." She looks at the river. "Half a season tied up on a low river and the mooring's due, wet or dry."
intro.again: Magda, mending the sweep.

options.text: Why is the river so low?

text.text: Magda on the quay, not on the Patience. The barge has the guild's green painted on her bow. "They took her at dawn," Magda says. "For the mooring. I'm on the winch Monday."
Magda on the Patience's roof, not mending anything. "The mooring's due at dawn," she says. "Eighty. I haven't got it." She does not ask you for it.
"Patience is paid up," Magda says. "First time in a year." She knocks on the deckhouse roof. "Ride when you like."
"Mm?" Magda twists the wire.

again.again: Magda, on the Patience.

options.text: Why is the river so low?

river.text: "The dam." She jerks her head north. "The city keeps the Water up there and lets it down when its card says, and the card says hardly ever. We go down half-loaded and we come up behind the guild's tug for a fee. When it does let the Water down, it's all at once in the spring and the meadows go under to the doorsteps." She bends the wire. "My grandmother said the dam was cracked. Everybody's grandmother says that."

load.text: "Pryce has a load for the city." She does not sound happy about it. "Sealed, twelve cases, a hundred and fifty Tolls, no questions. That's my mooring and some." She looks at you. "I need a second pair of arms at the sweeps through the Chute, and somebody awake on the night reach. The reed people come out there, and they know a guild load by its tarp. Half of it's yours."

crew.text: "Good." She hands you a folded paper. "Pryce's waybill. You carry the paper; I carry the oar." She nods at the cases under their tarp on the Patience's deck. "First light, when you're ready. Tell me."

paid.text: She looks at the money for a long time. Then she takes a copper ring off her finger, stamped PATIENCE, and puts it in your hand. "Ride on my account," she says. "Anywhere on the river. For as long as she floats."

intro.text: A man in a good coat with the guild's green on its cuff, at a desk in the barge office with a ledger open and a cup of something hot. "Factor Pryce. The guild's river." He does not get up. "Moorings, tows, the winch, freight. The river is a contract like any other. What can the guild do for you?"
intro.again: Pryce, at his ledger.

text.text: Pryce looks up from the ledger and looks at you for a long time. "The guild has a very long memory," he says pleasantly, "and a very large book."
"The river took a guild load," Pryce says, writing. "The guild will want its mooring from the Patience at dawn. Rivers are not insured."
"The guild thanks you," says Pryce, and makes a small note.
"Yes?" Pryce turns a page.

again.again: Pryce, at his ledger.

options.text: What does Emeka Uzor's paper cost?

load.text: "Machine parts for the guild's floor at the city's Docks, sealed." He sips. "The guild carries what the guild is paid to carry. Kowal carries what the guild pays her to carry. Everybody eats." He looks at you over the cup. "The waybill is in order. The seals are the Concern's. Nobody on the river opens a Concern seal and stays on the river."
load.again: "Nobody opens a Concern seal and stays on the river."

interject.text: "Machine parts," Odile murmurs outside. "Consigned to a guild floor that does not, to my knowledge, have any machines. Somebody is buying a future, my dear, and paying for its delivery in cash."

winch.text: "Debtors on paper. The guild's paper, bought at the Ninebridge block." He turns a page. "They haul the barges up from the city on the towpath and work the winch. When the paper's paid, they walk off. Most of them." He smiles. "Breakages add a month. Things break."

emeka.text: "Uzor." He finds the page. "One month to run. Thirty Tolls, and he walks." He waits.

decision.text: I bought the last month of Emeka Uzor's paper off the guild at Low Landing.

freed.text: He writes PAID across the page and blots it. "The guild thanks you for your custom." He does not look up again.

intro.text: A broad man on the winch house's capstan bar with four others, walking it round, with an old Ninebridge brand on his wrist and the guild's tally tag on a cord at his neck. He talks without stopping walking. "Uzor. On paper." Round. "Eleven months. One to go." Round. "Don't let him put you on paper. Whatever you owe. Don't."
intro.again: Emeka, walking the capstan.

options.text: Who else has walked this capstan?

again.text: "Round," says Emeka, walking it. "Round."
again.again: Emeka, walking the capstan.

options.text: Who else has walked this capstan?

month.text: "One month for nine." He laughs, without breath. "It was two months, last month. Then a hawser broke, and that's a month. Then the lamp in the bunkhouse broke, and that's a month." Round. "Things break."

text.text: "A man from the shore. Ibarra." Round. "Two years. Never said much. Said he had a wife on the stilts and a boat called a bird's name. He walked off when his paper ran out, south, toward the sea." Round. "I heard he got home. I hope he got home."

"Everybody." Round. "Men off the block, men off the shore, a boy from the Sink who cried every night for a month and then stopped. A man from the shore, two years: Ibarra. Said he had a wife on the stilts. Walked off south when his paper ran out." Round. "They all walk off, after. If they walk."

free.text: Emeka on the quay with a sack on his shoulder and no tag at his neck, looking at the river as if he had never seen it from this side. "Thirty Tolls," he says. "That's what I was." He shakes your hand, hard. "I'm going home. Wherever that is now."
free.again: Emeka, with the sack on his shoulder.

intro.text: A grey-moustached man behind a counter of coiled rope, cans of fuel and boxes of rivets, a pencil behind each ear. "Tran. Chandler." He spreads his hands at the shop. "Rope, rings, rivets. Everything a barge forgets. And a berth on the old hulk, dry, twenty-five a week, if the guild's doss house is too lively for you."
intro.again: Bao, behind the rope.

options.text: What were the big halls behind the town?

again.text: "Rope?" says Bao hopefully.
again.again: Bao, behind the rope.

options.text: What were the big halls behind the town?

berth.text: "The old hulk at the bottom of the quay. A cabin with a bed and a locker and a stove, and the river talking all night." He holds out a key. "Twenty-five."

berthed.text: He gives you the key and goes back to his rope. "Mind the plank. Everybody falls off the plank once."

halls.text: "The campus." He says it like a word from a story. "Before the Burn there were machines in those halls that thought, my grandfather said, thousands of them, so hot they needed a river to cool them. That's why the dam. That's why the Landing: this was the campus's lower landing, where the barges brought the concrete." He shrugs. "Now it's where we keep the rain off the fuel."

interject.text: "A compute campus," Nine says, looking at the shells through the window. "Ashby Station. It is in the old record, under losses." A pause. "The record still lists its water."

b.text: "Quiet on the water," says Bryony Sedge, and that is all she will say here.

look.text: Twelve wooden cases on the Patience's deck under a guild tarp, each banded with steel and sealed with the Concern's closed eye in lead. Stencilled on the end of each: MACHINE PARTS — CONCERN — THE DOCKS. One of them ticks, very faintly, as it warms in the sun.
look.again: The twelve sealed cases.

interject.text: Kes crouches by the ticking case and puts her ear to it, and then her palm, and sits back on her heels. "Kennel boards," she says. "Concern lineage. Asleep, waiting for a dog to put them in." She looks up at you. "Obviously."

options.text: (Look closely at the tags through the slats.)

mods.why: you know a board when you see one

inside.text: The seal comes up on its wire and goes back down again as if it had never moved. Inside, in straw: boards potted in black resin with the closed eye etched on each, a tag wired to each, KENNEL and a number, and on each underside a socket shaped for something's neck.
inside.again: KENNEL, and a socket for a neck.

tags.text: Through the slats, in straw: a black resin board with a wire tag: KENNEL 3. A socket on its underside, round and deep, as if for a neck.

seal.text: The lead is thicker than it looks and the wire is braided steel. You would leave a mark, and a Concern seal with a mark on it is a story the whole river would tell.

gone.text: The Patience's deck, bare, swept, the guild's tarp folded at the stern.

text.text: The Patience, the guild's green slapped across the name on her bow, a guild padlock on her deckhouse.

The Patience: a black flat barge forty feet long with a deckhouse aft, two sweeps lashed along her sides and a stern oar as long as a tree, her name painted on the bow in faded orange by somebody who had not done much lettering. PATIENCE. Her plank has a rope rail.

look.again: The Patience.

let.text: A cabin on the old hulk at the quay's foot: a bed, a locker, a stove. Chalked on the door: BERTH — 25 — SEE TRAN.

mine.text: Your berth on the hulk: the bed, the locker, the stove ticking, and the river going by under the planks all night, talking to itself.

w.text: The guild's winch: a pre-war capstan the height of a man on the quay's edge, a cable from it out to a barge in the stream, and men on paper walking its bars round. A chalked board: HANDS WANTED — A DAY — 10 TOLLS — NO PAPER FOR DAY HANDS.
w.again: The winch, the men on paper walking it.

options.text: (Take a bar for a day. 10 Tolls.)

day.speaker: narrator
day.text: Four hours walking the capstan round with men who are not allowed to stop, the cable groaning, a barge coming in out of the stream a yard at a time. You are paid at the end in guild Tolls. They are not.

short.speaker: narrator
short.text: Your legs give out before the barge comes in, and the man on the bar behind you walks your share without a word. The guild pays you for half.
short.again: Half a day on the winch.

look.text: A notice on the quay under oilcloth, with the city's seal: AUDIT OF DELIVERY — ASHBY — ELEVEN SEASONS SHORT OF SCHEDULE. INSPECTION PENDING. BY ORDER OF THE WATER OFFICE. Under it, smaller: THE CITY REGRETS ANY INCONVENIENCE TO RIVER TRAFFIC.
look.again: The city's notice on the quay.

look.text: A milestone at the foot of the embankment road, pre-war, its face scrubbed clean by somebody: MERIDIAN 198. Under it, cut with a knife: THREE DAYS IF YOU'RE LUCKY.
look.again: MERIDIAN 198.

table.speaker: narrator

text.text: The weigher's table, the scale on it, and the board behind it with the day's runs chalked and every one of them rubbed out: nobody goes on the glass on a kite day. Hester sits with her hands flat on the table and does not look at you.

The weigher's table: a pre-war school desk with a brass scale on it, and the runs chalked on the board behind it. THE EDGE — 3 HRS. THE CRATERS — 5 HRS — IODINE. THE PANELS — KITES. KELSO — SHUT. Hester writes your name up before you go and ticks it when you come back, and weighs what you bring.

table.again: The weigher's table and its scale.

edge_1.speaker: narrator
edge_1.text: Three hours along the edge where the scrub gives up and the glass begins, turning over the fused crust with a bar: glass that will cut, glass that will sell, and the scrap of a pre-war fence that was a fence for a mile and then was not.

edge_2.speaker: narrator
edge_2.text: In a drift of black sand against a fallen pylon, a pre-war power cell in its case, the kind a lineman carried, still holding a little charge after ninety years. Hester weighs it in her hand and nods, and does not say what it is worth, because she is going to buy it.
edge_2.again: The edge, and a lineman's cell.

edge_3.speaker: narrator
edge_3.text: Under a sheet of glass you have to break with your boot heel, a wrist: a soldier's, or a farmer's, ninety years in the crust, and on it a steel watch that still ticks when you wind it. You leave the wrist where it is. Hester gives you twenty-five for the watch without looking at it, and puts it in a drawer full of them.
edge_3.again: The edge, and a watch on a wrist.

craters_1.speaker: narrator
craters_1.text: Five hours among the craters under Kelso's fence, where the strikes threw half a base across the glass: cable as thick as your arm, a junction box full of boards gone green, and the iodine taste in your mouth the whole way.

craters_2.speaker: narrator
craters_2.text: At the bottom of a dry crater, a hound's housing split open like a seed pod, and inside it, potted in resin and untouched by anything, its controller. Pristine. Worth a rifle. You carry it back against your chest as if it might wake.
craters_2.again: The craters, and a hound's controller.

craters_3.speaker: narrator
craters_3.text: A field dressing station, half in a crater, half out: its roof gone, its cabinets fused shut, all but one. Inside it, in an army tin, three phials of the old flush and a purse of pre-war coin somebody meant to come back for. Delphine takes one phial off you at once and gives you Tolls for it.
craters_3.again: The craters, and the dressing station.

panels_1.speaker: narrator
panels_1.text: Six hours among the panel rows with a screwdriver and the sky in the corner of your eye: two of the array's junction cells, cool and heavy and full, unbolted from under a row that has not felt a hand since the Burn.

panels_2.speaker: narrator
panels_2.text: A kite down between two rows where it came in to perch and missed: wings folded wrong, its housing cracked on the glass, its board inside it whole. Hester holds it up to the light for a long time. "A winter," she says. "That's a winter, that is."
panels_2.again: The panels, and a fallen kite.

panels_3.speaker: narrator
panels_3.text: The silver in the panels' backs, scraped out of a whole row's cracked cells into a tin: Hester weighs it, and weighs it again, and pays you forty, and puts the tin in the strongbox under the scale where she keeps the things that matter.

run_wage.speaker: narrator
run_wage.text: Hours on the glass, the light coming up off it into your eyes, and what the glass gives up when it has given up its best already: a little scrap, a little wire, a few Tolls from the scale. Hester ticks your name.

run_fail.speaker: narrator
run_fail.text: The glass beats you: a wrong turn among craters that all look alike, the light off the crust closing your eyes to slits, and your water half gone before you have found anything worth carrying. You come back with nothing and Hester ticks your name anyway, because you came back.

text.text: The board: names out, names ticked back, a season of them. Four names at the bottom have a line under them now and, in Hester's square chalk, DEAD AT KELSO — A CARD THEY WERE GIVEN. Somebody has put a sprig of glass-thorn on the ledge under them.
The board: names out, names ticked. The newest is KWESI, and it is not ticked, and nobody has rubbed it out, and nobody will.

The board: a sheet of pre-war blackboard bolted to the hall wall, a season of names on it in chalk, each one ticked when its picker came back off the glass. Four at the bottom are not ticked: KELSO RUN — MATEI, SUNNIVA, OLU, DRAGOS — DUE BACK, and a date in the spring. Under them, newer: KELSO — SHUT — H.K.

look.again: The board, and the names on it.

intro.text: A tall woman in a re-dyed army jacket at the school's scale, her grey hair cropped to the skull, her forearms tight with old burn scars, reading your boots before your face. "New." Not a question. "I'm Hester. I weigh. If you go on the glass you put your name on the board first, and you come back and I tick it, and I buy what you bring at a fair weight. If you don't come back I don't come looking. Nobody does."
intro.again: Hester, at the scale.

interject.text: "Nobody comes looking," Tamsin says, very quietly, after. "She said that like it was the rules for a game."
"Fair woman," Wren says. "Scared of something. Look at her hands on that scale."

text.text: Hester at the scale with her hands flat on the table. She does not weigh anything. "The flag's up," she says. "He went to the panels at dawn."
Hester at the scale. She weighs what she is given and ticks what she is told and does not look up at anyone she does not have to, and least at you.
Hester at the scale, and her grandson on a crate by the stove pretending he is not listening. "Name on the board?" she says to you, and almost smiles.
"Weighing, or asking?" Hester does not stop sorting glass.

hub.again: Hester waits.

options.text: Four names on your board aren't ticked.
Who's the man in the clean coat?
Kwesi didn't go to the panels for cells. Your lodger paid him to map the kites.
Your four died at Kelso because of a card your lodger gave their guide.
Your four at Kelso died because of a card the Concern's man gave their guide.
I've an army board out of Kelso's shed. Is it worth anything here?

four.text: "Matei, Sunniva, Olu, Dragos." She does not look at the board. "Kelso, in the spring. The base on the March, a day east. Old army. Old boards, old chrome, if you can get at it. Matei had a way in, he said." She puts a piece of glass on the scale and takes it off again. "Parveen went with them and came back. Ask her. She won't tell you. Then I shut Kelso, and nobody's been since but the man in the clean coat, and he only goes as far as the gate."

interject.text: Ilya is looking at the board, counting. "Four out, one back," he says. "That's not the glass. The glass takes one at a time."

sorlie.text: "Sorlie. The Concern's." She says it the way people here say glass. "Contract man, up from the Skirts with paper. Pays double for the east room and doesn't eat with us. Wants a guide into Kelso, pays three hundred. Matei's card was his." She looks at you for the first time properly. "I took his money for the room. I'm not proud. We had a thin winter."
sorlie.again: "I took his money for the room."

interject.text: "A contract man in the Ashlands with a card," Kes says. "Obviously he's not after old chrome." She rubs her neck without noticing.

kite.text: She speaks to the scale, not to you. "Pemberton. The panels. He wanted cells; he's sixteen; he wants everything. He went before light, and Ingmar ran the flag up at nine." Her hands stay flat. "You don't go out on a kite day. That's the law here. It's the only one I keep."
kite.again: "You don't go out on a kite day."

interject.text: "I'm going," Tamsin says, to you, not to her. "You're going. Aren't we."
Ash has his hat in his hands. "Sixteen," he says. "I'll carry him if he can't walk."

out.text: She hears you out. Then she gets up from the scale, which you have not seen her do, and walks to the east room, and you hear her voice through the wall, low, the whole of it said once and not repeated. When she comes back she sits down and picks up a piece of glass. "He's going," she says. "He can camp at Kelso's gate with his card and see who comes to him there." Then she goes to the board and chalks under the four names, and her hand is steady.

chalk.text: She goes to the board and chalks under the four names, DEAD AT KELSO — A CARD THEY WERE GIVEN, and stands looking at it. "He's gone, your clean coat," she says. "Gone or going. It doesn't bring them back. It goes on the board."

glass.text: "The March." She means the plateau. "The old border. The army kept it with machines, and when the war came the other side burned it flat and the machines with it, most of them. What burned is glass. What didn't is still out there doing what it was told." She weighs a shard. "We pick what the glass gives up. It gives up boards and cells and old chrome off the dead, and it gives up people who get greedy. I weigh both."

interject.text: "The March Command," Nine says. "It was in the city's defence schedule before the Burn: the eastern belt, contracted out. The record says it was decommissioned." A pause. "The record is wrong about some things."

pump.text: She turns it in her hands, and her face does something you have not seen it do. "Army. Before the Scald. Nobody in it." She sets it down very gently. "Our well's pump has run on a cracked board for twelve years, and every season it drinks a little more of what it brings up. With that in it, the water comes up clean." She looks at you. "Sixty Tolls, and the east room's yours free as long as I keep it. That's what I can give. It's worth more to anyone with a rail."
pump.again: "It's worth more to anyone with a rail."

decision.text: I gave the army board out of Kelso's shed to Spindle's well pump. The water there comes up clean.

news.text: Spindle's well runs clean on an old army board a stranger brought in off the glass

pumped.text: She has the pump's housing open before you have finished speaking, and an hour later the well's handle is going up and down under a child's hands, and what comes out of the spout is clear. Hester fills a tin cup and drinks it standing, all of it, and then sits down at the scale as if nothing has happened.

intro.text: A boy of sixteen on a cot in the west room with a sheet of glass across his knees, scratching on it with a nail. He hides the glass as you come. "Have you been out? Out far? Kelso, or the panels?" He does not wait. "Gran says I can do the edge when I'm seventeen. The edge is for babies. There's nothing on the edge."
intro.again: Kwesi, with his sheet of glass.

again.text: "Have you been to the panels yet?" Kwesi asks, as if the question had been waiting all day.
again.again: Kwesi waits.

drawing.text: "Nothing." It is lines: rows, and loops over the rows. "Birds." He puts it under the cot. "Gran says don't go on about the panels."

text.text: Kwesi, with the shaking gone out of him and something else come in instead. "You shot them," he says. "Two. Out of the sky. Nobody does that." He looks east. "Gran says something will have counted."

Kwesi on a crate by the stove, not drawing anything. "He gave me a coin," he says, before you ask. "The clean man. For the turns. How they fly round. I didn't know what for." He looks at his hands. "I still don't."

Kwesi's cot. Under it, a sheet of glass scratched with a nail: Pemberton's rows, and over them the turns the kites fly, loop after loop, every one dated, a month of mornings. And wedged into the cot's frame where a boy hides what matters, a coin that is not a Toll: white metal, the closed eye on one side, a number on the other. Concern scrip.
A cot in the west room, a blanket folded square, and under it the edge of a sheet of glass.

look.again: Kwesi's cot.

options.text: (Look at the glass and the coin.)

seen.text: A month of kite turns over Pemberton, careful, in a boy's hand; and a coin a contractor pays with when he wants a thing done that he will not do himself.

interject.text: "Scrip." Kes turns the coin over. "They pay the Skirts in this. Nobody up the hill would pay a boy for bird pictures." She looks east. "They want to know how the kites guard something."

intro.text: A big man at the foot of the tower with a pre-war spotting scope slung on his back and his eyes red-rimmed from the glass light. "Lund. I watch the sky." He jerks his head up at the pole with its folded black square. "When I see a kite I run the flag, and everybody goes in, and nobody argues. That's all I do. It's enough."
intro.again: Ingmar, at the tower's foot.

text.text: Ingmar at the tower's foot with the scope at his eye, pointed south-east at nothing you can see. "Three up," he says. "Over the panels. Working the rows."
Ingmar sits at the tower's foot with the scope across his knees and nothing to point it at. "Came down one at a time," he says. "Like birds that forgot how. I don't know what to do with my days."
Ingmar has the scope on the horizon. "Clear," he says. "For now."

hub.again: Ingmar, with the scope.

options.text: Where do they go at dusk?

kites.text: "Army machines. Wings like a gull and a lens underneath." He does not take his eye from the scope. "They fly on the sun. All day they quarter the glass and anything that moves on it they stoop at, and they don't miss twice. At dusk they go down to the panels at Pemberton and sit on poles at the ends of the rows, and drink." He lowers the scope at last. "Something there still feeds them. Ninety years. A hut that hums."

interject.text: "What they stoop at," Ilya says. "Movement or heat?" Ingmar looks at him with new respect. "Movement. Heat close up." Ilya nods. "Then you don't move."

east.text: "The ones that don't sit at Pemberton go east, past Kelso, to a ridge we call Saddleback, and over it, and down." He shrugs. "Nobody's been over Saddleback and come back to say. There's a valley. They circle it the way a dog circles a sheep it's minding." He points with the scope. "Take the track east out of Kelso if you want to look. Lie down at the top. Don't stand up against the sky."

boy.text: He is quiet a long time. "They're working the rows, not the hut. He'll be in the hut if he's got sense; it's the only roof out there. At dusk they go down to drink, and then there's an hour of dark before the moon when nothing up there can see much." He hands you nothing, says nothing about going. "Hester won't ask you. She can't."

intro.text: A woman in a canvas apron in a scrap shack that smells of vinegar and iodine, washing a picker's eyes out with a squeeze bottle. "Arcand. Doctor, near enough." She does not stop. "Show me your hands. Show me your eyes. Iodine before you go out, flush after you come back if you were long in the craters, and don't look at the glass at noon. That's all the medicine there is, out here."
intro.again: Delphine, with the squeeze bottle.

hub.text: "Hands," Delphine says, by way of hello, and looks at yours.
hub.again: Delphine waits.

options.text: Parveen Rao. What happened to her hands?
What does the glass do to people?

parveen.text: "Glass." She sets the bottle down. "She came back across the apron at Kelso on her hands and knees in the noon light, a mile of it, because her legs had stopped. The palms are healing. The rest of her isn't." She looks out of the door to where Parveen sits by the fire. "She won't let me dress them any more. Bring her something for them yourself and she might talk to you. I'm the one who told her they'd heal, and she's angry at me for it."

interject.text: Ash says nothing until you are outside. "Angry at the one who says it'll heal." He nods slowly. "That's the right person to be angry at. It's the only one who'll stay."

sealed_nine.text: Nine stands before the rack the way a clerk stands before a bench. "Unit to unit," it says. "Standing order: await lawful command. meet.text: A picker hauling a laden sled by a harness across his chest, two more behind him with their goggles up and their scarves at their throats. He stops when he sees you, and counts you, and relaxes. "Spindle's that way," he says. "Names on the board?"

text.text: "Empty sky." He shakes his head, still not believing it. "We walked the panels at noon. At noon. My father never once in his life." Then, quieter: "Somebody'll come. Something that big doesn't stay open long."
"Bad," he says. "Kelso's three walked off the apron after the bang. Nobody knows where. We see one on a ridge sometimes, just standing." He tightens the harness. "They don't keep to anything now."
"Kites over the panels, the three at Kelso walking nights, the craters hot as ever." He shrugs. "Same as my father's day. Same as his. The glass doesn't change. You do, or it has you."

word.text: Chela Ortega at the lane's west end with her rifle across her knees and West Halt's watch spread along the hedge behind her. "The halts got fed when nobody else would feed us," she says. "Openfield took the twelve and asked nothing. So." She shrugs. "Nobody hurt, if we can help it. That's still my rule."

interject.text: "Not raiders," Wren says to you, watching the watch settle along the hedge. "Told you. Raiders don't sweep the brass."

word.text: Yaw Boateng sits on the store's step among the Choir's old ones with his hands in his lap, the way they sit. "They walked us here in the night when we were paper," he says. "I can sit in front of a door for them. It's not hard. It's just long."

Desmond Achebe with his cap lamp off and six of Number Four's miners at his back on the green. "No paper past the cage," he says. "Four said it. Four meant it. Here's Four." He looks at the guild's wagons. "They paid us double for tin for fifteen winters. We know what their paper is worth."

interject.text: Kes grips Desmond's arm. "You came down off the mountain for farmers," she says. "Obviously you did. Obviously."

word.text: Maren Okafor herself, off the Line with the Shift's committee, coughing into a rag and folding it. "We go up together," she says. "This is up. A store of seed and some people who won't be moved off it." She puts her hand flat on the store's door, the way she puts it on a table when she has decided. "I know what a lockout looks like."

interject.text: "You came," Kes says. She cannot say anything else. Maren puts a hand on the back of her neck, over the place, and leaves it there.

word.text: Rafe Ansel behind the lane's hedge with the Shift's armed, the Lodge's powder in their packs. "Maren's way is to sit," he says. "Mine isn't. I say what I'll do and then I do it." He checks a fuse. "If they ride at the old ones, I'll do it."

Vasha Kade at the head of her riders, sitting her bike like a judge. "It's written," she says, of the store, of the night, of all of it, and smiles. "Somebody holds the pen. Tonight it's whoever has the most rifles on the lane."

interject.text: Ilya does not speak to her. He looks at her for a long time over the bike's bars, and then he walks away, and his hands are steady, and that is the frightening part.

intro.text: Elder Mason on a bench in front of the seed store's door with his hands on his knees and his hat on the bench beside him, the way a man sits who means to be there all night. Behind him the guild's notice is nailed over the Choir's tally board, and across the green the city's order is nailed to the well. "You came." He does not get up. "The sky keeps no books. The guild does, and the city does, and both of them have written this store down as theirs, on the same night."
intro.again: Mason on the bench before the store.

interject.text: Ash takes his hat off and stands by the bench, and says nothing at all, and Mason puts a hand on his arm without looking up.
"They want the seed," Tamsin says, very low, to you. "The guild and the city. The same seed. And these people want to sit in front of it."

hub.again: Mason waits on the bench.

options.text: What will you do when they come?
Where did the guild get a claim on your harvest?
What if they all sat at one table?

news.text: a stranger has said they will stand at Openfield's store with the Choir when the guild and the city come for it

decision.text: I stood with the Choir for Openfield's Long Night: the store, the people and the fields against the guild's paper and the city's order.

plan.text: "Sit." He means it exactly. "In front of the door, all of us, the old ones in front. We will not fight for seed. Seed is for planting, not for killing over." He looks across at the lane, where the guild's lamps are. "Petra will not sit. Some of the young ones will not. I cannot make them. I have tried for nine years." His voice does not change. "The city's paper says Openfield burns tonight. I have read it. I would rather it burned with us sitting than with us shooting."
plan.again: "I would rather it burned with us sitting."

interject.text: Ilya looks at the lane, and the riders' lamps, and the bench. "Sitting," he says. "I've seen men ride through sitting people." He does not say what he did about it.

text.text: "The guild's paper is on six crates of seed that will grow nothing." He almost smiles. "They bought chaff at a future's price, and now they want the real thing for it. You were there. You know what they hold is a lie we sold them."

"Ishan sold a crate a night to the guild's hand, and their factor wrote each crate down as a share of this harvest. The boy keeps the yard. The guild keeps the paper." He looks at the store. "The paper is what they came for."
"Seed walked out of here all season and somebody took a tenth of it." He does not look at you. "The guild wrote every crate down as a share of this harvest. I do not know who else wrote it down."

"The Choir's children sold the harvest forward, a crate at a time, to a guild hand on the lane who paid twelve Tolls and wrote each one down as a share. Now the shares fall due, all at once, on one night, and the guild's riders are here to collect."

paper.again: The guild's shares on the harvest.

petra.text: "My daughter keeps no likeness and has her own night planned." He turns his hat over on the bench. "The Grand Factor of the guild is sleeping on our lane tonight, in a wagon, and is on the city's list as its Treasurer. Petra has read that list too." He is quiet. "Ask her. I do not. If I ask, she will tell me, and then I will have to choose between her and what I believe, tonight, and I am too old to do it well."

calla.text: "The order's first name." He closes his eyes. "She came from Shale to sit with us. They read her name off the paper at the well and took her to the Line before she had put her bag down. A warden car, west." He opens them. "I will not ask you to go after her. I will tell you that the Line is not the guild's everywhere, and that the halts have their own rules about which trains move."
calla.again: "The Line is not the guild's everywhere."

table.text: "The common hall has a table forty feet long." He considers it, honestly. "They would not sit at it for me. They might for someone each of them owed. A guild factor sits for a debt. A warden captain sits for a lawful reason. Petra sits for nobody." He looks at you. "If you can make all three of them owe you on one night, you are a more dangerous person than I took you for."
table.again: "A more dangerous person than I took you for."

pledge.text: He looks at you for a long time. Then he picks his hat up off the bench and puts it down on the other side of him, leaving the place next to him empty. "At dusk, then," he says. "Whoever comes, comes. Sit with us, or stand at the lane, or go where you are needed. The sky does not mind which."

interject.text: Ash sits down in the hat's place on the bench, slowly, like a man getting into cold water. "Then I'll be here," he says. "At the door. Not first. Never first."
Tamsin lets out a breath. "Good," she says. "Good. I didn't want to have to argue with you."
"The Dogs'll come if they're asked," Wren says. "Some of them. They hate a rider more than they hate a farmer." She grins. "That's what passes for love, with us."
"The city will call its units in tonight," Nine says. "I will answer. I will be on the other side of the lane. Lawfully." It pauses. "I will be careful whom I count."

"The city will call its units in tonight," Nine says. "I will answer, and I will read its order aloud at the well, and I will log every line of it that cannot be made lawful as an error." It looks at the store. "There will be several."
"You'll starve the Precinct a winter," Odile says, not unkindly. "My dear, I approve. I just want you to know you're doing it."

text.text: Mason at the store's door, his hat in his hands, looking at what the night left.
"At dusk," Mason says. "Whoever comes."
"A table forty feet long," Mason says, "and all of them at it." He shakes his head slowly. "I do not know whether to thank you or pray for you. The sky does not need either."
Mason on the bench, with the place beside him empty. He looks at you, and away. "Go and stand with them, then," he says. "We will sit."

intro.text: Petra at the sky-shrine's fire with her scarf at her throat and her back to the green, the way a person sits who does not want to be counted. She does not look round. "You came for the store," she says. "Everyone came for the store. My father is going to sit in front of it and let them have it gently." She feeds the fire a stick. "The guild's Grand Factor is sleeping on our lane tonight. She is on the city's list. Treasurer. Did you know?"
intro.again: Petra at the shrine's fire.

text.text: Petra at the fire, her knife in its sheath on the stone beside her, where you can see it. "I said I wouldn't," she says. "I keep what I say. It's the only thing I keep."
Petra at the shrine's cold fire. She does not look up.
"Well?" Petra feeds the fire.

hub.again: Petra waits.

options.text: What do you mean to do about the Grand Factor?
Don't. Sarr dead won't save one seed, and the city will have its reason to burn you.

mods.why: Ash stands beside you and has refused his own orders
you are a sister or brother of the Open Sky
her father would not ask her, and you did
you brought Calla back without a knife

decision.text: I talked Petra Mason out of the knife she meant for the guild's Grand Factor on the Long Night.

options.text: Do what you have to. I won't stand in your way.

knife.text: "The city wrote her down as its Treasurer. Tolls on schedule. The Plan needs her alive and counting." Petra turns the stick in the fire. "The Unwritten break what the Plan needs. Some of us with words. Tonight, some of us with a knife, on the lane, in the small hours, while my father sits with his hands in his lap." She looks at you for the first time. "The sky keeps no books. Somebody has to tear the pages out of theirs."
knife.again: "Somebody has to tear the pages out of theirs."

interject.text: Ash has gone very still. "I burned my letter, Petra," he says. "I'm not burning anybody else's."
Ash says nothing. He is looking at the lane, and at the guild's wagons, and his face is the face of a man doing a sum.
Odile's hand has closed on Petra's wrist before anyone sees her move. "That is my student," she says, very pleasantly. "That is the price I told you about, my dear. Don't make me pay it."

down.text: She is quiet a long time. Then she takes the knife off her belt, sheath and all, and lays it on the shrine's stone where anyone can see it, and sits back. "Not tonight," she says. "Not because you're right. Because if I'm wrong my father burns for it, and if you're wrong it's only you."
down.again: The knife on the shrine's stone.

down_no.text: "No." Not angry. "You came here with the city's face on a paper in your pack. You don't get to tell me what the Plan needs."

yes.text: "I didn't ask your leave." But she nods, once, the way Unwritten nod to each other on a road. "Stay off the lane in the small hours."
yes.again: "Stay off the lane in the small hours."

intro.text: Imelda Sarr, the Grand Factor of the guild, on a folding chair in the lee of three wagons on Openfield's lane with a rug over her knees and a clock open on her lap, its back off, its works in the lamplight. She does not get up; she never gets up. "The harvest's shares fall due tonight," she says. "Every one of them signed. I came to collect in person because I wanted to see the Elder's face when I did." She closes the clock. "And because the city has nailed a paper to his well that says it is all theirs. Not at that price."
intro.again: Sarr, on her folding chair, with the clock.

interject.text: Odile stops at the wagons' edge. "Imelda." "Odile." Neither says anything else for a moment; it is a long moment. Then Sarr says, "You look well, for a woman who left," and Odile says, "You look rich, for a woman who stayed," and both of them almost smile.

text.text: Sarr, packing her clock into its case.
"Ask," Sarr says, "and I will tell you the price."

hub.again: Sarr waits.

options.text: What do I get, standing with you?
Someone means to put a knife in you tonight, on this lane.

news.text: a stranger has signed on with the guild's riders for Openfield's harvest

decision.text: I stood with the guild and the Concern for Openfield's Long Night: their contracts honoured, the store theirs, and the city kept off it.

text.text: "Six crates of chaff, sold to my hand at a future's price, and every crate written down as a share of this year's seed." She does not raise her voice. "I do not mind being cheated. I mind being cheated by people who pray. The shares stand. I will take good seed for them, or I will take the store."

"Shares in this harvest, bought a crate at a time from the Choir's children by my hand on the lane, paid in coin, signed, witnessed. A contract." She folds her hands on the clock. "The city's Ledger cannot void a lawful contract. It has tried, in its fashion: it has nailed up an order that says the store is the Precinct's. Tonight we find out which paper the glass believes."

offer.text: "Two hundred and fifty Tolls, tonight, as a factor's fee. The guild's gratitude, which is worth more and is rarer." She tilts her head at the next wagon, where a man in a clean coat sits writing. "The Concern's man will tell you what Halcyon offers the Choir's people: contracts, terraces, a roof. Order, on the Flats, for once." She opens the clock again. "And the city goes home with its paper. I am told you have reasons to want that."

interject.text: "Contracts," Kes says. "Terraces. A roof." She touches her neck. "And the thing in your neck that comes with the roof. Ask him about that."

warned.text: She is not surprised. That is the worst of it. "I have known since the docket," she says. "The city wrote me down as its Treasurer forty years before I was one, and the Choir's hard children read the same list." She winds the clock, three turns. "Thank you. It is a debt. I pay my debts." She looks at you over it. "I will not sleep on the lane."
warned.again: "I will not sleep on the lane."

interject.text: Odile lets out a breath you did not know she had been holding. "Imelda," she says, "for once in your life, do as you're told."

pledge.text: She counts two hundred and fifty onto the rug from a purse that does not get lighter, and pushes it toward you with one finger. "Good," she says. "At dusk the riders take the lane. At midnight the city will try its paper on the store, and the Elder's daughter will try something worse. Be where I need you." She closes the clock. "Not at that price, I said, to the city. To you, at this one."

interject.text: Wren looks at the riders, and at the Tolls on the rug, and at you. "I'll see this night out," she says. "Because I said I'd walk with you. Then I'm gone." She does not raise her voice either.
Kes has gone white. "You've handed them the Flats," she says. "Obviously you know that. I'll stay till it's light. Don't talk to me."
Ash turns his hat in his hands. "Then tomorrow I'll be at the store door," he says, "on the other side of you." He walks away down the lane toward the green.
"She rides with them," Ilya says. He does not need to say who. "You know that. You've put me on her side of the lane." He checks his rifle's bolt twice.
"Well," Odile says, "Imelda always paid on the nail." She pockets nothing; it is your money. "My dear, I hope you know what the nail is."

text.text: Lucien Roux, the Concern's bond officer from Carrick, at a camp desk in the next wagon, in a clean coat, writing. He recognises you and finishes his line before he looks up. "The weighbridge," he says. "Every box to the plate, now. That was you." No heat in it. "The Concern backs the guild tonight. It also remembers."

A man in a clean coat at a camp desk in the next wagon along, writing in a ledger by a hooded lamp: Lucien Roux, the Concern's bond officer from Carrick. He sees you, and for the first time since you have known him he stands up before he has finished the line. "Designate. The Board wrote that you had taken its seat." He offers his hand, and holds yours a moment longer than a hand needs. "Then tonight we are on the same side of a fence, whichever side of it you stand on. You will forgive me for hoping it is ours."

A man in a clean coat at a camp desk in the next wagon along, writing in a ledger by a hooded lamp: Lucien Roux, the Concern's bond officer from Carrick. He finishes his line before he looks up, and then he looks at you for exactly as long as the lens over Director Soto's door did. "Designate. The Board writes that you have a seat in waiting." He sets the pen down. "Director Soto writes separately, as she always does."

A man in a clean coat at a camp desk in the next wagon along, writing in a ledger by a hooded lamp: Lucien Roux, the Concern's bond officer from Carrick. He finishes his line before he looks up. "Designate. The Board writes that you declined its seat." No heat in it. "It is noted. It is not held against you. Tonight is a farm, not a chair."

A man in a clean coat at a camp desk in the next wagon along, writing in a ledger by a hooded lamp: Lucien Roux, the Concern's bond officer from Carrick, here because the guild's claim on Openfield's seed is underwritten by Halcyon. He finishes his line before he looks up. "Good evening. The Concern backs the guild's claim. I am here to see it honoured."

intro.again: Roux, at the camp desk.

options.text: Why does the Concern want seed?

hub.text: "Yes?" Roux keeps his pen on the line.
hub.again: Roux waits, pen on the line.

options.text: Why does the Concern want seed?
What have you brought for the night?

news.text: a stranger has signed on with the guild's riders for Openfield's harvest

decision.text: I stood with the guild and the Concern for Openfield's Long Night: their contracts honoured, the store theirs, and the city kept off it.

vault.text: "Halcyon keeps a seed vault under its gardens: every grain line the old world bred, held cold. Openfield's seed is ninety years of the glass selecting what will grow in it. There is nothing like it anywhere." He sets the pen down at last. "In a timber shed it will rot, or burn, or go to the Precinct's ration bins. In the vault it will outlast all of us. That is not a threat. It is the best argument I have, and it happens to be true."

interject.text: "Kept cold under a mountain where nobody can plant it," Tamsin says. "Like the Cistern." She looks at Roux. "We were kept too. Ask us how that went."

people.text: "Contracts." He says it as a kindness. "Terraces on the Teeth, rooms, rations, a clinic. The Concern takes anyone who signs. A farmer who can grow in glass is worth a great deal to us." He pauses. "Chrome, for those who want it. It is better chrome than anyone else's. It does come with terms of service. Everything does."
people.again: "It does come with terms of service."

interject.text: Kes laughs, short and ugly. "Terms of service," she says. "Ask me what's in mine."

text.text: "Kennel Seven's first pack walked west out of the Ashlands four days ago." He says it as a man reads a delivery note. "Recovered thanks to you, I believe. They will be on the lane by dusk. I would ask your friends not to run from them."

"Kennel boards, delivered to the guild's floor at Carrick by barge this season, and the units they speak to." He nods toward the dark beyond the wagons, where something on four legs is sitting very still. "A few. Enough to keep a lane."

"Riders. Rifles. Paper." He looks at you a moment longer than he needs to. "There was to be more. A reserve in the Ashlands we expected to recover this season. Somebody sealed it against us." He picks the pen up. "We noticed."
"The guild's riders and the guild's paper. The Concern does not bring its own people to a farm." He picks the pen up. "Unless it has to."

"Is a seat at the table that decides what the Reach eats in ten years." He turns the ledger so you can see a page already written in his clean hand: your name under the Board's, and a date left blank. "Tonight is not that day. Tonight the guild holds a farm's seed on paper and the Concern underwrites the paper. If you stand with the guild, the Board will hear it was done by one of its own." He lets that sit. "If you do not, it will hear that too, and it will not be surprised. A seat is not a leash. Not yet."

"A seat in waiting." He says it as if tasting it. "Director Soto believes about half of what she is told and writes down all of it. She wrote that you were very gracious." He meets your eye. "Whatever you meant on the hill, tonight is a farm. If you meant it, stand with the guild. If you did not, I will know by morning, and so will she, and the seat will still be waiting. The Board never withdraws an offer. It lets it cost more."

"Was declined." He nods, as if confirming an entry. "The Board never withdraws an offer; it lets it cost more. You will hear from it again, at a worse price, on the day you take the sash." He closes the ledger. "Tonight I am only a man who underwrites a farmer's debt, and you are only someone standing between me and the farm. That is a simpler thing, and I prefer it."

seat.again: What the Board's seat means tonight.

interject.text: Kes has gone very still at your shoulder. "He means it kindly," she says afterward, low. "That's the bit that gets you. They always mean it kindly."

pledged.text: Roux writes a line, blots it, and turns the ledger so you can see your name in it in a clean hand under the day's date. "The Concern remembers its friends," he says, "in writing." Two wagons down, Sarr's purse comes open.
pledged.again: Your name in the Concern's ledger.

post.text: A post by Openfield's well where the Choir pins its notices: a call for hands at harvest, a child's drawing of the sky, nothing that wants anything of you.

text.text: The city's order, in a clerk's square hand under the Ledger's seal, nailed to Openfield's well post: THE HOLDING KNOWN AS OPENFIELD IS RETURNED TO THE SCHEDULE. CLAIMS UPON ITS STORES BY ANY PARTY ARE VOID AGAINST THE CITY. STORES: TO PRECINCT SUPPLY. PERSONS: AS THE RECORD HOLDS, SAVE THAT ANY PERSON STANDING AT THE READING MAY BE ENTERED LIVING AND HEARD (COURT OF ACCOUNTS, R30: THE RECORD YIELDS TO A LIVING PERSON). FIRST NAME TO BE READ: CALLA, SISTER, OF SHALE — SEDITION. And under it, the date the order takes effect, which is tonight's.

The city's order, in a clerk's square hand under the Ledger's seal, nailed to Openfield's well post: THE HOLDING KNOWN AS OPENFIELD IS RETURNED TO THE SCHEDULE. CLAIMS UPON ITS STORES BY ANY PARTY ARE VOID AGAINST THE CITY. STORES: TO PRECINCT SUPPLY. PERSONS: THE RECORD DOES NOT HOLD THE OCCUPIERS (UNRECORDED).
