And under it, the date the order takes effect, which is tonight's.

The city's order, in a clerk's square hand under the Ledger's seal, nailed to Openfield's well post: THE HOLDING KNOWN AS OPENFIELD IS RETURNED TO THE SCHEDULE. CLAIMS UPON ITS STORES BY ANY PARTY ARE VOID AGAINST THE CITY. STORES: TO PRECINCT SUPPLY. PERSONS: OCCUPIERS UNRECORDED; REMOVED WITH THE HOLDING'S CONTENTS AS PROPERTY (COURT OF ACCOUNTS, R30) TO PRECINCT LABOUR. FIRST NAME TO BE READ: CALLA, SISTER, OF SHALE — SEDITION. And under it, the date the order takes effect, which is tonight's.

The city's order, in a clerk's square hand under the Ledger's seal, nailed to Openfield's well post: THE HOLDING KNOWN AS OPENFIELD IS RETURNED TO THE SCHEDULE. CLAIMS UPON ITS STORES BY ANY PARTY ARE VOID AGAINST THE CITY. STORES: TO PRECINCT SUPPLY. PERSONS: AS THE RECORD HOLDS. RELOCATION ON SCHEDULE. FIRST NAME TO BE READ: CALLA, SISTER, OF SHALE — SEDITION. And under it, the date the order takes effect, which is tonight's.

order.again: The city's order on the well post.

interject.text: Nine reads it twice, the way it reads a form it has been asked to sign. "Claims by any party void against the city," it says. "That clause cannot void a lawful contract. It can only say so." It touches the seal. "The Precinct's clerks know that. They wrote it anyway, because the schedule says Openfield burns tonight, and a paper that says so makes it easier."
"Relocation on schedule," Tamsin reads. Her voice has gone thin. "That's the word. That's the word MOTHER said no to. Three times."

copied.text: You copy it out on the back of something, every word, the seal drawn as a circle.

text.text: The seed store's door, charred to its frame, and the tally board beside it burned to a black square. Somebody has chalked on the stone of the step, in a child's hand: WE SAT.
The seed store's door with a new lock on it and the guild's half-moon branded into the wood, and under it a Concern stencil: PROPERTY OF HALCYON SEED VAULT — CONSIGNED.
The seed store's door under the city's seal, a strip of grey paper across the jamb: STORES TO PRECINCT SUPPLY — EMPTIED — R30. The store is empty. So is the green.

The seed store's door with three marks on it in three hands: the guild's half-moon, the city's seal, and a circle for the sky. Under them a tally of thirds, kept by Doria, checked by a clerk and countersigned by a factor's hand.
The seed store's door, scorched along its foot where the fire got that far and no further, and the Choir's tally board back over the guild's notice. COUNTED AT DUSK. COUNTED AT DAWN.

The guild's notice, nailed over the Choir's tally board on the seed store's door: SHARES IN THE OPENFIELD HARVEST FALL DUE THIS NIGHT. CLAIMED UNDER CONTRACT, GUILD OF TOLLS. I. SARR, GRAND FACTOR. Somebody has written under it in pencil, very small: THE SKY KEEPS NO BOOKS.
The seed store's tally board on its door: COUNTED AT DUSK. COUNTED AT DAWN. Doria's marks, every day of the season.

look.again: The seed store's door.

read.text: Under the notice, pinned behind it, a sheaf of the guild's chits: OPENFIELD — ONE CRATE — ONE SHARE — 12 T — witnessed by the guild's hand on the lane, a season of them. Every one of them a child of the Choir's name, signed.
read.again: The guild's chits.

text.text: Captain Idris Lowe of the Precinct's wardens by Openfield's well, in grey, with the order's copy in a case at his hip. He straightens when he sees you, which he has never done before. "Designate." He does not like saying it. He says it. "The schedule holds. Tonight it holds here. I would rather it held with your hand on the paper than mine."

Captain Idris Lowe of the Precinct's wardens by Openfield's well, in grey, a long way from the city, with the order's copy in a case at his hip and three wardens at the lane's west end. He looks tired in the way of a man who has carried out a great many lawful things. "The schedule holds," he says. "Tonight it holds here. I am not going to pretend to you that I like it."

intro.again: Lowe, by the well.

interject.text: "Captain." "Unit nine." Lowe looks at it a long moment. "You were called in." "I was," Nine says. "I am here." Neither of them says on which side.

options.text: Tell me what the city wants.

"PERSONS: AS THE RECORD HOLDS, SAVE THAT ANY PERSON STANDING AT THE READING MAY BE ENTERED LIVING AND HEARD (COURT OF ACCOUNTS, R30: THE RECORD YIELDS TO A LIVING PERSON)." He folds it. "And the first name to be read. You know whose."

He takes the copy out of its case and reads it to you in full, the way he would read it to the holding, without leaving a word out: the holding returned to the schedule, every claim on its stores void against the city, the stores to Precinct supply. "PERSONS: THE RECORD DOES NOT HOLD THE OCCUPIERS (UNRECORDED). THE CITY CAN NEITHER MOVE NOR SHELTER THEM (COURT OF ACCOUNTS, R30). THEY REMAIN ON THE HOLDING WITHOUT STORES." He folds it. "And the first name to be read. You know whose."

He takes the copy out of its case and reads it to you in full, the way he would read it to the holding, without leaving a word out: the holding returned to the schedule, every claim on its stores void against the city, the stores to Precinct supply. "PERSONS: OCCUPIERS UNRECORDED; REMOVED WITH THE HOLDING'S CONTENTS AS PROPERTY (COURT OF ACCOUNTS, R30) TO PRECINCT LABOUR." He folds it. "And the first name to be read. You know whose."

He takes the copy out of its case and reads it to you in full, the way he would read it to the holding, without leaving a word out: the holding returned to the schedule, every claim on its stores void against the city, the stores to Precinct supply. "PERSONS: AS THE RECORD HOLDS. RELOCATION ON SCHEDULE." He folds it. "And the first name to be read. You know whose."
"She is on the Court of Accounts' docket. Sedition, listed." He does not look away. "You have seen the docket. The order reads the docket's names first, wherever they are found. She was found here."

"The record holds a sedition docket in her name. The order reads the docket's names first, wherever they are found." He does not look away. "She was found here. She is on her way to the city to be heard."

calla.again: "She is on her way to the city to be heard."

text.text: "Bread." He says it plainly. "The Sink kept its pumps this spring and the Precinct's supply came in short, and it will be short again this winter. The schedule makes the shortfall good from the Flats, from this store. Without it the Precinct rations by the spring, and you have seen what the Precinct does when it rations." He breathes out. "I will not tell you the Sink should have drowned. I will tell you there is a bill, and this is where it is sent."

"Water and bread. The city's plan was recomputed on a smaller lake this season, and the Precinct's growth with it. The schedule makes up the difference here." He looks at the store. "Somebody told the truth about a dam. This is what the truth costs, on paper."

"The Precinct eats this winter." He says it as if he has said it to himself many times. "The schedule writes Openfield's stores into the Precinct's supply, and the guild off the Flats with them. Order, and bread, for four hundred thousand people inside the Wall." He looks at the Choir on the green. "And these people somewhere else. The schedule holds."

why.again: "The schedule holds."

text.text: He hands you the order's copy out of its case, and does not let go of it for a moment. "Then you read it," he says. "At the well, when it is time. It is better coming from you." He lets go. "Designate."

He nods once, the nod of a man whose night has become slightly easier and much worse. "At dusk the line forms at the west end. At midnight the order is read at the well. The guild will contest it. So will the Elder's daughter." He looks at you. "Be at the well."

interject.text: "This is what they'd do to the Cistern," Tamsin says. She is not shouting; it is worse. "Exactly this. A paper on the door and a captain who doesn't like it." She walks away from you across the green.
Ash looks at you for a long time. "I'll see it," he says. "I owe them that. I owe you nothing after."
"I will stand at the well with you," Nine says. "And when the order is read, I will log every line of it that cannot be made lawful. Aloud." It does not look at Lowe. "That is what I am for."
"Then we will make it lawful," Nine says, "line by line, and I will log what could not be softened." It sounds, for once, very old.
"The city," Wren says. She has her goggles down. "The rope's city." She does not say anything else, and does not look at you.

plain.text: The common hall's long table: forty feet of scrubbed planks, benches down both sides, a bowl of something at the end for whoever is hungry.

table.text: The common hall's long table, empty, forty feet of it under the lamps. Through the door: the guild's wagons on the lane east, the wardens' line at the west end, the Choir on the green between them. Each of them is here for the same shed. None of them will sit down for the others. They might sit down for you, if each of them owed you something they could not refuse.

passives.label: West Halt
passives.text: The Line's halts owe you their trains: no guild rider or warden car moves on the west sections tonight without them.

passives.label: Gull Stilts
passives.text: The Stilt Court owes you its boats: whatever comes down the delta comes in hulls the shore lends.

passives.label: Low Landing
passives.text: The Wet owes you its barges: the river carries what you say it carries.

passives.label: Carrick
passives.text: The Stand at Carrick owes you: the dockers can black any freight on the quay, the guild's and the Concern's.

passives.label: The Shift
passives.text: The Shift owes you: the miners of the Teeth will send people, and the Concern knows it.

passives.label: The Court
passives.text: The city's own court has a ruling of yours in its register: a record yields to a person who stands up.

passives.label: Kelso
passives.text: You sealed the Concern's sleeping army in the Ashlands against every code, and the Concern knows whose doing it was.

passives.label: Bridgeward
passives.text: The Rust Dogs hold Bridgeward's near end and owe you for it: the Crown's road and the guild's go round them.

passives.label: Sister Calla
passives.text: You took the order's first name back off the Line. The Choir owes you, and the city knows it was you.

options.text: (Send to the lane, the well and the green: all three to sit at this table at dusk, on two favours owed.)

sit.text: They come, because you have called in what they owe. Sarr with her rug and her clock and Roux at her shoulder; Lowe with the order's case, and two wardens he leaves at the door; Mason, with his hat, and Doria with the tally book; and, last, Petra, who does not sit, and stands against the wall with her arms folded where she can see everyone's hands. Nobody speaks. Every one of them is looking at you.
sit.again: All of them at the long table, looking at you.

interject.text: Odile takes the bench beside you and lays a pencil down on the planks in front of her, square to the edge. "Shall we begin, my dears?" she says to the whole table. "I'll keep the book."

options.text: (Make the truce: a third of the store to each claim, the eviction stayed at the rail, the people stay, and every one of you owes me.)

news.text: the guild, the city and the Choir sat at one table at Openfield because one stranger had a hold on all three

decision.text: I put the guild, the city and the Choir at one table in Openfield's common hall and made a truce out of what each of them owed me.

options.text: (Let them go back to their sides. Choose one.)

truce.text: It takes until the lamps are low. Sarr prices every word and you pay for each one with something she owes you; Lowe will not void his order and you do not ask him to, only to stay it at the rail, a season, person by person, which the record allows; Roux writes everything down and says nothing; Mason says "yes" once, at the end, to everything, and Petra unfolds her arms. A third of the store to the guild's shares at the price they were bought at. A third to the Precinct's ration, by the city's carts. A third stays in the shed, counted at dusk and at dawn. The people stay. When it is done every one of them stands up and looks at you the same way, and it is not gratitude. It is the way people look at somebody who now holds a piece of each of them.
truce.again: The truce, written, and the way they looked at you.

interject.text: "Everybody owes you," Wren says on the step after, quietly. "Nobody'll stand next to you." She bumps your shoulder. "Except us, I suppose. Somebody has to."
Tamsin is shaking. "Nobody got shot," she says. "Nobody got shot." She sits down on the step quite suddenly.

broke.text: It does not hold. Sarr prices a word you cannot pay; Lowe will not stay what the schedule holds; Petra laughs, once, against the wall. One by one they stand up and go back to their sides of the green, Mason last, his hat in his hand. The table is empty, and will not be full again. You will have to stand with one of them, or none.

none.text: You could walk away from all of them. The guild's paper and the city's order would meet at the store in the small hours without you, and the Choir would sit in front of it, and the night would go the way the city's forecast wrote it: Openfield burns, the Elder with it, the stores to the Precinct.
none.again: The night, as it is written.

options.text: (Stand with none of them. Let it come as it is written.)

decision.text: I stood with none of them for Openfield's Long Night, and let it come as it was written.

none_said.text: You say so, to nobody in particular, in an empty hall. Nobody comes to argue. It is not that kind of night.

broken.text: The long table, empty under the lamps. They will not sit at it again.

text.text: The long table, three marks on its end in three hands, and Doria asleep at it over the tally book.
The long table, empty under the lamps. You have chosen your side; the table is for people who have not.

after.text: The common hall's long table, scrubbed, the benches pushed under it.

text.text: Dusk at Openfield. The Choir sits down in front of the seed store, the old ones in front, Mason on his bench with his hat beside him, children sent to the long hall and not staying there. On the lane east the guild's lamps come on one by one. At the west end the wardens' line forms in grey, very straight. Between them, the green, and the well with the order on it, and you.

Dusk at Openfield. The guild's riders take the lane in pairs and the wagons are drawn across it, beds empty, waiting for the store. At the west end the wardens' line forms in grey. On the green the Choir sits down in front of the seed store, the old ones in front, and does not look at you.

Dusk at Openfield. The wardens' line forms at the west end, very straight, and moves up to the well, and Lowe stands by the order with its copy in his hand. On the lane east the guild's lamps come on. On the green the Choir sits down in front of the store, the old ones in front, and Petra and her young ones are nowhere you can see.

Dusk at Openfield, and for once nobody forms a line. The guild's carts come up the lane with a clerk walking beside them; the city's carts come from the west with a warden walking beside them; Doria opens the store's door and stands in it with her tally book, and counts the first third out, crate by crate, and nobody shouts.

Dusk at Openfield. The Choir sits down in front of the store. The guild's lamps come on along the lane. The wardens' line forms at the west end. Nobody looks at you, because you have told them you are nobody's tonight.

passives.label: West Halt
passives.text: West Halt's watch walk down the track from the Line at dusk: Chela Ortega in front with her rifle slung, a dozen behind her, the brass tags on their collars catching the lamps. "The halts were fed when nobody else would feed them," she says. "Openfield fed the twelve."

passives.label: The twelve
passives.text: The twelve off the stock car, who have lived at Openfield since they walked south from West Halt, come out of the long hall together and sit down in front of the store with the old ones, without being asked. Yaw Boateng in the middle.

passives.label: Number Four
passives.text: Desmond Achebe and six of Number Four's miners off the evening's barge and the long walk, lamps on their caps, picks on their shoulders. "No paper past the cage," Desmond says. "No paper past the store, either."

passives.label: The Shift
passives.text: A committee from the Skirts off the Line: a dozen of the Shift with their lamps down, the way they go up from a mine, and a note in Maren Okafor's hand: WE GO UP TOGETHER. THIS IS UP.

passives.label: The Shift, armed
passives.text: Rafe Ansel and twenty of the Shift's armed, with the Lodge's powder in their packs and their faces set. They do not sit. They take the lane's hedge and lie down behind it with their rifles.

passives.label: The Rust Dogs
passives.text: Rust Dogs, a ragged twenty of them, down from the road on bikes with no lamps, Bridgeward's paint still on their jackets, and they put themselves across the east end of the lane between the guild's wagons and the green, and grin.

passives.label: Sister Calla
passives.text: Sister Calla, back off the Line, walking among the people sitting at the store with a basin and a cloth, the way she walked her tent in Shale. Where she passes, people sit straighter.

passives.label: Unit nine
passives.text: At the well, when the wardens' line forms, Assessor Nine steps out of it and reads the order aloud before the captain can, every line, and after each line it cannot make lawful says, level, "Logged as an error." The wardens shift their feet.

passives.label: The guild's Line
passives.text: The seven o'clock comes into West Halt with guild riders in every coach, and they are at Openfield by dusk, forty of them, the guild's green on their cords.

passives.label: The Concern's freight
passives.text: A sealed Concern car on the through's path, run west on green and stopping for nobody but this: men in clean grey get down from it at West Halt's siding and walk south.

passives.label: Kennel boards
passives.text: In the dark beyond the guild's wagons, things on four legs sit in a row, very still, their lenses lit, waiting to be told what a lane is.

passives.label: Kennel Seven
passives.text: Out of the east at dusk, a pack: thirty hounds off the March at a steady run that does not tire, grey plates under the glass dust, and they lie down in rows behind the guild's wagons like a sown field.

passives.label: Vasha Kade
passives.text: Vasha Kade rides in with the guild's riders at the head of a dozen of her own, sitting her bike like a judge, and looks across the green at the store the way she looks at everything: as if it were already written.

passives.label: The shore's oil
passives.text: Guild trucks, running on Hum's oil off the shore, grind up the lane in low gear with empty beds for the store.

passives.label: Unit nine
passives.text: Assessor Nine stands in the wardens' line at the well, its cap square, and when the order is read it makes each line lawful as it goes, and the wardens stand straighter for it.

passives.label: The designate's warrant
passives.text: The wardens' line knows whose hand is on the order. They stand differently for it: like men who will be thanked.

passives.label: The city's kennel
passives.text: Behind the wardens' line, the kennel boards the city seized off a barge, and what they speak to: three hounds in the city's grey paint, sitting.

passives.label: Against: hounds
passives.text: Across the lane, things on four legs in a row behind the guild's wagons, lenses lit.

passives.label: Against: Kennel Seven
passives.text: Out of the east at dusk, a pack off the March that lies down in rows behind the guild's wagons.

passives.label: Against: Vasha Kade
passives.text: Vasha Kade, at the head of a dozen riders, looking at the store as if it were already written.

passives.label: Against: the guild's Line
passives.text: Forty guild riders off the seven o'clock, at the lane by dusk.

passives.label: Against: unit nine
passives.text: Assessor Nine in the wardens' line, making each line of the order lawful as it is read.

passives.label: Against: unit nine
passives.text: Assessor Nine stepping out of the line to log the order's errors aloud, and the wardens shifting their feet.

passives.label: Against: West Halt
passives.text: The halts will not carry your side's men on their sections tonight: the request flags stay down and the pilots stay home.

passives.label: Against: the Shift
passives.text: Rafe Ansel's armed men behind the lane's hedge, rifles out, for the Choir.

passives.label: Against: the Rust Dogs
passives.text: Rust Dogs across the east end of the lane, for the farmers, grinning.

interject.text: Wren is off the green and among the Dogs before you can say a word, slapping backs, swearing, laughing. She comes back with her goggles up. "Told you," she says. "They hate riders worse than farmers."
Kes sees Maren's note in the committee's hands and has to sit down. "We go up together," she reads, and wipes her nose with the back of her hand. "Obviously she'd say that. Obviously."
Ilya has seen Vasha. He does not say anything. He lies down behind the well's wall with his rifle and does not take his eye from the glass for the rest of the night.

Ilya has seen Vasha, across the lane, at the head of her riders. He does not say anything. He lies down behind the well's wall with his rifle and does not take his eye from the glass for the rest of the night.

Tamsin sits down among the Choir on the step of the store, between an old woman and a boy, and folds her hands in her lap the way they do. "I want to see what it's like," she says, "sitting in front of a door." She does not look at you.
"The city has called its units in," Nine says. "I will be at the well. I will come back." It goes, and does not look back, and you are not sure, until the order is read, which way it will turn.

text.text: Midnight. The guild's riders come up the lane at a walk with lamps and the wagons behind them, for the store; and from the west, the wardens' line, at a walk, for the well and the order. The Choir sits. Somebody in it has started singing, badly, and the others have joined in to cover for them.

Midnight. The wardens' line comes up to the well and Lowe begins to read the order aloud. The riders draw in round the store. And from the store's side, low, fast, three of Petra's young ones are moving along the long hall's wall with something that smells of lamp oil.

Midnight. Lowe stands at the well with the order in his hand and the wardens at his back. The guild's riders draw up on the lane to contest it with their paper and their rifles. The Choir sits in front of the store, and does not move, and has started to sing.

Midnight. The second third goes out on the city's carts. A rider and a warden share a cigarette by the well, not speaking. Mason sleeps sitting up on his bench. It is the strangest night anybody here has ever kept.
Midnight. The riders come up the lane. The wardens come up to the well. The Choir sits. You watch.

core.speaker: narrator
core.text: The core is warm in your hand, its lamp green, and across the lane every lens on four legs turns to it at once. Then, one after another, as if their names had been said, the guild's hounds lie down on the dirt and put their heads on their forelegs, and do not get up again whatever their handlers shout. The riders look at their dogs, and at you, and at each other.

interject.text: "Don't," Kes says, very quietly, at your shoulder. "Don't ever do that again. Please." Her hand is on her neck.

mid_fail.speaker: narrator
mid_fail.text: It does not go your way. Words are not enough tonight, or not yours, or not these; the night goes on past you and you have to run to keep up with it.

sit_fail.speaker: narrator
sit_fail.text: You sit, and the riders come on at a walk, and you are up and out of the way before the first horse reaches you, with the Choir's old ones sitting on behind you while the riders go round them, and you are ashamed of it all night.
sit_fail.again: Up and out of the way.

interject.text: Ash does not get up. The riders go round him. When you look back he is still there, beside Mason, his shotgun on the ground in front of him.

fire_fail.speaker: narrator
fire_fail.text: You are a breath too late. The oil goes over the store's back wall and a lamp after it, and the fire goes up the old timber like a word said aloud. The riders get half the store out before the roof comes in. Petra's people are gone into the dark.

text.text: The lane, after: the guild's lamps out, a wagon on its side, riders down and riders gone back to Sarr's chair at a run, and the Choir still sitting in front of the store as if nothing had happened, because to them nothing has that they did.
The well, after: the wardens' line broken and gone back to the west end in pieces, the order torn off the post, Lowe on one knee by a man in grey who is not getting up.

The small hours. The lamps on the lane are low. Down among the guild's wagons, where the Grand Factor sleeps in the middle one on her rug with her clock, something moves that is not a rider: three shapes in grey scarves, along the wagons' shadow, low.

The small hours. The lamps on the lane are low, the wardens' line is a row of grey shapes sitting on their packs, the Choir sleeps sitting up against each other in front of the store. Nothing moves that does not have to.

options.text: (Ash is already moving. Toward the wagons.)
(Get between the knives and the Grand Factor's wagon.)

ash_stands.speaker: narrator
ash_stands.text: Ash goes down the lane in the dark faster than a man that size should, and when the three grey shapes reach the Grand Factor's wagon he is already standing in front of its step with his empty hands out. One of them is Petra. "Brother," she says. "Sister," he says, and does not move, and the knife that was meant for the wagon goes into his forearm instead, and he does not move then either. They go. Sarr wakes to a man bleeding on her step and a clock that has stopped.

ash_knife.speaker: narrator
ash_knife.text: Ash goes down the lane in the dark with his shotgun left on the store's step and his knife in his hand, and you understand what the sum on his face was, and you have a breath to decide.

options.text: (Say his name, the way he once said yours.)

mods.why: he trusts you

ashk_stopped.speaker: narrator
ashk_stopped.text: He stops in the middle of the lane with the knife in his hand. He stands there a long time. Then he puts it away and walks back up to the store's step and sits down beside Mason's bench and puts his face in his hands, and does not say anything until it is light.

ashk_done.speaker: narrator
ashk_done.text: He does not stop. You hear the wagon's door, and nothing else, because he is good at it, he always was; and then he walks back past you up the lane, and does not look at you, and does not stop at the store, and goes on west into the glass with Petra's three behind him, and you do not see him again.

knife_stopped.speaker: narrator
knife_stopped.text: You reach the wagon's step a breath before they do, and they see you, and stop, and one of them is Petra, and she looks at you over her scarf with an expression you will remember. Then they are gone into the dark the way they came. Sarr, awake, sits up on her rug with the clock in her lap. "Thank you," she says. "That is a debt."
knife_stopped.again: The wagon's step, and Petra's look.

knife_late.speaker: narrator
knife_late.text: You are a breath too late. They are already coming back past you along the wagons' shadow, and one of them is Petra, and her knife is in her hand and not clean. In the middle wagon the clock has stopped.

knife_shout.speaker: narrator
knife_shout.text: You shout, and the riders' lamps swing, and the three grey shapes break and run, and two of them get away into the glass. The third does not: the riders bring Petra Mason back up the lane by the arms with her scarf torn off her face, the face she has kept from every lens for ten years, in the lamplight, in front of the whole Choir.

knife_done.speaker: narrator
knife_done.text: You do not move. Neither does anything else on the lane, for a while. Then three grey shapes go back along the wagons' shadow the way they came, unhurried, and in the middle wagon a clock has stopped.

dawn.speaker: narrator
dawn.text: Dawn comes up over the glass.

choir_stands.speaker: narrator
choir_stands.text: The guild's wagons go back down the lane at first light with their beds empty, and the wardens' line folds its tents at the west end and walks away west behind Lowe, slowly, the way men walk who will have to explain. The order is still on the well. Nobody has taken it down; nobody needs to. Openfield stands. The store stands, counted at dawn. Mason gets up off his bench at last, very stiffly, and goes to the store's door and puts his hand flat on it, and stands there a long time.

news.text: Openfield stood its Long Night: the guild and the city both went home without the store

decision.text: Openfield stood through the Long Night: the guild went home with its paper and the city with its order, and the store was counted at dawn. The Precinct will be short this winter.

interject.text: Tamsin is asleep against the store's door when the light comes, among the old ones, her hands still folded in her lap. When she wakes she looks at the empty lane for a long time. "We sat," she says. "We just sat. And they went home."

choir_scorched.speaker: narrator
choir_scorched.text: At first light the guild's riders go back down the lane, and as they go they put their lamps to the rows. By the time the Choir is on its feet the east fields are burning, a year's harvest going up into the sky the Choir keeps no books for. The wardens watch from the west end and do not help and do not stop it, and fold their tents. The store stands. The seed is counted at dawn. The halls stand. Mason watches the rows burn with his hat in his hands.

news.text: Openfield kept its seed store through the Long Night; the guild's riders burned its fields as they left

decision.text: Openfield held its store through the Long Night, but the guild burned the east fields as it went. The seed is safe; the year's harvest is not. The Precinct will be short this winter.

choir_thin.speaker: narrator
choir_thin.text: Too few. At midnight's end the riders and the wardens reach the store together from two sides, and in the dark nobody can say afterwards who threw the first lamp. The store goes up. The long hall after it. The Choir goes on sitting, and then the old ones in front are not sitting, and then everybody is running, and Mason is not: he is in the store's doorway with his back to the fire, as if he could keep it in.

mods.why: Ash goes in with you

news.text: Openfield burned in the Long Night, as the city's forecast said it would

ct_pulled.speaker: narrator
ct_pulled.text: You go in. You do not remember most of it. You remember the heat and the sound, and that he was heavier than he looked, and that he did not help, and then the green under you and the sky over you and Mason beside you on the grass with his beard burned off one side, breathing.

ct_lost.speaker: narrator
ct_lost.text: The roof comes in. The doorway goes with it, and the man in it. In the morning the Choir builds his cairn in the burial ground under the dead windpump, without his name on it, as he would have wanted, and every one of them puts a stone on it.

seed_shore.speaker: narrator
seed_shore.text: But not the seed. In the small hours, while the riders and the wardens watched the store, Doria and the twelve carried the seed out of its back in sacks and down the track to West Halt, where the halt's pilot would not let the guild's trains move, and on the seven o'clock it went west to Carrick, and off the quay into hulls the shore had lent, and down the delta into the drowned town where nobody will ever find it but the people who put it there.
seed_shore.again: The seed, gone down the delta.

decision.text: Openfield burned, but its seed went west on the Line and down the delta in the Stilts' boats, hidden in the drowned town.

seed_north.speaker: narrator
seed_north.text: But not the seed. In the small hours Doria and the twelve carried it out of the store's back in sacks and down the track to West Halt, where the halt's pilot would not let the guild's trains move, and on the seven o'clock it went west, and at the river onto a barge the Wet had promised you, and up the Water to Sawtown, where it is in a loft over the cookhouse under Dorit Avraham's eye.
seed_north.again: The seed, gone up the river.

decision.text: Openfield burned, but its seed went west on the Line and up the river on the Wet's barges, to a loft at Sawtown.

seed_lost.speaker: narrator
seed_lost.text: And the seed with it: ninety years of the glass choosing what would grow in it, gone up into the sky in one night. Doria sits in the ashes of the store with the tally book in her lap and does not write anything in it.

decision.text: Openfield burned in the Long Night, and its seed store with it.

guild_company.speaker: narrator
guild_company.text: The order is read at the well and meets the guild's paper and the guild's rifles, and the city's line goes home with it at first light. The store is opened with the guild's keys and emptied onto the guild's wagons, crate by counted crate, and the Concern's stencil goes on every one: HALCYON SEED VAULT — CONSIGNED. Roux sits at his desk on the green and signs the Choir's people onto contracts as they come to him, one by one, the young first. Mason does not come. At noon he picks up his hat and walks out of Openfield west with the ones who will not sign, and does not look back.

news.text: Openfield is the guild's now, and its seed the Concern's; the Elder walked out west with the ones who would not sign

decision.text: The guild took Openfield's store through the Long Night and the Concern consigned its seed to Halcyon's vault. Openfield is a company farm now; the Elder walked out with those who would not sign.

interject.text: "Order," Odile says, watching Roux's queue. "On the Flats, for once." She does not sound pleased. She sounds like a woman reading a price she wrote herself.

guild_scorched.speaker: narrator
guild_scorched.text: The guild holds the lane and the city's line goes home at first light, but the store is half ash: whatever Petra's people threw over the back wall at midnight took the old timber and half the seed with it before the riders beat it out. What is left goes onto the guild's wagons under the Concern's stencil. Roux signs contracts on the green. Mason walks out west at noon with the ones who will not sign, and the halls stand empty behind him.
guild_scorched.again: The store, half ash, under the guild's mark.

news.text: Openfield is the guild's now; half its seed burned rather than go to the Concern

decision.text: The guild took what was left of Openfield's store through the Long Night; the Unwritten burned half the seed rather than let it go to Halcyon. The Elder walked out west.

guild_burned.speaker: narrator
guild_burned.text: Not enough. The city's line and the guild's riders meet at the store in the dark, paper against paper and then rifle against rifle, and the Choir sitting between them. Somebody's lamp goes into the timber. The store goes, and the long hall, and the riders fall back down the lane with nothing on their wagons, and the wardens fall back west with nothing in their hands, and in the store's doorway, with his back to the fire, as if he could keep it in, is Mason.

news.text: Openfield burned in the Long Night between the guild's riders and the city's wardens

gb_pulled.speaker: narrator
gb_pulled.text: You go in, and come out with him, and lie on the green with his weight on you and the sky going grey over the smoke. Nobody thanks you. The guild's wagons are going down the lane empty.

decision.text: Openfield burned in the Long Night between the guild's riders and the city's wardens, with the store. I pulled the Elder out of its doorway.

gb_lost.speaker: narrator
gb_lost.text: The roof comes in, and the doorway with it, and the man in it. The guild's wagons go down the lane empty. Petra stands in the ashes at noon and does not let anyone near her.

decision.text: Openfield burned in the Long Night between the guild's riders and the city's wardens, and the Elder with his store.

ledger_evicted.speaker: narrator
ledger_evicted.text: The order is read at the well, every line, and kept. The guild's riders contest it with paper and lose, and are put off the Flats with their wagons by a line of grey that does not raise its voice; the city's carts come up the lane and the store is emptied onto them, crate by counted crate, under the Ledger's seal, for the Precinct. Nothing burns. Openfield is returned to the schedule. Mason walks out west at noon, alive, with his hat, at the head of whoever is let go.

news.text: the city emptied Openfield in its Long Night, the store to the Precinct, the guild off the Flats, and nothing burned

decision.text: The city's order was kept at Openfield through the Long Night: the store went to the Precinct under the Ledger's seal, the guild was put off the Flats, and the holding was returned to the schedule without burning.

ledger_scorched.speaker: narrator
ledger_scorched.text: The order is read and kept. The guild's riders contest it and are put off the Flats. Then, at first light, by the order's own last line, the wardens clear the holding: they put the rows to the torch so nothing grows here that the schedule did not plant. The halls stand, empty. The store goes west on the city's carts under the Ledger's seal. Mason watches his fields burn from the lane with his hat in his hands, and then walks west, alive, with whoever is let go.
ledger_scorched.again: The rows, burning, by the order's last line.

news.text: the city cleared Openfield in its Long Night and burned the rows by order

decision.text: The city's order was kept at Openfield through the Long Night; the guild was put off the Flats, the store went to the Precinct, and the wardens burned the rows at dawn.

ledger_burned.speaker: narrator
ledger_burned.text: Too thin a line, and too many against it. The order is read at the well and the guild's riders and Petra's young ones both answer it at once, and in the dark between them the store goes up, and the long hall after it, and the wardens fall back to the west end with the order still in Lowe's hand. Openfield burns, exactly as the city's forecast wrote it would. In the store's doorway, with his back to the fire, is Mason.

news.text: Openfield burned in the Long Night, as the city's forecast said it would

lb_pulled.speaker: narrator
lb_pulled.text: You go in, and come out with him, and the wardens at the west end watch you do it and do not move. When Lowe comes to look at the ashes at noon he stands by Mason on the grass for a while and then takes his cap off, which you have never seen him do.

decision.text: Openfield burned in the Long Night, as the city's forecast said it would. I pulled the Elder out of the store's doorway.

lb_lost.speaker: narrator
lb_lost.text: The roof comes in, and the doorway with it. The forecast is kept, to the letter. Lowe reads the order's last line to the ashes at noon, because the schedule says it must be read, and his voice does not change, and his hands do.
lb_lost.again: The order's last line, read to the ashes.

decision.text: Openfield burned in the Long Night, as the city's forecast said it would, and the Elder with his store.

people_heard.speaker: narrator
people_heard.text: And the people, by the precedent in the Court's register: every one of them who stood up at the reading and gave a name was entered living and heard. Forty-one of them did, which is forty-one faces the Ledger never had, and they are tenants of the holding now, on the record, under the schedule. The rest walked west with the Elder rather than be seen.
people_heard.again: Forty-one faces given to the record.

people_outside.speaker: narrator
people_outside.text: And the people, by the precedent in the Court's register: the city can neither move nor shelter a person the record does not hold. So it did neither. The Choir's people sit on the holding they no longer own, with no store and no fields, in the open, and nobody is obliged to help them.
people_outside.again: The Choir, on land it does not own.

people_property.speaker: narrator
people_property.text: And the people, by the precedent in the Court's register: unrecorded occupiers of a vacant holding are removed with its contents, as property. They go west on the city's carts with the store, counted with the crates, for the Precinct's labour lines. The wardens are gentle about it, the way you are gentle with things on an inventory.
people_property.again: The Choir, counted with the crates.

people_relocated.speaker: narrator
people_relocated.text: And the people, as the record holds: relocated on schedule, to wherever the schedule has room. Some go. Most walk west with the Elder before anybody can read them a destination.

truce_dawn.speaker: narrator
truce_dawn.text: Dawn, and the last third still in the shed, counted by Doria with a guild clerk and a city clerk reading over her shoulder. The guild's carts are gone east with their third; the city's carts west with theirs. The order on the well has a second paper pinned over it: STAYED AT THE RAIL — ONE SEASON — PERSONS TO BE HEARD. The Choir gets up off the step, stiff and astonished, and goes back to the fields. Nobody thanks you. Each of them, passing, looks at you the way you look at a creditor.
truce_dawn.again: Openfield, standing, and every side in your debt.

news.text: Openfield came through its Long Night whole: the store split three ways at one stranger's table

decision.text: I made a truce at Openfield on its Long Night: the store split three ways, the eviction stayed at the rail a season, the people kept their fields. The guild, the city and the Choir all owe me now, and none of them trusts me.

none_dawn.speaker: narrator
none_dawn.text: It goes as it was written. The riders and the wardens reach the store together in the dark and nobody can say afterwards who threw the first lamp; the store goes up, and the long hall, and the Choir runs at last, all but one. Mason is in the store's doorway with his back to the fire when the roof comes in. At first light the city's carts come up the lane and take what the fire left, under the Ledger's seal, and the guild goes home with its paper, and the order on the well is exactly right.
none_dawn.again: Openfield, burned as it was written.

news.text: Openfield burned in the Long Night, as the city's forecast said it would, and a stranger watched

decision.text: I stood with nobody on Openfield's Long Night, and it went as the city's forecast wrote it: Openfield burned, the Elder with his store, and what was left went to the Precinct.

calla.speaker: narrator
calla.text: At the Line, at dawn, the warden car the order's first name was put into goes west to the city on the seven o'clock, because nobody took her off it. Sister Calla will be heard by the Court of Accounts, as the docket holds. She will be heard, and then she will be written down, as the forecast said.

decision.text: Sister Calla was carried west on the Line to the city in a warden car on the morning after the Long Night, to be heard for sedition.

text.text: Nine comes back from the well at first light with its cap in its hand and dust on its grey. "I logged eleven errors in the order," it says. "Aloud. The captain wrote down that I had. The schedule will have to read them." It stands beside you. "I came back. I said I would."

Nine comes back from the well at first light, its cap square. "Every line of it made lawful," it says, "that could be. I have logged the ones that could not be softened." It is quiet a moment. "There were fewer than I wished. I came back. I said I would."

rl_ash.speaker: narrator
rl_ash.text: Ash finds you on the lane when it is light. He does not raise his voice; he never has. "I said I'd see it. I saw it." He looks at Openfield, at what the night did to it, and then at you, for a long time, the way he looks at a cairn. "You stood with them. Against this." He puts his hat on. "Go well, friend. Not with me." He walks west into the glass toward the burial ground, and does not look back.

decision.text: Brother Ash left me after Openfield's Long Night, for standing against the Choir.

rl_wren.speaker: narrator
rl_wren.text: Wren is waiting by your gear when you come back up the lane, with her own pack on her shoulder. "I saw it out," she says. "Like I said I would." She pulls her goggles down. "You shook their hands. The ones who sell people on paper. I can't walk next to that. I won't learn it." She goes east down the lane past the guild's wagons without looking at them, and is a long way off before you understand she meant it.

decision.text: Wren left me after Openfield's Long Night, for standing with the guild and the Concern.

rl_kes.speaker: narrator
rl_kes.text: Kes has not spoken to you since the pledge. She speaks now, once, at the edge of the green, with her hand on the back of her neck. "You handed them the Flats. And everyone on them who signs." She does not cry; she has decided not to. "I said I'd stay till it was light. It's light." She goes north toward the Line, and the Teeth, and the Shift.

decision.text: Kes left me after Openfield's Long Night, for standing with the Concern.

rl_odile.speaker: narrator
rl_odile.text: Odile sits in the middle wagon a long time with the stopped clock in her lap. When she comes out her coat is buttoned to the throat. "I told you my price, my dear," she says. "You heard it. That is a cost." She walks east down the lane toward the bridge where she was born, and does not hurry, and does not look back.

decision.text: Odile left me after Openfield's Long Night, because the Grand Factor did not walk out of it alive.

close.speaker: narrator

text.text: Openfield, in the morning, getting up off its step and going back to the rows. The basin will hear of this night all winter, every telling different. Somewhere west, in the city, a schedule is being recomputed.

Openfield, in the morning, under the guild's half-moon and the Concern's stencil, its young ones in a queue at a desk on the green. The basin will hear of this night all winter. Somewhere west, in the city, a schedule is being recomputed.
Openfield, in the morning, empty, its store under the city's seal, its green trodden flat by carts. The basin will hear of this night all winter. In the city, the schedule holds.
Openfield, in the morning, and the smoke going up straight into a sky that keeps no books. The basin will hear of this night all winter, every telling different.

close.again: The morning after the Long Night.

text.text: A warden by the well, in grey, very tired. "The holding is returned to the schedule," he says, as if he had been told to say it to anyone who asked.
A warden of the Precinct in grey with a carbine across his chest, a long way from the city. "Stand clear of the line. The order will be read at the well."

look.again: The warden, in grey.

look.text: One of the guild's riders, the half-moon on his cord, dust to the knee, rifle slung. "Contract business," he says. "Nobody has to get hurt over seed." He does not sound sure.
look.again: "Nobody has to get hurt over seed."

text.text: A warden car on West Halt's platform road, its windows plated, its door chained, standing where it has stood since it came in, because the section past West Halt is worked by pilot and no pilotman of West Halt will take it on. Through the slot in its door, Sister Calla, sitting on the bench inside with her hands in her lap. "You came," she says. "You shouldn't have. Don't get yourself shot for me."

A warden car on West Halt's platform road, waiting on the section's token from Four Ways' box, which has not come and will not come tonight: the box's instrument for this section is down, and there is no spare. Through the slot, Sister Calla, on the bench inside. "They say a wire has to say yes," she says. "It keeps saying nothing. I have been praying to it."

A warden car on West Halt's platform road, its windows plated, its door chained, waiting for the seven o'clock to take it west. Through the slot in its door, Sister Calla, sitting on the bench inside with her hands in her lap. "You came," she says. "You shouldn't have. Don't get yourself shot for me."

freed_watch.text: Chela listens, and nods, and at the change of the escort's watch the car's door is open and Calla is in West Halt's water tower, where twelve people hid before her, and by morning she is walking south with the twelve's old route in her head.

freed_lift.text: In the dark the car's chain is an old city lock and gives with a sigh, and Calla comes out of the door into your arms as light as a bundle of sticks, and you are off the platform road and into the scrub before the escort has finished its cigarette.

chela_no.text: "Not for you," Chela says. "Not a city prisoner, with the city looking straight at us. Not yet." She looks at the car. "Ask me when you've got something better than asking."

lift_no.text: The chain rattles. The escort's lamp comes round. You are flat in the ditch by the rails for an hour before it goes back, and the car is still chained.

freed_fare.text: Henrike Dahl reads the Act off her knee on the Customs House steps at six, the way she reads it every morning: a person landed on this quay is a passenger who owes her fare. You pay it. The wardens look at the Act, and at the Harbour Master, and at each other, and unchain the door, because the Ledger enforces the Harbour Act and nothing else here, and the Harbour Act has been read.
freed_fare.again: The Act, read on the steps.

freed_court.text: Dahl hears it on the steps at six with the Act on her knee and the wardens standing in front of her. She reads Schedule 2 aloud: no persons. "A person on my quay is a passenger," she says. "Pay her fare, or work it, but she is not freight." The wardens unchain the door. Somebody on the Stand cheers, once, and is hushed.

freed_cradle.text: In the dark, past the Bond's white lights, to Crane One and the basket on its cable, and Kobby at the winch saying nothing at all. Calla goes out over the dry riverbed among the hulls with her hands on the basket's rim and her face turned, at last, toward the sea.

court_no.text: "The Act says cargo, livestock, mails, stores, ballast," Dahl says. "It does not say prisoners, and it does not say persons." She closes it. "Bring me something the Act can read."
court_no.again: "Bring me something the Act can read."

cradle_no.text: The escort's lamp swings across the quay as you reach the car, and holds on you. You walk on, as if you had been going somewhere else.

text.text: Calla among the Choir with a basin and a cloth. "You took me off a train," she says. "I have been thinking what to give you for it, and I have decided it is this: I will not tell anyone it was you." She wrings the cloth. "They will know anyway."
Calla, back at Openfield, walking among the people at the store with a basin and a cloth as if she had never been away. "You shouldn't have," she says. "Thank you."

seal.text: The Ledger's grey seal, and under it the city's even hand: BY COURIER — TO THE DESIGNATE — RESERVE 9 (THE MOUTH). The courier stood over you while you signed for it, then went without a word, the way the city's people do when the paper has said everything.

text.text: Three sheets, the city's even hand on all of them. Under it, the reason, set down the way the Precinct sets down weather: AN ORDER OF EVICTION WAS BROKEN IN THE OPEN AT OPENFIELD BY PERSONS WHO KEEP NO RECORD. THE PLAN'S DISSENT IS MOVING ON ITS CORE. THE SCHEDULE IS BROUGHT FORWARD. And at the foot of the last sheet, one line corrected in the same hand: PUBLIC STEPS REOPEN R49, the 49 ruled through and 30 written over it. Under that, small, the line the city prints at the foot of every order it has ever sent: OBJECTIONS LIE TO THE COURT OF ACCOUNTS.
