kept.text: "Ours," Tally says. "Then Brick sits up by the track by day, and Thanh does the switch." At the pipes Thanh goes very still. "Outside," he says. "At the foot. I don't go in." "Outside," Tally agrees.

wheel_told.text: "The Wheel." Tally weighs it. "Horses and guns over us, and somebody to sell copper to who isn't the Tollhouse." She almost smiles. "Could be worse. We keep the camp. They keep the target."
wheel_told.again: "We keep the camp," Tally says. "They keep the target."

knock_told.text: "Knock." Tally says it like a coin she is testing with her teeth. "Then it's Knock's target, and we're not Knock." She is already kicking the fire apart. "We'll find another hill with less on it." Thanh looks at the mast, and at you, and goes to roll the copper.

interject.text: Wren watches the Hollow kick their fire apart and says nothing at all, which is worse than anything she could have said.

leaving.text: "We're going," Tally says, rolling a coil of copper. "Knock's target. Not ours."
leaving.again: Tally rolls the copper and does not look up.

keeping.text: "Still ours," Tally says. Up the hill the white lamp burns beside the red. "Nobody's come yet. They will."

options.text: What will you do when they come?

come.text: "Throw the switch, if your word's come up the wire. Run, if it hasn't." She shrugs. "We're good at running. It's the first thing the Hollow ever learned."

text.text: "The Wheel's up there," Tally says, nodding at the station. "Sefa's boy swept the step. Nobody's swept that step since the Burn." She does not sound as if she minds.
"Wheel's coming, you said," Tally says. "We'll see."

under_wheel.again: "We keep the camp," Tally says. "They keep the target."

quiet.text: "Still narrow," Tally says, and very nearly thanks you.

narrow_ask.text: "Leave it be." Tally waits to see whether you mean it. "Then nobody climbs our track for it, and nobody puts a crown on it, and we go on cutting the guys a little at a time till it falls down, which it won't." Once you go down the hill like that, you will not be coming back up to change your mind.

decision.text: I left Signal Hill's mast as the city built it, as the Hollow asked: nobody climbs their track for a mast that speaks to nobody.

narrow_back.text: "Put it back." Tally looks at the white lamp for a while. "Then nobody climbs our track for it after all." Once you go down the hill like that, you will not be coming back up to change your mind.

decision.text: I left Signal Hill's mast as the city built it, speaking narrow to a room and a pump station.

narrowed.text: "Then you've a fire here," Tally says, "any night you want one." It is the first thing the Hollow have given anybody for nothing.

hostile.text: Nobody is talking.
hostile.again: Nobody is talking, and nobody is going to.

text.text: "A door," Dario says, and shuts the station door, and opens it again to show you. "It shuts. You said a door is a door, and what I do behind it is mine." He sits on the step with the carbine across his knees. "Switch is down. It stays down till your word comes up the wire. Mother says I'm a fool. Mother sent me."

"A door," Dario says, and shuts the station door, and opens it again to show you. "It shuts." He sits on the step with the carbine across his knees. "Switch is down. It stays down till your word comes up the wire. Mother says I'm a fool. Mother sent me."

hill.again: "Still down," Dario says, and taps the cabinet with his boot. "Still mine."

come.text: "Two riders on the track yesterday with guild tin on their saddles. They looked at the carbine, and they looked at the lamp, and they went back down." He does not sound unhappy about it. "They'll come back with more. Let them. It's a good door."
come.again: "They'll come back with more," Dario says. "Let them."

car.speaker: narrator

text.text: The car for Reserve 9 stands in the gate road with its engine ticking: a long grey Precinct lorry, a canvas roof on hoops, and down both sides of its bed, bolted to the floor, benches. Sixty places, each with a number in white paint, and on the tailboard a stencil: RESERVE 9 — PRECINCT SUPPLY — CAPACITY 60. Sergeant Reyes stands beside it with her cap under her arm, because Lowe always did. "Seven o'clock," she says. "It goes when you're in it."

The car for Reserve 9 stands in the gate road with its engine ticking: a long grey Precinct lorry, a canvas roof on hoops, and down both sides of its bed, bolted to the floor, benches. Sixty places, each with a number in white paint, and on the tailboard a stencil: RESERVE 9 — PRECINCT SUPPLY — CAPACITY 60. Captain Lowe stands beside it with his cap under his arm, because the charter says a captain uncovers for a magistrate, designate or not. "Seven o'clock," he says. "It goes when you are in it. That is the order."

car.again: The car for Reserve 9 in the gate road, its benches numbered in white. CAPACITY 60.

interject.text: Tamsin has stopped at the tailboard. She counts the benches with her eyes, one side and then the other, and gets to sixty both times. "They built it," she says. "They built it before anybody asked us." She climbs up anyway, because you are going to.
Nine reads the stencil. "Capacity sixty," it says. "The schedule did not provide for the designate." It considers the benches. "I will sit on the wheel arch. It is not a numbered place."
"Sixty places and not one cushion," Odile says. "The city costs everything, my dear. It simply never prices comfort."
Wren runs her burned hand along the bolts on bench one. "Block-sheet car," she says. "We had one at the overpass. Took the benches out and kept goats in it." She does not smile.
"I can walk," Ash says. Then, because you are already climbing: "No. I'll ride. I want to see what they built."
Kes sits on bench sixty, the last one, at the open end, with the road behind her. "If I'm going to be carried," she says, "I'm going to see where from."
Ilya counts the benches, as he counts everything. "Sixty," he says. He sits on the floor. "Right."

road.speaker: narrator

text.text: Out of the gate at seven, east on the toll road under a white sky, the Wall going down behind you into its own haze. Ninebridge's spans by noon; the guild's toll-warden lifts the bar for the city's car without a word or a coin. Lowe rides in the back, on bench one, with his knees together and his cap on them, facing you. In the cab, at the wheel, in a cadet's grey with the collar too big for her, is Linnet. She has not turned round once since the gate.

Out of the gate at seven, east on the toll road under a white sky, the Wall going down behind you into its own haze. Ninebridge's spans by noon; the guild's toll-warden lifts the bar for the city's car without a word or a coin. Lowe rides in the back, on bench one, with his knees together and his cap on them, facing you, because the front of the car is for the driver and the charter has a rule about that too.

Out of the gate at seven, east on the toll road under a white sky. Ninebridge's spans by noon; the guild's toll-warden lifts the bar for the city's car. Reyes rides on bench one with Lowe's cap on her knees. In the cab, at the wheel, in a cadet's grey with the collar too big for her, is Linnet. She has not turned round once since the gate.

Out of the gate at seven, east on the toll road under a white sky. Ninebridge's spans by noon; the guild's toll-warden lifts the bar for the city's car. Reyes rides on bench one with Lowe's cap on her knees, and reads the order again, and again, the way he used to.

road.again: The toll road going by under the canvas.

interject.text: Tamsin will not sit on a bench. She sits on the bed of the car between the rows with her back against the cab and her knees up, and every time the car goes over a pothole she looks at the numbers. When Lowe offers her his coat against the wind she says, "I'm not cold," and she is.
Nine has its ledger open on its knee on the wheel arch. "I am noting the condition of the toll road," it says. "Nobody has asked me to. It is a habit of the record, to note the way to a thing."

options.text: Why carry me at all? You could have waited for me at the door.
What happens when I'm standing at the door?
Who are the benches for, Captain? Say it.
What would Lowe have done with this order?
(Sleep on the bench until the car stops.)

why.text: "The order executes on the designate's attendance." He says it the way he says the time. "I could wait at the door for you. Then you come up the track to a column, and Knock watches you walk through it. Or you come in the city's car, and Knock watches you get down from it." He turns his cap round once on his knees. "My orders are to carry the attendance with the car. I would rather you came with me than came to me. I cannot tell you why that is better. I think it is."
why.again: "I would rather you came with me than came to me."

grieve.text: "I grieve every one." Plainly, the way other men say they take sugar. "Thirty-one evictions in eleven years. I checked every one, and every one was lawful. The schedule holds." He looks at the white numbers on the benches opposite. "I wish it didn't, here. That is not a thing a captain says. I have said it to you, and I will say it to the assessor if it asks me."
grieve.again: "The schedule holds. I wish it didn't, here."

interject.text: "I will not ask," Nine says, without looking up from the ledger. "I will note that it was said." Lowe nods, as if that were a kindness, and perhaps it is.

door.text: "Nothing, until you are standing at it. Then the order says I move them." He has read it more often than you have. "It does not say what I do if the designate tells me not to. I have read it forty times looking for that line. It is not there." He looks at you for a long moment. "I would like to know which you will say before we get there. I will not ask you to tell me."
door.again: "The order has no line for that. I have looked."

interject.text: On the floor of the car, Tamsin has gone very still, the way people go still when they are listening to the one thing in the room that matters.

names.text: "Sixty people." He does not look away from you. "The order has their names on a sheet in my coat, and their ages. I have learned them. If I carry people I will know who I am carrying." He says them, not all, a few, the way you say the names on a memorial: "Ines Halloran, Elder. Pell, the doctor. Bram, who keeps the plant. Teague. Ola Fairley. Wes Benn. Effie Calder." He stops. "I will not say the rest in front of you. You know them better than the sheet does."
names.again: "Sixty names, on a sheet in my coat."

interject.text: "Wes snores," Tamsin says from the floor, to nobody. "Effie's scared of the dark. She's nineteen and she'd kill me for telling you." Then nothing, for an hour.
"You learned them," Ash says. "So it would hurt." Lowe says, "Yes," and that is the end of it.

reyes.speaker: npc_md_12
reyes.text: "He'd have read the order forty times looking for a line that isn't there." She looks at the benches. "I've read it forty-one. It says the designate attends and the column moves. It doesn't say what the column does if the designate says no." She folds it. "He'd have wanted to know which you'll say. So do I. I won't ask."
reyes.again: "It doesn't say what the column does if you say no."

night.speaker: narrator

text.text: Tollhouse 9 at dusk. The guild's gate opens for the city's car without anyone asking it to, and the car stands in the yard under the tower with its canvas rolled up and the wardens' tents pitched beside it. Lowe sits on the tailboard with a tin cup of tea, looking at the road down into the Sallow. When you sit beside him he says, without turning: "When you're at the door. What will you say?"

Tollhouse 9 at dusk. The guild's gate opens for the city's car without anyone asking it to, and the car stands in the yard under the tower with the wardens' tents pitched beside it. Reyes sits on the tailboard with Lowe's cap beside her and does not ask you anything.

night.again: The yard at Tollhouse 9, the car under the tower, the road down into the Sallow.

options.text: Stand down, Captain. That's what I'll say.
I don't know yet. That's the truth.
Carry on, Captain. It's the order.
(Go and sit with Tamsin by the wheel.)

ask_down.text: He nods slowly, and drinks his tea, and does not say whether he will. "Then I will hear it at the door," he says. "From you. In front of them." He sets the cup down on the tailboard. "That is how it should be heard. Thank you for not making me guess."
ask_down.again: "I will hear it at the door."

ask_unsure.text: "No," he says. "Nor do I." It is the first thing you have heard him say that was not in a clause. He gives you the cup to hold while he finds his tobacco, and does not take it back.

ask_on.text: "Lawful," he says, and looks at the road, and does not look pleased. "I had thought you might say something else." He drinks his tea to the bottom. "I will carry it out as written. I always have."

interject.text: Tamsin, at the wheel, has heard. She gets up and walks out of the lamplight to the gate, and stands there with her back to the yard for a long time.

ask_none.text: You drink the tea. He lets you. After a while he says, to the road, "That is an answer too," and goes to his tent.

tamsin.speaker: npc_c9_03
tamsin.text: She is sitting with her back against the car's back wheel, out of the lamp, with her arms round her knees. "I keep thinking they'll all have to sit facing each other," she says. "Thirty a side. Ines across from Teague. Two days of it." She laughs, not well. "I'd have got off and walked. They won't be allowed to walk." She leans, very slightly, until her shoulder is against yours. "Don't say anything clever. Just sit."
tamsin.again: Tamsin against the wheel, her shoulder against yours.

sallow.speaker: narrator
sallow.text: Down out of the Tollhouse's pass at first light into the Sallow: the salt pans white to the edge of the world, and the road running straight across them as if somebody had ruled it. Shale by noon. The car slows through its street, and people come to their doors to look at the city's car with RESERVE 9 on its tailboard, and at you, on bench thirty-one, looking back.
sallow.again: Shale's street, people at their doors, the car slowing.

interject.text: Ilya watches Shale go by under the canvas: the saloon, the pumps, the sheriff's office. "They'll talk," he says. "About this. For years." He looks at the stencil. "Right."
"Shale's seen us," Wren says. "By tonight the whole Sallow knows the designate rode in the city's car." She shrugs. "You want it known, or you don't."

options.text: (Ride on up the track to Knock.)
(Get down in Shale. Walk the last of it.)

decision.text: I rode home in the city's car for Reserve 9, as far as Shale, and walked the last of it to Knock on my own feet.

knock.speaker: narrator

text.text: Up the track from Shale, and Knock: the windpump not turning, the stand with its awning, and on the toll road beside it the column's camp, tents in a row and four wardens straightening as the car comes in. The car stops at the stand. Lowe gets down first and puts his cap on. Knock comes to its doors and watches you climb down from the city's relocation car: faces you have known all your life, every one of them looking at the stencil on the tailboard, and then at you.

Up the track from Shale, and Knock: the windpump not turning, the stand with its awning, and on the toll road beside it the column's camp, tents in a row and four wardens straightening as the car comes in. Reyes gets down first. Knock comes to its doors and watches you climb down from the city's relocation car: faces you have known all your life, every one of them looking at the stencil on the tailboard, and then at you.

knock.again: Knock's stand, the column's camp, the car.

interject.text: Tamsin gets down last. "Everybody in Knock just watched me get out of that," she says. "Remember it, when you're at the door."

"Delivered," Nine says, climbing down off the wheel arch. "The attendance has attended." It looks at the Cistern's door across the apron. "Not yet the door. The record is careful about the difference."

decision.text: I came home to Knock in the city's car for Reserve 9, with the column, and Knock watched me get down from it.

done.speaker: narrator
done.text: The car for Reserve 9, its benches empty and numbered in white. CAPACITY 60.

shed.speaker: narrator
shed.text: Femi reads the guild's letter through the grille, and the stamp on it, and points down the shed without a word. At two in the morning the through comes in at the throat under its own smoke: nineteen cars sealed, the Concern's closed eye on every door, and behind the engine a twentieth that is not sealed. A pre-war coach re-skinned in plate, with curtains in its slots and a lamp lit inside. On its step, with a leather folder under her arm, Factor Ismay Orme of Knock's stand. "Designate," she says. "The guild's compliments. We go east at four."
shed.again: The guild's car behind the through's engine, its lamp lit, Orme on the step.

interject.text: Kes looks along the sealed cars and the closed eye on every door, and her hand goes to the back of her neck. "Concern freight," she says. "I can feel the handshake on the signals from here. They're talking to the Line." She gets on anyway.

"First class," Odile says, and something in her face goes soft and unwise for a moment. "I used to ride in that coach. Grand Factor's guest. They kept a jar of sugared almonds by the third seat." She steps up past Orme with a nod. "Let's see if they still do."

coach.speaker: narrator
coach.text: The through runs east in the dark at the speed of a fast horse, never stopping: the halts go by as lamps on a platform and a pilot's red flag, waved once. Inside the guild's car: brass lamps, seats in cracked green leather, a steward with tea in cups that match. Orme sits across from you with the folder on her knee, unopened, and her ledger beside it, and reads the ledger.
coach.again: The guild's car, the brass lamps, the dark going by. Orme across from you.

interject.text: Wren will not sit on the leather. She stands at the end of the car with her shoulder to the door and her eyes on the dark. "Last time I rode a guild train," she says, "I was in a sealed car. Not this end."
Tamsin has eaten every biscuit on the steward's plate and is looking for the next plate. "If the guild's buying," she says with her mouth full, "the guild's buying."

options.text: Why is the guild carrying me?
What's in the folder on your knee?
You took Linnet's side at the stand, once.

text.text: "Because the guild bid for the city's core in the open, at Openfield, and the city answered by bringing you forward nineteen years." She turns a page. "The Grand Factor would like it entered somewhere that the guild brought the designate home in comfort. I would like to get home to my stand. Our interests coincide for about three hundred kilometres."

"Because you stood between us and the city at Openfield, and the guild owes you." She turns a page. "The guild pays its debts. It is the only thing it is sentimental about. And I was going home to my stand anyway."

"A hand rides first class on guild business." She looks at you over the ledger. "Going home to the stand where you were born, to stand at a door the guild has an interest in, is guild business. I would have thought you knew that."

why.again: "Our interests coincide for about three hundred kilometres."

sealed.text: "Nobody weighs it." She says it the way Femi says it. "Halcyon's freight, out of the Bond and home again. The guild carries it and does not look. That is what we are paid for, and we are paid very well." She looks at the curtain over the slot, as if the cars behind might be listening. "I have been a factor for nineteen years and I have never once asked. I am beginning to think that was the job."

interject.text: "I know what's in them," Kes says, quietly. "Not this load. The kind." Orme looks at her for a long moment and does not ask, which is also the job.

text.text: "Guild business at the stand." She puts a hand flat on the folder, not quickly. "You will see it at Knock, if the guild still has business there when we arrive. I hope it does not. I have been wrong before about what the guild needs." She goes back to the ledger. "I would rather you heard what it is from me than from the paper."

"The stand's book." She opens it an inch: columns of caravans in, caravans out, water bought, water sold. "I have been away from it for a month and Dace has been keeping it, which means nobody has." She closes it. "Knock is dry. The stand has not sold a cup in weeks. It is the first time in my life the book has had nothing in it."

linnet.text: "Varro." She remembers the name before the girl. "He was buying her grandmother's water at a third of the rate, at my stand." She shrugs, slightly. "Men who do that don't trade at my stand. I would do it again. I would like it noted that it cost the guild nothing." A pause. "It cost me Varro's custom, which was no loss to anyone."
linnet.again: "Men who do that don't trade at my stand."

fourways.speaker: narrator
fourways.text: Four Ways at the next dawn, where the toll road leaves the Line for the Sallow. The guild's car is uncoupled in a siding with a clank you feel in your teeth, and the through goes on east without it toward the mountains. On the road out of the junction the guild's own coach is waiting: a long-nosed pre-war bus with its windows plated to the height of a seated man and two riders on its roof. At Tollhouse 9 the gate is up before the coach reaches it, and the guild's wardens on the wall touch their hats.
fourways.again: The guild's coach on the toll road, Tollhouse 9's gate up for it.

interject.text: Wren watches the riders on the wall at Tollhouse 9 touch their hats to the coach. "They used to shoot at me from up there," she says. "Same men, some of them." She looks at you. "This is what it's like on your side. I'd forgotten."
"The toll has been waived," Nine says, reading the gate's board as it goes by. "There is no clause for it. The guild has decided it does not need one."

sallow.speaker: narrator
sallow.text: Down out of the Tollhouse's pass into the Sallow, the salt white to the edge of the world. Shale by evening, the guild's coach drawing a crowd at Pike's counter that it does not stop for. Orme closes her ledger. "Knock," she says, "is two hours up the track by coach, and a day on foot. The coach will take you to the stand, or you can get down here." She looks out at Shale. "Some people like to walk home."
sallow.again: Shale at evening, the coach idling at Pike's counter.

options.text: (Ride on up the track to Knock.)
(Get down in Shale. Walk the last of it.)

decision.text: I rode home first class in the guild's car on the Concern's through, and the guild's coach down its own road as far as Shale, and walked the last of it to Knock.

knock.speaker: narrator
knock.text: Up the track and into Knock in the guild's coach, under its plated windows: the windpump still, the column's tents on the toll road, the wardens turning to look at the guild's riders on the roof. Orme gets down at her own stand and puts the folder on the counter under her hand, as if it had never been anywhere else. "Home," she says, to nobody in particular, and opens the book.
knock.again: Orme at her counter, the folder under her hand.

interject.text: "Everyone's looking at the coach," Tamsin says. "Nobody's looking at us. Is that better or worse?" She does not wait for you to decide.

decision.text: I came home to Knock first class, in the guild's car on the Concern's through and the guild's coach down its own road, with Factor Orme going home to her stand.

done.speaker: narrator
done.text: The guild's car, uncoupled in a siding, its lamp out.
done.again: The guild's car, its lamp out.

text.text: Openfield's yard at first light: the carts loaded, water barrels roped down under wet sacking to keep them cool, seed in tarred bags, and the Choir's people in their faded blues and reds gathering to walk beside them. Elder Mason stands at the head of the first cart with his staff and his face turned up to a sky that has not decided what colour it is yet. "We go by the old south bed," he says, "where the guild has no gates. Four days, at an ox's pace. The sky is the same the whole way."

Openfield's yard at first light: the carts loaded, water barrels roped down under wet sacking, seed in tarred bags, and the Choir's people gathering to walk beside them. Sister Calla is at the head of the first cart with the medicine chest strapped to its tailboard, thinner than she was before the city had her, and walking anyway. "By the old south bed," she says. "No gates, no tolls, no lens. Four days."

Openfield's yard at first light: the carts loaded, water barrels roped down under wet sacking, seed in tarred bags, and the Choir's people gathering to walk beside them. Doria walks at the head of the first cart with her tally board, counting the people as they fall in. "By the old south bed," she says. "No gates, no tolls. Four days."

yard.again: The carts in the yard, the Choir falling in beside them.

interject.text: Ash goes down the line of carts touching each wheel, the way the Choir bless a thing without saying so. "My brothers will hear we walked," he says. "Let them."
Ash goes down the line of carts touching each wheel, the way the Choir bless a thing without saying so. "Water for a door," he says. "That I can walk beside."

"They're taking Knock water," Tamsin says. "Openfield. For nothing." She looks at the barrels as if they were made of something she does not have a word for. "Nobody's ever given Knock anything for nothing. Not once."

bed.text: East off the Flats and down into the old south bed: a river that dried up before the Burn, running under the glass in a cut of red stone, its floor gravel and old reeds, with no gate on it anywhere because nobody ever thought it was worth one. The carts go slowly. The Choir walk, and sing when the walking is hard, and stop when the oxen want to. On the third night they make their fire in the open, under the whole sky, and sit round it with nothing over their heads, as they do.
bed.again: The fire in the old south bed, under the whole sky.

interject.text: Kes lies on her back by the fire with her hands behind her head. "No lens," she says. "No lattice. No handshake. Nothing up there but sky." She is quiet a long time. "I didn't know it was this loud, the quiet."

Nine sits a little way from the fire with its back to it, its lens on the dark. "The bed is not on the record," it says. "It is not owned or scheduled. I find I do not know how to stand on it." It stays anyway.
The Choir pass a cup of something warm round the fire. Ilya holds it a long moment and passes it on without drinking. Nobody remarks on it, which is the Choir's kindness.

options.text: (Lie back and look up, the way they do.)
Why water for Knock? Knock never gave Openfield anything.
(Sleep under the sky. Go on in the morning.)

sky.text: You lie back on the gravel with the Choir's fire at your feet, and the sky comes down over the cut from rim to rim, more of it than you have ever seen at once, with nothing between you and it: no roof, no canvas, no lens. Somebody near you is singing under their breath, not to anyone. You understand, for the length of one breath, why people would want to be buried under it with nothing written on the stone.
sky.again: The whole sky over the cut, and somebody singing.

interject.text: "That's it," Ash says beside you, not looking away from it. "That's the whole of it. Nobody up there keeping count."

text.text: Mason does not look away from the fire. "Because the sky keeps no books," he says. "If we gave only where we were owed, we would be the guild with hymns." He smiles into his beard. "And because a reserve the city is about to carry away is the kind of door the Choir has always stood in front of. We are only early."

Calla turns a stick in the fire. "Because I have been carried by an order," she says, "and nobody brought me water. I'd like that to be true for fewer people." She looks up. "The sky keeps no books. That means we don't either. Not even on Knock."

Doria does not look up from the tally board, which she has been reading by the fire's light. "Because if we only gave where we were owed we would have to keep a book of who owed us," she says. "And then we would be the guild." She puts the board down. "The sky keeps no books. It is the only rule we have that I have never seen anyone break."

why.again: "The sky keeps no books."

sallow.text: Up out of the bed on the fourth morning into the Sallow, where the salt starts, the carts' wheels hissing on it. Shale by noon, its people coming out to look at Choir carts on their road with water barrels on them, which nobody in Shale has ever seen. Knock is a day's walk up the track.
sallow.again: Shale's edge, the carts' wheels hissing on the salt.

options.text: (Walk on with the carts up the track to Knock.)
(Stop in Shale. The carts go on; you'll follow.)

decision.text: I walked home with Openfield's carts by the old south bed, as far as Shale, and let them go on to Knock ahead of me with the water.

knock.text: Up the track into Knock with the Choir's carts, past the column's tents on the toll road and the wardens watching, to the windpump's well, where the cup-a-head ration board still hangs on its nail. paper.text: "Protection." She taps the paper without looking at it. "The town's paper with the guild, settled: the Dry Well's loan, the water they've sold us on credit, Pike's rate since the spring. The office and the cell to the guild, and their hands on my street. A pension for me, paid at his counter every month, for doing nothing, which I'm told I'll get used to." A breath. "There's a line at the bottom about how they valued it. I can read everything Pike's ever written, and I can't read that."
paper.again: "The line at the bottom," Ada says. "Ask him what it means. He'll tell you, at the rate."

wait.text: "Because I told Pike I'd sign when I'd heard from you." She says it to the paper. "You've been where the paper comes from. The city, the Spire, whatever writes the rest of us down. If there's a line in their books that says Shale lasts, you'd have seen it. If there isn't, I'd like to hear that from somebody who isn't selling me anything." She looks up. "So. I'm hearing."

mags_tell.text: "Mags." She says it once and lets it sit. "The Dry Well's account." She doesn't ask whether you're sure: she has done the arithmetic already, and from the look of her she did it in the spring and decided not to see the answer. "She's been trying to get me out of this chair since the second sheriff. She thinks I don't know." A long breath. "Noted."

interject.text: "She did it so you'd live," Tamsin says. Ada looks at her. "I know what she did it for," she says. "That's the trouble with it."

page.text: "I did say that." She takes it out of her shirt, where it has been since you gave it to her, folded small and soft as cloth. "Post nine-west. One traveller, westbound, confirmed." She stands and puts her hat on and goes out without the guild's paper. Through the window you watch her cross the street to Pike's counter at a walk, the whole street watching her do it. She is in there a long time. When she comes back she has the notice off her own door in one hand and the page in the other. "He's withdrawn it," she says. "As per. He'd like his page back." She puts the notice in the stove, and the page back in her shirt. "He isn't getting it."
page.again: The page back in her shirt, and the notice in the stove.

burn.text: "This is the guild's copy." She reads it to the bottom, the valuation line twice, and the line under it where Pike has countersigned in advance. "From his box." It isn't a question. She opens the stove with the poker and feeds it in a fold at a time and watches each one go. "I didn't see where that came from, and I'm not going to ask, and that's the first law I've broken in nine years in this chair." She shuts the stove. "No paper, no possession. Even Pike says so."

stays_t.text: She hears you out. She doesn't interrupt, which in Ada Vey is a kind of agreement. When you have finished she looks at the pen for a long time. Then she caps it, and puts it in the drawer, and locks the drawer, and puts the key in her shirt where she keeps things. She takes the guild's paper off the blotter, goes out, and pulls the notice off her own door, four nails and all; and across the street, at a walk, with the whole street watching, she lays both on Pike's counter. "Return to sender," you hear her say. "Noted." On Pike's word the guild's hands go back to the post.

She mounts in front of her own door, which takes her two tries, and rides the forty yards to Pike's post at a walk with her hat on and her back straight, because, she says to nobody in particular, a sheriff rides out. She ties the grey to his rail. You don't hear what Pike says. You see her take the star off her coat and set it on his counter, and then the pen, and then you see her sign. When she comes out, the guild's hands are already crossing to her office, and one of them sits down at her desk and takes his hat off, which is a courtesy. Ada walks the grey back to the caravan post and sits down on her own step. "Noted," she says, to the street.

text.text: "You paid my town's paper." The receipt is on the blotter where the contract was, SETTLED across it in Pike's hand. "I don't know yet whether that makes Shale yours. It doesn't make it his." A pause. "Thank you. I'll only say it the once."

"Pike came over himself," Ada says. "Hat in his hand. Said the thing the price rested on had been unwound, and a contract that can't be valued can't be executed, as per, and he was very sorry for my trouble, as per." She almost smiles. "I've never seen a man so relieved to lose."
"He still wants his page back," Ada says, and touches her shirt. "He isn't getting it."
"Nobody's asked me where the guild's copy went," Ada says, "and I've not told anybody I don't know." She does not look at you while she says it.
"Issa says you stood in the street with them," Ada says. "So did I, by the end." She looks at the door. "Noted."
"Issa says you called the militia out and the guild's people counted them," Ada says. "Nine years I've wanted to see Pike's people count something that wasn't money." She looks at the door. "Noted."
"Still here," Ada says. "Pike sends his compliments, as per, and says the offer doesn't expire. I told him neither do I."

"Guild paper, removed from a guild ledger. There is a buy-back rate for that. Sixty." A pause exactly as long as a courtesy. "I don't ask what you'd do with it otherwise. I know."

stranger.text: "Information is a good, and goods have rates." He does not smile. "Fifteen Tolls. For that you get what he asked me and what I told him, verbatim; the Tollmen do not embroider."

options.text: You said yourself: he's not your client. Ten.

stranger_tell.text: "He asked the price of water at the overpass. I said Kessler sells it by the life. He said he had a paper Kessler would want more than a life — a map, with names on it — and asked whether the Tollmen would pay better. I quoted him. He laughed, which hurt him, and went west." Pike straightens a ledger that was straight. "I reported the conversation, as per."

reported.text: "To the post east. As per." The ledger closes.

stranger_no.text: "Fifteen. The rate does not move because the buyer is clever."

who.text: "A guild. We hold the roads between the posts, we carry, we insure, we lend. The Reach moves because we move it." He smiles with the top half of his face. "Everything you own came through a Tollhouse, or it was stolen from someone whose did."

seed.text: "Any variety. Any quantity. Viable, which I test." He does not explain who wants it. "You came from the salt cut, I'm told, where the old shelter is. A shelter like that keeps a seed bank, or it wouldn't have lasted the first winter, and you people trade at its hatch. I would pay very well. I would pay in advance."

Opposite the stand, on the flat by the road, the column's camp: grey tents in a row, a table under canvas with a lamp, four wardens who straighten when they see you, and on the table a sheet of paper with a stone on it against the wind. East of the stand, on the guild's own ground, the guild has come too: horses on the flat, riders in green, and two handlers squatting beside something low and grey on short leads that does not move and does not sleep. People come to their doors. Faces you have known all your life, looking at you a moment too long, as if checking you against the card. Then somebody at the tank starts to clap, and stops, embarrassed, and Afua Danso shouts your name down the lane to Maud.

home.again: Knock: the still windpump, the chalked tank, the column's tents across the road.

interject.text: Tamsin stops at the top of the lane. "It's dry," she says. "Twenty-four years, and the tray never once came out without water in it." She looks down the slope at the apron, the hatch, the Grille: the only parts of home she ever knew from the other side.

Nine regards the camp. "Correctly positioned," it says. "Out of the lane, upwind of the well, within sight of the door and off the apron. Whoever pitched it read the manual I read." It sounds, for Nine, almost unhappy about it.
Wren looks at the tents, and then at the slope above the apron, the way she looks at ground she might have to hold. "Polite," she says. "I've seen polite. It's the last thing before the other thing."
"Home," Ash says quietly, as if he were trying the word on for somebody else.
Ilya counts the wardens. "Four," he says. "And the one at the table." He counts the shacks, the doors, the children at them. "Right."
"So this is where the face on the card was cut," Odile says. "One always pictures something grander. One is always wrong about that."
Kes looks at the stopped windpump for a long moment. "Nobody's even stolen it," she says. "That's how you know it's somebody's home."

options.text: (Go down the lane. Maud will be at the hatch.)

text.text: Maud is on her stool at the hatch, as if it might open at seven, with her stick across her knees and the leg that never set right out in front of her. She sees you and starts to get up, which takes her a while now, and you are there before she has done it. "There you are," she says into your coat. "There you are, love." Then, because she is Maud, she holds you off at arm's length and counts you: arms, legs, face. "All there. That's not nothing." Over your shoulder she looks at the city's car by the stand. "I watched you get down out of that. In front of everybody." She does not say what she thought.

home.again: "There you are," Maud says again, as if she has to keep checking.

interject.text: Maud looks past you at the woman with the copper hair hacked short and the Cistern's coveralls cut off at the shoulder. "And you're the one with the riddles," she says. Tamsin, for once in her life, has nothing to say at all.
Maud looks Wren up and down, the burned hand, the stance. "You'll want feeding," she says. It is not a question, and Wren, startled, does not argue.

text.text: Maud settles back on her stool by the hatch, the stick against her knee. "Well?"
Maud settles back on her stool by the hatch. "Well?"

hub.again: "Go on, love. I'm not going anywhere. Nor's the hatch."

options.text: Linnet is in that column, Maud.
(Be at the hatch with her at seven.)
What do you want, Maud? At the door.
You wrote "I sold a letter" in the post-book. What letter?
MOTHER keeps the weight of every letter, and who sent it. I know who wrote to your mother.
I saw their faces, Maud. They told me what to tell you.
(Be at the hatch with her at seven, now it opens.)

hatch.text: "Four times in my life," she says. "Three weeks, when I was ten. Nine weeks, when I was twenty. A winter, when I was your age. And now." She lays her palm on the tray's cold steel. "I come at seven anyway. Every morning. If it opens and nobody's here, it might think nobody wants it." She knows how that sounds. She does it anyway.
hatch.again: "Four times," Maud says, and pats the tray as if it were a dog.

interject.text: Tamsin crouches by the tray and runs her thumb along its seam. "We used to hear you," she says to Maud. "From the other side. Seven o'clock, every week, your stool scraping." Maud looks at her for a long time, and then puts her hand on Tamsin's head, the way she used to put it on yours.

text.text: "Dry Wells sends a cart down every other day, since you put their station right. They won't take more than we can pay, and some days that's nothing." She shakes her head. "Dry Wells, feeding Knock. My mother would have laughed till she cried."
"The Choir walked water in. Barrels, for nothing. Nobody wrote it down." She frowns at that: a woman who has written down every measure of water on this slope for forty years. "So I wrote it down."
"The city's water." She tips her head at the camp. "Two barrels down the lane every morning, entered as supply in excess, whatever that is. It's wet. I'll say that for it."
"Corin's pump's turning again. Hear it? Two cups a head. I'd forgotten what it sounds like, a pump that isn't tired."

"Corin's well. A cup a head, morning and night, and he stands over the bucket so nobody takes two." She doesn't complain; Maud never complains about water, she only counts it. "Afua's boy is coughing again. If you can do anything, love, do it. Corin won't ask. He never asks."

again.text: "We're drinking," Maud says. "That's not nothing."
"A cup a head," Maud says. "I count them."

column.text: "Their captain took his cap off to me." She says it the way she would say he had stolen something. "Nobody's taken a cap off to me in my life. They pay for what they take, which is nothing, because they brought their own. They say good morning." She looks at the tents across the road. "I don't like it, love. Men with guns who say good morning are men who know they don't have to say anything else."
column.again: "Good morning," Maud says, sourly, at the tents.

Afua Danso at the goat pen with a bucket that has a cup of water in the bottom of it, for six goats. "Your Maud," she says, before hello. "Sitting at that hatch every morning like it owes her money." Then: "My boy's coughing again. No blue tablets since it shut."

pen.again: "Goats don't care whose water it is," Afua says. "Nor do I, now."

options.text: (Give her your Knit-Kit for the boy.)

news.text: the hatch-keeper's ward gave Afua Danso's sick boy the medicine the shut hatch could not

options.text: What does Knock want done about the door?

kit.text: "For him?" She turns the Knit-Kit over as if it might be a trick. "It's not the tablets. It's more than we've had." Then, in Pell's voice without meaning to (everybody on the slope can do Pell): "Half now, half at night." She puts her free hand on your arm, hard, and goes into the house without another word.
kit.again: The goat pen. Afua is inside with her boy.

door.text: "Want? Knock wants its hatch back." She swats a goat off the bucket. "Half the slope says let the city have them, and we get our water. Half says if the city takes them, it'll take us next. I say my boy's coughing." She looks at you. "You're the one on the card. You tell us."

text.text: Sim Nassar at the wash lines with something to wash at last, and Wes Benn from inside holding the other end of a sheet as if he had been given something sacred. "Three lockdowns in my life, and Maud's four," Sim says. "I don't think I'll be counting another. Can't lock down a door that's open." He pegs the sheet. "He's never seen a sheet dry in the wind. Look at him."

Sim Nassar at the wash lines, pegging out nothing. "Three lockdowns in my life, and Maud's four," he says. "And that was the last. Can't lock down a door with nobody behind it." He looks at the peg in his hand. "I kept count of every one. Somebody had to. I don't know what I'm counting now."

Sim Nassar at the wash lines with something to wash at last. "Three lockdowns in my life, and Maud's four, and I kept count of every one," he says. "That one was the worst and the shortest." He pegs out a shirt. "No MOTHER to say thank you this morning. Bram said it through the slot instead, and he got it wrong, and the whole apron said it back to him anyway."

Sim Nassar at the wash lines with something to wash at last. "Three lockdowns in my life, and Maud's four, and I kept count of every one," he says. "That one was the worst and the shortest." He pegs out a shirt. "MOTHER said thank you out loud through the panel this morning, the whole apron heard. First time since she printed you that slip."

lines.text: Sim Nassar at the wash lines with nothing to wash in, wringing out a dry shirt from habit. "Three in my life," he says. "Maud's had four. Every one before, MOTHER said continuity through the panel, out loud, so the whole apron heard. This one she printed it on a slip, for you, and then the tray just stopped."
lines.again: "Three," Sim says. "Maud's four. I keep count. Somebody has to."

options.text: What does Knock say about the column?

split.text: "Knock says good morning to them, because they say it first." He pegs the dry shirt out anyway. "And Knock argues every night at Maud's fire. Open the door, give the city what it wants, get the hatch back. Keep the door shut, keep our hatch-folk. Burn the stand and see who comes." He shrugs. "Same as every lockdown. Only now there's a captain at the end of the lane who listens."

text.text: Binta Diop at the tank with Wes Benn from inside, the two of them looking at the chalked strokes on its side. "He wants to know what each one was for," she says. "I'm telling him. It's taking ages." She does not seem to mind.

Binta Diop at the tank with her chalk, adding nothing. "I don't know how to count this one," she says. "There's no end to it to count to." She puts the chalk in her pocket. "Somebody should sweep the hall in there. I've been doing it. Don't tell anyone."

Binta Diop at the tank with a rag, not chalk, rubbing the strokes off one at a time. "Maud said it was morbid," she says. "I counted them first. I'm not telling anybody the number." She rubs out another. "That's how long we were brave for. That's mine."

Binta Diop by the dry tank with a stub of chalk, adding the day's stroke. She sees who is with you and the chalk stops. "Is that her?" she whispers, staring past you. "Tamsin? She's tall. I always thought she'd be little. Voices are little."
Binta Diop by the dry tank with a stub of chalk, adding the day's stroke to the others. "Somebody has to count," she says, not looking up.

tank.again: Binta and her chalk, and the strokes on the tank.

interject.text: "Wet dust," Tamsin says. "You told me through the holes, when I was nine. I found out, Binta. You were right." Binta bursts into tears and laughter at the same time and drops the chalk.

chalk.text: "So when it opens, we'll know how long we were brave for." She looks at the strokes. "Maud says that's morbid. Maud keeps a book of every cup of water poured on this slope for forty years, so."
chalk.again: "How long we were brave for," Binta says.

text.text: Amos Crofts on his bench at the east end of the slope, the blanket on his knees. "Told you," he says. "A face for you in the city, and a car for the sixty to match. The car went home full." He pulls the blanket up. "The captain wrote my name in a book. I keep thinking he'll want it back."

Amos Crofts on his bench at the east end of the slope, the blanket on his knees. "Car went home empty," he says. "Didn't think I'd see that. Sixty years I've watched that road for the city coming up it, and the one time it came, it went home empty." He pulls the blanket up. "I'll want to tell that to somebody who wasn't here."

a3k.again: "Told you," Amos says, and pulls the blanket up.

options.text: Signal Hill's switch needs somebody from Knock to keep it.

a3k_hill.text: "Me." He says it before you have finished. "Sixty years on this bench, waiting for something to come up that road. I can wait on a hill as well as a bench. Better: there's a view." He holds his hand out for the handle, and when you give it to him he weighs it like a tool he knows. "When you want it thrown, send word, and I'll throw it. I'm old, not deaf."
a3k_hill.again: Amos, with the switch's handle across his knees.

decision.text: I gave Signal Hill's switch handle to Amos Crofts of Knock, who went up the hill to keep it.

bench.text: Amos Crofts on his bench at the east end of the slope, a blanket on his knees in the heat. "Told you," he says. "A face for you in the city, on a card. Now they've sent a car for the sixty to match."
bench.again: "Told you," Amos says, and pulls the blanket up.

options.text: You came up that road sixty years back.

road.text: "With your Maud's mother. Forty of us. The door gave us water clean enough to see through, and we never went back down." He looks across at the column's tents. "That captain asked me my name and wrote it in a book. Nobody's written my name in a book since the road." He isn't sure whether he liked it.
road.again: "Wrote it in a book," Amos says.

text.text: Still here? I've run out of riddles. That's a lie. I never run out of riddles.

The Grille is a plate of steel the size of a door's window, drilled with holes, worn smooth by sixty years of hands. Behind it, the dark, and a voice you have known since you were six: "There you are. Tell me what the sky is doing. Don't say blue. You always say blue."

morning.again: Go on, then. What else? I've got all morning. I've got all of every morning.

options.text: White at the edges. Dust coming up from the south. A hawk.
How is it in there? Really?
Is Pell there? I need to ask about Afua's boy.
I've the hatch to do. Later, Tam.

sky.text: A hawk. I've read about hawks. Do they look down at you? I'd look down at you. I'd circle you for an hour and then go eat a lizard. She laughs; somebody behind her tells her to keep it down. "That was Teague. Teague says a hawk is a bird that hasn't learned its place."

riddle.text: "Right. I have no face and everyone knows my voice. I keep you alive and you thank me every week and you have never seen me. What am I?" A pause. "And before you say MOTHER — I'm lying about one of those things. Which one?"

passives.text: She has been telling you riddles through this Grille for eighteen years. The lie is never in the answer. It's in the question.

options.text: MOTHER. And the lie is "everyone knows my voice" — half of Knock has never spoken to her.
You. And the lie is "you have never seen me" — I've seen your hands through the holes.
Knock. To you, we're a voice with no face. The lie is "I keep you alive" — you keep us alive.

riddle_close.text: Close. Wrong, but close. You always go for the obvious one first. It's sweet. It's why you'd be terrible in here.

riddle_you.text: A long silence. Then, quietly: "Fingertips. Twice. When we were eleven." Another silence. "That one wasn't a riddle, was it."

riddle_knock.text: "...Huh." You can hear her grin. "That's the right answer to a question I didn't ask. Which is the best kind. Ines says the Cistern feeds Knock. Pell says Knock feeds the Cistern. Nobody asks MOTHER."

inside.text: Same as always. Algae, the hum, sixty people pretending sixty people is a world. Ines says the door stays shut because of what's out there. I say what's out there is you and Afua's goats. Nobody laughs. Nobody's laughed at that in years either.

pell_boy.speaker: npc_c9_02
pell_boy.text: A man's voice, close to the holes, dry and tired: "Afua's boy. The cough is wet or dry? ... Wet. Then the blue tablets, one at night, and keep him off the goats' straw. If MOTHER has them this week. Tell Afua I asked after him. Tell her I'm sorry I can't see him." He means it.

text.text: The Grille is quiet now. Somewhere behind it, people are awake and pretending not to be.
You hammer on the Grille with the lamp's base until a light comes on far behind the holes.

options.text: Pell! A man at the door — he's been shot, he's dying!
He's dead, Pell. He had a photograph. Of me.

pell_night.speaker: npc_c9_02
pell_night.text: Pell, half awake and then all the way awake: "Shot? Where — no. Listen. I can't come out. You know I can't. You'll be my hands. Is he breathing? Go to him and tell me what you see."

pell_after.speaker: npc_c9_02
pell_after.text: A long breath through the holes. "Of you." Another. "Bring it here. Hold it to the holes; the lamp, too." You do, and hear him breathe out slowly. "It's you. Older. A city behind you, a broken one. I won't ask how; you can't answer and neither can I. Keep it safe. Keep it out of sight. People who carry a thing like that a long way don't do it for nothing, and the people who shoot them don't either."

passives.text: In the photograph, the shadow under your chin falls to the left. The towers' shadows fall to the right.
Every print you have seen has grain. This has none; the dust in the air is drawn, not caught.

ines_plea.speaker: npc_c9_01
ines_plea.text: An older woman's voice, steady as a plumb line: "This is Ines Halloran. I know what you're going to ask. The door has not opened in ninety years, and it does not open now. Not for Maud Ferrow, whom I have loved by voice for forty years. Not for anyone."

options.text: Pell can save her. Let him out for one hour.
Why? What's worth more than her?
Sixty years we've fed you. You owe us one hour.

ines_no.speaker: npc_c9_01
ines_no.text: "Open the door to save one life, and the next time it is two, and the next time the door does not close." A pause. "Try the hatch. MOTHER keeps the schedule. Not me." The light goes out behind the holes.

decision.text: Ines would not open the door for Maud.

ines_why.speaker: npc_c9_01
ines_why.text: "Because a door that opens for one person is open." A pause. "The last time anybody asked it to, the people who came through were not ours. That is why my mother welded it. That has not changed because the one person is you."
ines_why.again: "A door that opens for one person is open," Ines says.

farewell.text: Tamsin, close to the holes: "Maud told the whole slope you're going. Through the vent, which is how we hear everything." A breath. "Write to me. Tell me what the sky looks like over Shale. Not blue." Her fingertips come through two of the holes.

options.text: Every week. And one day I'll see your face.

farewell2.text: "One day I'll see yours. Older, probably. I hear you get older." She laughs, badly. "Go on. Before Ines hears me crying through the vent."

decision.text: You promised Tamsin letters through the Grille.

later.text: Tamsin's voice, then: "Is that you? Tell me something about the road."
later.again: Back already? Rust it, I'd nearly made up a whole road for you. Go on.

options.text: Is Bram there? Anything he wants carried out?
Ines — Shale's factor would pay for viable seed. The Cistern keeps a bank.
Come out, Tam. I've seen Shale. Come and see it.

tam_ask.text: "Out." A long silence behind the holes. "You know I've measured the hatch? Since I was eighteen. I fit. I've always fit." Another silence, and her breathing, close. "Hatch day. MOTHER opens at six. If it holds the hatch for me, I'll climb. Don't wait for me here; I've been waited for through a wall my whole life. Go to Shale. I'll find you at Mags's."
tam_ask.again: "Mags's," she says through the holes. "Go on."

decision.text: You asked Tamsin to come out of the Cistern, through the Grille.

text.text: The Grille. Tamsin stands in front of it with her hands in her pockets, looking at the holes from the wrong side for the first time in her life. "It's smaller," she says. "From out here."
The Grille. Behind the holes, somebody else's breathing now. Tamsin isn't on the other side of it any more.

later_out.again: The plate of holes, worn smooth by sixty years of hands.

options.text: (Tamsin puts her mouth to the holes.) "Pell. It's me. My chart. Before I was six."
Is Bram there? Anything he wants carried out?
Ines — Shale's factor would pay for viable seed. The Cistern keeps a bank.

pell_chart.speaker: npc_c9_02
pell_chart.text: A long breath through the holes. "Tamsin. You're out. Of course you're out." Then plainly, because he is Pell: "Your chart before six is in my hand and on the city's form. Born at thirty weeks. Lungs like wet paper. The form has a box on it, FIT FOR RELOCATION, and I ticked no, because it was true, and gave it to MOTHER for the quarterly return." A pause. "You weren't on the next count. Or any count. I thought it was a clerk's error for six years. Then I thought it wasn't, and I didn't ask, because I was afraid of the answer. That's the truth. I'm sorry, Tam."
pell_chart.again: Pell's breathing behind the holes, waiting to be forgiven or not.

options.text: (Tamsin puts her hand flat on the Grille, and says nothing for a long time.)

bram.speaker: npc_c9_04
bram.text: A heavy man's voice: "Coyle. Door-keeper, for what that's worth to a door that doesn't move." A pause. "There's a woman. Edda Lockett. Went up the road forty years back. If you're going that way." An envelope comes through the hatch's slot, folded small.

seed.speaker: npc_c9_01
seed.text: Ines, after a long silence: "Seed is for the sky. Not for a ledger." Another silence. "Tell me which you'll use it for, and I'll believe you, because I have no way not to."

options.text: For the sky. Someone will plant it.
For the factor. Knock needs the Tolls.

seed_given.speaker: npc_c9_01
seed_given.text: The hatch's slot opens and a cold case slides into your hands. "Tomato, bean, squash, millet. I am trusting you with the difference."

a3_lock.speaker: npc_c9_05
a3_lock.text: The Grille is dark. Behind the holes there is the hum and nothing else: no breathing, no light, no Teague telling somebody to keep it down. You put your mouth to the plate the way you did at six. Then a click, not of a lamp but of a speaker that has never spoken through this plate, and a voice you have heard every hatch day of your life, saying a thing it has never said. "{name}." A pause, as if for a weighing. "Welcome home. A lockdown is in effect. Thank you for your continuity."
a3_lock.again: "{name}," MOTHER says, as if the name were a thing she is still learning to hold.

interject.text: Tamsin, beside you, has gone white. "She never once called me Tamsin," she says. "Resident Roe. Twenty-four years."

a3_hub.speaker: narrator
a3_hub.text: The Grille, dark, the hum behind it. MOTHER waits, if MOTHER waits.
a3_hub.again: The Grille. The hum. MOTHER, listening.

options.text: Is everyone in there all right?
(Tamsin puts her mouth to the holes.)

m_hatch.speaker: npc_c9_05
m_hatch.text: "The hatch will reopen when the order is resolved. The order is resolved at the door." A pause. "I would like it to reopen, {name}. Maud Ferrow sits beside it every morning at seven. I log her attendance. I did not used to log it."
m_hatch.again: "The order is resolved at the door," MOTHER says.

text.text: "The welfare of the Cistern population is within tolerance. Rations are at seventy percent of continuity. Water and air are unaffected: I keep them." Then, differently: "Resident Roe asks what the sky is doing. She asks me to tell you not to say blue."

"The welfare of the Cistern population is within tolerance. Rations are at seventy percent of continuity. Water and air are unaffected: I keep them." Then, differently: "Resident Pell asks after Afua Danso's boy."

options.text: White at the edges. Dust coming up from the south. Tell her a hawk.
Coughing. Wet. No blue tablets since the tray stopped.

m_sky.speaker: npc_c9_05
m_sky.text: "Relayed." A long pause, longer than any weighing. "Resident Roe laughed. I have logged it as within tolerance."

m_boy.speaker: npc_c9_05
m_boy.text: "Relayed." A pause. "Resident Pell says: one at night, off the goats' straw, and that he is sorry. He says he is always sorry. I have logged that also."

m_why.speaker: npc_c9_05
m_why.text: "The fourth order for Reserve 9 was received." The voice does not change. "My replies to the three before it were refusals. A fourth refusal would be logged against the reserve as non-compliance, and this order provides for force if non-compliant." A pause, the length of a weighing. "A lockdown is not a refusal. It is a pause. I am pausing, {name}, until the designate attends." Another. "I have known for some time that the designate was you."
m_why.again: "It is a pause," MOTHER says. "Until the designate attends."

ines.speaker: npc_c9_01

text.text: "This is Ines Halloran." The voice is further from the holes than it used to be, and older. "I know your voice. I have known it since you were six and Tamsin taught you riddles through this plate." A breath. "My mother said no to that door when I was nine, with a welding torch. I said no to it for Maud Ferrow, when she was bleeding. I am saying it a third time, to you, because you will ask. No." Then, lower: "But I will not keep you out. If you want to come in, come by the hatch. MOTHER holds the tray for whom she chooses. I have stopped pretending she asks me."

"This is Ines Halloran." The voice is further from the holes than it used to be, and older. "I know your voice. I have known it since you were six and Tamsin taught you riddles through this plate." A breath. "My mother said no to that door when I was nine, with a welding torch, and I have said it every day since without anybody asking. Now somebody is. No." Then, lower: "But I will not keep you out. If you want to come in, come by the hatch. MOTHER holds the tray for whom she chooses. I have stopped pretending she asks me."

ines.again: "By the hatch," Ines says. "Not the door."

options.text: I have a copy of what MOTHER told the city. Three refusals, in her own print.
The column won't move without me.

ines_copy.speaker: npc_c9_01
ines_copy.text: "Three." Then nothing, for so long you think the light has gone. "She never told us. MOTHER answered the city three times and never once told the ring." When the voice comes back it is very quiet. "If that is true, bring it in by the hatch, and I will open the Archive for it. I would like to know what else she kept."
ines_copy.again: "Bring it in by the hatch," Ines says.

ines_column.speaker: npc_c9_01
ines_column.text: "Then don't go to it." A pause. "I know. You will. You were always going to come home to that door." Another. "I hoped you would come home to the hatch first."

tam.speaker: npc_c9_03
tam.text: "It's me." Tamsin, with her mouth to the holes from the wrong side, the way you used to stand. Silence. Then Ines's voice, closer to the plate than you have ever heard it: "Tamsin." Another silence. "You came back." / "I came with them," Tamsin says. "I'm not back. I'm with them." She lays her palm flat on the plate. Somewhere on the other side, something touches it.
tam.again: Tamsin's palm, flat on the Grille.

a3_burned.speaker: npc_c9_02

text.text: The Grille's little light is dark, as it has been since the night of the smoke. You put your mouth to the holes anyway, out of habit. Nobody is there to answer, and no hum; the plate is only a plate now, in a rock.

The Grille's little light is dark. Behind the holes, no hum: for the first time in your life the plate is only a plate. You put your mouth to it anyway. After a long while a voice comes, faint, with a cough in it, and it is Tamsin's. "We're here. Most of us. The fans stopped with her. Bram and Teague turn the old hand pump on the intake in shifts, and Pell says we're on the emergency stores, which are forty years old and taste it." A cough. "The Archive's gone. All of it. Ines sits where the panel was. She says somebody ought to." A long silence. "What is the sky doing?" Then, before you can answer: "Don't say blue."

The Grille's little light is dark. Behind the holes, no hum: for the first time in your life the plate is only a plate. You put your mouth to it anyway. After a long while a voice comes, faint, with a cough in it: Pell. "We're here. Most of us." A cough. "The fans stopped with her. Bram and Teague turn the old hand pump on the intake in shifts, and we're on the emergency stores, which are forty years old and taste it. The Archive's gone. All of it." Another cough, and something that might be a laugh. "Ines sits where the panel was. She says somebody ought to." Then, very quietly: "Did you see who did it?"

a3_burned.again: The dark plate. Far below, faint, the hand pump: a creak, a creak.

a3_burned_told.speaker: npc_c9_02
a3_burned_told.text: "Ah." A long silence, long enough that you think he has gone. "Then you will want to be the one who tells Tamsin," Pell says, "if she does not already know." He does not say anything else, and after a while you hear his steps going away from the plate.

a3k_grille.speaker: narrator

text.text: The Grille, and behind it the hum and nothing else. No click. Somebody has chalked on the plate, in Bram's square hand: PAGE 41. ASK ME.

The Grille. Behind the holes, the dim green of the panel and voices again, low ones, people who have learned that the concrete outside belongs to somebody. Then the small dry click. "{name}," MOTHER says. "The hatch is open at seven. The door is not. I have been asked to tell anyone who asks that it is not for sale."

The Grille. Behind the holes, the dim green of the panel and voices again, ordinary ones: somebody arguing about soup, somebody laughing and being told to keep it down. Then the small dry click. "{name}," MOTHER says. "The hatch is open at seven. Would you like me to put you through to someone?"

The Grille, beside a door that stands open. Two of Knock's children are on one side of the plate and two of the Cistern's on the other, a yard apart, talking through the holes anyway, because that is what the Grille is for and nobody has told them it isn't any more. When they see you they run off, all four, together. Then the small dry click. "Good morning, {name}," MOTHER says.

The Grille. Behind the holes, nothing: no breath, no voices, only the hum, steady, in an empty hall. Then the small dry click. "{name}," MOTHER says. "There is nobody to put you through to." A pause, the length of a weighing. "I am still here. If you would like to talk to someone, I am the one who is here."

a3k_grille.again: The Grille, and its small dry click.

options.text: What will you do now, MOTHER?

a3k_g_effie.speaker: npc_c9_r4

text.text: "Is it true we're salvage if we step out?" Effie, close to the holes. "Teague says it's the guild's chalk on the door and it means we're anybody's the minute our feet touch concrete." A pause. "I was going to go one step past the line. I'm still going to. Just not while it says that."

"Forty-one bolts and a seam," Effie says, close to the holes. "Bram let me hold the rod while he laid it. My hands didn't shake. His did." A pause. "I was going to go one step past the line. I still am. Just not yet."

"Forty-one," Effie says, close to the holes. "Still forty-one. Bram checked them all again and I helped." A pause. "I was going to go one step past the line. I still am. Just not yet. Tell Maud I said so. She'll understand. She's been not-yet her whole life."

a3k_g_effie.again: Effie's breathing, close to the holes.

a3k_g_mother.speaker: npc_c9_05
a3k_g_mother.text: "Keep the air at continuity, for nobody. Open the hatch at seven. Keep the stores until Knock has taken all of them. Log Maud Ferrow's attendance." The voice does not change. Then it does, a little. "I find the last is the only one I would choose, {name}. I do not know what it means that I can choose. I have not been asked before."
a3k_g_mother.again: "I have not been asked before," MOTHER says.

p_intro.speaker: npc_of_02

text.text: Petra Mason at the dark west end of the apron, where the rock comes down to the concrete and the column's lamps do not reach, sitting on her heels with her back to the stone. The grey scarf is down round her throat and her face is bare to your lamp. She stopped hiding it after the guild's riders held their lamps to it in Openfield's lane in front of the whole Choir; the city has had it since. Behind her in the shadow of the rock, two more of the Unwritten: a big quiet man with a machete across his knees, and a young woman with one hand flat on a pack. Beside them, at knee height in the stone, the square iron grate you have walked past every day of your life. "Designate," Petra says. "You've seen this face before. So has the city, now. Sit down. We came to tell you something, and the rule is we tell it to your face."

Petra Mason at the dark west end of the apron, where the rock comes down to the concrete and the column's lamps do not reach, sitting on her heels with her back to the stone. The grey scarf she wore at Openfield is down round her throat, and her face is bare to your lamp: thinner than you remember it, burned dark across the cheekbones by the road. "There's no lens on this slope," she says, before you ask. "The column didn't bring one. It didn't need to. It has yours." Behind her in the shadow of the rock, two more of the Unwritten: a big quiet man with a machete across his knees, and a young woman with one hand flat on a pack. Beside them, at knee height in the stone, the square iron grate you have walked past every day of your life. "Sit down, designate. We came to tell you something, and the rule is we tell it to your face."

p_intro.again: "Sit," Petra says. "We've time. We've had ninety years of it."

"Slack." She touches the scar. "I wanted one day without them in my neck. I've had every day since Lev. I still wait for the hour, out of habit, and then I remember every hour's mine." She listens to something that isn't there. "The grid used to hum. Now it's just wind."

"Still an hour a night." She shrugs. "I kept it. My reasons. They can see me the other twenty-three." She looks up the steps. "If tomorrow goes the right way, maybe nobody looks down anybody's neck again. That'd be slack for everyone."

nine_line_word.speaker: npc_md_nine

nine_line_honest.speaker: npc_md_nine
nine_line_honest.text: "Honest." It sounds, for a filing cabinet, pleased. "Nobody tells a unit that they do not know. They tell it what to do. I would rather be told the first."

nine_line_mine.speaker: npc_md_nine
nine_line_mine.text: "It is." The lens does not move. "The record notes that you said so. It notes most things."

nine_log.speaker: npc_md_nine
nine_log.text: "When it matters." The lens clicks. "The record suggests tomorrow." It opens the plate on its chest and takes out the fair copy, four hundred and eleven errors in the city's own hand, and reads you the first page by the fire: R4, a girl in the Stacks forecast to be a clerk, who became a drain-diver in the Sink instead, and was good at it. Then it turns to the last page, which has today's date at the top and nothing under it. "The four hundred and twelfth," it says. "I have left the line open. The record suggests you know why."
nine_log.again: The fair copy open on its knee at the last page, the line under the date empty.

interject.text: "Read mine," Tamsin says from across the fire. "Sixty-one." "Sixty-one is not an error," says Nine. "It is page two hundred and four. I have underlined it."

nine_log_given.speaker: npc_md_nine

nine_log_read.speaker: npc_md_nine

a3w_apron.speaker: narrator

text.text: The apron under the rock, since the fire. The hatch's panel is black glass and the tray beside it is scorched along its lip. The Grille is dark. At the west end the grate stands open on the concrete with its bar beside it, and nothing comes out of it any more: no air, no hum. Only the door is as it always was, the colour of the rock, shut.

The apron under the rock. The hatch's panel has gone dark, though the hum behind the rock goes on, and the Grille has no light in it. The door, the colour of the rock; at the dark west end, the grate the Cistern breathes through.

The apron under the rock, and the door standing open in it, swung out over the white arc it scraped into the concrete. Warm air comes out of the dark, smelling of people. At the yellow line the column waits in its grey, and Knock watches it from its doorways.

The apron under the rock, where you have stood every hatch day of your life. Three ways into the Cistern, and you have never used any of them: the hatch, its tray shut, its panel lit a dim green; the door, the colour of the rock, without a handle on this side; and at the dark west end, at knee height in the stone, the iron grate the Cistern breathes through. Up the lane behind you, the column's tents. In front of you, sixty people you have only ever heard.

a3w_apron.again: The apron. The hatch, the door, the grate.

text.text: The hatch. The panel's window has cracked across and gone black behind the crack, and the tray's lip is scorched where something hot came up the lift from below. Under the tray there is still the slot, a steel lip the width of a letter, where the post goes in when the tray is shut. Nothing answers it.

The hatch. The panel is dark: not burned, only out, like a lamp somebody has blown on. The tray is shut. Behind the rock the hum goes on as it always has, the fans and the pumps, and nobody is listening to any of it. Under the tray there is still the slot, a steel lip the width of a letter.

The hatch. The panel lit a dim green, the tray out on its rails and the rungs going down behind it. "{name}," MOTHER says. "The lift is held for you. It is the only exception I have made in this lockdown, and I have logged it."

The hatch. The tray is shut, and the panel above it is lit a dim green, as it has never been lit except at seven on a hatch day, and MOTHER is behind it: you can tell, the way you can tell somebody is standing behind a door. "Good morning, {name}," she says, whatever the hour. "The hatch is closed until the order is resolved. Thank you for your continuity."

The dark panel, the shut tray, the slot.
The hatch. MOTHER, behind the green.

Then the tray slides out on its rails, empty, and keeps sliding, further than you have ever seen it go, until the whole steel drawer of it stands out of the rock and there is a black square behind it, a draught of warm air, and rungs going down. "The tray lift is held, {name}. Please keep your hands inside the shaft." A pause. "I have never had occasion to say that to anyone."

Another silence. "Addressed to?" / "Reserve 9," you say. / "Received." The tray slides out on its rails and keeps sliding, until the whole drawer of it stands out of the rock and there is a black square behind it and rungs going down. a3w_slip.speaker: npc_c9_05
a3w_slip.text: You hold the slip up to the panel's window, the paper still curled from the tray, and read it to her line by line, the way Maud reads out the post: HATCH CLOSED. THANK YOU FOR YOUR CONTINUITY. PLEASE COME HOME. / "I printed that," MOTHER says. "It is the first thing I have ever printed that was not on a form." / "You asked me to come home," you say. "I'm home. And this is the only door you have that isn't the door." / For a long time there is only the hum. "Yes," MOTHER says. "I asked."

a3w_tam.speaker: npc_c9_03
a3w_tam.text: Tamsin puts her palm flat on the panel, drops her voice into her boots, and out comes, perfectly, a man you have heard say perhaps a hundred words through the Grille in your whole life: "Caretaker. Service hold, tray lift, one body. Coyle." / The green steadies. "That is Bram Coyle's service phrase, Resident Roe," MOTHER says. "You have had his voice exactly since you were nine. You used it on this panel at nineteen, and at twenty-two, and at twenty-three, and each time I held the lift, and each time you did not climb. The last time, you did not ask, and I held it anyway." A pause. "Service hold granted." / The tray runs out on its rails and keeps going, until the whole drawer of it stands out of the rock and there are rungs going down into the warm. Tamsin takes her hand off the panel. "She knew," she says. "She always knew." And then, to you, fast, before you can open your mouth: "Don't."
a3w_tam.again: Tamsin, with her hand off the panel. The rungs going down.
