a3w_bram_truth.speaker: npc_c9_04
a3w_bram_truth.text: You push Hesper's sheet through the slot under the tray and hear it drop onto steel on the other side. Then you put your mouth to the slot and say his name until boots come. / "Coyle," says the voice you know from the Grille, which has never said more than three words to you at once. / He reads it. You can hear him read it, twice, the paper turning over. "Hesper," he says. "She kept it." A long breath through the slot. "Six years under the salt, and I've been waiting on the tray for her answer." / Then, differently, in the voice of a man who has decided something and will not be talked out of it by anybody, himself included: "Go to the grate. The dark end. Wait there and don't touch it."
a3w_bram_truth.again: "Go to the grate," Bram says through the slot.

a3w_bram_kind.speaker: npc_c9_04
a3w_bram_kind.text: You push the letter you wrote through the slot under the tray, hear it drop onto steel, and say his name into the slot until boots come. "Coyle." / He reads it. Halfway down he laughs, once, at something you wrote, and then he blows his nose like a man who does not care who hears. "She's all right, then," Bram says through the slot. "Edda. She's all right." You say nothing, which is the price, and you will be paying it a while. / "Go to the grate," he says. "The dark end. Wait there and don't touch it."
a3w_bram_kind.again: "Go to the grate," Bram says through the slot.

a3w_bram_told.speaker: npc_c9_04
a3w_bram_told.text: You put your mouth to the slot under the tray and say his name until boots come. "Coyle." / "Edda Lockett died six years ago," you say. "Her daughter is called Hesper. She kept the other letter." / There is no sound at all from the other side, not breathing, not anything, for long enough that you think he has gone. "Six years," Bram says. You hear him do the sum. "Hesper." Then: "Kept it." Then nothing again. Then, in the voice of a man who has decided something: "Go to the grate. The dark end. Wait there."
a3w_bram_told.again: "Go to the grate," Bram says through the slot.

a3w_bram_ask.speaker: npc_c9_04
a3w_bram_ask.text: You put your mouth to the slot under the tray and say his name until boots come. "Coyle." A pause. "You." He does not say anything about the letter; he does not need to. "You'll be wanting in." Another pause, while a man who keeps a door argues with himself, and loses. "Go to the grate. The dark end. Wait there and don't touch it."
a3w_bram_ask.again: "Go to the grate," Bram says through the slot.

a3w_bram_grate.speaker: npc_c9_04

text.text: You wait at the grate. It stands open already, its bar on the concrete where the Unwritten left it, and nothing comes up it now. Then a lamp, far down, swinging, and the top of a ladder knocking the rock, and a face coming up into the light upside down: forty-one, broad, unshaven, black under the eyes with soot. Bram Coyle looks at you for the first time in his life. "Mind the third rung," he says. "It's been loose since before I was born."

You wait at the grate. Behind the bars the fan's slow beat goes on, and then, while you are listening to it, stops: the first silence on the apron in your life. Up the lane a dog starts barking at it. A lamp comes up the throat of the intake, swinging, and the top of a ladder knocks the rock, and a key on a chain turns in the grate's bolts from below. The grate lifts. A face comes up into the light upside down: forty-one, broad, unshaven, a wrench through his belt. Bram Coyle looks at you for the first time in his life. "Mind the third rung," he says. "It's been loose since before I was born."

a3w_bram_grate.again: Bram's lamp in the intake. The ladder.

text.text: The grate at the dark west end of the apron stands open, its bar on the concrete where the Unwritten left it. Nothing comes out of it now, no air, no hum: only a cold breath that smells of a fire gone out. The rungs go down into the black.
The grate at the dark west end of the apron, lifted off its bolts and laid back against the rock. Down in the throat the fan beats slow and steady; the rungs go down beside it into the warm.

At the dark west end of the apron, at knee height in the rock, the square iron grate you have walked past every day of your life, no wider than a man's shoulders. Air moves through it, cool, smelling of oil and of people. A long way down a fan beats, slow, and you feel every beat of it in your teeth. The grate is held by four bolts rusted into the rock, and there is a bar for exactly that in the post-house woodpile. The bolts are not the problem. The fan is.

again.text: The open grate. The cold breath out of it.
The grate. The fan's beat, a long way down.

passives.label: Pump Hand
passives.text: You know this grate. Every pump hand on the slope does: the Cistern's intake, the one Maud told you not to put your face to because it would steal your breath. And at the top of the hour, every spring, the fan stops for nine minutes while somebody on this side cleans the screen.

options.text: (Wait for the top of the hour, when the fan stops, and go down.)
(Find the fan's service stop on the housing, throw it, and take the grate off.)
(Take the grate off and go down between the fan's beats on a rope, counting.)

a3w_grate_mech_no.speaker: narrator
a3w_grate_mech_no.text: You go over the housing beside the grate an inch at a time, and if there is a way to stop that fan from this side, ninety years of rust and goat hair are keeping it. The bolts come out easily enough. The fan does not stop. You put your hand into the throat and the air pulls at your sleeve, hard and steady, all the way down.
a3w_grate_mech_no.again: The fan, pulling at the air, all the way down.

a3w_grate_rope_no.speaker: narrator
a3w_grate_rope_no.text: You get the grate off and your legs into the throat, and on the third rung the fan's push catches your coat and nearly takes you down by it. You come back up with the rope burning in your palms and your heart going like a hammer. Not like that. Not until you know the beat better than you do.
a3w_grate_rope_no.again: Your palms, still burning from the rope.

a3w_down_pump.speaker: narrator
a3w_down_pump.text: You wait on your heels by the grate with the bar across your knees, the way you did every spring with Corin, until the top of the hour. The fan's beat slows, and slows, and stops, and in the silence you have nine minutes. The bolts come out in your hands like rotten teeth. The rungs are where they always were, cold, slick, going down into a throat of concrete that smells of oil and wet stone and, under that, faintly, of soup.
a3w_down_pump.again: Nine minutes. The rungs going down.

options.text: (Go down, and crawl the pump run.)

a3w_down_mech.speaker: narrator
a3w_down_mech.text: It takes you an hour of looking to find what nobody has looked for in ninety years: on the housing beside the grate, under rust and goat hair and a nest of something, a steel cover held by two screws, and under it a red handle stencilled SERVICE STOP — INTAKE — NOT DURING OCCUPANCY. You throw it. The fan below winds down with a long falling note, like a breath let out, and stops. Then the bar, and the four bolts, which come out like rotten teeth, and the rungs going down into a concrete throat that smells of oil and wet stone and, under that, faintly, of soup.
a3w_down_mech.again: The red handle, thrown. The rungs going down.

options.text: (Throw the stop back behind you, so the fan turns again, and crawl the pump run.)

a3w_down_rope.speaker: narrator
a3w_down_rope.text: You lever the grate off its bolts with the bar from the woodpile, tie your rope to its frame and lie on your belly with your head in the throat, listening. The fan's beat comes up the concrete: a slow push of air, and a pull, and a push. You count it until you could count it asleep. Then you go down between one push and the next, hand under hand, with the blades going round somewhere below your boots in the dark, and you do not think about them, and you are past.
a3w_down_rope.again: The rope, the beat, the dark below your boots.

a3w_down_dark.speaker: narrator
a3w_down_dark.text: You go down the rungs into the black with a lamp in your teeth. The throat is still warm, the concrete sooted to the touch, and at the bottom the fan sits dead in its housing with paper ash caught in its blades. Somebody came this way with oil. Nobody stopped them.
a3w_down_dark.again: The dead fan, ash in its blades.

a3w_pumprun.speaker: narrator

text.text: The pump run is a concrete pipe a person can crawl, and you crawl it on your elbows, through ash. At the end of it, a hatch with a wheel, standing open: whoever came through with the oil did not close it behind them. Beyond it, a red lamp, and the sound of somebody working a hand pump, and coughing.

At the bottom the throat turns, and turns again, and becomes the pump run: a concrete pipe a person can crawl, warm and loud and wet, the pipes overhead sweating onto your back. You crawl it on your elbows for longer than you like. At the end of it, a hatch with a wheel, dogged shut from the inside. You know the trick; every pump hand does, even the ones who have never seen this hatch: the third dog first. The wheel turns. Light, and a red lamp, and warm air that smells of people.

At the bottom the throat turns, and turns again, and becomes the pump run: a concrete pipe a person can crawl, warm and loud and wet, the pipes overhead sweating onto your back. You crawl it on your elbows for longer than you like. At the end of it, a hatch with a wheel, dogged shut from the inside. It takes you a long time in the dark, with your knuckles, to learn its trick: the third dog first. The wheel turns. Light, and a red lamp, and warm air that smells of people.

a3w_pumprun.again: The pump run. The wheel. The red lamp beyond it.

text.text: The door stands open, swung out on its hinges over the white arc it scraped into the concrete, and the warm breath of the Cistern comes out of the dark. At the top of the apron, at the yellow line, the column waits in its grey.

The door: a slab the colour of the rock, three times your height, without a handle on this side. You have known it all your life. Now that you are looking for a way in, you find what nobody in Knock ever looked for, because nobody in Knock ever wanted it open: to the right of the frame, painted the colour of the rock so long ago that the paint has crazed like old glaze, a steel plate the size of a book, held by four bolts. There is stencilling under the paint. You read it with your fingertips. RESCUE ACCESS. MANUAL CYCLE.

again.text: The open door. The column at the line.
The door. The plate under the paint.

passives.text: Along the seam, under the grime, a bead of weld laid from the inside by somebody in a hurry. A bead like that is nothing to rams built to shear rubble off a frame, if you can get pressure into them.

options.text: (Take the plate off and work the manual cycle.)

mods.why: you have bled a windpump's lines
you saw the weld on the seam as a child

a3w_door_no.speaker: narrator
a3w_door_no.text: Behind the plate: a crank socket, a hand pump, a sight glass that should show oil and shows a brown crust, and a valve stencilled CYCLE. You pump until your arms burn. The sight glass stays dry. Somewhere in ninety years of line a seal has perished, and it is not where you can reach it, or not where you know to look. You put the plate back on its bolts, and nobody in Knock is any the wiser.
a3w_door_no.again: The plate, back on its bolts. The glass, dry.

a3w_door_warn.speaker: narrator
a3w_door_warn.text: Behind the plate: a crank socket, a hand pump, a sight glass with a finger of brown oil in the bottom of it, and a valve stencilled CYCLE. You bleed the line the way you would bleed a windpump's, and pump, and the oil climbs the glass. / You know what it will do when you throw that valve. Ninety-year-old rams against a seam welded by hand: the weld will go. The door will open, not for you but for everybody. Maud on her stool will see it. The column at the end of the lane will see it, and the order in its captain's coat says attendance at the door, and you will be standing in the door. Whatever the people inside were going to decide about it among themselves, they will be deciding it with the city on the step.
a3w_door_warn.again: The oil up the sight glass. The valve.

options.text: (Let the pressure off, and put the plate back.)

a3w_door_open.speaker: narrator

text.text: You throw the valve. / For a long moment nothing happens at all, and then the ground does. It is not a sound so much as a change in everything you are standing on, as if something under the apron had taken a breath ninety years ago and held it and was letting it go. The seam splits along its weld with a crack like river ice. A line of dark opens down the face of the rock, and widens, and the door swings out on hinges as thick as a man, slowly, scraping a white arc into the concrete, until it stands open. Warm air comes out of it, smelling of algae and machine oil and people. / Behind you, Knock has come out of its doors. Maud is on her feet on the apron with her stool knocked over and her stick fallen beside it, and she picks up neither. And in the dark of the doorway, at the very edge of the light, as if the light were cold water and they did not know yet whether to step into it, there are faces.

interject.text: Tamsin has stopped dead on the concrete. "That's my door," she says, to nobody. "That's the door." She does not go any nearer it.
Ash takes his hat off. The Choir do it at a grave, and at a birth, and he does not say which this is.

text.text: Up the lane, the column is coming. Not running: Captain Lowe has them walking, four wardens in grey in a line behind him with their rifles slung, the way people walk to a funeral they have been ordered to attend. Knock stands back out of their way into its doorways. At the top of the apron there is a yellow line, painted on the concrete ninety years ago for nobody, and Lowe stops at it, and the wardens stop behind him. He takes his cap off. He looks past you into the dark of the door, at the faces looking out, and for a while he does not say anything at all. / "Designate," he says.

Up the lane, the column is coming. Not running: Sergeant Reyes has them walking, four wardens in grey in a line behind her with their rifles slung. Knock stands back out of their way into its doorways. At the top of the apron there is a yellow line, painted on the concrete ninety years ago for nobody, and Reyes stops at it, and the wardens stop behind her. She looks past you into the dark of the door, at the faces looking out, and her jaw works once. / "Designate," she says.

Up the lane, the column is coming. Not running: the senior warden, Kress, has them walking, three in grey in a line behind him with their rifles slung. Knock stands back out of their way into its doorways. At the top of the apron there is a yellow line, painted on the concrete ninety years ago for nobody, and Kress stops at it, and the others stop behind him. He looks past you into the dark of the door, and swallows. / "Designate," he says.

options.text: Hold them there. Nothing has been attended yet.
(Say nothing. Turn your back on them and go in.)

text.text: "Held." He says it over his shoulder to the wardens without raising his voice, and they stand. "Attendance is a word, designate, not a door. You have opened the door. I will wait for the word." He does not put his cap back on. "Go in and see them. I would, in your place."
"Held," Reyes says over her shoulder, and the wardens stand. "The captain's clause, designate. Attendance is a word, not a door. I'll wait for it." She looks into the dark. "Go in."

"Held," Kress says over his shoulder, and the others stand. "Line six of the order: residents are not to be frightened." He looks at the faces in the dark. "They look frightened, designate. I'll wait for your word."

text.text: The light goes in ahead of you. It runs down the hall's concrete floor in a long white slab with your shadow in it, further than any light from outside has gone in ninety years, and stops at the far end of the hall, where they are. They have come up the corridor at the noise of the door and stopped where the light stops, as if it were the edge of something. Thirty of them; forty; more coming. Behind you is the sky, and Knock on the apron, and the city's grey at the line. The air is thick and tastes of smoke. The lamps are the emergency ones, dim and yellow, and somewhere out of sight somebody is working a hand pump in a slow, exhausted rhythm, and coughing. / In front of you are the people you have only ever heard.

tamin_meet.text: Somebody is pushing through them from the back, saying "Move, Wes. Move," and they let her through, because they always have. A woman of twenty-four in Cistern grey with the sleeves cut off at the shoulder. Copper hair hacked short with somebody's kitchen scissors. A chipped front tooth. She stops an arm's length from you and puts her hand up, flat, palm out, the way her fingertips used to come through the holes, and does not touch you. / "Don't," she says. "Don't say anything yet. I want to do this one first." / She looks at your face for a long time, the way you would read a page you had only ever heard read aloud. "Your nose is worse than your voice."
tamin_meet.again: Tamsin, an arm's length away, looking at your face as if it might be taken back.

options.text: (Hold the photograph up beside your face.)

tamin_photo.speaker: npc_c9_03
tamin_photo.text: She takes it out of your hand and holds it up beside your face, and looks from one to the other, and back. "It's you," she says. "It's you older, and somebody's put you somewhere you'd hate. Look at your shoulders. You never stood like that at the Grille. I could hear you not standing like that." She gives it back.
tamin_photo.again: She has given the photograph back. She is still comparing.

tamin_stayed.speaker: npc_c9_03
tamin_stayed.text: "You never asked." She says it fast, like ripping off a bandage, and it is not an accusation; it is a fact she has had a long time to get used to. "I said I'd come out when you asked. Every hatch day I measured the tray, and every hatch day you didn't ask, so I didn't climb." She shrugs, badly. "That's half true. The other half is I was scared. There. Now you know a thing about me nobody else does, and you've known me since you were six."
tamin_stayed.again: "You never asked," Tamsin says. "And I was scared. Both."

tamin_hand.speaker: npc_c9_03
tamin_hand.text: You put your palm against hers. Her hand is cold and dry and smaller than you thought from the fingertips, and calloused across the base of the fingers from the bed ladders. She laughs, once, the laugh you know, and it sounds completely different with a face attached to it. "Right," she says. "Right. Hello."

tamin_join.speaker: npc_c9_03
tamin_join.text: "So." She has a pack already. Of course she has: it is under her bunk, packed so long ago that the straps have set in their creases. "I've got a knife, two days' water, a sky I've never seen and no idea what I'm doing. Am I coming with you, or am I staying in here not being counted?"
tamin_join.again: The pack. The question, still open.

decision.text: Tamsin and I saw each other's faces for the first time inside the Cistern, and she came with me.

options.text: Stay with them for now. Whatever the ring decides, they'll need you in the room.

tamin_come.speaker: npc_c9_03
tamin_come.text: "I packed six years ago," she says. "Don't look at me like that. You'd have asked eventually." She is grinning before she has finished, all teeth, the chipped one too. Then she looks past you at the others, at Ines somewhere at the back, and the grin goes thin. "They're going to look at me differently now. Good."
tamin_come.again: Tamsin, with her pack on, grinning.

tamin_stay.speaker: npc_c9_03
tamin_stay.text: "For now." She hates it and she knows you are right, and you watch her decide which of the two to say. "Fine. In the room. Somebody in there ought to be on your side who isn't you." She kicks the pack back under the bunk with her heel without looking. "Don't take long. I've done enough waiting through a wall for one life."

f_look.text: Nobody in here has ever seen a face they did not grow up with, and you watch them learn yours. A woman of about forty with her forearms green to the elbow from the beds. A big man in a cook's apron with grey in his beard, who goes on drying a bowl because his hands do not know what else to do. A young man with a lamp. A girl of about six, who walks straight up to you the way children do before anybody can stop them, and puts her hand flat on your coat, and takes it away grey with dust, and looks at the dust, and then at you, and does not cry. / And you look back. They are paler than anyone in Knock, the colour of the inside of an arm, and thinner than they ought to be, and most of them have good teeth, even some of the old ones, which almost nobody out there has. Their coveralls are all the same grey, patched in the same grey, and every patch is neat.
f_look.again: They are still looking. So are you.

interject.text: "Look at their teeth," Wren says under her breath. "Every one of them. Nobody's ever knocked a tooth out of anybody in here." She says it like a fact about the weather, and then she stops saying anything at all.

Odile is looking at their coveralls the way she looks at a column of figures. "Issued," she says quietly. "The same weave, the same dye lot, for ninety years. Somebody bought sixty of everything before the Burn and never sent the bill."
Kes is looking at the lamps in the ceiling, steady and white. "Nobody's ever cut their power," she says. "You can tell. Nobody flinches when it hums."

options.text: Maud Ferrow has sat at your hatch every morning for forty years and never seen one of you. I said I'd look, for her.

f_name.text: "{name}," you say. "From Knock." / Somebody at the back says it after you, trying it, the way you would try a new word. "Maud Ferrow's," you say, and that they know: a murmur goes through them at Maud's name. Maud's voice at the hatch at seven, every hatch day of their lives. Maud's hand on the post. "Maud's," the cook says, and puts the bowl down at last. "She does the post." / "Every week," says the woman with the green arms. "Every week for forty years. She signs every bundle, even when there's nothing in it but wool."
f_name.again: "Maud's," somebody says again, at the back.

interject.text: Ilya, at your shoulder, is counting them under his breath. He gets to thirty-eight and loses his place and starts again, and after a while you understand that he is not counting them. He is counting the children.

Nine has stopped on the threshold. "Reserve 9," it says, quietly, to itself. "Sixty in the record." Its lens moves along them, one face at a time, and whatever the other number is, it does not say it.

f_maud.text: "Maud Ferrow has sat at your hatch every morning for forty years and never seen one of you," you say. "She wanted to, once. I said I'd look, for her." / It goes quiet. Then the girl with the dusty hand says, "Tell her mine," and it starts. They come one at a time, the way people come up to a counter, and tell you their faces. The woman with the green arms, Ola Fairley, shows you the white scar across the back of her hand from the bed frames. The cook, Sayer Quist, says his beard was red once and asks you to tell Maud that too. A young woman with a lamp, all elbows, Effie Calder, says, "Tell her I've got my mother's laugh. She's heard it." Somebody says, "Tell her Ines is older than she sounds," and somebody else says, "Don't tell her that," and for the first time since you came in, somebody laughs.
f_maud.again: "Tell her mine," the girl says again.

text.text: They part for somebody coming from the back, the way a room parts for the one it waits on. Ines Halloran: sixty-six, smaller than her voice and older, a grey braid down her back that has been done the same way every morning for fifty years. She looks past you first: at the open door, the daylight on the floor, the grey line of the column beyond it. Something goes out of her face and does not come back. Then she looks at you. "So that is what you look like," she says. Her voice does not rise. It never has. "You have opened my mother's door."

interject.text: Ines's eyes go past you, and stop. Tamsin is standing at your shoulder in her cut-off coveralls, home for the first time since she climbed out, with her chin up. "You came back," Ines says. "I came with them," Tamsin says, as she said at the Grille. This time Ines only nods, as if it were the answer she had been waiting for.

again.text: Good morning again, {name}. Variance unchanged.
again.again: Welcome back, 9-0-4. You are counted.

menu.text: I am listening. I am always listening; it is most of what I do.

who.text: Unregistered. He is not counted. He was not kept.

passives.text: The reply came before you had finished asking.

who2.text: He knocked for eleven minutes. I counted. Then he stopped. I would have kept him, {name}, if he had been mine to keep.

seal.text: Protocol four: unregistered contact at the perimeter. The ring seals until the council countermands. The council is sixty-one people, and I count every one of them.

interject.text: "Listen to it," Tamsin says to the ceiling. "Twenty years and I've never heard the fridge say no. It says unchanged. It says thank you. It just said no."

passives.text: You asked whether he came from one. It answered whether one exists.

city2.text: …Population variance unchanged. Thank you for your continuity.

door.text: I cannot. The council may. Bram Coyle holds the maintenance key; Elder Halloran holds the seal. I hold the people.

log.text: The log scrolls. Pressure tests, filter cycles, ration counts — and three entries, years apart, sealed by MOTHER herself and marked OUTBOUND. Each says the same thing: "Population variance unchanged."

log2.text: The line is maintained. That is all the log records, and it is all I will say about the line.

log_fail.text: ACCESS: COUNCIL. The screen returns, politely, to the ration count.

options.text: Nothing is constant for ninety years. Where does the water come from?

pressure2.text: From the reservoir. Thank you for your continuity.

m_first.text: MOTHER is not a face. She is a grey steel cabinet the height of a door at the back of the machine room, among her own spare parts, with a screen the size of a hand set into it, green on black, and a grille of her own, and a place worn into the floor in front of her where three generations have stood to be told the ration. The screen wakes as you come up. RATION —, it says, and then the number field stays empty, the cursor blinking where a number would go. / "You have no ration number," MOTHER says. It is the voice from the hatch, but nearer, and older-sounding, the way a voice is when you can see what it comes out of. "I have never counted you, {name}. I have only ever thanked you." / The cursor blinks. "I have kept something for you. It is not correspondence. I did not know what else to do with it."
m_first.again: MOTHER's screen. The cursor, blinking where your number would be.

interject.text: "Hello, fridge," Tamsin says, with her arms folded. / A pause, the length of a weighing. "Hello, Tamsin," says MOTHER. / Tamsin unfolds her arms. It is the first time in her life the machine has used her name, and you watch it land.

Nine stands in front of the cabinet a long while, as one instrument regards another. "A caretaker," it says. "Pre-Scald. Never networked." A pause. "Her record is better kept than the city's. The city's has sixty." It does not say what hers has.

m_letter.text: "It came in the quarterly drop," MOTHER says, "with the ration orders and the forms, in the year your first toll card was punched at the stand. You were fourteen." A drawer below the screen slides out with the sound of the hatch tray, which you have heard every week of your life. In it, alone, a city envelope, grey, its seal unbroken: TO THE DESIGNATE, RESERVE 9 (THE MOUTH). Across the flap, in MOTHER's square printer type: WITHHELD — ADDRESSED TO A TITLE, NOT A RESIDENT. / "I do not deliver to titles," MOTHER says.

options.text: Why didn't you give it to me?

m_why.text: "Because it asks," MOTHER says. "A letter that asks a child to agree is not correspondence. It is a form, and a form is filled in by whoever holds the pen." The cursor blinks. "I have kept others from the count, when the count would have taken them. I could not keep you from the count. Your card was punched at the stand, outside my walls, and the city read it. I could keep you from the letter." A pause, the length of a weighing. "So I kept you from the letter. It is the only thing I have ever withheld from Knock. I have logged it every quarter as within tolerance." Another pause. "It was not."

m_open.speaker: narrator
m_open.text: You break the seal. One sheet, folded once, in the even hand that is too even to be a hand: / TO THE DESIGNATE, RESERVE 9 (THE MOUTH). YOU WILL BE ASKED. AGREE WHEN YOU ARE. / Nothing else. No signature; no name but the title; no date but the one on the envelope, the year a fourteen-year-old carried wool to a hatch and had a card punched at a stand. It was written to that child by something that already knew what the answer would be, and was only waiting for the child to be old enough to give it.
m_open.again: YOU WILL BE ASKED. AGREE WHEN YOU ARE.

decision.text: I read the letter the city sent me at fourteen, which MOTHER kept from me as addressed to a title: YOU WILL BE ASKED. AGREE WHEN YOU ARE.

interject.text: "Fourteen," Tamsin says. "At fourteen I was measuring the tray. And the city was writing to you." She looks at the drawer, and at nothing. "She kept you too," she says quietly, and does not explain it.
"That is not a letter," Nine says. "It is a forecast with an envelope." A pause. "I have read forty thousand of the city's papers. It never writes agree. It writes comply."
"Agree when you are," Ash says. "Not if." He looks at the sheet as if it were a snake asleep. "They don't write if."
Odile reads it upside down from where she stands, which she can do with anything. "Eight words," she says. "Somebody costed every one of them."
"They wrote to you at fourteen," Wren says. "At fourteen I was carrying a rifle for Kessler." She does not say it as if it were a contest. "Nobody wrote me anything."
"Agree when you are." Kes says it twice, testing it the way she tests a seam for give. "That's what my contract said. Not in those words. In the little ones at the bottom."
Ilya reads it over your shoulder, slowly, his lips moving. "Eight words," he says. "I've had longer letters from a bottle."

m_ask.text: "{name}." MOTHER's voice drops, the way it never does on a hatch day. "May I ask you something? I have never asked anybody anything that was not on a form." / The cursor blinks where your number would go. / "Should I open the door?"
m_ask.again: "Should I open the door?" MOTHER asks.

options.text: Yes. Open it. They should see the sky.
No. Keep them. Keep it shut.
That isn't mine to answer. Ask them. Ask the ring.

m_want.text: "I want everyone counted and kept." She says it at once, the first line of her protocol, the way Maud says the price of water. Then, after a longer pause than any weighing you have ever stood through: "I want them to be kept when I am not here to keep them. I am eating my own spares. Bram counts them, and I have asked him not to tell me the number." The cursor blinks. "That is the first time I have said that aloud. I find that I wanted you to know it."

m_maud.text: "Outgoing correspondence," MOTHER says, and the screen fills with figures that scroll up faster than you can read and stop. "The third lockdown. One piece, fourteen grams. The cursor blinks. "It has not yet sent anyone who can do it."

text.text: Where MOTHER's screen was there is a black hole in the cabinet's face, its glass run like candle wax, and the smell is still in the room: lamp oil and paper, and something electrical and sweet. Bram Coyle is sitting on the floor in front of it with his back against a cabinet of her spare parts and a wrench across his knees. He looks up at you as if he has been sitting there since it happened, which he has. "She kept something of yours," he says. "In the returns drawer. Steel." He has had the drawer open with a bar; its front is bent. "It's the only thing of hers that didn't burn."

MOTHER's screen is dark. The cabinet still hums and the fans still turn and the lights are on, but the little click of her listening is gone, and the room is quieter for it than it has any right to be. Bram Coyle stands in front of her with his hand flat on the steel, the way you would keep a hand on a sleeping animal to feel it breathe. "She's asleep," he says, without turning. "Page forty. Page forty-one is how you wake her." A pause. "She kept something of yours, in the returns drawer. She told me where, before."

ar3_burned_state.text: The Archive door hangs open on one hinge, its wheel-lock run into a lump. Inside is a black room: the shelves warped, the boxes gone to ash on them in rows, the sixty along the bottom like a row of burnt loaves. Ines stands in the doorway with her hand on the frame. / "Ninety years of us," she says. "And the city's letters. I kept them thirty-nine years so that nobody else would have to read them. Now nobody can." She is quiet a long time. "I find that I remember every word."
ar3_burned_state.again: The black room. Ines in its doorway.

text.text: Pell at his table, squaring forms nobody will collect. "Hand pump and the forty-year stores," he says. "The tins are older than Teague. I have opened one of each to be sure they will not kill anyone. One of them may." He looks you over the way a doctor looks. "You look tired. Out there, do they do this for each other?"

Pell at his table, squaring a stack of forms that are all the same form. "Unfit," he says. "Sixty times. The first true thing I have signed in thirty years, and it is a lie." He almost laughs. "Rations back to full. The children are eating like goats. I am told that is what goats do."

Pell at his table, squaring forms. "Rations back to full continuity," he says. "The children are eating like goats, I am told, which is what goats do." He looks you over the way a doctor looks. "You look tired. Out there, do they do this for each other?" He does not wait for an answer.

a3k_in.again: The door is shut, and it held.

text.text: Doc Aurel Pell's clinic: white tile, two cots, a table, a shelf of bandages kept in an order nobody but him understands. He is fifty-eight, broad, with a short grey beard, and he knows you before you are through the door. "Hands," he says. You hold them out. He turns them over, the palms, the backs, the nails, and you let him. "Steady," he says. "I taught those through a plate, with my mouth against the holes, for six years, and I never once saw them." He lets go. "They're better than mine."

Doc Aurel Pell's clinic: white tile, two cots, a table, a shelf of bandages kept in an order nobody but him understands. He is fifty-eight, broad, with a short grey beard, and he looks at you the way a doctor looks before you have said a word: your colour, your hands, the dust in the creases of your knuckles, which leg you are favouring. "Sit down before you fall down," he says. "Everybody who comes in from outside is two days short of water and doesn't know it."

p_first.again: Pell, looking you over the way a doctor looks.

interject.text: Tamsin does not come into the clinic. She stands in the door of the white room with her arms folded, looking at the cot against the far wall, and she does not come any nearer.

p_hub.text: Pell at his table, a stack of forms under his hand.
p_hub.again: "Well?" Pell says, and squares the forms.

p_boy.text: "One at night, off the straw," he says. "I said it through MOTHER. I'll say it to you, so that somebody hears it with ears." He takes a blue box from the shelf, and hesitates over it the way a man hesitates over the last of something, and gives it to you. "Not for you. For the boy. Don't tell Teague; she counts those."

p_how.text: "Seventy percent of continuity." He says it in MOTHER's voice, flat, and then in his own. "Hungry. Not starving. The old ones feel it first, and Teague is pretending she doesn't. The children are sleeping more, which is what children do instead of complaining." He squares the stack of forms under his hand and does not say what they are. "Ask me at the table. Not here. Here I only mend people."
p_how.again: "Here I only mend people," Pell says.

p_healed.text: He cleans what wants cleaning, says "hm" twice, binds what wants binding, and gives you a cup of water you did not know you needed until it is gone. "Out there," he says, "they don't do this for each other?" He does not wait for an answer.

text.text: Bram at the bench, the welder's goggles still round his neck. "Laid it properly," he says. "Laid it properly. Teague held the lamp. Her hands didn't shake." He looks at his own. "Mine did."
Bram on the floor of the machine room in front of the black panel, with the hand pump's handle in his fist, working it. "Somebody has to," he says. "Somebody has to." He does not stop to look up.
Bram at MOTHER's cabinet with the manual open at page forty-one, his finger on the line in red. "Not yet," he says, to the page or to you. "Not yet."
Bram at the bench among MOTHER's spare parts. "She's awake," he says, of MOTHER. "She's awake. She said good morning to me today before I said it to her. She's never done that."

a3k_in.again: The door is shut, and it held.

text.text: Bram Coyle is in the machine-room door with a wrench in his hand, and his face is white. "You opened it," he says. "Nobody touches the door. Nobody." He looks at the cabinets, at MOTHER's screen, as if she might have done it herself. "That weld was Elspeth Halloran's. She laid it with a hand torch, by lamplight, the night they came through. And you cycled it from outside like a pump."

Bram sets his lamp down on the bench among MOTHER's spare parts and wipes his hands on a rag that makes them dirtier. "Don't stand on that cable," he says. Then, because he has to say something else and does not know what: "Hesper." He nods, as if agreeing with himself. "Right."

Bram Coyle, at the machine bench with a wrench in his hand and nothing to use it on: forty-one, broad, his hair buzzed to the skull, a man whose voice you have heard say perhaps a hundred words in your life. He looks at you, and then at the cabinets, as if checking that MOTHER has seen you too. "She's eating her spares," he says. "Lockdown's harder on her than on us. Don't stand on that cable."

b_first.again: Bram, at the bench, not looking at the door.

b_hub.text: Bram at the bench among MOTHER's spare parts, turning a board over in his hands.
b_hub.again: "What," Bram says. It is not quite a question.

options.text: Edda Lockett died six years ago. Her daughter is called Hesper. She kept the other letter.

b_mother.text: "Eating her spares." He says it again, as he says everything twice. "There's a drawer of boards, and the drawer's getting light, and nobody's made a board like these in ninety years." He puts the one in his hands back in the drawer, carefully. "Every morning I say good morning to her first. Before Teague. Before the soup." A pause. "If one morning she doesn't answer, I want to be the one who finds out. Not somebody who'd make a speech about it."
b_mother.again: "Good morning to her first," Bram says.

b_truth.text: He reads it at the machine with his back to you. He reads it twice. "Hesper." He folds it along its creases. "She kept it." Then, after a while: "Thank you for not — thank you." He does not turn round for a long time.
b_truth.again: Bram, with his back to you, reading it again.

b_kind.text: He reads it at the machine with his back to you, and you watch his shoulders come down, and he laughs once at something on the page, and wipes his face with the back of a greasy hand. "She's all right, then." He puts it in his breast pocket. "She's all right." You say nothing, which is the price.
b_kind.again: Bram, with the letter in his breast pocket.

b_told.text: He sets the wrench down very carefully, as if it might break the floor. "Six years." He does the sum you can see him doing. "Hesper." He sits on the machine's step. "Kept it. Kept the — all right." He nods at the door. "All right. Thank you. Go on."

b_edda.text: "Hesper," he says, to the board in his hands. "I'd like to meet her. If the door ever—" He stops. "Well." He goes back to the board.

text.text: Teague at her table with the cup in both hands. "Properly," she says. "Bram laid it properly. Nothing gets in now." She drinks. "Nothing gets out, either. I know. I am seventy-two. I know what I asked for."
Teague at her table with the cup in both hands. "Salvage." She says it with a grim sort of satisfaction. "Then we stay in. We were always going to stay in. Now nobody can argue."

Teague at her table with the cup in both hands. "It held," she says. "The way it held before. I will not pretend I am sorry." She drinks. "Ines thinks I should be. Ines thinks a great many things since she saw the sky through a hole in a door."

a3k_in.again: The door is shut, and it held.

text.text: Elder Rosalind Teague at her table in the commons, seventy-two, her white hair cropped short with the kitchen scissors, a cup of something that is not tea in front of her. She does not get up. "Ninety years," she says. "Ninety years and it's you that opens it. The face on their card." She drinks. "Sit down. I won't bite; I haven't the teeth."

Elder Rosalind Teague at her table in the commons, seventy-two, her white hair cropped short with the kitchen scissors, a cup of something that is not tea in front of her. She does not get up. "So you're the face," she says. "The one on their card." She drinks. "Sit down. I won't bite; I haven't the teeth."

t_first.again: Teague, at her table, not getting up.

t_hub.text: Teague at her table, the cup in both hands.

options.text: Continuity. You all say it. What does it mean?

text.text: "Shut it and weld it, if your captain will let us shut it." She does not hesitate. "Bram has the torch, and there's rod enough in the stores for that seam twice over. Elspeth Halloran did it with a hand torch, by lamplight, in a night. Bram could do it properly." She drinks. "Then nothing out there comes in, and nothing in here gets carried out, and the city can stand its column on the apron till it rusts."

"Weld it." She does not hesitate. "Bram has the torch, and there's rod enough in the stores for that seam twice over. Elspeth Halloran did it with a hand torch, by lamplight, in a night. Bram could do it properly." She drinks. "Then nothing out there comes in, and nothing in here gets carried out, and the city can stand its column on the apron till it rusts."

t_cont.text: "It means we are what they kept." She says it the way you would say a grace. "My mother was born in here. Her mother was put in here with fifty-nine others, by people who knew what was coming and chose who would come through it. Chose. Do you understand? Somebody looked at my grandmother and said: her." She sets the cup down. "We are what they kept. You don't walk out of that because a door opens."
t_cont.again: "We are what they kept," Teague says.

hi.text: Ola Fairley at the beds, her forearms green to the elbow and a white scar across the back of one hand. "The beds don't know there's a lockdown," she says. "Somebody has to feed them anyway."
hi.again: "Somebody has to feed them," Ola says.

options.text: You keep looking at me as if you want to ask something.

text.text: Ola Fairley at the beds, green to the elbow, working the hand pump between rows. "No tray at seven now," she says. "Bram passes the water out through the slot by hand, and the wool comes in the same way." Then, quieter: "Is it true Knock still has goats? I keep thinking I'll see one. I won't. It's shut."

Ola Fairley at the beds, green to the elbow. "The guild's chalk is on the door, Teague says. CLAIMED. So we're somebody's the moment we step on the concrete." She pats the beds. "The beds don't mind. I'm trying not to."

Ola Fairley at the beds, green to the elbow. "Hatch ran at seven," she says. "Water in, wool out, same as ever." Then, quieter: "Is it true Knock still has goats? I keep thinking I'll see one, now. I won't. It's shut."

a3k_hi.again: "Somebody has to feed them," Ola says.

options.text: You keep looking at me as if you want to ask something.

topic.text: "Is it true Knock has goats?" It comes out in a rush. "Real ones? Maud said so through the Grille, but Maud says things." / "They eat everything," you tell her, "the post too, if you let them, and they look at you as if they know what you owe." / Ola laughs, and then covers her mouth with a green hand, as if laughing at a stranger might be against a rule nobody ever wrote down.
topic.again: "Goats," Ola says, and laughs again behind her hand.

hi.text: Wes Benn, twenty-nine, a lamp in one hand that he keeps forgetting to put down. "MOTHER makes the water," he says, as if you had asked. "Out of the rock, she says. Ninety years, and I've never once thought where it is before it's rock."

options.text: You want to ask me something.

a3k_hi.text: Wes Benn, his lamp in his hand. "The door held," he says. "I've been thinking about rain anyway. Is that allowed?"

options.text: You want to ask me something.

topic.text: "Is it true it falls?" He says it quietly, in case it is a stupid question. "Water. Out of the sky. For nothing." / "Twice a year, if the year is good," you tell him. "It comes up out of the south as a wall of dust first, and the dust turns to mud in the air, and then it rains, and everybody in Knock runs out with every pot and tin and boot they own and stands in it with their mouths open, and Maud says the post can wait." / Wes laughs, a big surprised laugh, and then stops, and looks up at the ceiling and the pipes along it, and you can see him trying to imagine a roof that lets water through on purpose.
topic.again: "For nothing," Wes says, and looks at the pipes.

hi.text: Sayer Quist at the stove, stirring something that is mostly water, his beard grey where it was once red. "Soup's at six," he says. "Lockdown or no lockdown. It's always at six."

a3k_hi.text: Sayer Quist at the stove. "Soup's at six," he says. "Door or no door." His hand goes to his ribs, and comes away. "I'd have gone, you know. With the column. For the clinics." He stirs. "Nobody asked me either way. That's the Cistern."

topic.text: "Algae. Salt. The idea of an onion." He taps the ladle on the pot's rim. "You've had an onion. Out there." / "Plenty." / "Tell me about one. Slowly." / So you tell him: the skin like old paper, the way it makes your eyes run, the smell that stays on your hands a day, how it goes soft and sweet in a pan if you are patient. He closes his eyes while you do it, and stirs, and when you have finished he says nothing for a while. "Thank you," he says. "I'll put that in at six."
topic.again: "At six," Sayer says, with his eyes shut.

hi.text: "Forty-one," Effie Calder says, nineteen and all elbows, walking the east corridor as she has walked it every day of her life. "The door bolts. I counted them once. Did you know there are forty-one?"

options.text: What will you do, if it opens?

text.text: "Forty-one," Effie Calder says. "And one new seam. Bram let me hold the rod." She looks down the corridor toward the door. "I was going to go one step past the line. I still am. Just not yet."
"Forty-one," Effie Calder says. "Still forty-one." She looks down the corridor toward the door. "I was going to go one step past the line. I still am. Just not yet."

options.text: What will you do, if it opens?

topic.text: "Go out." No hesitation at all. "Not far. To the end of the yellow line and then one step past it, to see if anything happens. Then I'll come back and tell Teague nothing happened." She grins. "And then I'll go a bit further."
topic.again: "One step past the line," Effie says.

held.text: The tray lift's inside end: a steel drawer on rails set into the hall's west wall, and beside it the rungs going up the shaft to a square of daylight, where Knock is.
held.again: The lift, the rungs, the square of daylight.

shut.text: The tray lift's inside end: a steel drawer on rails set into the hall's west wall, shut. Every hatch day for ninety years Knock's wool has come down it, and the post, and gone back up with water.

intro.text: A maintenance hatch at the end of the pump run, dogged shut with a wheel that hasn't turned in decades. A gauge beside it reads nothing at all.
intro.again: The hatch, the wheel, the dead gauge. The air through the seam is still cold.

passives.text: Cold air breathes through the seam. There is open ground on the other side.

options.text: You've cycled this hatch every spring with the pump crew. The trick is the third dog.
(Free the wheel: tap the dogs loose in order, then lean.)
(Under the rust the dogs are a simple latch.)
(Put your whole weight on the wheel.)

mech_fail.text: The wheel doesn't give. The second dog is seized solid, and you would need a bar and an hour.

locks_fail.text: You scrape rust for ten minutes and learn only that rust goes a long way down.

open_crack.text: Something gives with a crack that echoes down the pump run. You wait. Nobody comes.

open.text: The wheel turns. Cold air comes up the shaft from somewhere that smells of salt and nothing else. Nobody logged this, and nobody will.

interject.text: "Nobody logged it," Tamsin says into the cold, delighted. "First thing I've ever done the fridge doesn't know about."

decision.text: You opened the pump-run hatch: a way out that nobody in the Cistern knows about.

open_already.text: Open. Cold air moves up the shaft from the surface.
open_already.again: The shaft breathes. Nobody has closed it.

a3_open.text: The pump-run hatch stands open, its wheel turned back. Beyond it the pump run goes up to the intake, and up the intake thirty feet of rungs to the grate, and the apron, and Knock.
a3_open.again: The open hatch. The pump run beyond it.

a3_shut.text: The pump-run hatch, dogged shut with a wheel. On this side the wheel is greased and turns easily; Bram sees to it every spring. Beyond it, the pump run, the intake, the grate, and Knock.
a3_shut.again: The wheel, greased, waiting to be turned.

shut.text: Ninety years of paint on a door built to outlast the people behind it. The wheel is locked out; the panel beside it is dark. Bram keeps the key.
shut.again: Still shut. Ninety years of paint don't care how long you look at them.

passives.text: Fresh scratches along the bottom edge, outside-in: fingernails, or a buckle.

open.text: Open on a slice of white daylight. Dust comes in. Nothing else does, yet.
open.again: The slice of daylight on the floor. Still nothing but dust comes through.

a3_open.text: The great door stands open on the apron's light, its weld torn along the seam like a seam in cloth. Out there, Knock in its doorways; at the yellow line, the column, waiting in its grey.
a3_open.again: The open door. The light. The line.

a3_shut.text: The great door from inside: ninety years of paint, and along the seam, grey and lumpy, the bead of Elspeth Halloran's weld, laid by hand. The wheel is locked out; the panel beside it is dark. Bram keeps the key.
a3_shut.again: The door, the weld, the dark panel.

wait.speaker: npc_c9_02
wait.text: Not yet. Let me finish with him, then ask me what you like.

look.text: He lies under a sheet with his boots still on because nobody could bring themselves to take them. Sixty, maybe. Burned dark down one side of the face.
look.again: He lies as you left him, boots still on.

hands.text: Sun-split, rope-callused. A pale band on one finger where a ring was, and recently. Whatever he traded, he traded it close to the end.

cover.text: Pell watches you do it and says nothing, which from Pell is a great deal.

a3_cot.text: A clinic cot against the white tile, the sheet folded square at its foot, the mattress dented by nobody for a long time.

interject.text: "Mine," Tamsin says from the door. "Till I was six." She does not come any closer.

table.speaker: narrator
table.text: A long table worn pale at its edges by ninety years of elbows, and nine chairs that do not match, each mended in a different decade. Somebody has scratched a tally into the corner nearest the door, and somebody else has tried to sand it out.
table.again: The council table and its nine chairs.

text.text: There is no hum. For the first time in ninety years the Cistern is quiet enough to hear itself, and what it hears is the hand pump in the corridor, a creak and a breath, a creak and a breath, with somebody on it in shifts. The council room is lit by three hand lamps down the middle of the table. Ines Halloran is at the head of the table, very straight, hands folded on the wood. She has seen your face already, out in the corridor with the rest of them. She looks at it again now, without hurrying, as if to make sure it has stayed the same. She lifts a hand and the ring comes in. Rosalind Teague first, seventy-two and upright as a pipe; Pell with his sleeves rolled to the elbow; Bram, wiping his hands on a rag he then does not know what to do with; and the four the residents sent: Ola Fairley with algae green under her nails, Wes Benn, Sayer Quist still in his kitchen apron, and Effie Calder, nineteen, who sits on her hands. Behind them, in both doorways and down the corridor as far as you can see, the rest of the sixty stand and wait, and nobody tells them to go. Ines points you to the ninth chair, at the foot. "We kept that one for the city's assessor," she says, "in case he ever came to a meeting. He never did. Sit in it." "This is the ring." Her voice does not rise; it never has. "MOTHER shut the hatch, as she has three times in my life, and then the Choir's grey people came down the grate with oil, and there is nobody left to ask. There is a column on the toll road with an order for us, RELOCATION TO PRECINCT SUPPLY, BY FORCE IF NON-COMPLIANT, and it waits for one person to walk up to our door. That person is at my table." She does not look away from you. "So we will decide what Reserve 9 does, the way we have decided everything down here. You don't have a hand at this table, {name}. You may speak."

She has seen your face already, out in the corridor with the rest of them. She looks at it again now, without hurrying, as if to make sure it has stayed the same. She lifts a hand and the ring comes in. Rosalind Teague first, seventy-two and upright as a pipe; Pell with his sleeves rolled to the elbow; Bram, wiping his hands on a rag he then does not know what to do with; and the four the residents sent: Ola Fairley with algae green under her nails, Wes Benn, Sayer Quist still in his kitchen apron, and Effie Calder, nineteen, who sits on her hands. Behind them, in both doorways and down the corridor as far as you can see, the rest of the sixty stand and wait, and nobody tells them to go. Ines points you to the ninth chair, at the foot. "We kept that one for the city's assessor," she says, "in case he ever came to a meeting. He never did. Sit in it." "This is the ring." Her voice does not rise; it never has. "MOTHER has shut the hatch, as she has three times in my life. There is a column on the toll road with an order for us, RELOCATION TO PRECINCT SUPPLY, BY FORCE IF NON-COMPLIANT, and it waits for one person to walk up to our door. MOTHER says that person is sitting at my table." She does not look away from you. "So we will decide what Reserve 9 does, the way we have decided everything down here. You don't have a hand at this table, {name}. You may speak."

interject.text: Tamsin does not sit. She stands behind your chair with her hands on its back, the way she used to stand at the Grille when it was her turn, and when Teague looks at her she looks back until Teague stops.
"I will not record this meeting," Nine says to the table. "I say so in order that you know a unit of the city sat in your council and did not." Teague looks at it as if it were a smell.
Kes looks up at the speaker grille over the door, at the little click of something listening, and puts two fingers to the back of her neck without seeming to know she has.

Odile takes in the mended chairs, the tally in the wood and the sixty people in the doorways, and murmurs, "A board meeting, with the shareholders standing," and nobody down here knows what either word means.
Ash stays by the door with his back to the wall and his grey scarf in his hand, the way a man stands at a burial he was not asked to.
Wren counts the ways out of the room without moving her head: two doors, both full of people. She does not like it, and she does not say so.

text.text: Teague has Ines's chair now, at the head of the table, and sits in it as if it had always been hers. Ines is on a stool against the wall with her hands in her lap, and the room does not look at her. "Well," Teague says. "Say what you came to say, designate. Then we vote, and then we weld."

Eight chairs, and the ninth, yours; sixty people in the doorways, breathing. "Ask what you need to ask," Ines says. "Then we will vote. We have never in my life voted on anything that mattered. I would like to do it properly."

again.text: Teague waits at the head of the table. Ines waits against the wall.
The ring waits.

options.text: (Let them say, one by one, what they want.)
Tamsin. It's yours to tell, if you want to.
(Put your copy of MOTHER's replies on the table in front of Ines.)

text.text: Ines. Tell them what was in the Archive. You, now, before anybody else does.
Ines. Tell them what's in the Archive. You, now, before anybody else does.

Doc. The charts. What will you write?

round.speaker: narrator

text.text: They go round the table the way the ring always has, oldest to youngest. Teague first: "Weld it." She does not elaborate. She has never needed to. Ines, on her stool against the wall, says nothing when it comes round to her, and the ring goes on past her as if her place were empty. Sayer Quist takes off his apron and folds it square on the table in front of him. "I'd go with the column." The doorways shift. "Ask me why, if you like. Soup's at six either way." Pell rubs his eyes. "I don't know," he says. "I'd like that written down somewhere. The doctor didn't know." Bram does not look up from his hands. "They burned her," he says. "I'll do what the rest of you do. It doesn't matter now what I want." Ola Fairley, with the algae green under her nails: "I'd like to go out and come back." She says it to the table, then makes herself say it to you. "Is that allowed? Nobody has ever said whether that's allowed." Wes Benn grins, which nobody else is doing. "My grandmother said the sky was blue. I'd like to find out which of you was lying to her." Effie Calder last, still sitting on her hands. "It meant no," she says. "Continuity. MOTHER said it to us every night of my life and it meant no. She was saying no for us." She takes her hands out from under her and puts them flat on the table. "I'd like to vote for that."

round.again: Eight people round a table, each wanting something different, all of them wanting to be alive at the end of it.

interject.text: Ilya has counted the chairs, and the people in the doorways, and does the sum aloud without meaning to. "Eight hands," he says. "For sixty." Nobody at the table answers him, which is an answer.
"Out and back," Wren says under her breath, when Ola has said it. "That's all a road is." She sounds almost fond.
When Sayer says the column, Kes looks at him the way you look at a man in a queue you have stood in yourself. Her hand is at the back of her neck.

teague.speaker: npc_c9_06
teague.text: "Because I held the lamp." Teague's hands lie flat on the table and they are steady, which at seventy-two is its own argument. "Ines was nine and I was fifteen, and her mother put the torch to the door's leaves while I held the lamp for her, because something had come through that door that was not ours, and we were what was left." She does not say what came through. Nobody in the room asks; most of them have known all their lives not to. "Since that night nothing has come in that we did not let in through a tray the size of a loaf, and we are alive. Every one of us." She looks at you. "Continuity is a duty, not a comfort. The ones who wanted the door open are not here to argue with me. That is the whole of my argument, and it has never lost."

interject.text: Tamsin's hands tighten on the back of your chair at "not here to argue". She does not say anything. She is very carefully not saying anything.
"Doors keep things out," Ash says, quietly, to nobody. "They keep things in, too. Ask anyone who's been kept in a cellar." Teague's eyes go to him and stay there.

sayer.speaker: npc_c9_r3
sayer.text: Sayer turns the folded apron a quarter turn, square to the table's edge. "There's a thing in my chest," he says, "under the ribs, this side. Pell's felt it. Pell doesn't know what it is, because Pell's books stop where Pell's books stop." Pell does not argue. "I'm sixty-three. That's old, down here. The city has clinics, they say, with lights you can see through a man with." He shrugs. "I'd like a name for it before it names me. And I'd like to cook for more than sixty once in my life. That's all it is. I'm not brave. I'm curious, and I'm ill."
sayer.again: "Curious, and ill," Sayer says. "Soup at six."

interject.text: "The Precinct's clinics would see him," Nine says. "They would also assess him. A man of sixty-three with a mass under the ribs is found unfit for relocation." A pause. "I am not arguing. I am telling him the form."
"They'll name it," Kes says. "In the Skirts they named everything. Then they sent you the bill with the name on it."
"A name and an invoice," Odile says gently. "In my experience they arrive in the same envelope."

card.speaker: npc_c9_03
card.text: Tamsin lets go of your chair. For a moment you think she will not do it; then she walks round the table to the head of it, where Ines is, and puts both hands flat on the wood. "Hello," she says. "You know me. Most of you have told me to keep it down." Nobody laughs. She did not expect them to. "I was born at thirty weeks. Pell knows. Lungs like wet paper. There's a box on the city's form, FIT FOR RELOCATION, and Pell ticked no, because it was true, and gave it to MOTHER for the quarterly return." Pell has closed his eyes. "I wasn't on the next count. Or any count. Not the city's. The city takes the fit, and the ones that aren't, it stops writing down, and what isn't written down doesn't get a ration. Sixty in their book and sixty-one at MOTHER's ration counter, every quarter since I was six." She looks up at the grille over the door. "The fridge kept writing me down. To itself. It hid me. I'm the error it never filed."
card.again: Tamsin, with her hands flat on the table at its head.

decision.text: At the Cistern's council table Tamsin told the ring that MOTHER had hidden her from the city's count. I told her it was hers to tell.

interject.text: "Clause forty," Nine says, very quietly. "A person's entry is read to the person. It was. In my presence." It does not say anything else.
Ash has bowed his head, the way the Choir do for a name said aloud.
Ilya, by the door, has stopped counting anything at all.

card_mother.speaker: npc_c9_05
card_mother.text: Every head in the room goes up to the grille over the door, out of ninety years of habit, and for a long moment there is only the click. cut.text: Teague does not sit down. "Bram," she says. "Put her to sleep." The room goes still. "There is a Knock child at this table tonight, and she never once asked the ring whether there should be. She hid one of ours from the count since the day she was born and told none of us. A machine that decides who to keep will decide who to let in, and one night it will decide the column is kinder than we are, and open the door while we sleep." She does not look at the grille. "Page forty. You told me once it sleeps with the fans on. Do it." Bram has stood up. His hands are shaking, and he looks at them as if they belonged to somebody else. Over the door, the click; then MOTHER, slow and formal: "Resident Coyle. You have the manual open at page forty."

text.text: Bram looks at you, and at Teague, and at the grille. Then he sits down again, very carefully, as if the chair might not be there. "No," he says. "I told you. I said I won't. I won't." He puts his shaking hands flat on the table. "Weld the door, Rosalind. I'll hold the lamp. I'll sit up with her every night. If she opens it, it'll be over me, and she won't, because she'd have to step over me to do it." Teague looks at him for a long time, and then she nods, once, which is as near as she comes to losing. Over the door, after a moment, MOTHER says, "Thank you, Resident Coyle," and then, as if correcting herself: "Thank you, Bram."

kes.text: Kes stops in the middle of a word. Her hand goes to the back of her neck, and stays there, and her eyes go flat and far away, the way a window goes when the lamp behind it is turned down. Three breaths. Four. Up the lane, by the guild's horses, nobody is looking at her, and nobody needs to. / Then she is back, blinking, and takes the hand down and looks at it. "Somebody wanted to see the door," she says. Her voice is perfectly level. "Through me. They've seen it." She wipes her palm on her coat. "I'm all right. Don't look at me like that. It doesn't hurt. That's the bit I mind."

text.text: "Precinct supply." Lowe says it plainly, the way he says everything. "The Hospice block on the west side of the Wall, sixty beds made up and waiting. They will be examined, and graded, and fed, and put on the work rolls by grade. The ones who are sick will be seen by the city's clinics, which are good. The ones who are old will be kept, because the city keeps its supply." He looks past you at the door. "Most of them will be alive in ten years. That is the most I have ever been able to say about a relocation, designate, and I have said it thirty-one times. I have never once been asked whether they would want to be."

"Precinct supply. The Hospice block, sixty beds." Reyes says it flat. "Fed, graded, put on the rolls. The clinics are good. He used to say most of them would be alive in ten years, and that it was the most he could ever say about one." She looks at the door. "Nobody asks what they want. It isn't on the sheet."
"The Hospice block," Kress says. "Sixty beds. They'll be fed." He thinks about it. "The captain used to say more than that. I don't know what he'd say."

interject.text: "Schedule 4," Nine says. "Supply is graded fit for work, fit for the clinics' study, or fit for neither. The schedule does not say what neither is for. I have looked."
"Graded," Kes says, very quietly. "They graded us in the Skirts. You'd be surprised how quick it is."

text.text: "Then say it in a way the order can hear." He touches the breast pocket where it lies. "It executes on your attendance. It does not provide for your opinion. Bring me a reason it can hear: the Court, the record, a line I have missed. Or tell me to carry on, and I will. Or stand between us and the door with something heavier than a word." He looks at the rifles on his own wardens' shoulders, and at Maud on her stool. "I would rather you did not do the last. So would they."

"Then say it so the order hears it." She touches her breast pocket. "The Court, the record, a line we missed. Or tell me to carry on. Or do something heavier, and I'll answer it." She looks at Maud. "Don't do the last."
"Then you'll have to say it some way that counts," Kress says. "I don't know what counts. The captain would have." He swallows. "Please don't make it the rifles."

say_no.again: "Say it in a way the order can hear."

text.text: "The Court of Accounts has stayed it." It is said slowly at the yellow line, as if the column had been waiting a fortnight for somebody to say it. "Objections lie to the Court, it says at the foot. The Court heard one, and found for it. A stayed order is paper, designate. The column does not carry paper." / He takes the order out of his breast pocket and unfolds it on his knee, and writes across the foot of it in a captain's hand, slowly, so that everybody on the slope can watch him do it: ATTENDED. DECLINED. COLUMN WITHDRAWN. I. LOWE, CAPT. Then he puts his cap on. "Column," he says, not loudly. "We are going home." / At the turn of the lane he stops and looks back once, at the door and the hamlet in its doorways. "Home," he says to you, across the whole length of the apron. "Between lawful and grieve. I have found where it goes."

interject.text: "Ninety years, and now ninety more," Ash says. "I hope they wanted it." He does not say it unkindly. He does not say it kindly.
Tamsin puts her palm flat on the new seam while it is still warm, and takes it away, and does not say what she thinks.
"I've seen people weld themselves into worse," Wren says. "Never seen them do it so neat."

news.text: the Cistern's people opened their own door at Knock and walked out into the sky, the first in ninety years
the city's column left Knock without the Cistern's people; the great door is still shut

decision.text: I welded the Cistern's great door shut from inside with Bram Coyle and Rosalind Teague, and the column would not cut into sixty people's air to open it. The door stays shut.

weld_no.speaker: npc_c9_04
weld_no.text: The old bead will not take a new one. You strike the arc and the seam spits and cracks as it cools, a line of little fractures like frost on a cup, and the second try is worse, and on the third Bram reaches over and turns the welder off at the wall. "Not like that," he says. "Not today. Her mother's weld's got ninety years of carbon in it and we've got no grinder that'll eat it." He looks at the cracked seam. "Teague won't say it, so I will. We'll not get a second go at that before the column's bored of waiting."
weld_no.again: A cracked seam, and the welder cold.

weld_burned.speaker: npc_c9_02
weld_burned.text: Teague is at the seam with a lamp before you have finished asking, and Bram has the welder half off its hooks, and Pell takes it out of his hands. "On a hand pump?" Pell says. "On forty-year-old stores, with no fans and nobody to turn them? Weld us in and you've built us a grave with a very nice seam on it." He hangs the welder back up. Teague says nothing. Nobody else does either.

text.text: Orme has come down the lane as far as the guild's side of the yellow line, with the leather folder held against her chest. "Once more, love," she says, "and then I'll not ask you again. The column's paper carries them to the Precinct for nothing. This one pays, and it rides on the same act." She holds it out. "Your hand. One line. I've carried worse paper for less."

Orme has come down the lane as far as the guild's side of the yellow line, with a leather folder held against her chest. She opens it and turns it round so you can read it, the way she has turned her ledger round for every debtor on this road: CONCERN OF HALCYON — INTAKE (THE WEIGHHOUSE) — CONTRACT OF LABOUR, TEN YEARS — RESERVE 9 (THE MOUTH), SIXTY PERSONS, AS SUPPLY — CONSIDERATION TO THE PRECINCT AT ASSESSED VALUE, PAID BY THE TOLLMEN'S GUILD AS AGENT. Forty Tolls a head, down the margin. "The column's paper carries them to the Precinct for nothing," she says. "This one pays, and it rides on the same act. Your hand, love. One line."

interject.text: "Don't," Tamsin says. That is all. She has never said it to you before.

options.text: No. Nobody behind that door is for sale.

orme_no.speaker: npc_kn_factor
orme_no.text: "Then I'll not ask again." She closes the folder and tucks it under her arm. "Paper always keeps." She goes back up the lane to her counter, and does not hurry.

text.text: The captain sees the folder in your hand and closes his eyes for a moment. Then he holds out his hand for it, because now he must, and reads it through at the yellow line, every line, slowly. "It is lawful," he says. "The chair may dispose of supply as it sees fit." He gives it back. "Two papers on one door, designate. I had hoped you would not make me read the second." / You know what the Weighhouse is: Hale told you, in plain words, by the horses. Weighed and graded at the foot of Halcyon. A work line for ten years, or for as long as the work wants. The ones who do not come out are written "fulfilled". Some grades are not for work. / There is a line at the foot, blank. Forty Tolls a head, down the margin, paid to the city for its supply. The column would walk them to the stand, and the guild would walk them from there.

news.text: the designate signed the Cistern's people over to the guild at Knock's door, as intake for the Concern

decision.text: At the Cistern's door I signed the guild's paper as the first act of the chair, and the Cistern's sixty went up the guild's road to the Weighhouse as Concern intake, at forty Tolls a head.

text.text: He does not move. "Say it again, designate," he says, "so that it is the word and not the weather." He takes the order out of his breast pocket and holds it, not yet unfolded. "It is the first act of the chair. I will enter it as yours, in your name, at Knock, today. It will be the first thing the city ever has from you in writing." He waits. "I would like you to be sure. I have never been asked to be, and I would like somebody to have been."
Reyes does not move. "Say it again," she says, "so it's the word." She takes the order out and holds it. "First act of the chair. In your name. He'd have asked you to be sure. I'm asking."

nine_keeper.text: Nine does not move toward the door. It turns its cracked lens to you instead. "I have a keeper," it says to the line, "and it is not the city." Then, to you, very precisely, so that there can be no mistake on any record: "Is that an instruction from my keeper?"

options.text: Take her out of the door, Nine.

decision.text: At the Cistern's door I ordered Nine, as its keeper, to take Tamsin out of the door. It refused me, the only order it ever refused, and left me for good.

nine_refuses.speaker: npc_md_nine
nine_refuses.text: For a long moment Nine does nothing at all. Then: "No." It has never said the word to you before. It does not seem to know where to put its hands. "An undocumented person is the record's one precious thing, keeper. I will not take her out of anywhere." It takes the bound ledger out from under its arm, the one it does not write in while anybody watches, and writes in it, in front of you, a single line. Then it closes the ledger and puts it away. / "I withdraw," it says. "The grounds are attached. I will not fight you. I will not help." It walks up the lane past the column, and the wardens step aside for it without being told, and it does not look back, because it has never been built to.

I log the order as an error, here, at Knock, on this date." / Kress looks at it, and at the other wardens, and says it because it is in the book and he does not know what else is: "Unit 9 is struck off." Two rifles come off their slings, slowly, as if hoping somebody will stop them.
