decision.text: When the wardens turned their rifles on Nine at the Cistern's door, I stood between them, and it came to a fight on the apron.

nine_spared.speaker: narrator

text.text: The captain lets out a breath. "Struck off," he says, "and not mine to dispose of. The order says nothing about units." He lifts a hand without turning, and behind him the rifles go back on their slings. "Stand aside, unit." Nine stands aside, and keeps its lens on the woman in the door.
"Struck off," Reyes says, "and not mine to dispose of." She lifts a hand; the rifles go back on their slings. "Stand aside, unit."
"Struck off," Kress says, and it is clear he is relieved to have been told what to do. "Not mine to dispose of. Rifles down."

nine_spared.again: Nine, struck off and standing aside.

nine_struck.speaker: narrator
nine_struck.text: The wardens do it the way they do everything at Knock: politely. Nine does not lift a hand. It stands on the apron with its cracked lens on the woman in the door, and when the first round takes it in the chest it says, quite clearly, "Logged," and when the second takes it in the head it says nothing. It goes down all at once, like a stack of ledgers, and lies on the concrete with one hand open. / Nobody in Knock has ever seen a machine die. Nor had you.
nine_struck.again: Nine, on the concrete, one hand open.

news.text: the city's wardens shot their own unit dead on Knock's apron when it refused an order

decision.text: Nine refused the city's order at the Cistern's door, and the wardens struck it off there, on the apron, and I said nothing.

nine_deputy.speaker: npc_md_nine
nine_deputy.text: Nine does not move toward the door, and it does not refuse. It turns its cracked lens to you. "Designate," it says. "I am the city's. The city has given me a lawful order, and I am a deputy; I make the city's orders lawful line by line." A pause, measured to the tick. "I would like you to tell me to refuse. I find I cannot do it on my own. I would like it to be a word from the chair."
nine_deputy.again: "I would like you to tell me to refuse."

decision.text: At the Cistern's door I told Nine to obey the captain, and it carried Tamsin out of the door so the column could go in.

text.text: "On the designate's word," Nine says, "I refuse." / The captain looks at it, and at you, and something in his face that has been held tight for a fortnight lets go a little. "A unit acting on the designate's word is acting on the chair's," he says. "I will enter it as the chair's first countermand." He writes it on the foot of the order, under the space where the designate's name will go. "It does not move her out of the door."

"On the designate's word," Nine says, "I refuse." / Reyes looks at it, and at you. "Acting on the designate's word is acting on the chair's," she says. "Entered. The chair's first countermand." She writes it on the foot of the order. "Doesn't move her out of the door."

"On the designate's word," Nine says, "I refuse." / Kress looks at it, and at you, and writes something on the foot of the order because it seems to be expected. "The designate's word," he says. "All right. She's still in the door."

nine_obeys.speaker: narrator
nine_obeys.text: Nine walks down the apron to the door. Tamsin sees it coming and gets up, and it waits until she is up, and then it picks her up the way you would pick up a sleeping child, one arm under her knees, and she fights it, hard, all the way, with her fists and her teeth and her heels, and it does not let go and it does not hurt her and it does not say anything at all. It carries her the length of the apron and sets her down beside Maud, on her feet, and holds her by the shoulders until she stops, and then lets go. / "Precious," it says to her, quietly, and nobody else hears it but you. Then it walks back and stands beside you, and does not look at you.
nine_obeys.again: Tamsin beside Maud, out of the door.

news.text: the city's column carried the Cistern's people out of their door at Knock, on the designate's word

decision.text: At the Cistern's door I gave the designate's word, "carry on", and the column carried Reserve 9 to the city as Precinct supply: the first act of the chair.

news.text: the designate signed the Cistern's people over to the guild at Knock's door, as intake for the Concern

decision.text: At the Cistern's door I signed the guild's paper as the first act of the chair, and the Cistern's sixty went up the guild's road to the Weighhouse as Concern intake, at forty Tolls a head.

order.speaker: narrator

text.text: The door is already open. They come out of it because there is nowhere else to go. / The car is at the stand already, where it brought you home, with its tailboard down and its sixty numbered benches. / They come out one at a time, in issued grey, carrying what they can carry, and they stop on the concrete and look up, because they have never had a sky. The wardens do not push. They do not need to. Ines comes out last but one, with Teague behind her, and walks the length of the apron and up the lane to the stand with her hands folded in front of her and her eyes on the car, and climbs up, and sits on the bench with her number on it. Sayer Quist does not go. Pell wrote his "no" true, and the captain reads it off the chart at the line and stands him aside, and he stands in the empty door in his kitchen apron and watches the rest of them climb up, the one man in the Cistern who wanted to. Cadet Ferrow walks beside the line with her clipboard and says each name out loud as they pass her, every one, so that somebody in the grey has said it. / Maud stands on the apron and watches every one of them go past her. She has wanted to see their faces all her life. She sees them now.

Kress takes the plate off the RESCUE ACCESS panel and works the manual cycle, because there is nobody inside to open it any more, and the door swings out over the concrete with a crack like river ice. / The car comes down the toll road from the gate where it has waited since the order came, a long grey lorry with a canvas roof, and backs up to the stand with its tailboard down and its sixty numbered benches. / They come out one at a time, in issued grey, carrying what they can carry, and they stop on the concrete and look up, because they have never had a sky. The wardens do not push. They do not need to. Ines comes out last but one, with Teague behind her, and walks the length of the apron and up the lane to the stand with her hands folded in front of her and her eyes on the car, and climbs up, and sits on the bench with her number on it. / Maud stands on the apron and watches every one of them go past her. She has wanted to see their faces all her life. She sees them now.

"As the designate says." / Kress takes the plate off the RESCUE ACCESS panel and works the manual cycle, because there is nobody inside to open it any more, and the door swings out over the concrete with a crack like river ice. / The car comes down the toll road from the gate where it has waited since the order came, a long grey lorry with a canvas roof, and backs up to the stand with its tailboard down and its sixty numbered benches. / They come out one at a time, in issued grey, carrying what they can carry, and they stop on the concrete and look up, because they have never had a sky. The wardens do not push. They do not need to. Ines comes out last but one, with Teague behind her, and walks the length of the apron and up the lane to the stand with her hands folded in front of her and her eyes on the car, and climbs up, and sits on the bench with her number on it. / Maud stands on the apron and watches every one of them go past her. She has wanted to see their faces all her life. She sees them now.

The captain takes the order out of his breast pocket and writes on the foot of it, in your name, at Knock, today, and holds it out to you, and you sign under it. Then he puts his cap on. "Carry on," he says to the wardens. Bram works the cycle with Ines beside him, and the seam splits along her mother's weld with a crack like river ice, and the door swings out over the concrete, and the light goes into the hall. / They come out the way people come out of deep water, a few at a time, shading their eyes. Effie Calder first, nineteen, all the way out onto the concrete, where she stands with her arms held a little away from her sides, as if the air were something she had to keep her balance in. Wes Benn after her, looking up for rain. A girl of six with dust on her hand. Ines last but one, very straight, and she stops at the edge of the apron and looks up, and stays like that. / Nobody has told them what to do next. Nobody has to. Knock comes down the lane, slowly at first and then not slowly, with cups. / Maud said once that she would like to see a face. She stands on the apron with her stick and sees sixty, one after another, and does not say anything, and does not need to.

opened.again: The door, open. People on the apron, looking up.

interject.text: Ash has taken his hat off. He does not put it back on. "There," he says. "There it is." He is looking at the sky, not at them, as if checking it had come for them.

Tamsin is down the apron and into the middle of them before anybody can say anything, and Effie Calder grabs her by both arms and the two of them stand there in the light, laughing, saying nothing that makes sense.
"Look at them," Wren says. "Look at them look." She sounds as if she has been hit.
Odile watches them come out and does not say anything clever at all, which is the most she has ever said.
Kes watches a girl of six put her hand flat on the sunlit concrete and take it away and look at it. "Yeah," Kes says, softly. "That's what it's like."
Ilya counts them out. When he gets to sixty he says it out loud, "Sixty," and nobody knows why he is crying, and he does not say.

wren_sold.speaker: npc_rd_03
wren_sold.text: "Forty." Her pack is already on; it was packed before you signed. "Forty a head. That's what they were to you." She does not raise her voice; she has never needed to. "I keep my count. You know where you are on it now." She walks up the lane past the guild's coach and does not look at the people climbing into it, because she cannot stand to, and is gone up the toll road before the coach is loaded.

decision.text: Wren left me at Knock for signing the Cistern's people over to the guild.

wren_gone.speaker: narrator
wren_gone.text: Whatever you had with her, she took it up the road with her.
wren_gone.again: The toll road, with nobody on it.

tam_back.speaker: narrator
tam_back.text: In Shale, at Mags's, when the news comes up the track that the Cistern's door held, a woman behind the bar with Nell puts down a clean glass and goes to the door and stands in it a long time, looking south. She will hear the rest from you. She will want to.
tam_back.again: Word going up the track to Shale.

decision.text: The Cistern's door held, and Tamsin, who walked out on me in the city, heard it at Mags's. The door is the one thing that could have brought her back.

tam_hears.speaker: narrator
tam_hears.text: The news will be at Mags's by the next caravan: the Cistern's door opened from outside, and its people taken away on the designate's word. You know who will hear it, behind the bar, with a clean glass in her hand. You know she will not come down the road to ask you why.
tam_hears.again: Word going up the track to Shale.

decision.text: Tamsin heard at Mags's that I had let the Cistern's people be taken away. She did not come back.

options.text: Come out of the door, Tam.

out.text: "When they've gone." She picks at the concrete with a thumbnail. "Or when I have. You pick." She still does not look at you. "You already did, actually. You just haven't said it to him yet."

sorry.text: "Don't." Very quietly. "Sorry is for after. Tell him something, or don't, and then be sorry."

text.text: The relocation car stands backed up to the buffer stop at the end of the freight shed, the way the guild's lorries back up to be unloaded: the long grey Precinct lorry with its canvas roof on hoops and RESERVE 9 — PRECINCT SUPPLY — CAPACITY 60 stencilled on the tailboard. The tailboard is down. Nobody has chained it. The people who came in it sit along the platform's edge with their bundles on their knees, and on every bundle a name, written in its owner's hand. Nobody in the car speaks above a whisper. All of them saw the door. / Beyond the car a trestle has been set up under the shed's last lamp with a board on it, PRECINCT SUPPLY — RECEIVING, and a clerk's stool with nobody on it; out past the shed's mouth, on the river road, two Precinct vans wait with their engines off. Sixty, the Line's engine, stands at the water column drinking, as she does every morning, as if nothing were behind her. Captain Lowe sits on an upturned crate at the tailboard with his cap on his knee. He has shaved. He stands when he sees you, and uncovers. "Designate." On the concrete beside the car, cross-legged against its back wheel, a woman with copper hair hacked short is talking through the slats in a low voice. She sees your boots, and does not look up. Cadet Ferrow sits at the far end of the tailboard with her clipboard on her knees. Every hour, Kress says later, she reads the sheet aloud to the car, every name, so that somebody in the grey has said them that day.

The people who came in it sit along the platform's edge with their bundles on their knees, and on every bundle a name, written in its owner's hand. / Beyond the car a trestle has been set up under the shed's last lamp with a board on it, PRECINCT SUPPLY — RECEIVING, and a clerk's stool with nobody on it; out past the shed's mouth, on the river road, two Precinct vans wait with their engines off. Sixty, the Line's engine, stands at the water column drinking, as she does every morning, as if nothing were behind her. Sergeant Reyes stands at the tailboard in Lowe's cap with her arms folded, and does not unfold them. "Designate." On the concrete beside the car, cross-legged against its back wheel, a woman with copper hair hacked short is talking through the slats in a low voice. She sees your boots, and does not look up. Cadet Ferrow sits at the far end of the tailboard with her clipboard on her knees. Every hour, Kress says later, she reads the sheet aloud to the car, every name, so that somebody in the grey has said them that day.

"We wanted the city because it has clinics, and the sky, and because a door that only opens one way is a cell however kind the warden. We did not want to be graded. Teague stayed with the door, and I let her think I was the brave one." She looks at Sayer Quist, who sits apart with his hand flat over his ribs. "Sayer will go in. He wants a name for what is under his hand, and the Hospice has the only doctors who could give it one. That is his to choose. The rest of us would like to walk off this platform on our own feet, as we walked onto it. If there is a way that is not the van, we would like to hear it. If there is not, we will get into the van. We are very good at waiting."

text.text: Six o'clock on the Customs House steps, at the change of shift. Henrike Dahl comes out with the Act under her arm and sits on the top step with it open on her knee, as she does every evening, and the quay comes to watch, as it does when there is something worth watching. You tell her what is standing at her buffer. You put it to her: the city's order calls these people supply, and on this quay supply is a word the Act already has. She turns to Schedule 2 and reads it aloud, all of it, slowly, while the shift changes behind you: cargo; livestock; mails; a ship's stores; ballast; and their forty definitions. Then she closes it on her finger. "Stores are a ship's," she says. "These are nobody's ship's. No persons." She looks down the steps at the column. "Finding. A person landed on this quay is a passenger. A passenger carried here on the Precinct's own road has had her fare paid by the Precinct." / Lowe stands at the foot of the steps with his cap under his arm and the order in his hand, and when she has finished he unfolds it once more and reads its last line, and folds it, and puts it away. "The Ledger enforces the Harbour Act on this quay," he says, "and nothing else." He says it to his wardens, not to you. "Fold the trestle."

stand.speaker: narrator

text.text: Constance Okoye hears it out with her hands in her coat pockets, and then walks to the Stand and says three words to the gang at the board, and the three words go along the quay faster than she does. Crane Two stops. Then Six. By the time she comes back to the shed there are dockers standing along the platform's edge from the water column to the buffer, shoulder to shoulder, in canvas and oilskin and tyre-rubber gloves, not saying anything, not holding anything, two hundred of them and more coming up off the barges. "We don't load people," Connie says to the column. "Never have. Ask the Bond about the girl." She folds her arms. "Nobody on this quay touches that car, or that van, or that board, until those people are off it. Stand there with your rifles as long as you like. We're good at standing. It's what we're called." / Lowe looks along the line of them for a long time. "I am not going to shoot dockers on a quay for the Hospice block," he says at last, to nobody in particular, and then to his wardens: "Stand back from the car."

cradle_day.text: "By day?" Kobby Ofori does not stop coiling the cable on the bank. "By day the winch is chained and the Bond's lights are the brightest thing on the quay, and every man in grey on that platform can see straight down my stairs." He looks across at the freight shed, at the car's canvas roof just showing over the platform's edge. "Come back when the Bond's lights are the only lights. Swing a lamp at me twice. Wait. Once."

cradle.speaker: narrator

text.text: Past midnight, when the Bond's white lights are the only lights on the quay, Kobby Ofori's granddaughter rides the basket out over the dry river toward Bridgeward with a lamp swinging on its rim, slow, the way it swings when the cradle is carrying somebody who matters, and every warden on the platform turns to watch it go. Behind their backs they get up off the platform's edge one at a time, in their stockinged feet, carrying their boots and their bundles with their names on, and go along the river wall in the dark to the stairs and down them onto the bed, where the Hulls' people are waiting with their hands out. Nobody speaks. A child starts to, and is lifted, and doesn't. / By the time Abena's lamp comes back across the bed the car and the stairs are empty, and on the Benguela Star, in the crew book that has been signed every Sunday for ninety years, Kobby is writing names in his slow square hand. "Crew," he says, when he sees you watching. "Schedule 3. A crewed vessel in port. Nobody moves her, and nobody moves her crew." He blots the page. "They'll have to learn to sign on a Sunday." / In the morning Lowe finds the car empty, and stands looking at it for a long time. Then he takes the order out and writes across its foot NOT FOUND AT RECEIPT, and initials it, and puts his cap on. "Clause twenty-two," he says to the wardens. "Written off." He does not look toward the river wall. He looks, very carefully, at the engine.

text.text: "Then say it so the order can hear it." Lowe does not move toward the trestle. "Say it, and I give the clerk your name, and the vans take them round by the river road, and in the morning they are graded." A pause. "Say it, or don't."
"Say it, then," Reyes says. "So the clerk can write it."
"You have to say it," Kress says. "Out loud. For the clerk."

decision.text: At Carrick's buffer I gave Precinct Supply my word, and the Cistern's people were received into the city.

text.text: The clerk comes out of the shed's office with his ledger and sits on the stool at the trestle and reads the names in a flat clean voice, and each of them comes to the board and says "Here," and is written RECEIVED. Ines first, as at the door. Sayer Quist with his hand over his ribs, gladly. Effie Calder last, who looks at you before she climbs into the van, and then doesn't. Lowe signs under the clerk's line and then, because the order requires it, holds the ledger out to you. When you have signed, he puts his cap on and does not take it off again for anybody on the quay. / When the clerk has read the last name Tamsin is still standing at the trestle. "And me," she says. The clerk runs his pen down the sheet and up it again. "Not listed," he says, politely. The van's door shuts a foot in front of her face. interject.text: Kes watches the vans go. "Graded by morning," she says. "I said." She does not look at you for the rest of the day.
"Received," Nine says. "Entered." It writes something in its own ledger, and does not read it back.
Tamsin, beside you, does not say anything. She watches the vans all the way to the end of the Wall, and then she looks at you as if she were learning your face for later.

walked.speaker: narrator

text.text: By morning the Hulls have more crew than they had, and nobody on the quay has seen them come. Below the river wall there is new washing on the Star's rail, in issued grey. Sayer Quist shakes everybody's hand on the platform, one at a time, and walks across the river road to the Hospice block's clinic on his own feet, to be graded, because he wants a name for what is under his ribs, and it is his to want. / Tamsin goes with them, at the back, with a child on her hip who is not hers. At the edge of the light she stops and looks at you. "Don't think it makes us square," she says. "It doesn't." She shifts the child to her other hip. "Thank you." Then she goes.

Tamsin has her hands in her pockets and is grinning at the shed's broken roof as if it were a joke only she had heard. "Passengers," she says. "Passengers."

text.text: Sixty at the buffer, drinking at the water column, and behind her nothing but the buffer stop and its lamp. Somebody has chalked on the shed's last pillar, in a hand that has only just learned the shapes: PASSENGERS.

Sixty at the buffer, drinking, and nothing behind her but the buffer stop and its lamp. On the Stand's tally board, under the day's gangs, somebody has chalked a gang that was never called on: RESERVE 9 — STOOD.

Sixty at the buffer, drinking. The trestle is folded against the shed wall with its board turned to the brick.

sealed.text: Tamsin sits on the apron with her back against the rock beside the shut door, in the place where she sat in it, her knees drawn up. She looks up when your shadow reaches her, and does not get up. "It held," she says. "You found another way. After you'd said the first one. Twice." She picks at the concrete with her thumbnail. "I know which one you said first."
sealed.again: Tamsin, against the rock beside the door.

opened.text: Tamsin, on the apron by the open door, with a girl of six on her hip, pointing at things for her: the windpump, the tank, a goat, the sky, the sky again. She sees you over the girl's head and her face closes, not hard, only shut, the way a door shuts that might open again some other year. "They opened it," she says. "Themselves. You didn't. Remember that, when you tell it."
opened.again: Tamsin by the open door, the girl on her hip.

sold.text: Tamsin sits in the open door of an empty hall, where the guild's green walked them out, with her back against the steel and nothing behind her but a swept floor and the hum. "Forty a head," she says, without looking round. "Kes told me once what's at the top of that road. Spare parts, she said. She was being funny." A breath. "She wasn't."

held.text: Tamsin, in the empty door again, with road dust to her knees. "I walked to the city," she says. "All the way, behind the car. At the buffer they let me sit by it, because I wasn't anything they had a word for." She does not look at you. "Then the clerk read the names, and I wasn't one of them, and the van's door shut a foot in front of my face." She laughs, once, with nothing in it. "Sixty at MOTHER's counter, and one more. Sixty on the city's sheet. I was right all along. It doesn't help."
held.again: Tamsin in the empty door, road dust to her knees.

buffer.text: Tamsin, on the platform against the car's back wheel, her shoulder to the slats. "All the way from Knock," she says, before you can say anything. "I walked behind it. Nobody stopped me. I'm not on the sheet, so I'm not anything they're allowed to stop." Through the slats beside her head somebody's fingers come out and hold her sleeve, and she lets them. "Get them off this car," she says. "If you can't, go away."

text.text: Tamsin on the Benguela Star's deck among them, a child asleep against her shoulder who is not hers, on a ship that has not moved in ninety years. "You got them off," she says. "I'll give you that. I'll give you that every day I live." She shifts the child. "It doesn't make me come back. You said the word first. I heard it."

hub.again: Tamsin does not say anything else. She is waiting for you to go.

options.text: And if I can't get them off?

text.text: "No." Not cruel. Very tired. "Get them off the car."
"No." She shifts the child. "You got them off. You'd said the other thing first. Both of those are true, and I can only carry one of them, and I've got a child on this arm."
"No." She says it gently, which is worse. "You said carry on. You said it twice, so it would be the word and not the weather. I heard the word. I can't unhear it because the weather changed after."
"Then I walk behind the van." She doesn't look round. "If they let me in, I go in. They won't. I'm not on the sheet."
"Here, for now. They're crew, Kobby says. They have to sign on Sundays." She almost smiles. "I've never signed anything on a Sunday. I've never known what day it was."

"Here, for now. Connie says the quay always wants hands." She looks at Ines, who is learning how to carry a crate from a docker half her age. "Ines has never done a day's work she wasn't counted for. She's going to hate being paid."

"Go back to the city in a month, and stand at the Hospice gate, and say their names at it, one a day, until somebody comes out to make me stop." She means it. "Sixty days. I've done longer behind a wall."
"Go up that road, when I know where it ends." She doesn't say it like a plan. She says it like the weather. "Don't tell me you'll come."
"Teach sixty people what weather is." She almost smiles, and catches it. "Effie wants to see Shale. Wes is waiting for rain. Ola's in love with a goat. Somebody has to stop them dying of it."

"Sit here." She pats the concrete. "Somebody should, who's been on both sides of it. When it opens, if it ever does, they'll want somebody who knows what's out here and won't lie to them about it." She looks at you. "That isn't you. Not any more."
"Learn where Pell keeps the tablets before he forgets. He's the only doctor sixty people have ever had." She shrugs. "I said I'd keep them alive. That's what that is. It's boring. It's mine."
"Stay where they are." She shrugs. "They didn't choose the city. So I'm staying where they did choose."

next.again: Tamsin has said what she will do.

text.text: "Then do something about it," Tamsin says.
"I know." She does look at you, then. "Me too. Go on."
"Sorry's for after, I said." She looks at you properly for the first time. "This is after." A pause. "I know you are. It doesn't change where I'm sitting."

Ines Halloran at the Star's chart table with the crew book open in front of her, reading the names in it, ninety years of Sundays, slowly. "They signed every week," she says. "To say they were still aboard. We were counted every quarter to say we were still supply." She turns a page. "I prefer their reason."

Ines Halloran on an upturned crate in front of the Boxes with a tin cup of Espe Cardenas's soup, watching the cranes. "Nobody here has asked me for a number," she says. "I have been waiting all morning for somebody to. Nobody has." She drinks. "I find I keep standing up when a docker walks past, in case he wants the table."

hi.again: "Nobody has asked me for a number," Ines says.

text.text: "What we came for, without the part we did not." She sets the cup down. "Sayer has his clinic. The young ones want the Wheel, and Shale, and the sea, which Effie insists is real. The old ones want a wall with no door in it, so that nobody can open it from the other side." She looks at you. "I want to write to Maud Ferrow. I have never had an address before."

"Learn the quay. It has rules; I am good at rules." She sets the cup down. "The young ones want the Wheel, and Shale, and the sea, which Effie insists is real. The old ones want a wall with no door in it, so that nobody can open it from the other side." She looks at you. "And I want to write to Maud Ferrow. I have never had an address before."

Effie Calder halfway up the Star's ladder, as high as she can get without being on the rail. "It's a ship," she says, before hello. "Kobby says it floated once. On water. On top of it." She looks down at the dry bed. "I'm going to see the water it floated on. The Basin. Today. Don't tell Teague. Teague isn't here. I can tell her myself."

Effie Calder on the quay's edge with her boots off and her feet over the Basin, a yard above the water. "It's salt," she says, before hello. "I put my finger in it and licked it. Nobody told me it would be salt." She swings her feet. "Connie says I can try the call-on at dawn if I can lift a sack. I can lift a sack. I've been lifting sacks for nineteen years. Nobody ever paid me for it."

hi.again: "Salt," Effie says, and swings her feet.

topic.text: "Back where?" She means it as a real question. Then: "To see Maud. To see Knock, from the outside, on purpose. Not to the door." She looks at the Basin. "One step past the line, I said. I think I've gone a bit further than that."

text.text: Ines Halloran at the edge of the apron, where the concrete ends and the dust begins, standing very straight with her hands folded and her face turned up. Somebody has scrubbed the concrete behind her until it is paler than the rest. "I stepped round them," she says, without looking down. "The first thing I did outside in my life was step round the city's dead. I would like it to have been something else." Then she looks at you. "I had you taller. I have stopped minding. Everything out here is a different size from its voice."

Ines Halloran at the edge of the apron, where the concrete ends and the dust begins, standing very straight with her hands folded and her face turned up. She has been standing there, Maud says, since first light. "I had you taller," she says, without looking down. "I have stopped minding. Everything out here is a different size from its voice." Then she looks at you. "Maud is shorter than hers. So am I, she tells me."

hi.again: Ines at the edge of the apron, looking up.

text.text: "I stopped being the one at the table before the door opened." She considers the sky. "I find I do not miss it. Teague has the ring, and the ring has nothing left to decide, which she minds more than I would have." She looks at the open door. "Some of us will go to the city; Sayer has gone already, to have the thing under his ribs named. Effie wants the Wheel. The rest of us will stay where the water is, which is here. MOTHER says good morning now. It took her five days. She practised on Bram."

"Learn to be one of sixty instead of the one at the table." She considers the sky. "Some of us will go to the city; Sayer has gone already, to have the thing under his ribs named. Effie wants the Wheel. The rest of us will stay where the water is, which is here." She looks at the open door. "MOTHER says good morning now. It took her five days. She practised on Bram."

hi.text: Ola Fairley on the rail of Afua Danso's goat pen in her issued grey, with a goat eating her sleeve. She is letting it. "You didn't say they'd eat my sleeve," she says. "You told me everything. You didn't say sleeves." She laughs, and doesn't hide it behind her hand any more.
hi.again: "Sleeves," Ola says, and scratches the goat.

options.text: Out and back, you said. Will you go back in?

topic.text: "Every night. To sleep. I'm not mad." She scratches the goat between its horns. "Out in the day, back at night. Out and back. I asked the ring if it was allowed, and Ines said nobody's in charge of allowing now." She seems to find this frightening and wonderful in about equal parts.

hi.text: Wes Benn sitting on the edge of the apron facing south, a lamp beside him that he has finally put down. "Twice a year, you said," he says. "If the year is good." He hasn't taken his eyes off the edge of the sky. "I'm not going to miss it."
hi.again: Wes, facing south, waiting for rain.

topic.text: "I've waited twenty-nine years for water not to be rock." He smiles at the horizon. "I can do months. Afua says she'll shout when she smells the dust coming."

hi.text: Effie Calder at the head of the lane where it meets the toll road, as far from the door as she can get without being on the road. "I went past the line," she says, before hello. "One step. Nothing happened. Then I went a bit further." She points north up the road. "How far is Shale? Really? Don't say a day. Everybody says a day."
hi.again: "A day," Effie says, disgusted. "Everybody says a day."

topic.text: "Go to Shale. Then the Wheel, if they'll have me. Tamsin says they take anybody who can fix a track, and I can fix anything MOTHER ever broke." She grins. "Then I'll come back and tell Teague nothing happened. And then I'll go a bit further."

look.text: The Spire's close, after the card. The works have changed pace: the scaffold is coming down off the steps plank by numbered plank, the stone saws run from first light, and on the works board the 49 in PUBLIC STEPS REOPEN R49 has been painted out and a 30 lettered over it in a hand that does not slope. Nobody is on the steps who is not carrying stone. The wardens at the lane post have been doubled, and they watch the square the way people watch weather coming. q_what.text: "What is under your feet." He does not look down. "The Vault of Accounts, and the thing in it that keeps them. Ninety years of forecasts: every birth and death and harvest and riot in the Reach, a season early, at odds nobody else can make. The Exchange sells them by the sheet. The Board would like to own the press." A small, exact pause. "And the schedules attaching. The schedules are the valuable part. A forecast is a guess. A schedule is a guess with wardens."
q_what.again: "A guess with wardens," Quill says again.

interject.text: "With all schedules attaching," Odile says, very quietly, the way she reads a clause back to the man who wrote it. "That's the city, my dear. Not the machine. The city."
"The schedules are the record's obligations," Nine says. "They are not an asset. They are a debt the record owes the people in it." Quill, pleasantly: "Everything is an asset to somebody, Unit 9."

q_why.text: "Because nothing else will hold." He says it as if it were obvious, because to him it is. "The Ledger may void any transfer of the city's property but one: the first act of its own Magistrate. It promised that in the charter, ninety years ago, to whoever would sit in the chair, and it has never once had to keep the promise." He lets that sit. "A signature from anybody else is a document. Yours, as your first act, is the one paper in the Reach the Ledger has sworn never to tear up. We are not buying the core from the city. We are buying it from the chair." A small gesture: you. "You are the chair."

interject.text: "Clause one, the reserved act," Nine says. "It is real. I have read it. I had hoped nobody else had."
"So it's not the machine they need," Kes says. "It's you. Of course it is. It's always a person at the end. Somebody has to sign."

q_city.text: "It runs." Quill looks at the lamps, which work. "Clinics on contract, the Line on time, water by meter, the Sink pumped because pumping is cheaper than drowning. Everyone useful. Nobody waiting nineteen years for anything." The coat does not move. "There are costs. The Board does not pretend otherwise. Some people are more useful whole and some are more useful in parts, and the Clinic floors are where that is decided, by doctors, carefully. The hounds in the valley will answer the Board instead of nobody. And the leash the Concern already holds on every piece of its chrome will have a city at the other end." He meets your eye. "You will have heard all of this from people who would rather it were not true. I would rather you heard it from me. It is true."
q_city.again: "It is true," Quill says. "All of it."

interject.text: "Spare Parts," Kes says. "That's what we call the Clinic floors, down where I'm from. He said it nicer. He's paid to."

text.text: "Less than there was." He takes no pleasure in it, which is worse. "The Board has read the Skirts' file. The Shift marked you, and the Clean shut the gate on you, and the Board has a long memory for the people who stood in its gate. The seat is withdrawn." A figure, arrived at somewhere behind his eyes. "What remains is a sum: an annuity, paid at Ninebridge, for life, and the Concern's clinics at the end of it, which are the best in the Reach. And your life kept on file, which is a kindness you will not understand until you are old."

"The seat. You have the card." He does not need to look at it. "A seat at the Board's table on the terrace, a contract that is a citizenship, the gardens under glass, and the Board's season, which is longer than other people's. Considerably." He waits for you to ask what that means, and when you do not, he looks almost approving. "Nobody up there looks their age. You would not either."

It can wait for the next face the forecast finds; you would be surprised how many faces a city has." A beat. "If you say no, say it to me plainly, so that I can carry it plainly. I dislike carrying anything that rattles."

text.text: Captain Lowe at the foot of the steps, cap under his arm, in the same grey he wore on Knock's apron, pressed. "Designate." He does not salute; he never has. "The Precinct has given me the close until the designate attends. It considers that a reprimand. I wrote ATTENDED. DECLINED. COLUMN WITHDRAWN. across the foot of an order of the Ledger's, and a captain who does that is given a square to stand in." He looks at the square. "It is a good square."

Captain Lowe at the foot of the steps, cap under his arm. "Designate." He does not salute; he never has. "The order did not execute. Nobody stood it down. It is on my desk with a pin through it, and the Precinct has asked me what I intend to do with it." A pause the length of a clause. "I have said: wait. It is what the order does. I am learning it from the order."

Captain Lowe at the foot of the steps, his left arm strapped across his chest under the grey, standing as straight as the strap lets him. "Designate." He does not salute; he could not. "I yielded on your apron with two of mine on the concrete. I have written to their families. I write a bad letter. I have had practice, and it has not helped." He does not say it to wound you. He says it so that it has been said.

Captain Lowe at the foot of the steps, cap under his arm. He looks older than the grey. "Designate." The same voice he uses for everything, and it nearly holds. "Thirty-two doors, in eleven years and a month. I knelt by one of them." He does not say her name. He does not need to; it is in the way he does not say it.

Captain Lowe at the foot of the steps, cap under his arm. "Designate." The same voice he uses for everything. "Thirty-two doors, in eleven years and a month. Lawful, every one. I checked." He looks at the steps, not at you. "The Precinct has given me the close until the designate attends. It considers that an honour."

text.text: "An inquiry, after. Whatever comes after." He says it the way he says the weather. "The Precinct does not dismiss captains; it moves them to squares." Then, lower: "If one morning the lens has nothing to say to us, designate, the wardens will still be at their posts. Order is a habit before it is a schedule. I have spent eleven years on the schedule. I will spend whatever is left on the habit."

"Nothing, until the order does something." He almost smiles. "It is the first time in eleven years I have had a paper on my desk that I am not obliged to carry out and not permitted to throw away. I find I read it every morning. I find it reads the same."

"The Precinct will want to know why a captain yielded to a designate." He moves the strapped arm a quarter-inch and stops. "I will tell it: because the designate was standing in front of a door, and so was I, and only one of us was wrong. I expect it will not like the answer. I did not expect it to."

"Promoted, probably." Flat. "They promote the captains who carry. They are short of us." He turns the cap round once in his hand. "I have been told I may choose my next square. I asked for this one. I wanted to see what the first act of the chair looks like from the bottom of the steps."
"The close, until you attend. Then whatever the chair decides." He looks at you. "It will be you deciding. I would rather know that than not."

now.again: "The habit," Lowe says, "or the schedule." He does not say which.

text.text: "Behind their door." He nods once. "When the column went back up the lane, somebody inside knocked on it. Three times, slowly, the way you knock to say you are still there. I have not told the Precinct. It would want to know what it meant."

"Out." Something nearly like pleasure crosses his face and leaves again. "Some in the city, of their own will; I signed them through the gate myself, with their names. Ola Fairley asked me what the sky does at night. I told her. She did not believe me."
"On their feet, with their names." He looks at his hands. "I have never once carried people who asked to come. I did not know how to hold a door for them. Sayer Quist showed me. He held it for me."
"Up the guild's road, to the Weighhouse." He does not look away from you. "I read the paper, as you said I must. Two lawful papers on one door. I chose the one you signed."

"In the Hospice block. Graded. Fed. Most of them alive in ten years." His own words from the apron, said back without inflection. "Never asked." He turns the cap round once. "I go and look at them on my day off. I am not sure who that is for."
"Sixty names," he says, "and Knock's. I have them all. I had them before I came down the toll road."

interject.text: "He has the names," Ilya says afterwards. "He counts them like I count mine. Every night, the same number, in case it's changed."

text.text: "The Precinct keeps the close the day the designate attends. I keep the Precinct's close." He looks up the steps, and down to the steel door in the Spire's foot. "Whatever you do up there, I will be at the foot of these steps when you come down them." A beat. "If you come down them in a hurry, I will be a slow reader. I have always been a slow reader."

"The Precinct keeps the close the day the designate attends. I keep the Precinct's close." He looks up the steps, all of them. "I will be here when you come down. Whatever you are when you come down."

home.text: "Home." He says it the way he said it in Knock, as if checking that it is still a word. "Thirty-one evictions, and I did not know what the third word was until a reserve that had never seen my face told me without speaking." He looks at the square, and the city, and the lamps that work. "I have not been home in eleven years. I have a room in the Precinct with a desk in it. I find I would like to go home, after. I do not know where it is."

list.text: He takes it out of his breast pocket: a sheet folded so many times the creases have gone soft, EVICTIONS — SCHEDULED at the top in a clerk's hand and, under it, in his own, thirty-one names and dates, and a thirty-second line that is only the word KNOCK. "Every one I carried, or did not. I have read it every night for eleven years." He holds it out. "If you sit in that chair, read this before you sign anything. Not because it will change what you sign. So that you will know whose names were on the paper before yours."
list.again: The folded list is in your pack.

interject.text: "Thirty-one entries and a thirty-second," Nine says. "I have them too. His hand is better than mine."

"Captain, on paper, since your apron. The Precinct needed somebody to stand here. I asked to be the one." She looks at you the way you look at a bill. "He went down with his empty hand out. I want you to know I saw it."

p_intro.text: Petra Mason on the cold stone at the west end of the close, her hood down and her face bare to the city's lamps, which may be the bravest thing anybody has done on this square in ninety years. Thaddeus is beside her with the machete across his knees, not sharpened, only out; Rhoda has her back to the Spire. "We came east," Petra says. "Not for you. For the book." She looks up the steps to the doors, and down to the steel door in the Spire's foot. "It's under there. Everybody in the Reach is in it, a season early. And you're the only one it's going to open for."

p_do.text: "Wait." She nearly smiles. "You're the only book we allow, remember. Nothing happens unless you're on the stone to see it." She looks at the steel door again. "If you go down there and want it burned, we know fire. We know it better than anybody alive. If you don't, we'll have walked a long way to sit on cold stone in a city that counts us." A shrug under the homespun. "It's been done."
p_do.again: "Wait," Petra says. "We're good at it now."

p_sash.text: "Then you're not going down to the book. You're the book." Plainly, to your face, which is their rule. "I can't promise you Thaddeus then. Nobody can promise anybody Thaddeus. I can promise you I'll say it to you first, like this, and not from behind." She looks at you for a long moment. "Don't make me say it twice."

text.text: "He burned with the rows." She says it to the steps, not to you. "I wasn't there. I was told. He never fought for seed; he said that was the point. It was a good point. It didn't stop the fire."

"Walking somewhere with the guild's paper in his pocket that says Openfield is theirs." Her mouth goes thin. "He never fought for seed. He said that was the point. He's still making it, on a road, to anyone who'll stand still."

"At Openfield, singing at the seed store." She looks at her hands. "He thinks I'm in the hills. I let him. It's the kindest lie I know, and I know a lot of them; we keep no books, so we keep everything else."

walkin.text: Nine on a crate at the edge of the fire barrel's ring, its ledger on its knee and dust from somewhere outside the Wall on its plating. "NOT FOUND," it says, before you can ask. "I walked in through the Precinct gate at six this morning. The lens did not look up. An asset written off is not looked for; I have now tested this." The lens clicks. "The card said the designate will attend the steps. It did not say the designate would attend them alone. I have assumed an omission."

text.text: A sister of the Choir in undyed homespun gone grey on the road, on the cold stone below the planters with a dozen more behind her in a loose ring. Two of them are singing under their breath. "Keziah Abernethy. The Elder sent us." She does not get up; she pats the stone beside her instead. "The sky keeps no books, so nobody will write down that we came. We came."

A sister of the Choir in undyed homespun gone grey on the road, on the cold stone below the planters with a dozen more behind her in a loose ring. Two of them are singing under their breath. "Keziah Abernethy. Sister Calla sent us. She'd have come herself; she's setting a leg in Shale and won't leave it half set." She pats the stone beside her. "The sky keeps no books. We came anyway."

intro.text: A docker from Carrick in her work clothes, the tally hook still on her belt, sitting on the close's good stone as if she were pricing it. "Ifeoma Okonjo. Connie's on the quays; I'm the one she could spare." She nods back towards the docks, which you cannot see from here. "The Stand keeps the quays the night you go up, and every night after it has to. Nobody loads. Nobody unloads. Nobody burns anything they can't unburn."

intro.text: A young man from Bridgeward on the Court's side of the close, eating an apple down to the pips, wearing the three crews' colours in three different places, which in Bridgeward is a passport. "Tuan. I run for the chain." He nods at the lane as if Bridgeward were at the end of it. "Auntie Holt says the streets are kept. The Gilt keep theirs, the Pale keep theirs, the Rustmouths keep ours, and nobody likes it, which is how you know it's fair."

intro.text: Verity of the Saints on a bench by the empty plinth, a radio in her lap with the back off, listening to the hiss with her head on one side. "I said I would come if it came to reading." She does not take the earpiece out. "The girl stays in the tower. She hears it every night; she does not need to hear it on a stair." A small adjustment with a screwdriver. "If that night comes, the Saints read first, gently, on every set that listens. And if what has to be read has to be read here, at the source, I am here. I read slowly. Nobody has ever asked me to read anything fast that was worth it."

first.text: "The ones that have already happened." She turns the radio over. "A forecast that has already come true is only news, and people can hear news. "You will want to read the rest fast. Don't."

intro.text: Assessor Seventeen at the Court's door, where units stand, quite still: Nine's pattern, the Wet's wear, a lens with a hairline crack it has never had mended. "ENTERED: ATTENDING." Its voice has the dam's patience in it, somehow. "I have read one record aloud, to its keepers, at the speed it was written. The dam did not fall. I will read whatever is put in front of me." A click. "I am told that is too slow. I have never been told what it is too slow for."

long.text: "Ninety years, at the speed it was written." A pause. "I will not read all of it. Nobody could hear all of it. I will read what is put in front of me, every line, and I will not change a word, and I will stop when I am told to stop by somebody who has the right." The cracked lens turns to you. "I have not yet decided who that is. I am told it is you. I am waiting to be told by you."

first.text: Faulk's trestle stands under the scaffold lamp at the edge of the square, where the works lay out each morning's stones on paper: three planks on two horses, the plans weighted down with numbered offcuts. Tonight the plans are rolled and tied and stood in a bucket, and the planks are bare. Faulk is up on the scaffold and does not look round. Under the nearest stone is a note in a mason's capitals: FOR THE DESIGNATE. DON'T STAND ON IT. Whatever happens at the top of those steps, the city will have a night after it that nobody has planned for: the Precinct's lamps on or off, the radios loud or dark, a crowd at the foot of the steps either way. cold.text: The trestle is bare, the plank wiped clean, Faulk's numbered stones in a row along its edge as if they were waiting to be laid.

r_choir.speaker: npc_a3_31
r_choir.text: Keziah comes across from the planters with her hands tucked into her sleeves against the cold and looks at the bare plank as if it were a bed somebody was about to be laid on. "A vigil." She tries the word and puts it down again. "We don't keep vigils, child. A vigil is waiting for somebody to die or to wake. We sit." She sits, on the end of Faulk's trestle, which he would not like. "So we'll sit. On this stone, and on the Sink's stair, and at every pump the Precinct runs, one of us at each with a lamp and a pot of something hot, all night. We'll sing the long one, the one with no end, so anybody who can't see where they're going can walk toward the noise." She looks at the city's lamps. "If the lights go, people will be afraid of the dark first, before they get round to being afraid of anything else. We are not afraid of the dark. We'll lend them that." She chalks a small circle on the plank, the Choir's mark for an open sky, and nothing else.

interject.text: "The long one," Ash says, very low, when she has gone back to her stone. "I sang it all one winter in the Gully, to nineteen people who couldn't hear it. It was the only time it ever felt short."

r_stand.speaker: npc_a3_33
r_stand.text: Ifeoma Okonjo gets up off the good stone and comes to the trestle with the tally hook in her hand, and lays it on the plank between you like a pen. "Kept is already promised. What you're asking is how." She counts it off on the hook's tines. "The cranes chained at the jib by sundown. The fuel barges walked out to the middle of the river on their own warps, where nobody with a torch can reach them without a boat, and we have the boats. The Bond's doors chained from the inside by the people who work behind them. And nobody, not a warden, not a factor, not a man with a gun and a list, puts a person on anything that floats or rolls, that night or after." She picks the hook up again. "If the city burns, it burns without Carrick's fuel in it. That's the most a docker can promise, and it's more than anybody's ever had from a docker for nothing."

interject.text: "Fuel in the middle of the river," Kes says. "That's the cleverest thing anybody's said all week, and she said it like a shopping list."

r_gangs.speaker: npc_a3_34
r_gangs.text: Tuan comes over with a fresh apple and does not eat it, which from him you understand is formality. "Auntie said you'd ask it like that." He sets the apple on the plank like a paperweight. "Here's how. Every runner the three crews have, on the chain's links, one to a corner, all night. No crew crosses another's line, not even to help, because help across a line is how the last war started, and the one before it. The Saints' tower open to anybody who comes to its door. And the Gilt hold the foot of the Crown's stair." He grins. "First time anybody from Bridgeward's kept anything for the Crown. They'll want paying for it later. Later can wait." He takes the apple back. "You've heard that Bridgeward won't burn. What you haven't heard is that Auntie Holt said it with her hand on the chain. She's never done that for anything that wasn't a funeral."

interject.text: "Help across a line is how the last war started," Wren says afterwards. "He's four years younger than me and he's right. I hate that."

r_wheel.speaker: npc_a3_32
r_wheel.text: Lucan Begay comes to the trestle the way a rider comes to a fire, stopping a stride short. "Ahead." He nods slowly. "We've never once been asked to get somewhere before the news. We're usually after it, with a cart, picking up what it dropped." He lays it out with one finger in the dust on the plank: the stopping places on the roads in and out of the city, thirty-one of them, a rider at each by a lamp from sundown; the Line's halts; Four Ways; the toll road east to Tollhouse 9 and the Sallow. "Whatever comes down off this hill, the riders hear it from a Wheel mouth first, and they carry it out the same way, slow, and to faces. Nobody in the Reach hears what you did out of a box in a wall. They hear it from somebody who can be asked what it means and has to look at them while they answer."
r_wheel.again: "Thirty-one lamps," Lucan says. "One to a road."

interject.text: "A face you can ask," Ilya says. "That's all anybody in the Sallow ever wanted from the city. They got a list."

text.text: Lowe comes to the trestle and does not sit. He puts his cap down on the plank instead, crown down, the way a warden puts down a thing he means to pick up again. "You heard me say it: a habit before a schedule." He looks at the cap. "Then here is the habit, so that it is written somewhere. The Precinct's posts doubled at the clinic doors and at the pumps. Rifles slung, not carried. Line six of every standing order: residents are not to be frightened. The lane gates left open, not shut; a shut gate on a bad night is how a crowd learns to climb." He picks the cap up. "I cannot promise you the Precinct, designate. I can promise you the four who stood on your apron, and the ones they eat with. They are the ones who will be at the clinic doors. They have been told." A pause the length of a clause. "I told them before you asked. I wanted to see whether you would."

He picks the cap up. "I cannot promise you the Precinct, designate. I can promise you the four who stood on your apron, and the ones they eat with. They are the ones who will be at the clinic doors. They have been told." A pause the length of a clause. "I told them before you asked. I wanted to see whether you would."

interject.text: Tamsin watches Lowe pick up his cap and go back to the foot of the steps. "He told them before you asked," she says. "I don't know what to do with a warden I like. I'll think of something."

r_reyes.speaker: npc_md_12
r_reyes.text: Reyes hears it with her arms folded. "You want the wardens to keep order with nobody telling them what order is." She unfolds them. "That's called a job. Most of mine have never had one." Then, plainer: "Posts doubled on the clinics and the pumps. Rifles slung. Gates open. Anybody who raises a carbine at a resident that night answers to me, and I am worse than the schedule." She looks up the steps, and then at the place where he would have stood. "He'd have said it better. He'd have said it slower. It would have meant the same."

r_kress.text: You send to the lane post. Warden Kress comes up from it with his cap in his hand: the senior warden, who led the column only because there was nobody left above him to lead it, and went back to the ranks the day after. He hears the whole of it standing at attention, which on a man of fifty looks like it costs him. "Line six," he says at the end. "Residents are not to be frightened. I'll see to it, designate. I don't know who else will." He goes back down to the post, and you hear him at it for a long time afterwards, saying it to the young ones in the voice of a man reading it off a wall.
r_kress.again: Kress, at the lane post, saying line six.

r_saints.speaker: npc_bw_04
r_saints.text: Verity brings the radio with her, back still off, and sets it on the plank with the hiss turned low, so that it sits between you like a third person. "Gently is a method, not a mood." She ticks it off with the screwdriver. "Every set on every roof in Bridgeward on the hiss band from dusk. Twelve of us, a district each, with a list of who lives where. The girl hears the Ledger a breath before the rest of us, she always has, so we will know which lines are coming before they come." She looks at you over the radio. "And this, which nobody has ever done for anybody: if your name is coming, a Saint is at your door before it does. Nobody hears their own death from a stranger on our band. Not one person. I would rather walk all night."
r_saints.again: "A Saint at the door before it comes," Verity says. "Not one person."

interject.text: "A knock before the news," Odile says. "On the floor we called that a courtesy, and charged for it. She's giving it away."

r_saints_boy.text: It is a Saints' boy who comes across the close, with Verity's radio held against his chest like a baby, its back still off. "She'd have come," he says. "She said gently. We'll do it gently." He tells it the way she taught him: every set on every roof in Bridgeward on the hiss band from dusk, twelve Saints with a district each, and a Saint at the door of anybody whose name is coming, before it comes. "Nobody hears it from a stranger. That was the whole of what she said, every time." He chalks a small square on the plank, a radio, and goes back across the close without looking round.
r_saints_boy.again: A small square in chalk on the plank: a radio.

r_nine.speaker: npc_md_nine
r_nine.text: Nine sets its ledger on the plank and opens it at the back, where its own hand is smallest. "The errors first." The lens clicks, once. "Four hundred and eleven forecasts the record made since R4 and the world did not keep, each with the date it was made and the date it failed. At my speed, an hour and a quarter." It turns a page. "If anything is read tomorrow night, by anybody, at any speed, I will read the first page of this, and the last, and the number, and I will say before I begin that the record has been wrong four hundred and eleven times that it has written down, so that whoever hears what comes after hears it as the record and not as the sky." A pause the length of a clause. "A record that reads its own errors aloud before it reads anybody's future is a record that can be argued with. It is the only kind I have ever wished to be."

r_copy.text: You take Unit 9's fair copy out of your pack and chalk its first page and its last onto the bare plank in Faulk's chalk, and under them the number, four hundred and eleven, in figures a hand high. Then you say it to whoever is at the table: if anything is read tomorrow night, by anybody, at any speed, this is read first. The record has been wrong this many times. Start there. Nobody wipes it off. In the morning somebody has gone over the number again, harder, so the rain will not take it.
r_copy.again: The count, chalked on the plank, a hand high.

r_warned.text: You say it to the trestle, to whoever is at it: the names on the city's list that are still living people, the ones you could reach, have each had a letter in your hand with their own line copied out word for word, and have answered it. They will not hear it first from a box. The table is quiet for a moment, the way a table goes quiet when somebody has done a thing nobody asked them to and nobody can think of a reason why they would.

interject.text: "You warned them," Odile says. "Before the crash, in writing, in your own hand." She looks at you over her glasses for a long moment. "My dear. You would have been dangerous on the floor."
"The Unwritten would call it a waste of ink," Ash says. "The Choir would call it the only ink there is. I don't know tonight which I am."

text.text: Rafe Ansel is sitting on two greasy cases at the end of the trestle with a coil of fuse over his shoulder like a bandolier, the Shift's band on his arm, and a pump-casing out of the works' dead machine between his boots. He came up the Line with the cases the morning the Ledger's card came. "She'd have sent them herself," he says, meaning Maren, and says nothing else about her. "Two cases. Two's what's left." He looks at the casing. "Tell me what it's for and I'll tell you if two will do it."

Rafe Ansel is sitting on two greasy cases at the end of the trestle with a coil of fuse over his shoulder like a bandolier, the Shift's band on his arm, and a pump-casing out of the works' dead machine between his boots. He came up the Line with the cases the morning the Ledger's card came, because Maren said you would need them "when you need them, and not before", and he does not trust anybody else to carry powder on a train. "Six cases was what the magazine had. Two is what the Shift can spare." He looks at the casing. "Tell me what it's for and I'll tell you if two will do it."

A cage man from Number Six called Orrin is sitting on two greasy cases at the end of the trestle, a coil of fuse over his shoulder and the Shift's band on his arm. He ran the winch at Six for twenty years and fires the Shift's shots now that Rafe is gone; he came up the Line the morning the Ledger's card came, because the Shift said you would need what was in the cases and somebody had to sit on them. "Two cases," he says. "That's all there is now. What's it for?"

Six greasy cases out of Number Six's magazine, the Concern's mark on every lid, and a coil of fuse: you lay them on the plank one by one. The works' dead machine at the foot of the steps has a pump-casing in it that nobody will miss, and Faulk's box has a blasting detonator in it older than the Burn, which Faulk would tell you he keeps for stumps.

Twists of black powder bought off the road, four of them, enough for a hand-loader's winter or one bad idea; the pump-casing out of the works' dead machine; the detonator Faulk keeps in his box for stumps, older than the Burn. It is all here. Whether your hands are is another matter.

Faulk's box has a detonator in it older than the Burn, and the works' dead machine has a pump-casing in it. Neither is any use without something to put in it, and you have nothing that burns that hard.

ch_bench.again: The casing, the detonator, and the powder, on the plank.

ch_what.speaker: npc_hs_03
ch_what.text: Rafe turns the casing over in his hands. "A roof's not a quantity," he says. "Depends what holds it up. Stone that holds itself up, you'd want a quarry's worth. Anything held up by a machine, you don't bring the roof down; you bring the machine down, and the roof sees to the rest." He sets it on the plank. "Two cases brings down most machines. It'd bring this square's lamps down from here to the lane." He looks at the steel door in the Spire's foot and away from it again. "Don't ask me about that door. I don't want to know what's behind that door."
ch_what.again: "A roof's not a quantity," Rafe says.

ch_what_orrin.text: Orrin turns the casing over in his big hands as if it were a stone he meant to set. "A roof's not a quantity," he says. "Depends what holds it up. Stone that holds itself up, you'd want a quarry's worth. Anything held up by a machine, you don't bring the roof down; you bring the machine down, and the roof sees to the rest." He sets it on the plank. "Two cases brings down most machines. Don't tell me which one. I've been told enough for one life."
ch_what_orrin.again: "A roof's not a quantity," Orrin says.

ch_rafe.speaker: npc_hs_03

text.text: Rafe does it on the plank with the casing between his knees, the way a man does it who has done it in the dark at the face with a hundred tons over his head. "You're the one who told her," he says, not looking up. "About the cellar. She took it off me, and she was right, and I've hated you for it the regulation amount." He crimps the cap. He tapes the leads back. "Whatever it's for, don't do it with people under it. Maren took the powder off me before I could find out what that's like. Don't you go and find out instead." He holds it out, and does not let go of it for a moment, and then does.

Rafe does it on the plank with the casing between his knees, the way a man does it who has done it in the dark at the face with a hundred tons over his head. "You talked me out of the car," he says, not looking up. "I dream about it most nights. Not the car. The people who'd have been in it." He crimps the cap. He tapes the leads back. "So: whatever it's for, don't do it with people under it. I'm telling you what you told me. It was good advice. I've resented it ever since." He holds it out, and does not let go of it for a moment, and then does.

Rafe does it on the plank with the casing between his knees, the way a man does it who has done it in the dark at the face with a hundred tons over his head, tamping each handful with the heel of his palm. He crimps the cap with his teeth. He tapes the leads back so they cannot touch until somebody means them to. "Whatever it's for," he says, "don't do it with people under it. I nearly did, once. I still dream about the ones who'd have been there." He holds it out, and does not let go of it for a moment, and then does.

ch_rafe.again: Rafe sits on the empty cases, his hands in his lap.

interject.text: "That is an explosive device," Nine says, "and I am obliged to note it." A pause. "I have noted it. I have not noted where."
Ash looks at the casing for a long time. "The Unwritten would carry that up those steps and call it a prayer," he says. "I used to." He does not say what he calls it now.

ch_orrin.text: Orrin makes it up on the plank without a word, a handful at a time, tamping with the heel of his palm the way you would bed a pillar, and crimps the cap with a tool he has carried on a string round his neck since before you were born. He tapes the leads back. "Shot-firer's rule," he says, handing it over. "You count everybody out before, and you count everybody back after, and if the numbers don't match you don't go home." He sits back down on the empty cases. "I hope your numbers match."
ch_orrin.again: Orrin sits on the empty cases, counting something on his fingers.

ch_kes.speaker: npc_hs_01
ch_kes.text: Kes takes the leads off you without asking, which is how you know she has done it before. "Every kid on the Shelf can crimp a cap," she says, crimping one with her back teeth. "First thing they teach you, so you don't go up the face with somebody who can't." She packs the casing a handful at a time and tamps it with the heel of her hand, quick, bored, sure, and tapes the leads back. "There. It won't go off unless somebody means it to." She wipes her palms on her trousers and does not look at you. "Don't tell me what it's for. I can guess, and I'd rather guess."
ch_kes.again: Kes wipes the powder off her hands for the third time.

ch_made.text: You pack the casing a handful at a time, tamping with the end of Faulk's chisel handle because there is nothing softer, and wire the detonator with the leads crossed under tape so that they cannot find each other by accident in your pack. It takes an hour. Your hands are steady for all of it, and shake for a long time afterwards. It is heavier than it looks. Whatever it is for, it is for that now.
ch_made.again: The charge, heavier than it looks.

interject.text: "That is an explosive device," Nine says, "and I am obliged to note it." A pause. "I have noted it. I have not noted where."

ch_fumble.text: You get as far as the detonator. Then you look at the two leads in your hands and the powder in the casing and understand, very clearly, that you do not know which one does what in the way you would need to know it at the bottom of a stair with your hands shaking. You put it all back on the plank. Nothing is spent. Somebody who knows how could do it. It isn't you, not yet.

Rafe Ansel is sitting on two greasy cases at the end of the trestle with a coil of fuse over his shoulder like a bandolier, the Shift's band on his arm, and a pump-casing out of the works' dead machine between his boots. He came up the Line with the cases the morning the Ledger's card came, because Maren said you would need them "when you need them, and not before", and he does not trust anybody else to carry powder on a train. "Six cases was what the magazine had. Two is what the Shift can spare." He looks at the casing. "Tell me what it's for and I'll tell you if two will do it."

A cage man from Number Six called Orrin is sitting on two greasy cases at the end of the trestle, a coil of fuse over his shoulder and the Shift's band on his arm. He ran the winch at Six for twenty years and fires the Shift's shots now that Rafe is gone; he came up the Line the morning the Ledger's card came, because the Shift said you would need what was in the cases and somebody had to sit on them. "Two cases," he says. "That's all there is now. What's it for?"

Six greasy cases out of Number Six's magazine, the Concern's mark on every lid, and a coil of fuse: you lay them on the plank one by one. The works' dead machine at the foot of the steps has a pump-casing in it that nobody will miss, and Faulk's box has a blasting detonator in it older than the Burn, which Faulk would tell you he keeps for stumps.

Twists of black powder bought off the road, four of them, enough for a hand-loader's winter or one bad idea; the pump-casing out of the works' dead machine; the detonator Faulk keeps in his box for stumps, older than the Burn. It is all here. Whether your hands are is another matter.

The foot of the Spire's steps, and the lamp you have looked at in a photograph since Knock: the same lamp, the same stone, a stride to the left of where the picture was made. The scaffold has come down off the middle flight since the card came. The chain is off the great doors and lies coiled on the top step like something asleep, and one leaf of the bronze stands an inch open with a light behind it that is not a lamp. Nobody is on the steps. Behind you the close goes on: the fire barrel, the people who came, Faulk's trestle, the lane to the Precinct. In front of you the steps go up.

pnr_foot.again: The foot of the steps, under the lamp.

interject.text: Tamsin stops a step below you and does not come up level. "I'll be one step down," she says. "Like the picture. Somebody ought to be where the photographer was." She does not smile. "Go on, then. Or don't. I'm not going anywhere either way."
"The steps," Nine says. "A hundred and twenty years I have walked past them. Today, if you go, I am walking up." The lens clicks. "I have logged it. It seemed the kind of thing that ought to be."
Wren looks up the steps the way she looks at a place she means to come back to in the dark, and then, for once, does not. "No way down but through," she says. "I know the kind."
"Twenty-two to the first landing," Ilya says. "Counted them last night." He does not say why, and you do not ask.

"Every sheet I ever wrote had a date on it that somebody would one day reach," Odile says. "I always wondered what it felt like from their side." She looks at you. "No. Don't tell me. I'd only price it."
Ash stays on the bottom step, where he stood the first time. "I said I'd not climb them," he says. "I'll climb them today." He does not say which of the things he carries is coming up with him.
Kes puts her hand flat on the lamp post, the way she puts it on a machine to hear it. "It's cold," she says, surprised. "I thought it'd hum. Everything in this city hums."

arrive.text: You go up. They are the same steps: the cracks where the print has them whole, the chisel marks where Faulk's men have numbered the stones, a plank somebody forgot. On the fourth step you stop without deciding to, because your feet know it before you do: the lamp behind your left shoulder, the doors above, the Crown's glass going up out of sight on either side, the wind off the canal in your face, making you squint. Above the doors, in the lintel where a carved crest has been chiselled smooth, something the size of a coin turns in its socket and finds you. It clicks. Somewhere inside the Spire the city has just made the first picture of you that is a photograph: your own age, your own face, no sash. Behind you, the close has come up to the foot of the steps.

three.speaker: npc_ar_01
three.text: Assessor Three comes down from the doors the way it walks the length of its bench: no hurry, no weight wasted. It stops one step above you, so that its lens is level with your eyes, and holds out its forearm with the sash folded over it like a cloth over a waiter's arm. Grey wool, hand-woven, darned in two places with a thread that does not quite match; a band of dark blue down its length; a clasp of old brass worked in the city's crest, the one somebody chiselled off the lintel. MAGISTRATE OF ACCOUNTS, stitched along the blue, so small you would have to lean to read it. It smells of a drawer. "Designate." The voice it uses for everything. "The steps are reopened. The Ledger thanks you for attending. The chair is the designate's. This is the chair's." It does not offer to put it on you. It holds it out, and waits, as it has waited on its bench for thirty years for somebody to bring it something to read.
three.again: Three, one step above you, the sash over its forearm. It waits.

interject.text: "Darned," Odile murmurs, behind you. "They kept it ninety years in a drawer and darned it. That is either thrift or love, and in this city I could not tell you which."

what.speaker: npc_ar_01
what.text: "It does nothing." Three considers that, and corrects it, as it corrects the register. "It is cloth. The charter reserves certain acts to the Magistrate of Accounts, and the Magistrate is whoever the Court sees wearing it. The vault under the Spire opens to the chair. The chair's first act is the one act the Ledger may not void. That is the charter's single exception, and the reason the Ledger has wanted a Magistrate for thirty years." A pause the length of a clause. "Unit 3 would add that the vault opens to the designate whether the sash is worn or not. The Ledger has asked to be seen before it is judged. It used those words. Unit 3 has entered them."
what.again: "It is cloth," Three says. "The rest is the charter."

interject.text: "Seen before it is judged," Nine repeats. Its lens has stopped moving. "It has never asked anything of anyone. It schedules. I would like that entered as well."

text.text: You say it, all of it, out loud on the steps with the close listening: the names on its list and what became of them, the people its schedule moved who would not be moved, the units of its own that did not do as they were told, and that you agreed with it once, at the top of its stair, and were wrong. When you stop, the silence is long enough for the child on the woman's hip to ask what is happening and be hushed. Then: "Contested." Not the way it says noted. steps_worn.text: The scaffold came down in the first week, and the masons mended the fourth step before any other, because the Magistrate came down it every morning. The board was carried off: it had nothing left to promise. Three stood a step below the sash and read the day's schedule aloud, as the Plan had written it thirty years before, and the close listened the way people listen to weather. The lamp burned all night. The photograph had been out by a stride, and in the spring the Ledger had the lamp moved.

ledger_dark.speaker: narrator
ledger_dark.text: Under the Spire's foot the racks stood in their rows in the dark, and the note they had held for ninety years was gone. Nothing would be forecast again: not a death, not a toll, not a face on a step nineteen years away. For a month the couriers' slot at the foot of the steps filled with paper addressed to the Vault of Accounts, schedules and objections and letters asking what to do, and then people stopped writing. The city's drains ran on what was left in the pipes. Nobody knew for how long.

Its people came down the couriers' shaft with soft lamps and gloves, chalked a number on every rack and lifted them out in the order they had gone in, and the note went with them in sealed crates down the Line and up the hill to Halcyon, where it began again in a cleaner room. cistern_opened.text: The great door stood open all that year, propped with a sandbag nobody took away. The sixty went out through it the way people go into cold water, a step at a time and then all at once. Some walked to the city of their own will, for its clinics and its schedules; some built against the shacks on Knock's slope; four went south with the Wheel and wrote home from places nobody inside had a word for. Wes stood on the apron every morning facing south, waiting for rain. When it came, he did not go in.

They lived aboard among the rust and the washing lines, learned the names of the parts of a ship that would never sail again, and in the first week Effie climbed to the top of its mast.

They walked off the car at Carrick between two hundred dockers who did not load people, and the wardens stood back because the quay was against them.
