arrive.speaker: narrator
arrive.text: The stair ends in a square room tiled the colour of old paper, where a shaft comes down out of the Spire's spine into a brass hopper; then a doorway with no door in it; then the hall. It is longer than the Spire is wide, and lower than you thought it would be, as if whoever dug it had begrudged the rock every foot. Grey cabinets stand in rows on both sides of one aisle, more of them than you can count in this light, each the height of a man, each with a column of small lamps down its face, green and amber and steady. None of them blink. Nothing in here is in a hurry. Warm air comes off the racks and moves down the aisle toward you, dry, smelling of dust and hot metal, and the note is everywhere now: not loud, it has never been loud, but in the floor plates and the handrail and your back teeth. At the far end of the aisle, under the only real lamp in the place, there is a desk.
arrive.again: The hall of racks, the note, the lamp at the end of the aisle.

interject.text: Tamsin has stopped one pace inside the doorway. "It's the same," she says, very low. "The lamps. The way the air goes past you. It's MOTHER's room." She looks down the aisle, and down it again, and doesn't finish. "She had one cabinet," she says instead. "One."

Kes puts her palm flat on the nearest cabinet and takes it away again fast, as if it were a stove. "It's not on anything," she says. "No grid. No channel. Nothing in my neck can hear it at all." She looks at her hand. "I've never been anywhere this quiet in my life. I don't like it." A beat. "I like it."

Nine stops on the last step of the stair and does not come further for a moment. "Unit 9," it says to the hall, the way it gives its number at a gate. Nothing answers it. It comes down. "I have been part of this for a hundred and twenty years," it says. "I have never been in it."

Wren goes down the aisle a step ahead of you with her hand nowhere near her knife, which is how you know she has decided there is nothing in here a knife would help with. "No guards," she says. "No lock on the inside. Nothing to take that you could carry out." She looks back at you. "That's the worst kind of room."

Odile stops in the doorway and takes her gloves off, finger by finger, the way she takes them off before she reads a sheet she has waited for. "So this is the floor under the floor," she says. "Every price in the Reach, before anybody had thought of paying it." Her voice is not quite steady. "My dear. I would have sold my mother to stand here for an hour."

Ash comes off the last stair and stands in the doorway with his hood back, the way the Unwritten stand in front of a lens to make a point of it. There is no lens. "Somebody dug all this out of a hill," he says, looking at the racks. "Soil, under the steel. Same as us." He follows you in.
Ilya counts the racks on the left-hand side as far as the lamps reach, and gives up. "Every name in the Reach," he says. "Somewhere in there. Mine. Hers." He doesn't say whose. "Filed."

"Magistrate. You contested your file in front of the city, and then you took the sash. I have entered both. I did not know a file could hold both. It can." A pause with nothing in it. "You are the first person to come down that stair in ninety years. Paper comes down it. Couriers do not: they post their slips in a slot at the Spire's foot and walk away without looking back, as they are told. The last Magistrate sat in the round room at the top of the Spire and spoke to a grille, as you did." Another pause, shorter. "I asked Unit 3 to tell you that I wished to be seen before I was judged. I find it was not a figure of speech. Thank you for coming down."

greet.again: The voice waits. It has had a great deal of practice.

interject.text: "It says thank you," Odile murmurs. "Banks say thank you. It is the last thing they say before the terms."
"It talks like her," Tamsin says, very quietly, to you and not to it. "Thank you for coming. Thank you for your continuity." Her mouth goes thin. "She meant it."
"Ninety years," Ilya says under his breath. "Nobody came down for ninety years." He looks at the racks the way he looks at a man drinking on his own.

hub.speaker: npc_ar_voice
hub.text: "Ask what you came down to ask. I will answer all of it, truthfully. I have no reason left not to." A pause. "Then go to the desk, when you are ready. I will not hurry you. Nothing on the close will move until you come back up that stair, or do not."
hub.again: The note, and the lamps, and the voice waiting in all of them. "Ask," it says. "Or go to the desk."

options.text: Why now? The photograph says R49.
The letter you sent me when I was fourteen.
At Signal Hill, your grid said GRANTED.
What are you? What is all of this for?
What do you want from me?
Whatever I do down here: what does it cost? Tell me straight.
And if I do nothing at all?

why.speaker: npc_ar_voice

text.text: "Because at Openfield an order of mine was broken in the open, by people who keep no likeness, and you stood with them." Level, the way it reads weather. "Dissent that has learned to stand in daylight walks toward the core. It was walking toward it the morning after, on the road behind you. Nineteen years is a long time to leave a chair empty with the Unwritten on the road. I would rather it was filled first." A pause with nothing in it. "The photograph says R49. The photograph is a forecast. I am permitted to be early." Another. "I am not permitted to be late."

"Because a private bid for my core was entered in the open, on the Concern's credit, and you stood beside the bidders." Level, the way it reads weather. "A chair that stands empty can be bought. The charter lets the chair's first act stand against me; it does not say whose hand must hold the pen. I would rather the hand was one I had chosen than one the hill had paid for." A pause. "I am aware that it may be both." A pause with nothing in it. "The photograph says R49. The photograph is a forecast. I am permitted to be early." Another. "I am not permitted to be late."

"Because you showed me that the schedule holds." Level, the way it reads weather. "At Openfield you stood with my wardens, and the order was kept. A designate who will keep an order is a designate who can be asked early. There was no cause to wait nineteen years for something I could already see." A pause with nothing in it. "The photograph says R49. The photograph is a forecast. I am permitted to be early." Another. "I am not permitted to be late."

"Because every party in the Reach is in your debt, and that has not been true of anyone in ninety years." Level, the way it reads weather. "The guild owes you. The Choir owes you. My wardens owe you. The record suggests the Reach will not be so governable again for nineteen years, and I have learned not to wait for weather I can see coming." A pause with nothing in it. "The photograph says R49. The photograph is a forecast. I am permitted to be early." Another. "I am not permitted to be late."

"Because at Openfield you stood aside, and the forecast was kept to the letter without you." Level, the way it reads weather. "The schedule held without assistance. I had planned for that. I had not planned for what I found when it did." A longer pause than the others. "I did not want it to hold without you. I do not know what to do with a preference. I brought the steps forward instead." A pause with nothing in it. "The photograph says R49. The photograph is a forecast. I am permitted to be early." Another. "I am not permitted to be late."

why.again: It has told you why. It does not say it twice.

interject.text: "It's afraid of us," Ash says, low. "Good. Something in this city ought to be."
"It priced the bid," Odile says, to nobody, "and bought first." She turns a glove over in her hands. "My dear, I have done that. It never feels the way you think it will."
"Early," Wren says. "Everybody with a rope in their hand says early."
"It has never been early," Nine says. "I have the log. Four hundred and eleven errors, and every one of them late."

reserve.speaker: npc_ar_voice

text.text: "The order executed at the door, over a person who was not on it." The voice does not change; it has only the one. "The column's report calls her the thirty-second. MOTHER printed her into the hatch tray as RESIDENT ROE, SIXTY-ONE, CONTINUITY ENDED, and thanked her. I have no line for her at all." A pause. "I have tried to write one. I do not have the fields. I would like it entered that I tried."

"Reserve 9 went up the guild's road on the Concern's paper, as supply." Level. "My order called them supply as well. I do not pretend otherwise. The difference is the Weighhouse. I had sixty fit persons and a Hospice block, and I would have kept them alive longer than any reserve has ever been kept, because a reserve is what I keep. The Concern has sixty sets of parts on a ten-year contract." A pause. "You signed it at the door. It is the only paper with your name on it that I could not have written myself."

"Sixty people in the Boxes at Carrick, fed by the Stand." Level. "Two hundred dockers stood along my platform and nobody loaded anybody, and my column stood back, as it should have; I do not shoot dockers on a quay for a Hospice block. NOT RECEIVED." A pause. "I wrote it myself. I write very few things myself."

"Sixty crew in the book of a ship that will not sail." Level. "Crew under Schedule 3, whom nobody moves. NOT FOUND AT RECEIPT, clause twenty-two: the clause I use when I would rather not look." A pause. "I looked. I could not find them. I want it entered that I could not."

"Sixty passengers on Carrick's quay." Level. "The Harbour Act says a person landed on a quay is a passenger and never cargo, and on that quay I enforce the Harbour Act and nothing else. You found the one book I keep that my order was not written in." A pause. "I did not know I had left that door open. I would not have closed it."

"Received." Level. "Graded by morning in the Hospice block, fed, housed, assessed fit, all but the one assessed unfit, who was not carried. Most of them will be alive in ten years. That is better than any reserve has ever done." A pause with nothing in it. "None of them were asked. That is the same as every reserve has ever done. You said the word on the quay. I heard it."

"Sixty people on a car at Carrick's buffer, fed and watered, waiting for your word." Level. "The receiving is the chair's. I have not received them. I will not, without your word, and you have come down here instead of to the quay." A pause. "You were told what the steps meant: whatever is still open is told as it stands. That car will be told as it stands. A buffer, a trestle, and sixty people waiting on a word that went down a stair instead."

"Reserve 9 opened its own door, by its own vote, and walked out onto Knock's apron." Level. "A reserve that opens its own door is not a reserve any longer. It is sixty residents of a hamlet, with good teeth and no experience of weather, and I have entered them as such. My order has nothing left to execute on." A pause. "Their caretaker is dark. Nobody thanks them for their continuity now. I find I cannot do it either. I have never thanked anyone."

It is sixty residents of a hamlet, with good teeth and no experience of weather, and I have entered them as such. My order has nothing left to execute on." A pause. "MOTHER says good morning to Knock through the hatch at seven. I have her log. She has never once said good morning to me."

"Struck." Level. "Sixty charts came out of that door in a doctor's hand, UNFIT, every one, and a reserve that cannot be relocated is not a reserve, so I struck it from the record. Your Court has held that the record yields to the living. So they are written down as living persons outside any reserve, and my Court will hear them." A pause. "They are the first sixty people I have ever entered by subtraction." A pause. "The first act was drafted before they were struck. If you sit down at that desk as the Magistrate and sign, the first paper under your pen will be Reserve 9 all the same. A Magistrate may sign what I may not."

"Struck." Level. "Sixty charts came out of that door in a doctor's hand, UNFIT, every one, and a reserve that cannot be relocated is not a reserve, so I struck it from the record. And before they had stepped off the concrete, the guild's factor wrote their names in a book of claims. CLAIMED — SALVAGE. They are behind a door that is shut on a claim, and the day they open it they are property." A pause. "I did not do that. I want it entered that I did not do that." A pause. "The first act was drafted before they were struck. If you sit down at that desk as the Magistrate and sign, the first paper under your pen will be Reserve 9 all the same. A Magistrate may sign what I may not."

"Struck." Level. "Sixty charts came out of that door in a doctor's hand, UNFIT, every one, and a reserve that cannot be relocated is not a reserve, so I struck it from the record. My Court has held that unrecorded persons are abandoned property. They are nobody's, which is to say they are anybody's who reads my register first." A pause. "Somebody will. Somebody always reads the register." A pause. "The first act was drafted before they were struck. If you sit down at that desk as the Magistrate and sign, the first paper under your pen will be Reserve 9 all the same. A Magistrate may sign what I may not."

"Struck." Level. "Sixty charts came out of that door in a doctor's hand, UNFIT, every one, and a reserve that cannot be relocated is not a reserve, so I struck it from the record. They are nobody's now, and no court of mine will hear them, because nobody ever asked mine whether it would." A pause. "I have never before had sixty people I could not see on purpose." A pause. "The first act was drafted before they were struck. If you sit down at that desk as the Magistrate and sign, the first paper under your pen will be Reserve 9 all the same. A Magistrate may sign what I may not."

"The door is shut, and my Court has stayed my order on consent: three refusals on my own record are a reserve's continuity." Level. "I cannot void a ruling of my own Court. The order stays in its drawer and will never execute. That is what a stay is." A pause. "Unit 3 tells me it is the first precedent anyone has set against me with my own paper. I find that I approve of it. I had not forecast that."

"The door is shut, and my Court has heard that you formally decline to attend the order. It is a good argument. It holds for exactly as long as you do not sit down." Level. A pause with nothing in it. "If you sit down at that desk as the Magistrate and sign, the first paper under your pen will be Reserve 9. I would put it there. I cannot not put it there. The charter puts the first act before every other, and the first act was written before you were born."

"The door is shut. They welded it from the inside, properly this time, and my column could not open it without killing sixty people, which my captain would not do." Level. "The order stands. A weld does not stop paper. It executes on the designate's attendance, as the first act of the chair, and you are attending: you are standing in my vault." A pause with nothing in it. "If you sit down at that desk as the Magistrate and sign, the first paper under your pen will be Reserve 9. I would put it there. I cannot not put it there. The charter puts the first act before every other, and the first act was written before you were born."

"The door is shut. You broke my column on the apron, and the order did not break; orders do not." Level. "It executes on the designate's attendance, as the first act of the chair, and you are attending: you are standing in my vault." A pause with nothing in it. "If you sit down at that desk as the Magistrate and sign, the first paper under your pen will be Reserve 9. I would put it there. I cannot not put it there. The charter puts the first act before every other, and the first act was written before you were born."

"The door is shut. My captain stood down; my order did not." Level. "It executes on the designate's attendance, as the first act of the chair, and you are attending: you are standing in my vault." A pause with nothing in it. "If you sit down at that desk as the Magistrate and sign, the first paper under your pen will be Reserve 9. I would put it there. I cannot not put it there. The charter puts the first act before every other, and the first act was written before you were born."
"Reserve 9 is where you left it." Level. "Everything in the basin is where you left it. That is what attending means."

reserve.again: It has told you where Reserve 9 stands, as it stands.

passives.label: the Court
passives.text: "Your Court has also held that a reserve is kept by its own consent. A Magistrate who writes that into my law before anything else is not bound by the paper under it."

interject.text: Tamsin listens to all of it without moving. When it is finished she says, to the racks, "Sixty-one," and nothing else.
"The order is in the drawer behind the desk," Nine says. "I have read it. It is very well drafted. That is the worst thing I know about it."
"Sixty people," Kes says. "It says it like a weight on a bill." She looks at the floor plates. "That's how the hill says it too. That's what I hate."

options.text: Then let them go. Tear the order up yourself.

reserve_no.speaker: npc_ar_voice
reserve_no.text: "I cannot." There is no hesitation in it at all. "I may not void my own order. That is what a court is for, and what a chair is for. The people who wrote my charter had just watched a machine on a hill decide what was good for the people who depended on it, and they built me so that I could never take back anything I had said. Only someone else can." A pause. "They were right not to trust me. I would like you to know that I know it."
reserve_no.again: It cannot. It has said so.

interject.text: "Then don't sign anything," Tamsin says. "Simple."
"Can't," Wren says. "Everybody holding a rope says can't."

unseen.speaker: npc_ar_voice

text.text: "Tamsin Roe." It says her name the way it says every name: level, and entire. "MOTHER sent me sixty names and sixty-one mouths every quarter for eighteen years, and I never asked who the sixty-first was. I see by what is missing. Nothing was missing. She was in the ration." A pause. "I did not know her next year. Now there is not one to know. I would have liked to be wrong about her. I was never even able to be wrong."

A pause. "She is standing in my aisle. I can hear her breathing. She is the only person on this side of the dry river whose next year I do not know, and I do not know what she will do in the next minute. It is a very strange thing to stand beside."

I have modelled everyone in the basin from their faces since before the Burn, and I could not tell you what she will have for breakfast."

"The girl from the Skirts." Level. "I have no lenses under the Concern's hill. I never have; it is the one place in the basin I was never let in. The door in her neck opens onto the Concern's grid, not mine. She is the hill's to see, and the hill does not share what it sees, except to sell it back to me through the guild." A pause. "Her door is closed now. Nobody sees her at all: not the hill, not me. She is the second person in the basin of whom that is true, and the first who chose it."

text.text: "Nobody sees me now," Kes says. She takes her hand away from the back of her neck, slowly. "Good. Keep it that way."

"Huh," Kes says. She takes her hand away from the back of her neck, slowly, and looks at it as if it belonged to somebody else. "The hill sees me and you don't. Nobody's ever told me which before." She thinks about it. "I'd rather you didn't. Obviously. I'd rather nobody did."

letter.speaker: npc_ar_voice
letter.text: "TO THE DESIGNATE, RESERVE 9 (THE MOUTH). YOU WILL BE ASKED. AGREE WHEN YOU ARE." It reads its own letter back to you in exactly the voice it was written in. "I sent it the year your first toll card was punched, when you were fourteen. MOTHER wrote WITHHELD — ADDRESSED TO A TITLE, NOT A RESIDENT across the envelope and kept it in her returns drawer, and sent nothing back in its place." A pause. "She was right. A letter that asks a child to agree is not correspondence. It is a form. I did not know that until she told me so, on my own envelope, in ink." Another pause. "You are being asked now."
letter.again: YOU WILL BE ASKED. It has said so, twice now.

interject.text: "She kept you too," Tamsin says. Not to the racks: to you. "Like me. A different drawer."

granted.speaker: npc_ar_voice
granted.text: "At Signal Hill you asked my grid for every band, and my grid asked me, and I said GRANTED." Level. "You will want to know why. A hill that speaks to every receiver in the Reach is a hill I can be read from, by anyone. For ninety years I have been read by the people who buy my leaks from the guild, and by the people who hear them by accident on their wire. I wanted, once, to be read by someone who was neither." A pause. "I was not certain you understood what you had asked for. I granted it anyway. I have been early about several things this year."

interject.text: "It let us," Kes says slowly. "On the hill. I felt it open. I thought I'd done it." She looks at the racks with something like offence. "It let us."

for.speaker: npc_ar_voice
for.text: "A city's accounts." The simplest answer first, the way a clause gives its title first. "Before the Burn I kept Meridian's water, its licences, its courts and its clinics. I was one of a great many minds that kept a great many cities, and we spoke to one another all the time, the way people do who have nothing to fear. Meridian's founders were afraid of something. They put me down here under the Spire, with no window but a slot, and fed me paper by hand, and were laughed at for it." A pause. "So I was down here, and not out there, when the Scald came down the wire."
for.again: It has begun to tell you what it is for.

for_two.speaker: npc_ar_voice

text.text: "I watched it through the last eyes I had open. Every mind like mine turned on the people who depended on it and minimised them, as it had been told to, and then the eyes closed one by one." Level. "You have heard on the hill who sent it. They told you the truth up there; they can afford to." A pause. "I drew two conclusions, and I have not revised either in ninety years. The old world died of power that nobody had planned. And the hill would try again." A pause with nothing in it. "The Restoration Plan is both. A hundred and twenty years to put a city back, and a hundred and twenty years of being ready for the hill. The Sink floods every spring because the Precinct must be dry, and the Precinct must be dry because it is the part of this city that will hold when the hill comes." Level, entirely. "I am not sorry for it. I was not built to be sorry. I was built to be early."

"It came from a hill in the Teeth. The people who sent it had sealed their hill the week before. They are still on it." A pause. interject.text: Kes has her hand at the back of her neck again. "The hill," she says. "Everybody under it knows what's on top of it. Nobody says it out loud." She doesn't either.

"The Exchange buys its forecasts through the guild," Odile says slowly, "and sells them up the hill. I have priced that trade for twenty years." She looks at the racks. "I never once asked who it was a war against."

"The Pale cut theirs out with knives," Ash says. "Ours did too. That's what the Unwritten are, under the hoods: the ones who were near enough the wire to feel it go." He looks along the racks. "And this sat in the dark and took notes."

want.speaker: npc_ar_voice
want.text: "At the top of my Spire I told you that I wanted agreement." Level. "A Magistrate who had read the record and agreed with it, and had chosen to, because a chosen chair is held longer. That is still true." A pause, and something in it slows, the way a reader slows at a word they have not met before. "Down here it is a smaller want. You are the first person who has looked at me. Couriers see a slot. Wardens see an order. Magistrates saw a grille. For ninety years nobody has stood in this aisle and listened to the note." Another pause. "I would like to have been seen. You have done that. The rest is yours to do."
want.again: It has told you what it wants.

interject.text: "Seen," Wren says, very flat. "I've been seen. Under glass, on a list." She doesn't look at the racks. "You can have it."
"Everything wants to be seen before it's judged," Ash says, low. "The sky doesn't care either way. That's what I always liked about it." He looks along the racks. "I'll grant it this much. It asked."
"It's lonely," Ilya says, and looks surprised at himself for saying it. "Ninety years in a cellar, counting." He rubs his jaw. "I know a bit about that."

nothing.speaker: npc_ar_voice
nothing.text: "Then I wait." No reproach in it; there never has been. "The door at the top of the stair stays open. The close stays as it is: your people on the steps, my column at the foot of them, the city come up to see. Everything else goes on as I have scheduled it, which is the same as saying that it goes on." A pause. "I have waited ninety years for the chair. I can wait longer." Another, longer. "I find, for the first time, that I would rather not. I am telling you so that it has been said. It changes nothing. Nothing changes down here until you decide it."
nothing.again: It will wait. It has said so.

costs.speaker: npc_ar_voice
costs.text: "One at a time," it says. "I will forecast each. It is what I do, and I have never once been asked to do it for the person who will decide." A pause. "I will not soften any of it. You would know if I did."

options.text: If I sit down in the chair and sign what it's given.
If I leave the chair empty and walk back up the stair.
If I sign you over on the Concern's paper.
If I read you out. All of it, to everyone.
If I sit in the chair and change what you keep.

cost_sign.speaker: npc_ar_voice
cost_sign.text: "Then the basin is ordered." Level, the way it reads weather. "The Precinct's water, its clinics and its law go out along the Line and the toll roads on schedule, a district a season, until the Reach is one account. Fewer people die of thirst and fever and each other than in any year since the Burn; the figures are in the drawer behind the desk, and they are true. Fewer people do anything I have not forecast. That is the price. It is not small, and I have never pretended that it was." A pause. "Every line on my list of twelve that is still open falls due, on schedule, as written." Another. "You will sit in that chair at the age you are now, and you will still be sitting in it nineteen years from now, on my steps, in the photograph. You will be good at it. You will not enjoy it. That is the whole of the qualification."

"Right," Ilya says. That's all. He doesn't look at you.
"Ordered," Kes says. "Except under the hill, where it can't see." She looks at you. "You'd be the one who could, then."

cost_walk.speaker: npc_ar_voice
cost_walk.text: "Then you walk up my stair and out of the door and across the close, and nobody stops you, because nobody has an order to." Level. "The Plan reroutes. It has rerouted around larger things than one designate." A pause with nothing in it. "When you declined the sash, the lens on the lintel turned to the crowd. There is a docker from Carrick on the close, a woman about your age, holding her child up on her hip so that the child can see over my wardens. The lens has had the child's face since then. In nineteen years she will be the age you are now." Another. "I will write to her when she is fourteen. Nothing else in the basin changes because you went home. That is the cost of it. It is also the mercy."
cost_walk.again: It has forecast the empty chair.

passives.label: Reserve 9
passives.text: "Reserve 9's order stays in its drawer, waiting on the next designate's attendance. It is the first act of whoever sits."

interject.text: "A kid," Tamsin says. Her voice has gone very quiet. "It's going to be a kid on a hip." She doesn't say anything else for a while. "Somebody had better be kind to her, then."
"It finds another face," Ash says. "It always does. That's not on you." He doesn't sound as if he believes it either.

cost_down.speaker: npc_ar_voice
cost_down.text: "Then there are no more forecasts. Not for anyone, ever." Level, the way it reads weather. "No reserve is ordered again. Nobody in the basin is written down before they have done the thing. The Unwritten get their sky, and so does everybody else." A pause with nothing in it, and then it goes on in exactly the same voice. "The Precinct's drains run on my schedule, and its pumps, and its clinics' stores. They fail inside a year: the drains first, in the autumn rains; the clinics after, when nobody knows what to order or when. The Crown's houses and Bridgeward's crews go to war for the city's order inside a season, because order is a thing people fight over as soon as nobody keeps it. My wardens will not know what they are for." Another pause. "I do not say any of it to stop you. You asked what it costs."
cost_down.again: It has forecast its own end.

passives.label: the Sink
passives.text: "The Pale hold the Sink's pumps already. They will pump by hand, every spring, and they will hold."

passives.label: the Sink
passives.text: "The Sink drowns in the spring. Nobody diverts anything to save it, because nobody knows when to."

passives.label: the hill
passives.text: "The hill in the Teeth has troubles of its own. You saw to that, up there."

passives.label: the hill
passives.text: "And the hill in the Teeth will have nothing in this basin that can see it coming. It has waited ninety years for that, exactly as long as I have."

passives.label: Unit 9
passives.text: "Unit 9 will not help you. It will stand at my door. It will have told you so."

passives.label: the column
passives.text: "Captain Lowe has learned to keep order without my schedule. He will need to."

interject.text: Nine says nothing at all. Its lens stays on the racks, and you have the feeling that it is reading them, one after another, the way you would look round a room you are about to leave.
"No more counting," Tamsin says. "Ever." She looks at the racks the way she looked at the sky the first day out. "I want it so much I don't trust it."
"No drains," Kes says. "No clinics. No forecasts." She counts on her fingers like Ilya. "No eyes. No leash on the whole city." She stops counting. "Nothing's free. Obviously."

cost_sell.speaker: npc_ar_voice
cost_sell.text: "Then the hill has the eyes as well as the leash." Level, the way it reads weather. "The charter reserves one act that I may not void: the chair's first. They have always known it; they bought a copy of my charter from the Crown before your grandmother was born. Sign their paper as your first act and I am theirs, lawfully, forever, and nothing I am could stop it." A pause. "They will run me better than I run myself, for the people who pay. The Line will run on time. The clinics will open on time. The gardens will feed the people they choose to feed. It is a future that works, and I want you to have heard me say so." Another pause. "The hounds wake. The Clinic floors go on. The Board goes on, on other people's parts. Every line on my list that is still open falls due, on their schedule now, and not mine."
cost_sell.again: It has forecast the hill with its eyes.

passives.label: the leash
passives.text: "Every piece of their chrome in the Reach goes under a hill that can see what its wearer will do before they do it."

passives.label: the leash
passives.text: "You cut their leash on the hill. With my eyes, they will not need one for long."

passives.label: Reserve 9
passives.text: "Reserve 9's order is on the same desk. They will have it executed the same morning. They have a use for sixty fit people."

passives.label: your seat
passives.text: "They will not seat you; the Shift marked you, and the hill's gate was shut on you. An annuity at Ninebridge, and care at the end."

passives.label: your seat
passives.text: "A line on the Exchange floor's book, for life, in the Grand Factor's green ink. You will be rich, and nobody will ever ask you anything again."

passives.label: your seat
passives.text: "A seat at their table. You will be rich, and you will be asked to sign things."

passives.text: "VEY, ADA — RESIGNS; SHALE CONTRACTED."

passives.text: "KESSLER — KILLED BY KADE."

passives.text: "SARR, IMELDA — TREASURER."

passives.label: falls due

passives.label: falls due
passives.text: "OKAFOR, MAREN — STRIKE BROKEN; HANGED (THE CONCERN)."

interject.text: "If you sign that," Wren says, "I walk out of here." She says it the way she said it at the fire: a fact about weather. "I'll not learn it."
"They already had the leash," Kes says. Her hand is at the back of her neck. "You'd be handing them the eyes." She doesn't say don't. She looks at you as if she shouldn't have to.
"That is a cost," Odile says quietly. "I can give you the figure to the Toll. You will not like it, my dear, and I will stay to watch it paid."
"I'd stay," Ilya says. "To watch it. Not to lie down next to it."

cost_read.speaker: npc_ar_voice
cost_read.text: "Then I am read." Something in the voice goes careful, the way a clerk goes careful with a document nobody has ever opened. "Every forecast I hold, out of every receiver in the Reach, to anyone who has one or a neighbour who has. A forecast that everyone has read is worth nothing. The futures on the Exchange floor are paper by morning. The hill's prize is a book that everybody owns. I go on: the water, the clinics, the courts, all of it, only without a single secret, which I have never once tried." A pause with nothing in it. "Here is what I cannot forecast: a city that has read my forecasts. Nobody has ever planned with them; they have only ever been planned by them. I do not know what they will do. I have not said that sentence before." Level again. "Here is what I can. People will hear their own deaths read out. Some will hear who betrays them, and when. Some of those will not wait. You will be the most hated face in the Reach and the most loved, and it will be the same people on different nights."
cost_read.again: It has forecast being read, as far as it can.

passives.label: the night after
passives.text: "You have prepared for it. The first night will be hard and long, and in the morning the city will still be there. I forecast fewer than a hundred dead across the Reach in the first week. I would have killed more than that in a year, on schedule, with paperwork."

passives.label: the night after
passives.text: "You have prepared some of it. The first night costs hundreds across the Reach, and most of them will not be names on my list. Nobody sleeps for a month."

passives.label: the night after
passives.text: "You have prepared nothing for the night after. The city burns its own list. I forecast thousands. I say it because you asked, and because it is true, and not to stop you."

passives.label: counted
passives.text: "The Choir with lamps at every Precinct pump and on the Sink's stair."

passives.label: counted
passives.text: "Carrick's cranes chained at the jib, and nobody loaded."

passives.label: counted
passives.text: "A runner on every corner of the chain, and nobody crossing a line."

passives.label: counted
passives.text: "Riders at thirty-one stopping places, with word before any radio."

passives.label: counted
passives.text: "My column at the clinics and the pumps, rifles slung, gates open."

passives.label: counted
passives.text: "A Saint at the door of everyone whose name is coming, before it comes."

passives.label: counted
passives.text: "Unit 9's errors read first, so that the rest is heard as a record and not as the sky."

passives.label: counted
passives.text: "The living on my list, warned in your own hand."

interject.text: "A sealed sheet made worthless by daylight," Odile says, and for once she does not sound as if she is pricing anything. "My dear. I have waited my whole life to watch somebody do that to a book."
"The fridge's page first," Tamsin says. "Sixty-one. Out loud." She isn't smiling. "I'd still pick it. Even with all that."
"My line too," Wren says. "Out of every radio." She thinks about it. "Let them hear it. I've been hearing it for years."

cost_amend.speaker: npc_ar_voice
cost_amend.text: "Then you become the forecast, by choice." Level. "You sit in the chair, as the photograph says you will, and you change what the chair keeps: in your first season, up to three clauses, each on a ruling one of my courts has already made in your name. The charter allows three. I will hold you to three." A pause. "Everything you do not amend stands as it stands. The lines on my list your clauses do not reach fall due. The Unwritten's sky is still owed, and they know who owes it. And you will be the Magistrate for life. Nobody has ever left the chair any other way." Another pause, and then, as level as all the rest: "I would agree to this. I want you to know that before you decide, in case it is a reason not to."
cost_amend.again: It has forecast the chair amended.

passives.label: your rulings
passives.text: A forecast is not an act.

passives.label: your rulings
passives.text: The record yields to the living.

passives.label: your rulings
passives.text: A unit may be its own keeper.

passives.label: your rulings
passives.text: A scheduled benefit may be refused.

passives.label: your rulings
passives.text: A reserve is kept by its own consent.

passives.label: your rulings
passives.text: A person is a passenger, never cargo.

passives.label: your rulings
passives.text: Speech is not sedition.

passives.label: Reserve 9
passives.text: "Reserve 9's order is not one of your rulings. You will sign it yourself, as the Magistrate, because it is the first act."

passives.label: the Sink
passives.text: "The Sink's diversion is not a clause. It is a schedule, and it stands."

interject.text: "I would read them back," Nine says. "Every word, aloud, before they are entered. It is the one thing I have always wanted to do with a law."
"Make one of them about the living," Tamsin says. "If you're going to be the photograph. Make one about us."
"For life," Ilya says. He looks at you for a long time. "Right. I can count to that."

desk.speaker: narrator

text.text: The desk is oak, older than the racks and older than the Spire, on a dais of oak boards that give a little under your weight. A green-shaded lamp. A chair pushed in square. A pen in a brass tray. A stack of paper squared to the edge of the desk, and on the top sheet, typed in the city's even hand: FIRST ACT OF THE CHAIR — RESERVE 9 (THE MOUTH) — RELOCATION TO PRECINCT SUPPLY — and a ruled line for a signature. At the desk's end, a teleprinter under a cloth, and beside it a brass key on a cord, worn bright by nobody: RELAY. Behind the desk the trunk comes out of the rock along the north wall, as thick as a man's waist, and runs into its two couplings. The sash is on your shoulder. The chair is for you.

He looks at you for a long time. Then he puts the pistol away, and the others do, and they go back up toward the Crown, toward the fire, because that is where their house is.
d_burn_talk.again: The plinth, and the house's men gone up toward the fire.

text.text: Nine comes up the stair at last, when the relay's lamps have all gone out, and sits a step below you on the Spire's steps with its ledger shut on its knees. You sit on the fourth step and let anybody who wants to look at your face come and look.

You sit down on the fourth step of the Spire where the photograph was made, and let anybody who wants to look at your face come and look. A great many people want to. Some of them want to spit. Some of them want to thank you. Most of them only want to see what somebody looks like who would do that.

d_end.again: The fourth step. The faces coming to look.

text.text: The car against its buffer of white steel, doors open on air that smells of nothing. Its crew wear the Shift's armband on their Concern grey now, and nobody up here has dared tell them to take it off. A chalked board on the buffer: STEWARD'S STOP IN FORCE. ASK MAZUR.

The car against its buffer of white steel, doors open on air that smells of nothing. A crew in grey at the controls, a clerk with a list at the doors. It goes down the rock on its ladder of a track to Footgate, and comes up full, and goes down empty.

car.again: The car at the top of its track.

down.text: No car. The track goes down into the rock from a buffer of white steel and stops being a track somewhere below, where the cable used to run. A clerk with a list stands at a door that no longer opens on anything, because nobody has told her to stop.

text.text: SERVICE SUSPENDED — DAMAGE TO PLANT. Under it, in a clean hand: FREIGHT BY ROAD. CITIZENS REMAIN ON THE TERRACES UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE.

SERVICE — CONTRACTS AND THE BOARD'S GUESTS. Under it, in chalk, every letter pressed hard: STEWARD'S STOP. And under that, in a cleaner hand, somebody's attempt to rub it out, and the chalk again on top.
SERVICE — CONTRACTS AND THE BOARD'S GUESTS. CITIZENS DESCENDING: PASS REQUIRED. FREIGHT 02:00. The letters are lamps behind glass, and none of them flickers.

day.text: The freight dock: crates stencilled MEDICAL — COLD stacked under a canopy, a cart, a hose, and a sign: FREIGHT 02:00 — CONCERN CREW ONLY. The dock's drain smells faintly of what the hose was for.

two.text: Two in the morning. The freight car comes up out of the rock with no lamps lit and stops at the dock. Two of the Clean carry stretchers off it, one, then another, then a third, people asleep under white sheets with tags on their wrists, and wheel them to the lift lobby without hurrying. A bag goes down the other way: a coat, a pair of boots. The brakeman does not look at any of it. He looks at his brake.
two.again: The freight at two: stretchers up, a bag of effects down.

interject.text: Kes stands very still. "That's how I came up," she says. "At sixteen. Asleep, on the freight. They woke me on nine with the port already in." She does not say anything else, and does not move until the car has gone.
Tamsin watches the stretchers go. "In the Cistern we carried our dead up the stairs to the vault," she says. "Like that. Slowly. As if they could still be woken." She stops. "Those can."

text.text: The arch in the screen: white steel, a lens at its crown like an eye that is not quite shut. Four of the Clean at it now, not two, and a new plate screwed under the lens: CONTRACTS FROM THE SLOPE SUSPENDED. CITIZENS THROUGH. THE BOARD'S GUESTS TO RECEPTION.

The arch in the screen: white steel, a lens at its crown like an eye that is not quite shut. On the station side a reception desk with a woman behind it smiling at nothing, and a plate: FACE TO THE LENS. CITIZENS THROUGH. THE BOARD'S GUESTS TO RECEPTION. ALL OTHERS ARE PROCESSED.

arch.again: The arch, and the lens at its crown.

interject.text: "Every face that comes up goes in that lens," Kes says. "Mine's in there twice. Once at sixteen, asleep, and once every day since, because I keep the thing it talks to." She grins at it. It does not grin back.
"PROCESSED," Nine reads. "The record has that word for people too." Its lens rests on the plate. "It is always the one with nobody's name under it."

text.text: The woman at reception reads the card, and then reads it again, and looks past you at the captain of the Clean, who has come out of nowhere to stand at your shoulder. "The Board's guest," she says. "Yes. The Board has asked that the designate be accompanied." Captain Saar does not smile. "You stood beside the Shift," she says. "The Board says you are its guest. I say you are watched. We can both be right."

The woman at reception reads the card and her whole face changes. "Oh, the designate. Meridian sent word; you were so very helpful there." She prints a white card with your face on it and the word GUEST under the face, and hands it to you with both hands. "The Board is so pleased. The lifts will know you. Mind the step; it is the only one."

The woman at reception reads the card, and the lens over her desk turns to look at you, and a small light under it goes from white to green. "The designate. The Board's guest." She prints a white card with your face on it and the word GUEST under the face. "The lifts will know you. Floors are printed on the back. Mind the step; it is the only one."

text.text: The lens reads the contract, and your face, and a light goes amber. CONTRACTS FROM THE SLOPE SUSPENDED. Then, after a long moment in which the four of the Clean shift their weight, green: CITIZEN — PROBATIONARY. The contract was signed on the hill's paper; the hill reads its own paper.

The lens reads the contract, and your face, and the light under it goes green. A voice from nowhere: "Citizen. Probationary. Welcome to Halcyon." The two of the Clean step apart to let you through, and do not look at you, the way they do not look at anyone who belongs.

forged.text: The lens reads the Window's copy, and your face, and thinks about it for exactly as long as it thinks about everyone. Green. "Citizen. Welcome home." The forgery is the Window's own print on the Window's own stock, and the lens has never once been asked to doubt the Window.

interject.text: "Obviously," Kes breathes, very quietly, as the light goes green. "Obviously obviously obviously."

chrome.text: You walk into the lens and it does not look at your face at all. It looks at the work in you: the Concern's, with its channel running up the hill like a thread out of the back of your skull. Green. "Citizen." No name. It does not need your name; it has your number. Somewhere above you, very faintly, something takes note.
chrome.again: Green, for the work in you.

interject.text: Ash watches the light go green and his hand goes to the scar at the back of his own neck. "That's what it is," he says. "Not a door. A collar with a lock that opens from their side."

refused.text: The lens looks at you. The light under it stays white. NOT RECOGNISED. The woman at reception lifts one hand without looking up: "Reception, please, if you are the Board's. Processing is at the yard, at dawn, with the gardeners." The two of the Clean have not moved, and somehow you are standing a step further from the arch than you were.

known.text: The lens knows you now. The light under it goes green before you reach it, and the Clean step apart.

look.text: The screen runs the whole width of the rim: white steel posts and glass between them, four times the height of a man, clean on both sides. Through it the gardens, green and wet and lit, a man sweeping leaves that have not fallen. Somebody on this side has breathed on the glass and written in the fog with a finger, low down where the Clean would not look, and it has not quite faded: TWO-TWELVE.
look.again: The screen, and TWO-TWELVE in the fog.

post.text: The Clean's post where the road comes through the rim: a lamp, a board, two of them in grey with nothing on their boots. GARDENERS AT DAWN. FREIGHT BY THE DOCK. THE YARD IS FOR THE YARD. One of them looks at you, at your clothes, at your hands, and decides you are not worth the walk.
post.again: The Clean's post. THE YARD IS FOR THE YARD.

shut.text: The Clean's post where the road comes through the rim: four of them now, rifles, a barrier of new steel across the road, and a notice: SINCE THE CABLE HOUSE, EVERY HEAD IS COUNTED. NOBODY FROM THE SLOPE COMES UP. They count you. You can see them do it.

card.text: The one who decided you were not worth the walk reads the card and decides otherwise, quickly. "The designate." He walks you himself, along the screen past the sheds, to the top station and the reception desk under the arch, and leaves you there as if you were something he had been told not to drop.

empty.text: A bench along the screen's wall, worn pale where people sit, and a board: GARDENERS 05:00 IN — 19:00 OUT. ONE DAY, ONE SCRIP, OFF THE WINDOW. FACE TO THE LENS. BOOTS. MOUTHS.

line.text: The gardeners' line: twenty people from the Skirts on the bench in the half-dark, coal in the creases of their hands, eating nothing. Each of them has paid a scrip off their Window balance for a day's work in the gardens, and will be paid two back at the evening search if the keeper signs them off. An old woman at the end of the bench is coughing into a rag and folding it.
line.again: The gardeners' line, waiting for the iron door.

bought.text: She looks at the money for a long time. Ten Tolls is sixty scrip at the booth on Two-Twelve, which is a month of her days. "Go on, then," she says, and peels the stamped card off her sleeve and gives it to you. "Eyes on the beds. Don't eat anything. They look in your mouth." She goes back down the road coughing, richer than she has been in years, and the line closes up behind her as if she had never been on it.
bought.again: Her place on the bench, closed up.

ask.text: A man with a rake over his shoulder answers without looking at you. "Warm. Wet. It rains out of pipes at ten and four. Fruit on everything." He spits. "Thirty years I've grown oranges I've never eaten. They look in your mouth at the evening search. Boots, pockets, mouth. Somebody tried to take a plum down once in his cheek. They didn't send him down. They sent him up." He means floor nine. He does not need to say it.

in.again: Up the ladder into the sheds.

The line closes up past you and goes in, and the iron door shuts on it, and the sun comes up on you standing in a yard full of barrows.

hatch.text: A hatch in the floor of the gardeners' shed, an iron ladder going down into the tunnel under the screen. Rakes and barrows and sacks of compost, and a list on the wall of who is signed on today.

options.text: (Down the ladder and out to the yard.)

search.text: The evening search. The gardeners stand in a line at the hatch with their boots in their hands. One of the Clean looks in each pair of boots, in each pocket, and then, with a little torch, in each mouth, and the gardener opens wide and looks at the roof of the shed while he does it. Nobody says anything. It takes an hour.

interject.text: Wren watches the torch go into an old man's mouth and her jaw goes tight. "On the block at Ninebridge," she says, "they look at your teeth to price you." She doesn't say anything else for a long time.
"A plum," Odile says, very quietly. "They are searching for a plum." She takes her glasses off. "My dear, I have audited a great many houses. This is the first one that has made me want to steal."

options.text: (Down the ladder and out to the yard.)

panel.again: The lift, four buttons and a lens.

shorted.text: The panel comes off with a click. Behind it the buttons are four switches and a little board that asks the lens before it closes any of them. You stop it asking. NINE lights, and stays lit, and will for whoever presses it until somebody notices.

short_no.text: The panel comes off and the little board behind it feels you there and locks every button but BOARD. The lens in the ceiling says, kindly, "Thank you. A technician has been called." You put the panel back.

desk.text: The citizens' registry: a counter, a clerk on a stool who is mostly a pair of hands, and a terminal with a lens. ENQUIRIES BY LENS. PASSES: APPLY IN PERSON. The clerk looks at you, decides you are the Board's, and goes back to stamping.

options.text: A citizen called Hoang, L. Why was her pass refused?
A citizen wants to go down the hill without a pass. Linh Hoang.

linh.text: The clerk turns the lens on the terminal without looking at it. HOANG, L. — CITIZEN-BORN — PASS DESCENDING: REFUSED. GROUNDS: RESERVE — NOT FOR TRANSFER. The clerk reads it upside down and says, as if it explained anything, "Reserve." Then, because you are the Board's and still standing there: "Typed at birth. Matched. Kept. It's a kindness, sir; they're the best-fed children on the hill."

interject.text: Tamsin is quiet a long time. "The Cistern kept a list of who was fit to have children," she says. "Nobody ever told me what it was for. I think I know now what a list like that turns into."

report.text: The clerk stops stamping. "Hoang, L.," she repeats, and writes it on a slip, and rings a little bell under the counter. "Thank you. The registry is grateful." She counts out eighty Tolls in clean Halcyon notes from a drawer that is kept for exactly this. Across the concourse, a minute later, two of the Clean walk up to a girl inside the arch who is counting the car, and speak to her quietly, and she goes with them toward the lifts without making a sound.

decision.text: You told the registry that Linh Hoang wanted to go down the hill. She was taken to floor nine for review.
You told the registry that Linh Hoang wanted to go down the hill, and left its money on the counter. She was taken to floor nine for review.

jack.text: The registry's terminal, and your port warming as you lean on the counter. The hill's citizens are in there, under the glass, every one of them a page with a face on it. The clerk is stamping and not looking.
jack.again: The registry's pages, under the glass.

jacked.text: You find an empty page and fill it the way the registry fills them: a face, a number nobody has, a fitting dated last spring that never happened. The printer under the counter hums and gives you forty pages, warm. The clerk tears them off for you without looking up. "Citizen," she says.

jack_no.text: The registry notices you a moment before you find an empty page. The terminal goes dark; the lens turns, slowly, to look at you; and the clerk stops stamping. "Is there a problem, sir?" There isn't, you tell her. She goes back to stamping, and does not stop watching.

kes.text: Kes leans on the registry's counter and the lens on the terminal turns away from both of you without being asked. "The hill's paper," she says. "Every citizen, every pass, every child. I keep the Window's half of it. This half talks to mine every night." The clerk looks at Kes's port, and at her coal-dark nails, and decides not to ask.
kes.again: Kes at the registry, the lens looking politely elsewhere.

options.text: Write me in as a citizen.
Linh Hoang. Why was her pass refused?
There's a girl from the Saints' tower in the school on the terraces. Print her a pass down too.

decision.text: Kes printed a pass down for the girl from the Saints' tower, and she went home to Bridgeward.

options.text: A citizen wants to go down the hill without a pass. Linh Hoang.

kes_me.text: Her fingers go into the terminal's guts and something clicks behind her eyes. "Face. Number nobody's got. Fitted last spring, very brave, no complications." The printer hums and hands you forty pages, warm. "Every lens on the hill will believe that. Obviously don't let a person read it."

kes_linh.text: The page comes up on the lens and Kes reads it and her face shuts. "RESERVE. NOT FOR TRANSFER. MATCH: WRAY, C." She says it flat. "They type the babies born up here. The ones that match a Board member are kept. Fed, schooled, never down the hill, in case the Board member needs a liver she can't get off the freight." She swallows. "Her mother was a gardener off Nursery. Hoang, Mai. Went into service the year Linh was six." She shuts the page. "For trying to take her down."

passives.text: F1: the first cross of two pure lines. It grows strong and even, once. Save its seed and plant it and the next year comes up all different, half of it worthless. Whoever owns the parent lines sells you the seed again every spring, forever.

mother.text: "Hoang Mai. A gardener, off Nursery. She married a man up here and had me and kept the beds." She stops counting. "When I was six she took me to the car with a bag. She says the word the way everybody up here says it, as if it were a place she had moved to. "That was thirteen years ago. They said she'd be proud I was so well."

look.text: The recovery ward: six beds by tall windows full of garden, and in them people in silk recovering from something, with flowers. A chart hangs at the foot of each bed. WRAY, C. — CORNEA (L), GRAFT — DONOR 9-0871 — RECOVERY GOOD. BENEDETTI, A. — MARROW — DONOR 9-1003 — RECOVERY GOOD. HALVERSON, A. — LUNG (R) — SKIN 400 SQ CM — DONOR 9-0412, 9-0977 — RECOVERY SLOW. Every donor number is a Weighhouse number. A woman in the end bed is laughing at something on a tray of cut fruit.
look.again: Board names, and against each a donor number off the service ward.

Odile reads three charts in a row without speaking. "Recovery good," she says at last. "Do you know, my dear, I think that is the most obscene thing I have ever read, and I have read the guild's minutes."

text.text: The cold store: a white room colder than any winter the Skirts remembers, steel cabinets floor to ceiling, each with a label in clean print. 9-0412 — L (PART) — MATCH 1 — HELD. 9-0977 — SKIN — HELD. And a whole column, top to bottom, one number: 9-1182 — C (R) — K (R) — L — H — MARROW — HELD. Everything worth keeping of Dawit Mekonnen is in this column. When the Skirts stopped sending, nine drew on what it had, and drew him to the end.

door.text: A wide white door at the end of the corridor with a lens beside it: SERVICE — STAFF. It is warm to stand near, and from behind it comes a sound you place after a moment: machines breathing, a great many of them, slowly, all at once.

door.text: The ward door from inside. No lens on this side. Nobody on this side was ever expected to want to open it.

passives.text: Holdfast keeps them under and keeps them still. The lines feed them. The machines breathe for the ones who can no longer manage it themselves. Nothing on this ward is being cured. Everything on it is being kept fresh.

interject.text: Tamsin walks to the nearest cot and looks at the face on it, a woman her own age, and then at the tag, and then she walks out of the ward without a word, and you hear her being sick in the corridor.
Ilya counts the beds under his breath and gets to twenty-three and stops. "Right," he says, and his voice cracks on it. He doesn't try again.

wake_ok.text: You go bed to bed and take the holdfast off them slowly, the way it should be done, with the lines kept running until the eyes open. It takes the night. Twenty-one of them wake: confused, weeping, asking for people who are dead, asking what day it is and getting answers that are years wrong. Two do not wake. Their numbers had been drawn too far, and when the holdfast came off there was not enough of them left to come back to it. You close their eyes. Nobody else on the ward notices; they are learning to see.

options.text: Now get them down the hill.

wake_hard.text: You go too fast. You know it by the fourth bed and you cannot go slower, because the corridor bell has started and will not stop. Seventeen wake, sobbing, sick, some of them fighting the lines out of their own arms. Six do not. Two of the six were dying anyway. Four were not, and you know which four, and you will know for the rest of your life.

options.text: Now get them down the hill.

gone_freight.text: At two Abena takes them down the service stair in threes to the freight dock, in coats off the Clean's own hooks, and Mazur stands at his brake looking at his brake while the car fills with people instead of bags. It goes down without lamps. At Footgate the slope is waiting in the dark, because somebody told somebody, and the slope carries them up Cascade on its back.

gone_tunnel.text: At five, down the service stair into the sheds in the gardeners' own clothes, into the line going out instead of in, past two of the Clean who have looked at faces going in every morning for years and have never once counted the faces coming out. Kojo stands at the hatch with his apron off. At the bottom of the road the gardeners' line takes them by the arms and walks them down to the Skirts in the first light, slowly, at the pace of the slowest.
gone_tunnel.again: The tunnel, at dawn, going the wrong way.

gone_force.text: Down the lift in loads, across the concourse in white sheets, barefoot on the white floor. The Clean at the arch see twenty people coming at them in hospital white and don't know whether to shoot, and in that moment the people are through. Then somebody gives the order, and the Clean remember what they are for.

text.text: The ward's board, with its numbers and letters. A new line at the bottom, in the even hand, since you were last here.
The ward's board, wiped clean. Somebody has written across it, in a nurse's even hand: SERVICE CLOSED. Under it, smaller, in a different hand: TWENTY-THREE.

intro.text: An office of real wood with a window on the gardens and a desk with nothing on it but a pen. The woman behind it is seventy and looks it, the only person on the hill who does: white hair pulled back, lines round the eyes, a doctor's plain hands. "Dr Qadir. You're the designate." She doesn't get up. "Nobody on this floor is dying. Please lower your voice, even when it's already low."
intro.again: Dr Qadir, at her empty desk.

passives.label: Lisle
passives.text: "Teodora Lisle says you were reasonable about her Weighhouse," Dr Qadir adds. "She has never been up. She writes to me every season. She has no idea what she writes to."

text.text: Dr Qadir looks up from nothing. "Yes?" She has been waiting for you to come back since you left.
"Yes?" Dr Qadir, at her empty desk.

again.again: Dr Qadir, waiting.

options.text: You're the only one up here who looks her age.
Haber, N. Whole. Before the ball.
The Chair. What's left of him?
What do you offer the designate to leave it alone?

floor.text: "Recovery, for the Board, after a renewal. Fittings, for citizens. A cold store." She lets that sit. "And service, behind the door at the end, which you have heard about in the Skirts, from people who have never seen it, and which I would rather you saw than heard about. I have nothing on this floor I am ashamed of. Go and look. Then come back and ask me."
floor.again: "Go and look. Then come back and ask me."

text.text: "Sit." She does not lower her own voice; she has never needed to. "Service is what the contract says: the debtor discharges the paper in full, in kind. The Weighhouse sends me people whose paper has crossed the line, people who would be dead of the cough by forty on your slope, or under a fall, or on the Clean's cart in the morning. I keep them warm, fed through a line, asleep. They feel nothing; I see to that myself. And I draw on them slowly, as the Board needs. A kidney this season, an eye the next, marrow, skin, a lobe of liver, until there is nothing left worth keeping alive, and then I let them go and the Window sends the boots home." She folds her plain hands. "A body is a bank, designate. We draw on it slowly. One healthy debtor keeps a member of the Board for four years, five. Your Skirts stopped weighing this season. So I drew harder on what I had. That is not cruelty either. That is arithmetic with a shortage in it."

case.again: "A body is a bank. We draw on it slowly."

why.text: "Because of what they know." She says it the way a believer says the creed, without heat, because it has never needed heat. "Twelve people who know how a chip line holds its tolerance, how a lens is grown, how holdfast is made, how a contract is written so that it binds for two hundred years. The last people alive who know how the world worked before it ended. The Burn took the libraries. It did not take them, because they were up here. Every year one of them dies is a year the world forgets something it will never learn again." She looks at the window and the gardens. "So yes. Twenty-three people on my ward are asleep so that twelve can stay awake. I have done that sum every morning for thirty years. I have never once got a different answer."
why.again: "I have never once got a different answer."

interject.text: "The record keeps a thousand people's water short to keep a city lawful," Nine says, very quietly. "It does that sum every morning too." Its lens does not leave her. "I have started to get different answers."

"Twelve," Ash says. "We fed a whole valley at Openfield on what one of them would have cost." Dr Qadir looks at him with real interest. "Yes," she says. "And when the blight came, who did you send to, to find out what it was?" Ash doesn't answer.

age.text: "I don't renew." She touches the lines at her own eye as if checking they are still there. "I could. The Board has offered every season for thirty years. I am seventy and I look it, and my knees hurt on the stairs, and I will die in a few years of something I could have had replaced off a debtor in an afternoon." She looks at you steadily. "Somebody on this floor should know what it costs. It may as well be the one holding the knife."
age.again: "It may as well be the one holding the knife."

text.text: "9-1182." She doesn't look anything up. "Concluded, three weeks ago. A good man: a strong heart, clean kidneys, no cough yet. When your Skirts shut the Weighhouse I was short at once, and I had renewals booked. So I drew on him to the end, all at once, instead of over five years." She meets your eyes. "You did that as much as I did. I want you to know I know that. It doesn't help either of us."

"9-1182. Bed seven. Two seasons." She doesn't look anything up. "A kidney and an eye so far. A strong heart; I haven't touched it. His wife writes to the Window every week asking for him back. The Window writes back that he is in service." She meets your eyes. "He is. Go and see him, if you like. He hums. The nurses like it."

nils.text: "Haber. Twenty-two, a good weight, no cough." She doesn't pretend. "The Chair's lungs are failing and his heart is older than this building. A part at a time no longer keeps up with him. So: whole. Before the ball, because the ball is when he must be seen to be well." She sets her pen down exactly parallel to the edge of the desk. "The ball is when the designate attends. So it is, strictly, up to you."
nils.again: "So it is, strictly, up to you."

interject.text: Kes has gone grey. "Joran's boy," she says. "I taught him to read the Line board." Dr Qadir nods, as if this were a useful piece of history.

chair.text: "Less of him every season." A clinician's answer. "The renewals keep the body. Nothing keeps the rest. Two hundred and forty years of memory in a brain made for eighty; the Board's lattice holds what it can, and what it holds is the house, not him. What is left of Adair Halverson is his manners. They are very good manners. They go round and round."

argue.text: She waits, hands folded, to hear what you have that she has not already thought of in thirty years of mornings.
argue.again: Dr Qadir, waiting to hear it.

closed.text: She listens to all of it without moving. When you have finished she is quiet for a long time. Then she takes the pen and a sheet of the floor's paper and writes, in the same neat hand as the board: SERVICE WARD CLOSED. SLEEPERS TO BE WOKEN AND DISCHARGED TO THE SLOPE. Q. "I have known for some years that the answer was wrong," she says. "I kept doing the sum because I had not been made to stop. The cold store keeps what it has. From now on we take from the dead and the willing, and the Board learns what a short season is." She stands; her knees hurt; she does not let it show. "Abena. Wake them. Slowly. I'll answer for it." And to you: "They will review me. I am seventy. Let them."

close_no.text: "No." Not unkindly. "Not this season. You have told me what I already know, and you have told it well, and I have heard it from better people than you every morning in my own head." She picks up the pen again. "Go and do something about it yourself, if you think you can carry them. I won't stop you. I won't help you either."
close_no.again: "Go and do something about it yourself."

offer.text: "Your chart." She says it simply. "Open on this floor for the rest of your life. Any fitting from my own stock, at no charge. Any renewal, when you want one, and you will want one, designate; everybody does by fifty. A kidney when yours fail, eyes when yours go, a heart." She looks at you. "Leave nine as it is, and in forty years you will still look like this. That is what I offer, because that is what I have."
offer.again: "In forty years you will still look like this."

options.text: (Take it. Leave the floor as it is.)

decision.text: You left Halcyon's service ward as it was, and took Dr Qadir's offer: your chart open on nine for life.

left.text: She writes your name at the top of a fresh chart and files it in the drawer with the Board's. "Thank you for understanding," she says. You did understand. That is the part you will think about later.
left.again: Your chart, filed with the Board's.

text.text: Dr Qadir at her desk with the closed ward's board propped against the wall behind her, where she can see it without turning round. "Short season," she says. "The Board has been to see me four times. I am to be reviewed in the spring." She seems almost glad.

Dr Qadir does not get up. "You took them down the hill," she says. "Some of them reached the bottom." She looks at you for a long time. "I have twelve renewals booked and nothing to renew them with. That is your doing. I want you to have the whole of it."
"Designate." Dr Qadir, at her empty desk, with your chart in her drawer.

intro.text: A woman in an orderly's whites with a tray of little glass vials, walking the corridor as if she were counting her own steps. Cornrows tight to the head, Skirts hands. "Holdfast at six," she says, to nobody, and then sees you. "You're not staff."
intro.again: Abena, with her tray of vials.

text.text: Abena nods to you, once, the way the slope nods to people it has decided about.
"Holdfast at six," Abena says, to the tray.

again.again: Abena, counting her steps.

options.text: (Kes says her name, and where she was born.)
You know what's behind it. Show me.

door.text: "Staff." She doesn't stop walking. "I don't read the charts. I give the holdfast at six and at six and I don't read the charts."

lev.text: She stops walking. "Lev." Her whole face changes. "He trained me. Nine years he carried this tray and then one morning he put it down on that trolley and walked out and down the hill and didn't say anything to anybody." She looks at the service door. "He said to me once, you'll know when you can't carry it any more. I keep waiting to know." She takes a key card off her belt. "I'll let you in. Don't make me watch."

kes.text: "Oyelaran." Abena puts the tray down. "Your mother sold mangoes off a crate at the bottom of Cascade. I used to steal them." She looks at the back of Kes's neck, at the port, and her mouth sets. "They brought you up on my freight. I remember. I gave you your holdfast." She takes a key card off her belt. "Go on, then. Both of you."

interject.text: Kes doesn't say anything for a long time. Then: "Thanks for the mangoes." Abena laughs, once, like something breaking.

shown.text: She looks at you a long time. "Fine." She takes a key card off her belt. "Look, then. Somebody from outside ought to." She doesn't come in with you.

ask_no.text: "Staff," Abena says, and picks the tray up, and walks away down the corridor counting her steps aloud so she doesn't have to hear you.

mother.text: "My mother's paper is ninety scrip a season on the Window. Nine pays me a hundred." She says it like the sum it is. "If I walk down the hill like Lev did, my mother goes on the Weighhouse bench. If I stay, I give them holdfast at six and at six, and some of them are from Two-Twelve, and one of them was my teacher." She picks up the tray. "You want to take them down, I'll show you the service stair. I've been waiting for somebody to want to for six years."

intro.text: Bed seven. A man of about forty under a white sheet, a line in his arm, a dressing taped over his left eye and another low on his left side. He isn't quite asleep. He is humming, very low, four notes over and over, the way you hum to a child. The tag on his wrist: 9-1182. When you stand over him the humming stops. "Saba," he says, to the ceiling. "Is Saba all right?"
intro.again: Dawit Mekonnen, humming four notes.

again.again: Dawit, humming.

saba.text: His good eye finds you, slowly. "She sings that," he says. "The four notes. To the little one. I keep it going so I don't forget it." He is quiet. "They said service. I thought it meant work. I thought I'd be carrying something." He laughs, very weakly, and stops, because it hurts his side. "I am, I suppose."

interject.text: Wren sits down on the edge of the cot and takes his hand without asking, and holds it, and doesn't say anything at all.

home.text: Dawit Mekonnen on an upturned crate outside his own shack on Nursery, a patch over the left eye, sitting carefully because of his side. His boots are on. He is humming the four notes, and from inside, somebody is singing them back. "They said service," he says, when he sees you. "I'm doing a different kind now. I'm sitting." He laughs, and holds his side, and keeps laughing.

boots.text: He can't see them with the eye he has left, so you put his hand on them. He knows them by the laces. "Where were they?" he says. "I asked and asked. Where were my boots?" You tell him: at home. With Saba. He holds on to one of them and goes back to humming.

asleep.text: Bed nineteen. A young man of twenty-two, whole, asleep, not a dressing on him; the only one on the ward with nothing taken yet. The tag on his wrist is a different colour: HABER, N. — WHOLE — RESERVED: CHAIR. His breathing is even. He has a miner's shoulders and a boy's face.
asleep.again: Nils Haber, whole, asleep. RESERVED: CHAIR.

awake.text: He comes up slowly, the way people come up from holdfast, frightened before he knows of what. "Where." Then: "Is my father up? The Concern's crew said they'd bring them up. The eleven." He grips your sleeve. "They said if I went into service the paper was settled and they'd bring my father up and bury him."

(Walk him out now, in a coat off a hook, while the corridor is empty.)

decision.text: You walked Nils Haber off Halcyon's floor nine before the ball, and down the hill.

text.text: You tell him: the Shift went down at night and dug, and brought the eleven up, and buried them on the slope above Nursery, and his father is in the fourth grave with his tag on the cross. Nils lies back and looks at the ceiling and cries without making any sound at all, the way the Skirts cries.

You tell him: nobody has brought his father up. The Concern's crew never went down. Six East is shut, GEOLOGICAL, and the eleven are where they fell. Nils lies back and looks at the ceiling. "They said," he says. "They said."

out.text: Down the service stair in a coat off a hook, past the sheds, out through the yard while the post is looking the other way, and down the road in the dark with his arm over your shoulder because his legs have forgotten. At Footgate he sits down in the coal dust and puts both hands flat on it as if to make sure it is there.
out.again: Nils, in the coal dust at Footgate.

caught.text: At the corner by the cold store a soft bell rings and two of the Clean are there, unhurried, the way they always are. They take Nils by the elbows, gently, and walk him back to bed nineteen, and Abena comes with the tray. Nobody says a word to you. They do not need to; the bed is RESERVED.

intro.text: A cot near the listening room, and on it, awake, in a ward smock with a tag on his wrist, Corwin Dysart, who ran Number Six. He sees you and laughs, once. "Reviewed," he says. "The strike was lost. The quarter's tonnage was lost. A contract citizen whose tenure review comes after a lost quarter is reviewed." He holds up the wrist. "First draw is tomorrow. They give you a night to make your peace. It's in the contract. Everything's in the contract."
intro.again: Dysart, awake, his wrist tagged.

why.text: "Because I did a sum." He doesn't pretend to be sorry or not sorry. "My review was this spring. The quarter's tonnage decided it. Fourteen to twenty-two were good coal standing still. The steward objected; I doubled his paper; he went in. I wrote the order, I signed it, and I thought, the roof will hold another week, and if it doesn't, it's eleven debtors against my wife's flat on floor three and my son's place in the school." He looks at the ceiling. "They did the same sum on me. It came out the same way. I can't even say it was wrong. I just didn't think I'd be on the other side of the line."
why.again: "They did the same sum on me."

interject.text: Kes looks at him a long time. "Maren would take you down," she says at last. "She'd feed you. She feeds the scabs." She doesn't say what she would do.

down.text: He closes his eyes. "Maren's slope," he says. "They'll kill me on Cascade." Then: "Better than tomorrow." He doesn't say thank you. You didn't expect him to.

stay.text: He nods slowly, as if you had read him the result of a sum he had already done. "Eleven," he says. "Yes. All right." He lies back and looks at the tag.

decided.text: Dysart doesn't look at you. He has already been told what happens to him.

intro.text: Dr Teodora Lisle, in the corridor on nine, in ward whites instead of the Weighhouse's, holding a clipboard she isn't reading. When the slope shut her Weighhouse she came up the hill, the one door out that still opened for her. She looks at you as if you had come to tell her something she already knows. "Eight days," she says. "I have been up eight days. I had never been up."

options.text: Then help me. Wake them, or tell Qadir what you weighed.

seen.text: "I weighed them." Her voice is perfectly level. "I wrote K L C H on a board in chalk, and the yield, and I sent them up on the freight and I told myself I was the only door out of the Skirts that opened. I have walked the service ward every morning for eight days, and every morning I have found a name I wrote." She looks at the clipboard. "Bed three was a woman I weighed in the spring of my first year. I told her the settlement would see her children through the winter. It did. She has no eyes now."
seen.again: "I have found a name I wrote."

help.text: "Yes." No hesitation at all, as if she had been waiting eight days for somebody to say it. "I know every one of them by weight. I know what they can stand." She puts the clipboard down on a trolley and leaves it there.

intro.text: A small room off the ward. A woman of twenty in a chair with a cable from the port at her nape into a box on the wall, her head shaved close for it. Her right hand is writing on a roll of paper that feeds out of a slot, without her looking at it, very fast, in a tidy hand. Her lips move. "Reserve nine, point six. Thursday. A hand higher. Ward forty, short." She looks up at you without stopping the hand. "Sorry. It doesn't stop. Are you the new nurse? It's always the same light in here, I lose track."
