text.text: "Sela. I was a Listener at the Saints' tower in Bridgeward. Verity's." The hand writes. "I heard the city's wire in words, like the new one does. A man in a clean coat came with a radio that worked, when I was nineteen, and I thought I was going to be a citizen." The hand writes. "That was a year ago. They don't put anyone in the chair before nineteen; it's in the contract. So the new one, the girl from my tower, Immy, they've got her in the school on the terraces with the reserve children. Sixteen. Three years and then this chair, or the one next to it." She doesn't cry. She hasn't got time. "Somebody should get her out before she's nineteen."

"Sela. I was a Listener at the Saints' tower in Bridgeward. Verity's." The hand writes. "I heard the city's wire in words, the way some of us do. A man in a clean coat came with a radio that worked, when I was nineteen, and I thought I was going to be a citizen." The hand writes. "That was a year ago. I hear everything now. All of it. All the time. I haven't slept the night through since the port went in." She almost smiles. "Verity used to make us stop at two and drink something hot."

reads.text: "The Exchange desk, on the Board's floor." The hand writes. "The Ledger forecasts everything: reserves, prices, who dies. It leaks a little on its own wire, and a few of us hear the leak. The Concern buys ahead of the guild on what I write and sells to the guild after." She glances at the roll. "It's not enough for them. It's a keyhole. That's why they want the whole book, the one under the Spire. Then they wouldn't need me." She says it with something like hope.

immy.text: "The school's on floor five, by the registry. They keep the reserve children there and the bought ones. She's fed. She has a bed. She's frightened of the dark and they leave a lamp on." The hand writes. "Her paper's the Concern's. Anything the Concern owns, it sells, if you ask the right person. Or a pass. A pass down only says you can."
immy.again: "A pass down only says you can."

free.text: The box on the wall is simpler than it looks: the Concern never expected anyone to want to take its listeners off. You ease the feed down slowly, and her hand slows, and stops, and the roll of paper stops coming out of the slot. Sela sits looking at her own hand. Then she starts to cry, for the first time in a year, because it is quiet. Abena finds her a coat. She goes down the service stair and out with the morning's line, and doesn't look back at the chair.

free_kes.text: Kes kneels behind the chair and puts two fingers on the port at Sela's nape, the way you would take a pulse, and closes her eyes. "Shh," she says, to the box, not to Sela. The hand slows. Stops. The paper stops. "There," Kes says. "Quiet. Obviously it's weird. You get used to it." Sela turns round in the chair and holds on to Kes like somebody pulled out of a river.
free_kes.again: The empty chair, and the stopped paper.

unplug_no.text: You ease the feed down and her whole body arches in the chair and the hand writes so fast it tears the paper. You put it back. She sits panting. "Not like that," she says, when she can. "It holds on. Somebody who knows the grid. Please." The hand starts writing again.

intro.text: An office with real wood on the walls and a window full of the gardens. The woman at the desk is forty, or looks it: dark hair tied back, a plain grey suit with a single lit seam at the collar, a face that has been tired for a long time and slept well last night. She stands, which nobody else up here has done for you. "Pilar Soto. Director. Sit; I would rather talk to you than about you." She waits until you do. "The Board wants to buy something from you. I'm going to be honest about that, because the Chair is going to be charming about it, and you should hear it plainly from somebody first. We would rather buy than take. Purchase is kinder than war. I have counted the dead after the other kind."

what.text: "The Chair will tell you. He enjoys it, and it is his to tell; he has been planning it since before you were born." A faint smile. "There is a ball. There is always a ball. This season it waits for you: the card on the concourse says so. Go when you're ready. Before you do, Dr Qadir will show you floor nine if you want to see it. The Concern has no secrets from a partner, and I would rather you were angry with us before you sign than after."

war.text: "I was twenty." She doesn't look away. "The Concern took the Teeth's free pits by force, the last time anyone tried force. The Clean went into Number Two with gas and the Board's lattices in their heads telling them where everyone was hiding. I was the clerk; I counted for the minutes. Four hundred and six. Children in the count." She lets that sit. "After that I spent eighty years learning to buy things. It's slower. Nobody has to be counted."

interject.text: Ilya looks at her a long time. "And the ones you buy," he says. "Who counts them?" Soto meets his eyes. "Dr Qadir," she says. "Every morning."

age.text: "A hundred and twenty. I was born on this floor." She says it without any coyness at all. "I have been forty for eighty years. It is a good age. One knows things, and one's knees work." She turns the pen over. "The Chair is older. Most of the Board is older. Ask Constance Wray about the snow."
age.again: "I have been forty for eighty years."

chair.text: "The Chair is the Chair." The Board's formula, said flatly enough to sound like a warning. Then, lower: "Watch him at the ball. Watch him closely. Then come and tell me what you saw, if you saw anything." She picks the pen up again, which is how you know she has said more than she meant to.

kes_offer.text: Soto turns the folder round so Kes can read her own name on it. "Ms Oyelaran. The Concern would like to make you an offer." She lays it out in four sentences: tenure; a flat on the terraces; her two remaining years void; a citizen's contract for anyone she cares to name. "In return, the door you found. Kept, for us. You are the only person in ninety years who has found it from the outside. We would rather have you inside." She slides the contract across. Kes doesn't touch it. Then she does, and puts it in her jacket, folded small.

interject.text: "Obviously I'm not going to," Kes says to you outside, very fast. "Obviously. Tell me I'm not going to."

yes.text: Soto writes one line on the page in front of her and signs it. "Thank you." She means it, and she doesn't look pleased, exactly. "The Chair will be delighted. I am relieved, which is better." She hands you a letter on heavy card: SEAT IN WAITING.

no.text: Soto writes one line on the page and doesn't sign it. "Then we wait," she says. "We're very good at it." She looks at you with something like respect, and something like a price being revised. "So is the Chair. He has other ways to wait. I would rather you didn't find out what they are."

feigned.text: Soto looks at you for exactly as long as the lens over her door does. Then she writes one line, and signs it, and hands you a letter on heavy card: SEAT IN WAITING. "Thank you," she says. If she believes you, she is very good. If she doesn't, she is better.

caught.text: "No," Soto says gently. "You don't mean that." She writes one line, and doesn't sign it. "I'll put you down as a refusal. It's kinder than putting you down as a liar." She doesn't look angry. She looks like somebody who has been lied to by better.

give.text: "Tell me." She doesn't write. When you have said what you saw, she nods slowly. "The Board will need it in writing, or in a voice it can't argue with. A Chair who cannot answer is reviewed. It is in the bylaws; he wrote them."

Soto takes the chair at the head of the table. "He did the Scald," she says to you afterwards, very quietly. "He would have done it again. I would rather buy." She looks at the window. "I still want your city's book. Don't mistake me for kind."

give_no.text: The Board hears you out with perfect courtesy and the Chair thanks you twice, and nothing happens. Soto says afterwards, "Not enough. They've been looking away from him for twenty years. They need something they can't look away from."

kept.text: Soto looks at you for a long moment and then laughs, properly, for the first time. "Of course you are." She writes nothing down. "That's the most Concern thing anyone has said in this office in a year."

linh_no.text: "No." Mildly. "She's reserve. Reserve is the Board's, and I am not going to start my chairmanship, or my next eighty years, by giving away Constance Wray's liver to a stranger who asked nicely."

immy.text: "The Bridgeward girl." She doesn't need to look it up. "Bought, as written, from the man who sold us where she was." She lets that land on you. "Three hundred. That is what the Concern paid, and what the Concern charges. The Concern sells what it owns."

decision.text: You bought the girl from the Saints' tower back from the Concern for three hundred, and she went home to Bridgeward.

wants.text: The Chair sets his glass on the lectern. "Your city keeps a book of what will happen," he says, "and it is right far more often than anyone has a right to be. We should like the book. Not the city: it is ugly and it smells of its river. The book. The core under your Spire that writes the forecasts. In a little while the city will give you its sash; it has already written that it will. On that day the Magistrate may transfer the city's property, under the city's own law, with a signature. We would like your signature. On that day, and nobody's before. In return, a seat at this table, kept for you from the day you take the sash. And renewal, when you want it. Everyone wants it, eventually." He smiles. "You are wondering why. We sell futures, my dear designate. We always have: a chip, a contract, a season's term, a citizen's place on the terraces. It is the only product that never spoils. With the book we shall know what to sell, and to whom, and when; whom to renew, and with what, and who will be born on the slope in time to renew us. We shall not have to guess. I have been guessing for two hundred and forty years. I am so very tired of guessing." He picks the glass up again. "Director Soto would like to buy it from you. I would be happy to take it; there are things asleep in the Ashlands that would fetch it for us, and they do not tire. But the Board is fond of kindness, when it is cheaper. So. Nobody has to decide anything today." The hand on yours. "How kind of you to come."

interject.text: "Who will be born on the slope in time," Kes repeats, so quietly only you hear. Her hand is on the back of her neck.
"A futures contract on the future itself," Odile murmurs. "My dear, I have dreamed of that trade. I am so glad to find I never want to make it."
Wren is very still. "Things asleep in the Ashlands," she says. "He means the dogs."

text.text: "Thank you. Lungs, and a heart. A young man from your Skirts; Haber, Dr Qadir tells me. Whole, this time; she says a part at a time no longer keeps up with me." He touches his own chest, gratefully, as one touches a gift. "I am grateful to him. I always am. One should be."

"Thank you. A kidney this season, and a little skin. From your Skirts; Dr Qadir keeps the names, I keep the gratitude." He touches his own side, gratefully, as one touches a gift. "One should be grateful. One always is."

interject.text: Tamsin puts her glass down on a table very carefully, untouched, and walks out of the hall.

age.text: "Old enough to have skied the runs below this house when there was snow on them." He looks toward the windows as if the snow might still be there. "The lodge your Shift meets in. I had a fire there every evening of the winter of the Charter. Constance was nineteen; I taught her to turn on the black run." Pat, pat. "We were here before, and we shall be here after. How kind of you to come."

scald.text: "We did." He says it as pleasantly as everything else. "The Reach was coming apart: chrome everywhere, every gang its own lattice, nobody's hand on anything. Ninety years ago I signed an order that woke every piece of Concern work in the Reach at once and held its wearer still. Still is so much easier to govern. Then the fires came, and the people who were still could not leave them." He sips. "I am not sorry. There has been order of a kind ever since. Ask the city. It liked the arithmetic so much it wrote its whole Plan on the ashes."

interject.text: Ash makes a sound you have not heard from him before, and turns his back on the Chair, and stays like that.

house.text: Kes says something to the Chair that is not words, a run of sounds like a lock being turned in a language older than the lock. The Chair's face empties and does not fill. When he speaks it is his voice, without the courtesy, without anything. "HOUSE OF HALVERSON. CHARTER YEAR ONE. BOARD OF TWELVE, RENEWED. CHAIR: ADAIR HALVERSON. AGE TWO HUNDRED AND FORTY-ONE. COGNITION FOURTEEN PERCENT. COURTESY ROUTINE ACTIVE. ORDER OF THE SCALD: AUTHORISED BY THE CHAIR. RESERVE: ASHLANDS, KENNEL SEVEN, CONTROLLER IN THE CHAIR'S ROOM." Then Kes says one more sound and the Chair blinks and smiles at you and pats your hand. "How kind of you to come." Around you, very slowly, the hall has gone quiet.
house.again: COGNITION FOURTEEN PERCENT. COURTESY ROUTINE ACTIVE.

interject.text: Kes is shaking. "It's the same tongue," she says. "My door and him. The house wrote both." She wipes her mouth. "He's not in there. He's a door with a coat on."

toast.text: You raise your glass, and the hall turns, because the designate is raising a glass. You tell it what it already knows. The photograph of a winter meeting with snow on the lodge roof. The ages. The charts on nine with the Board's names on them, and the numbers against the names, and what the numbers are: people from the slope, asleep, drawn on a kidney at a time, a whole young man for one evening's good colour. You don't raise your voice. You don't need to; nobody in the hall is breathing. When you finish, the Chair thanks you, twice, and pats your hand. Then a woman near the windows puts her glass down on the floor and walks out, and then another, and the hall begins, very quietly, to empty.

interject.text: "Read into the record," Nine says, to the emptying hall. "Witnessed." It sounds, for once, like a judgement.

toast_fail.text: You raise your glass and say it, and the hall listens politely, and when you finish the Chair laughs, warmly, and says, "The designate has been to the Skirts. How kind of them to bring us the Skirts' stories," and the hall laughs with him, relieved to be told what to do. Two of the Clean are suddenly at your elbows, courteous as waiters. The glass is taken out of your hand.

yes.text: The Chair takes your hand in both of his. "Thank you. Thank you." The hall applauds softly, as if at a recital. A clerk appears with a letter on heavy card, SEAT IN WAITING, and the Chair signs it in a hand that has not changed in a very long time. "Nobody had to decide anything today," he says, delighted. "And you did anyway."

no.text: The Chair looks at you with perfect courtesy for a long moment. "Then we shall wait," he says. "We are very good at waiting. We were here before." Pat, pat. "And there are other ways to fetch a book." Across the hall, Soto sets her glass down.

text.text: "The leash." He says it plainly; he has had forty-one years to find the plain word. "Every piece of the Concern's chrome has a door in it and a channel behind the door, and the channel comes here, into the lattice in my spine. I see whoever wears it. When the Window says so, I make a limb heavy, or a hand quiet. Jun Baek's arm at the Pond; I know it by its hum. When his balance falls behind, I put it to sleep, and I hear him swear." He breathes. "After the Scald the Board would not trust its leash to a machine. Machines do what they're told. A man can be made to, which isn't the same, and the Board likes the difference." Then: "A patch came down the channel a while ago. A door in a grid-hand's port, shut from this end, because somebody sold it. They had me do it. I felt her go dark and stay dark. I'm sorry for whoever she was."

why.text: "A contract." He almost laughs. "Tenure. A flat on the terraces for my wife and my two girls, our paper void, a citizen's place for each of them. I was a grid-hand at the Window like your Kes, and I had found a door, like your Kes, and the Board made me an offer. Page thirty." He looks at nothing. "My wife died twenty years ago, up here, renewed twice and then not. My girls are fifty and forty-eight and look thirty, and they haven't come down to the works in twenty years. I don't blame them. I wouldn't visit this either."

stop.text: "Three ways." He has thought about this every day for forty-one years and it shows; it comes out in order. "Burn the channel at the trunk, and every door in the Reach loses its voice at once. People fall where they stand when it goes; I don't know how many get up. If I'm still on the end of it when it burns, it goes through me, and that's the end of me, which I don't mind as much as I should. Unless I burn it myself, slowly, from inside, letting it out of me a strand at a time, with somebody holding my head so I don't pull the cables out when it hurts. I have never had anybody to hold my head." He breathes. "Or cut the key out of my chair. The channel answers whoever holds the key. You could walk out of here with every Concern piece in the Reach in your pocket. Or leave it. Leave me. Somebody else will decide, eventually. Somebody always does."

When she comes back she says, "Told you it was a string," and, "Worth it," and she has them now, the fits, at night, like everybody else in the Reach who wore the Concern's work and got up again.

seized.text: The key is a lattice token the size of a thumb set into the chair behind his head. It comes out with a sound like a tooth. Femi Lawal gasps, and his hands open on the chair's arms, and the hum stops, because it is not his any more. It is in your hand, warm, and through it, very faintly, you can feel all of them: every door in the Reach, waiting to be told. He gets up. It takes him a long time. "The gardens," he says. "I'd like to see the gardens."
seized.again: The key in your hand, warm.

interject.text: Kes looks at the key in your hand for a long moment and doesn't say anything. With Kes, that is very loud.

left.text: Femi closes his eyes. "Yes," he says. "That's what everybody decides." The hum goes on.

after.text: "Designate." Femi, in his chair, holding his note. He doesn't ask you anything.

text.text: Femi Lawal on a bench in the gardens in his cardigan, with the scars on his neck open to the air, watching the rain come out of the pipes at four. "I could feel it from the chair," he says. "Every day. The citizens walking under it. I never once stood in it." He holds out his hand to the rain.
The keeper's chair, empty, the cables lying on the seat like something shed.

empty.speaker: narrator
empty.text: The keeper's chair, empty, burned black down one side, the cables melted into the seat. Nobody has cleaned it. Nobody comes down here now.

look.text: The trunk: a cabinet the size of a car at the end of the core where every cable in the room comes together before it goes into the chair. A console on its face with the closed eye, and a maintenance locker with a red stripe: CUTTING CHARGES — AUTHORISED STAFF.
look.again: The trunk, where every cable meets.

decision.text: You burned the Concern's channel from the grid core's trunk, and it went through its keeper and killed him. Every Concern piece in the Reach lost its voice.

news.text: every piece of Concern chrome in the Reach went dead at once for a moment; people fell where they stood, and got up again, most of them

options.text: (Set the cutting charges on the trunk and blow it.)

decision.text: You blew the grid core's trunk. The keeper died in his chair, the Clean came running, and every Concern piece in the Reach lost its voice.

options.text: (Put the keeper's key into the console and burn the channel with it.)

decision.text: You burned the Concern's channel with the keeper's key you had cut out of his chair. Every Concern piece in the Reach lost its voice.

news.text: every piece of Concern chrome in the Reach went dead at once for a moment; people fell where they stood, and got up again, most of them

burned.text: The console fights you, and then it doesn't. The channel burns from the trunk outward, an aisle at a time, and you feel it go out across the Reach like a breath let go. And it goes through the chair. Femi Lawal doesn't scream. He opens his mouth as if to say something courteous and the cables at his neck smoke, and he is still. The hum stops. In the quiet the cabinets tick as they cool.
burned.again: The keeper, still, and the cabinets ticking.

burn_no.text: The console takes your commands and gives them back to you, politely, one at a time, refused. On the chair, without turning his head, Femi says, "It knows me better than it knows you. It won't let you hurt me by accident."

blown.text: The charges are made for cutting steel and they cut it. The trunk goes up in a white flash that turns the core to noon, and the aisles go dark, and every door in the Reach loses its voice at once, and the keeper dies in his chair before the smoke reaches him. Then bells, everywhere, and boots on the gallery, and the Clean remembering what they are for.

blow_no.text: You get the locker open and the charges out and your hands wrong on them, and you put them back before they decide for you. When you turn round the guard from the door is standing at the end of the aisle, very still, with his hand on his radio. He hasn't pressed it yet.
blow_no.again: The guard, his hand on his radio.

keyed.text: The key goes into the console and the console knows it, and asks you, in the house's own tongue, what you would like. You tell it. The channel burns from the trunk outward, the way the keeper said it would, with nobody on the end of it. Every door in the Reach loses its voice at once. The key in the slot goes cold.
keyed.again: The cold key in the slot.

dark.text: The trunk, dark and cold. Nothing hums.

kes_fell.text: And in the dark, a sound behind you: Kes, on the floor, fitting, her own port still on the channel when it burned. You get to her and hold her head. It goes on a long time. When she comes back she says, "Told you it was a string," and, "Worth it," and she has them now, the fits, at night, like everybody else in the Reach who wore the Concern's work and got up again.
